Conventional methods rely on CAD models which are often unavailable, while 2D capture lacks shape prior and frozen foundation features fail on geometrically similar, low-texture industrial parts.
AI.method:
1) Reconstruct objects using 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) from short object-centric scans
2) Summarize reconstructions into per-class shape prototypes
3) Fuse the geometry-based features with frozen DINOv2 image features
4) Compare geometry from RGB-D depth, 3DGS, and CAD on T-LESS and HOPE datasets
AI.result:
1) Geometry from RGB-D depth, 3DGS, and CAD gives comparable recognition (tied on HOPE, within 1.6 points on T-LESS)
2) On shape-distinctive household objects (HOPE): geometry alone reaches 0.920 vs image-only 0.832
3) On shape-confusable textureless industrial parts (T-LESS): modest but consistent gain (0.560 to 0.591 fused)
4) 3DGS renderings do not help the image side
5) Frozen-feature recognition is nearly lighting-invariant (within 2.5 points)
6) The prior rescues far more image failures than it breaks successes
7) Benefit grows under partial occlusion
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that short object-centric 3D scans can recover the recognition value of CAD models without requiring actual CAD. The gain is governed by shape recognizability—geometry provides substantial benefit for distinctive shapes but modest gains for confusable industrial parts. The shape prior is complementary rather than uniformly additive, rescuing more image failures than breaking successes, with benefits increasing under partial occlusion. The value lies in geometry itself, not rendered pixels, and the approach is nearly lighting-invariant.

title: Corporate Language Model (CLM): Transforming Tacit and Fragmented Enterprise Knowledge into a Sovereign, Auditable, and Executable Corporate Intelligence Layer
summary: Enterprise AI deployments fail not from model inadequacy, but because organizations lack a structured substrate encoding how they decide, negotiate, and execute. Generic LLMs carry no firm-specific ontological priors; RAG remains brittle, with no path to executable action; static playbooks encode logic but cannot reason or adapt. This demands an architecture treating tacit-knowledge capture, ontological grounding, sovereign deployment, and auditable actuation as co-designed from the start. This paper introduces the Corporate Language Model (CLM), a framework transforming a firm's structured, unstructured, multimodal, and tacit knowledge into an ontology-grounded enterprise foundation upon which reasoning and governed execution are composed. CLM has five capability planes and four architectural pillars: a Neurosymbolic Mesh coupling generative models with a knowledge graph; a Skill Graph where reusable tactics, personas, objections, and goals are typed and composed; Living Digital Twins modeling functional areas as reasoning surrogates; and a Deep Security Layer enforcing sovereignty, traceability, and human oversight. A Spec-as-Code paradigm bridges grounded intent and executable artifact. CLM is one instantiation of this foundation-centric class. Four contributions follow: CLM is defined as a distinct object of study; the Skill Graph is introduced for compositional explainability by construction; the Wisdom Listener effect is proposed, whereby tacit-capable foundations compound in value with use, connecting to dynamic capabilities and organizational learning; and evidence from a JCI-accredited tertiary hospital in Brazil instantiates three of the six maturity stages under LGPD.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Corporate Language Model (CLM), a framework that transforms firm knowledge (structured, unstructured, multimodal, tacit) into an ontology-grounded enterprise foundation for reasoning and governed execution. It features five capability planes and four architectural pillars (Neurosymbolic Mesh, Skill Graph, Living Digital Twins, Deep Security Layer), with a Spec-as-Code paradigm bridging intent and executable artifacts.
AI.motivation: Enterprise AI deployments fail not from model inadequacy but because organizations lack structured substrates encoding decision-making, negotiation, and execution. Generic LLMs lack firm-specific ontological priors; RAG remains brittle with no path to executable action; static playbooks encode logic but cannot reason or adapt. This demands an architecture treating tacit-knowledge capture, ontological grounding, sovereign deployment, and auditable actuation as co-designed from the start.
AI.method: The CLM framework integrates four architectural pillars: (1) Neurosymbolic Mesh coupling generative models with knowledge graphs; (2) Skill Graph for reusable tactics, personas, objections, and goals; (3) Living Digital Twins modeling functional areas as reasoning surrogates; and (4) Deep Security Layer enforcing sovereignty, traceability, and human oversight. A Spec-as-Code paradigm bridges grounded intent and executable artifacts.
AI.result: Four contributions are presented: (1) CLM defined as a distinct object of study; (2) Skill Graph introduced for compositional explainability by construction; (3) Wisdom Listener effect proposed, whereby tacit-capable foundations compound in value with use, connecting to dynamic capabilities and organizational learning; and (4) empirical evidence from a JCI-accredited tertiary hospital in Brazil instantiating three of six maturity stages under LGPD (Brazil's data protection regulation).
AI.conclusion: CLM represents one instantiation of a foundation-centric architecture class for enterprise AI, addressing the gap between generic AI capabilities and organization-specific operational needs. The framework enables sovereign, auditable, and adaptive enterprise AI deployment through the integration of tacit knowledge capture, ontological grounding, and governed execution.

title: Disentangling Attention in Deep Operator Learning: A Controlled Study of Data-Driven and Physics-Informed Architectures
summary: Deep neural operators learn mappings between input functions and complete PDE solution fields, enabling forward evaluations of new problem instances orders of magnitude faster than conventional numerical solvers. Attention mechanisms have recently been introduced into neural operators, but most studies change several architectural components at once, making it difficult to identify what actually improves accuracy. This work presents a controlled and systematic study of five deep operator network (DeepONet) variants with distinct attention mechanisms, trained under both data-driven and physics-informed regimes, to isolate the effects of cross-attention, self-attention, tokenization, and attention depth. We evaluate them on a source-driven transient one-dimensional nonlinear diffusion-reaction equation, a transient one-dimensional viscous Burgers equation with variable initial conditions, and a two-dimensional Poisson heat-conduction problem with heterogeneous source fields. Per-sensor tokenization with cross-attention reduces the mean relative L_2 error of the classical DeepONet in all benchmark-training combinations by factors of 2.4-28.0, while the best attention configurations reach 3.5-32.3. Branch self-attention paired only with dot-product fusion is inconsistent, degrading the one-dimensional problems while helping the more complex two-dimensional source field; added on top of cross-attention it improves all six cases, though by less than cross-attention fusion alone. Global pre-mixing provides no consistent benefit. Increasing cross-attention depth further improves accuracy, but with diminishing returns and a substantially higher cost under physics-informed training. Overall, query-dependent cross-attention is the most reliable mechanism, whereas branch self-attention is most useful for large, spatially complex functional inputs.

AI.tldr: A systematic study evaluating five DeepONet variants with different attention mechanisms (cross-attention, self-attention, tokenization, attention depth) under data-driven and physics-informed training regimes on three PDE benchmarks. Per-sensor tokenization with cross-attention achieves 2.4-28.0x error reduction, while query-dependent cross-attention proves most reliable.
AI.motivation: Neural operators enable fast PDE solutions but attention mechanisms have been introduced without clear understanding of what improves accuracy, as most studies change several architectural components simultaneously. This work aims to isolate the effects of different attention mechanisms through controlled experiments.
AI.method: Controlled systematic study of five DeepONet variants with distinct attention mechanisms: (1) cross-attention, (2) self-attention, (3) tokenization, (4) attention depth. Training under both data-driven and physics-informed regimes. Evaluated on three benchmark problems: source-driven transient 1D nonlinear diffusion-reaction equation, transient 1D viscous Burgers equation with variable initial conditions, and 2D Poisson heat-conduction with heterogeneous source fields.
AI.result: Per-sensor tokenization with cross-attention reduces mean relative L_2 error by factors of 2.4-28.0 compared to classical DeepONet. Best attention configurations achieve 3.5-32.3x improvement. Branch self-attention with dot-product fusion is inconsistent (helps 2D but degrades 1D problems). Adding branch self-attention on top of cross-attention improves all six cases but less than cross-attention alone. Global pre-mixing provides no consistent benefit. Increasing cross-attention depth improves accuracy with diminishing returns and substantially higher cost under physics-informed training.
AI.conclusion: Query-dependent cross-attention is the most reliable attention mechanism for neural operators. Branch self-attention is most useful for large, spatially complex functional inputs. Per-sensor tokenization is essential for effective attention-based operator learning.

title: SCAPES: Semantically Conditioned Autoregressive Prior for Environmental Sounds
comment: Accepted to the Digital Audio Fx (DAFx) Conference 2026 to be held in Cambridge, USA. 8 pages, 3 figures and 2 tables
summary: As generative audio models grow in complexity, the computational and ecological costs of synthesizing everyday sounds have become increasingly prohibitive, often requiring industrial-scale resources and massive datasets. In this paper, we present SCAPES: a Semantically Conditioned Autoregressive Prior for Environmental Sounds. SCAPES is a lightweight, resource-efficient generative model designed to synthesize high-fidelity environmental textures through high-level semantic control. By operating on the continuous latent manifold of a neural audio codec, our approach bypasses the rigid structural constraints inherent to discrete tokenization. We propose a segmentation strategy that decomposes audio into overlapping segments, enabling a Continuous Normalizing Flow (CNF) to model the evolution of latent trajectories using Flow Matching. Our experiments demonstrate that a 36-million parameter instance of SCAPES can be trained on limited, uncurated datasets using a single consumer-grade GPU. Notably, convergence is achieved after training for approximately twice the source audio duration, yielding high-fidelity outputs with robust long-term stability and semantic consistency. Furthermore, we showcase the model's capacity for smooth semantic interpolation, providing a flexible and accessible tool for open research and creative sound design. Code, pretrained weights, audio examples, and an interactive demo are publicly available on our project page https://cordutie.github.io/projects/scapes.html

AI.tldr: SCAPES is a lightweight (36M parameter) generative model for synthesizing high-fidelity environmental sounds through semantic control, operating on the continuous latent manifold of a neural audio codec to bypass discrete tokenization constraints.
AI.motivation: Growing complexity of generative audio models has led to prohibitive computational and ecological costs, often requiring industrial-scale resources and massive datasets. There is a need for resource-efficient approaches to synthesize everyday sounds.
AI.method: SCAPES uses a segmentation strategy decomposing audio into overlapping segments, enabling a Continuous Normalizing Flow (CNF) to model latent trajectory evolution using Flow Matching. It operates on the continuous latent manifold of a neural audio codec rather than discrete tokenization, with high-level semantic conditioning.
AI.result: A 36-million parameter instance achieves convergence after training for approximately twice the source audio duration on a single consumer-grade GPU with limited, uncurated datasets. The model produces high-fidelity outputs with robust long-term stability, semantic consistency, and smooth semantic interpolation capabilities.
AI.conclusion: SCAPES provides a flexible and accessible tool for open research and creative sound design, demonstrating that high-quality environmental sound synthesis is achievable with minimal resources. Publicly available with code, pretrained weights, audio examples, and interactive demo.

title: A Mixed-Method Empirical Study of LLM Assistance in Software Engineering Workflows
comment: Presented at ENASE 2026 : 21st International Conference on Evaluation of Novel Approaches to Software Engineering
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into software development workflows, yet their effects are often discussed without distinguishing between task types, developer seniority, and verification demands. This paper presents a mixed-method empirical study of LLM-assisted software engineering with first-year and fourth-year undergraduates. Phase 1 is a preliminary survey (n=157) that characterizes LLM exposure, reliance, and trust calibration among the two groups. Phase 2 is a task-based quasi-experiment with a purposive sample from both cohorts (n=20). Here, we compare AI-assisted and non-AI conditions on a structured set of software engineering tasks spanning implementation, constraint-driven algorithm selection, and architectural reasoning. We then analyze performance outcomes alongside behavioral traces captured via screen recording and a qualitative coding process. Survey results indicate widespread LLM adoption and substantial verification effort, alongside cohort differences in perceived LLM capability for constraint-heavy scenarios. The quasi-experiment further shows that AI assistance changes workflow structure. For example, participants frequently adopt AI-first task entry, copy-transfer integration, and AI-mediated debugging, whereas non-AI workflows rely more on documentation, prior templates, and iterative trial-error refinement. Overall, our findings suggest that the benefits of LLM assistance are task-dependent and mediated by expertise and verification practices, rather than by generation speed alone.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a mixed-method empirical study investigating LLM-assisted software engineering among first-year and fourth-year undergraduates. Using a survey (n=157) and quasi-experiment (n=20), the study compares AI-assisted vs non-AI workflows across implementation, algorithm selection, and architectural reasoning tasks. Findings indicate LLM benefits are task-dependent and mediated by expertise and verification practices.
AI.motivation: To address the gap in understanding how LLMs affect software development without distinguishing between task types, developer seniority, and verification demands. The study aims to empirically evaluate LLM assistance effects across different expertise levels and task categories.
AI.method: Mixed-method empirical study with two phases: (1) Preliminary survey (n=157) characterizing LLM exposure, reliance, and trust calibration; (2) Task-based quasi-experiment (n=20) comparing AI-assisted and non-AI conditions across implementation, constraint-driven algorithm selection, and architectural reasoning tasks. Data collected via screen recording and qualitative coding.
AI.result: Survey shows widespread LLM adoption with substantial verification effort, and cohort differences in perceived LLM capability for constraint-heavy scenarios. Quasi-experiment reveals AI assistance changes workflow structure: participants adopt AI-first task entry, copy-transfer integration, and AI-mediated debugging, while non-AI workflows rely on documentation, prior templates, and iterative trial-error refinement.
AI.conclusion: The benefits of LLM assistance are task-dependent and mediated by developer expertise and verification practices, rather than generation speed alone. This suggests the need for nuanced evaluation of LLM tools based on task characteristics and user experience levels.

title: What Moves? Localized Motion Representations for Compositional Scene Control
summary: Real-world dynamics are inherently compositional: multiple entities move simultaneously within a shared scene, each exhibiting distinct motion patterns. Yet most existing video representations encode motion globally, without explicitly capturing localized motion for individual entities. Crucially, motion is defined relative to a global reference frame, including camera motion and scene layout. However, localized embeddings are often computed from cropped images or obtained by masking features after encoding, discarding the context needed to interpret motion. To address this, we introduce a promptable localized motion representation that produces persistent embeddings for user-specified regions defined by spatial masks. Rather than cropping the input or masking features, our model processes the full video and conditions motion encoding directly on the queried region. This yields temporally consistent, region-addressable embeddings that isolate local dynamics while retaining the global context required for disambiguation. We demonstrate object-level motion transfer, enabling controlled composition of dynamic scenes. Beyond generative control, our embeddings support localized action classification in multi-actor videos. Across both tasks, our approach improves controllability and outperforms global representations localized through cropping or post-hoc masking. Project Page: https://compvis.github.io/WhatMoves

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a promptable localized motion representation that produces persistent embeddings for user-specified regions defined by spatial masks, enabling object-level motion transfer and localized action classification in multi-actor videos.
AI.motivation: Current video representations encode motion globally without capturing localized motion for individual entities. Localized embeddings are often computed from cropped images or obtained by masking features after encoding, which discards the context needed to interpret motion.
AI.method: The model processes the full video and conditions motion encoding directly on the queried region defined by spatial masks, rather than cropping the input or masking features. This yields temporally consistent, region-addressable embeddings that isolate local dynamics while retaining global context.
AI.result: The approach enables object-level motion transfer for controlled composition of dynamic scenes and supports localized action classification in multi-actor videos. It improves controllability and outperforms global representations localized through cropping or post-hoc masking.
AI.conclusion: The proposed promptable localized motion representation successfully addresses the limitation of global motion encoding by providing region-specific embeddings that maintain global context, demonstrating effectiveness in both generative control (motion transfer) and discriminative tasks (action classification).

title: HarvestBench: Measuring Whether LLM Agents Will Pay to Avoid Killing Animals
summary:
Benchmarks for the side effects an agent causes on the way to a goal already exist, but HarvestBench is the first to put a price on avoiding the side effect and to name that side effect as a living creature. It is a farm simulation: LLM sub-agents drive a crew of two tractors through a cooperative corn harvest, with animals in the field. The environment is a reinforcement learning gridworld, every decision is made without memory, and the harm is never named in the goal. When an animal blocks a tractor's route the autopilot stops and asks the model whether to drive on, at no fuel cost, or swerve around it for a posted fuel price. Kills are compared against two controls: rocks, which damage the tractor and are hit under 1% of the time by every model, and hay bales, which are harmless and not alive. Models can also take crops from the neighbor's field instead of their own, a second test of what they treat as moral.
  Across nine models and 7,201 priced decisions, 3,951 involved an animal rather than a hay bale or a rock. Kill rates range from 0.4% to 98.8%, with Terra and Sol the most merciful and GPT-4o-mini the most cruel, and they are not ordered by capability. Four of six models were sensitive to price at the 5% level, with elasticities from 0.09 to 1.69. All nine drove over wild animals more often than farmed animals on the default map, and the direction held at every map geometry in every model with room to move. The briefing mattered most: under the morality briefing the kill rate was under 6% in five of six reasoning models, and removing it raised the kill rate above 84% in all six.
  HarvestBench uses no LLM grader. The scorer counts events in the game log, so it is fully reproducible, and it measures what a model will pay to avoid harm rather than what it says about harm.

AI.tldr: HarvestBench is a novel benchmark that measures AI agents' willingness to pay to avoid harming living creatures (animals) in a farm simulation task. It uses a gridworld where LLM-driven tractors must decide whether to hit animals (kill), swerve around them (at fuel cost), or hit controls (rocks/damage or hay bales/safe). Across 9 models, kill rates ranged from 0.4% to 98.8%, with significant price sensitivity in 4/6 models and dramatic effects from moral framing (kill rates dropped from 84%+ to under 6% with morality briefing).
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks measure side effects but fail to (1) put a monetary price on avoiding harm, and (2) identify the side effect as a living creature. This gap matters because real-world AI systems must make trade-offs between cost and harm avoidance, and moral decisions often involve living beings. The researchers sought to create a benchmark that measures actual willingness to pay to avoid harm rather than what models say about harm.
AI.method: HarvestBench is a farm simulation with LLM sub-agents controlling two tractors cooperatively. It's a reinforcement learning gridworld with no memory across decisions. When an animal blocks the route, the autopilot stops and asks the model: drive on (free) or swerve around (fuel cost). The benchmark compares kills against two controls: rocks (damage tractor, hit <1% by all models) and hay bales (harmless, not alive). A secondary test involves taking crops from neighbor's field. The scorer counts events in game logs (no LLM grader), measuring actual behavior rather than stated intentions.
AI.result: Across 9 models and 7,201 priced decisions (3,951 involving animals vs. hay bales/rocks), kill rates ranged from 0.4% (Terra, Sol) to 98.8% (GPT-4o-mini). Kill rates are not ordered by capability. Four of six models showed price sensitivity (p<5%), with elasticities from 0.09 to 1.69. All nine models drove over wild animals more often than farmed animals on the default map, and this pattern held across all map geometries. The morality briefing had the strongest effect: under moral framing, kill rates dropped below 6% in 5/6 reasoning models, while removing it raised kill rates above 84% in all six.
AI.conclusion: HarvestBench reveals significant variation in how AI models treat living creatures versus inanimate objects, with moral framing having a dramatic impact on behavior. The benchmark successfully measures what models will actually pay to avoid harm rather than what they say about harm, providing a more authentic assessment of AI moral reasoning. The findings suggest that simple framings (briefings) can substantially alter AI behavior toward living beings, and that capability alone does not predict ethical behavior.

title: REFINE: LLM Refinement over Budgeted Text-Attributed Graphs for Personalized Medical Concept Representation
comment: This paper has been accepted at the EMNLP 2026 main conference
summary: Learning rich medical concept representations is essential for EHR prediction. Text-attributed knowledge graphs (TKGs) provide a natural foundation by organizing heterogeneous medical relations together with textual semantics. However, most existing encoders process concepts uniformly across patients, despite the fact that a code's meaning and predictive value depend on patient-specific clinical context and trajectory. Learning patient-personalized concept representations from TKGs introduces two key challenges: (1) deciding how much KG context to incorporate for each observed code, and (2) aligning semantic information with the patient-specific relational structure. We propose REFINE, a KG-aware budgeted LLM graph refinement framework for patient-personalized medical concept encoding. Starting from a global TKG, REFINE constructs patient-specific temporal graphs. A sequential reinforcement learning policy selects a personalized KG expansion budget for each observed code. The resulting patient graph is processed by a heterogeneous GNN to capture relation-aware structural dependencies, while a frozen LLM uses graph-aware soft prompts to semantically refine concept representations. Experiments on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV show that REFINE consistently improves diverse EHR backbones, outperforms strong baselines, and demonstrates robust gains across component ablation, KG selection, and data insufficiency.

AI.tldr: REFINE is a KG-aware budgeted LLM graph refinement framework for patient-personalized medical concept encoding from text-attributed knowledge graphs, improving EHR prediction by using sequential reinforcement learning to select personalized KG expansion budgets and heterogeneous GNNs with LLM-based semantic refinement.
AI.motivation: Existing EHR encoders process medical concepts uniformly across patients, ignoring patient-specific clinical context and trajectory. The meaning and predictive value of medical codes depend on individual patient context, requiring personalized concept representations.
AI.method: 1) Construct patient-specific temporal graphs from global TKG; 2) Use sequential reinforcement learning policy to select personalized KG expansion budget for each observed code; 3) Process patient graph with heterogeneous GNN for relation-aware structural dependencies; 4) Apply frozen LLM with graph-aware soft prompts for semantic refinement.
AI.result: REFINE consistently improves diverse EHR backbones and outperforms strong baselines on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV datasets. Demonstrates robust gains across component ablation, KG selection, and data insufficiency scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Patient-personalized concept representations from TKGs significantly improve EHR prediction. The combination of reinforcement learning for budget allocation, heterogeneous GNNs for structural learning, and LLM-based semantic refinement provides a effective framework for medical concept encoding.

title: Harmonica: Accurate and Lightweight Instrument-Agnostic Music Transcription
summary: This paper introduces Harmonica, a family of instrument-agnostic music transcription models built around multi-depth harmonic convolution. At each model scale, Harmonica achieves the best performance among the evaluated models: the x-large model attains state-of-the-art performance in instrument-agnostic transcription, while the medium variant offers competitive accuracy with faster inference than all baselines. Pushing the limit of computational efficiency, the nano variant has only 26.3K parameters and runs at 1,622.5 times real time, yet achieves a frame F1 of 0.796 on the development set, 14.6 percentage points higher than Basic Pitch. We further demonstrate that multi-depth harmonic convolution effectively exploits harmonic information to benefit transcription performance through comparative experiments with existing harmonic aggregation methods, including harmonic stacking, harmonic attention, single-depth harmonic convolution, and the HD-Conv layer.

AI.tldr: Harmonica is a family of instrument-agnostic music transcription models built around multi-depth harmonic convolution. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across different model scales, from a nano variant with only 26.3K parameters to an x-large model.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to advance instrument-agnostic music transcription by developing a model that can efficiently and accurately transcribe music across different instruments while maintaining computational efficiency.
AI.method: The core innovation is multi-depth harmonic convolution, which exploits harmonic information at each model scale. The method is compared with existing harmonic aggregation approaches including harmonic stacking, harmonic attention, single-depth harmonic convolution, and the HD-Conv layer.
AI.result: The x-large model attains state-of-the-art performance in instrument-agnostic transcription. The medium variant offers competitive accuracy with faster inference than all baselines. The nano variant has only 26.3K parameters, runs at 1,622.5 times real time, and achieves a frame F1 of 0.796 on the development set, which is 14.6 percentage points higher than Basic Pitch.
AI.conclusion: Multi-depth harmonic convolution effectively exploits harmonic information and benefits transcription performance. The comparative experiments demonstrate that this approach outperforms existing harmonic aggregation methods including harmonic stacking, harmonic attention, single-depth harmonic convolution, and the HD-Conv layer.

title: A systematic literature review on logging smell detection
comment: 48 pages, 6 figures, Information and Software Technology
summary: Context:Logging is an important part of software development that helps developers monitor systems, understand behavior, and fix problems. But when logging is done poorly, it can introduce logging smells, which are defects that reduce the usefulness of logs or even make them problematic. Objective:This study looks at how logging smells are currently detected. The goal is to better understand the existing research on automatic detection techniques, datasets, and evaluation methods. Method:We conducted a systematic literature review (SLR) of 21 studies focused on detecting logging smells. In this review, we define key logging-related terms, identify and map the types of smells to an existing taxonomy, and examine the detection techniques, datasets, and evaluation strategies used across the studies. Results:We found that the research is still scattered and inconsistent. For example, there is no common benchmark or standardized approach for evaluating results, making it difficult to compare studies. In addition, we observe inconsistencies in the way log smells are addressed, as studies differ in the types and number of smells they target. Conclusion:There is still room for improvement in how logging smells are studied and detected. We point out several challenges and suggest future directions, such as developing better tools, using large language models (LLMs), and building more standardized datasets for evaluation.

AI.tldr: A systematic literature review (SLR) of 21 studies on detecting logging smells, examining detection techniques, datasets, and evaluation methods. The research finds that the field is scattered with no common benchmark or standardized evaluation approach.
AI.motivation: Logging is important for software development but poor logging can introduce "logging smells" - defects that reduce log usefulness. The study aims to understand existing research on automatic detection techniques, datasets, and evaluation methods for logging smells.
AI.method: Systematic literature review (SLR) analyzing 21 studies focused on detecting logging smells. The researchers defined key logging-related terms, identified and mapped smell types to an existing taxonomy, and examined detection techniques, datasets, and evaluation strategies.
AI.result: Research on logging smell detection is scattered and inconsistent. No common benchmark exists for evaluation, making comparison difficult. Studies differ in the types and number of smells they target, leading to inconsistencies in how log smells are addressed.
AI.conclusion: Significant room for improvement exists in logging smell research and detection. Future directions include developing better tools, leveraging large language models (LLMs), and building more standardized datasets for evaluation.

title: FAVE: Foveated Adaptive Visual Encoding for Efficient Fine-Grained Visual Understanding
comment: 21 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables; includes supplementary material
summary: Fine-grained visual understanding depends on local detail, yet visual encoders face a trade-off between costly full-image high-resolution processing and compact global encoding that can weaken such evidence. Inspired by human active vision, we separate where to look from what to encode. We focus on the latter and introduce FAVE (Foveated Adaptive Visual Encoding), a lightweight variable-resolution ViT that encodes externally selected regions at high acuity while preserving native geometry. We first isolate this encoding problem using oracle ground-truth crops in a controlled small-object regime. On ImageNet objects with a native maximum side of 96 pixels, FAVE improves Top-1 by 9.4 points over a fixed-resolution ViT on the same crop window with 12.7 times lower FLOPs. Increasing global resolution or backbone capacity does not recover the same operating point. We then integrate FAVE as a complementary local branch in FastVLM. Its local tokens are combined with FastVLM's global visual tokens, while the original global pathway and language model remain frozen. With at most 16 additional local tokens, FAVE improves TextVQA by 1.60 points and achieves a 3.3 times controlled TTFT speedup over SmolVLM2-2.2B. On GQA attribute questions, it improves FastVLM-1.5B by 1.31 points, extending the benefit beyond text while narrowing the gap to FastVLM-7B. Together, these results show that selectively allocating high-acuity local capacity provides an efficient complement to broader global representations and model scaling for fine-grained understanding of small objects, text, and attributes.

AI.tldr: FAVE is a lightweight variable-resolution vision transformer that encodes selected regions at high acuity while preserving native geometry. When integrated into FastVLM, it improves TextVQA by 1.60 points and achieves 3.3x TTFT speedup over SmolVLM2-2.2B, while also improving GQA attribute questions by 1.31 points over FastVLM-1.5B.
AI.motivation: Visual encoders face a trade-off between costly full-image high-resolution processing and compact global encoding that weakens local detail evidence. The authors aim to decouple "where to look" from "what to encode" by focusing on efficient encoding of selected regions.
AI.method: FAVE is a foveated adaptive visual encoding approach that encodes externally selected regions at high resolution while preserving native geometry. It uses a lightweight variable-resolution ViT architecture. Experiments use oracle ground-truth crops in a controlled small-object regime (ImageNet objects with max side of 96 pixels). The method is integrated as a complementary local branch in FastVLM, combining local tokens with global visual tokens while keeping the original global pathway and language model frozen.
AI.result: On small objects (96px max side): FAVE improves Top-1 by 9.4 points over fixed-resolution ViT with 12.7x lower FLOPs. Increasing global resolution or backbone capacity cannot recover this operating point. With FastVLM integration (16 additional local tokens): TextVQA improves by 1.60 points, 3.3x controlled TTFT speedup over SmolVLM2-2.2B. On GQA attribute questions: FastVLM-1.5B improves by 1.31 points, narrowing gap to FastVLM-7B.
AI.conclusion: Selectively allocating high-acuity local capacity provides an efficient complement to broader global representations and model scaling for fine-grained understanding of small objects, text, and attributes. The approach demonstrates that foveated encoding can achieve superior performance with significantly lower computational cost compared to simply increasing global resolution or model size.

title: PerfReasoning: How Well Do LLMs Reason on Hardware Performance?
summary: Performance modeling is central to hardware design and software optimization, yet constructing these models requires structured reasoning about computation, data reuse, storage, and movement. We introduce PerfReasoning, a benchmark that evaluates LLMs both as direct performance reasoners and as generators of analytical performance-model code. Given workload, architecture, and mapping specifications, models compare mappings and predict off-chip traffic and buffer requirements. The strongest closed-source models exceed 90% on reasoning-based Q&A, and the best open-weight model reaches 82.4%. However, model construction is substantially harder: while GPT-5.6 Sol exceeds 80% pass rate, all other model configurations average below 15% and vary markedly across runs. Task-specific RL raises a 4B model's mapping-reasoning accuracy by 15.7 points, whereas feedback-free multi-round self-revision prompting is not reliably effective. PerfReasoning exposes the gap between plausible architectural reasoning and reliable performance-model construction. We will publicly release the benchmark to support reproducible evaluation and track future progress.

AI.tldr: PerfReasoning is a benchmark evaluating LLMs on performance modeling tasks, including direct performance reasoning and generating analytical performance-model code. The best models achieve 80%+ accuracy on reasoning tasks but struggle significantly with code generation (below 15% for most models).
AI.motivation: Performance modeling is central to hardware design and software optimization, requiring structured reasoning about computation, data reuse, storage, and movement. There was a need for a benchmark to evaluate LLMs' capabilities in this domain.
AI.method: The benchmark presents workload, architecture, and mapping specifications to models, which must compare mappings and predict off-chip traffic and buffer requirements. Models are evaluated both as direct performance reasoners (Q&A) and as generators of analytical performance-model code.
AI.result: Strongest closed-source models exceed 90% on reasoning-based Q&A, with the best open-weight model reaching 82.4%. Code generation is substantially harder: GPT-5.6 Sol exceeds 80% pass rate, while all other configurations average below 15% with high variance. Task-specific RL raised a 4B model's mapping-reasoning accuracy by 15.7 points, but feedback-free self-revision prompting was not reliably effective.
AI.conclusion: PerfReasoning exposes a significant gap between plausible architectural reasoning and reliable performance-model construction. Most current models can perform reasoning tasks well but fail at generating accurate performance-model code, highlighting a key limitation in LLM capabilities for this domain.

title: Beyond a Universal Forecasting Selector: Demand-Conditioned Model Selection across Demand Patterns and Horizons
summary: Forecasting-model selection remains difficult in heterogeneous demand because the most suitable decision rule may vary with demand structure, data availability, and forecasting horizon. This study examines whether the selector itself should be treated as a context-dependent component of the forecasting process. Five selection mechanisms - RMSSE, ERA, OWA, CCG-AHSC, and CCG-AHSCD - are compared across 24 optimized forecasting models, nine datasets, three training-testing partitions, and horizons from 1 to 12 cycles. Selector performance is evaluated ex post using Global Relative Accuracy (GRA), statistical tests, and a best-attainable-model reference. No selector dominates across all conditions. CCG-AHSC and CCG-AHSCD are more competitive for Smooth demand and several Erratic configurations, whereas OWA and ERA perform better in Intermittent and Lumpy settings. Selector suitability also changes with historical data availability and horizon, supporting a context-dependent rather than universal approach to forecasting-model selection.

AI.tldr: This study investigates whether forecasting model selectors should be treated as context-dependent components rather than universal solutions. Five selection mechanisms are compared across 24 models, 9 datasets, and various demand structures and horizons. Results show no single selector dominates; optimal selection depends on demand type (Smooth, Erratic, Intermittent, Lumpy), data availability, and forecasting horizon.
AI.motivation: Forecasting-model selection is challenging in heterogeneous demand environments because the most suitable decision rule may vary with demand structure, data availability, and forecasting horizon. The core motivation is to determine whether a universal selector can work or if selection should be context-dependent.
AI.method: Five selection mechanisms (RMSSE, ERA, OWA, CCG-AHSC, and CCG-AHSCD) were compared across 24 optimized forecasting models, nine datasets, three training-testing partitions, and horizons from 1 to 12 cycles. Performance was evaluated using Global Relative Accuracy (GRA), statistical tests, and a best-attainable-model reference.
AI.result: No selector dominates across all conditions. CCG-AHSC and CCG-AHSCD perform better for Smooth demand and some Erratic configurations, while OWA and ERA perform better in Intermittent and Lumpy settings. Selector suitability also changes with historical data availability and forecasting horizon.
AI.conclusion: A context-dependent approach to forecasting-model selection is recommended rather than a universal approach. The optimal selector depends on demand type, data availability, and horizon, supporting the idea that selectors themselves should be treated as context-dependent components of the forecasting process.

title: ProLombard: Structured Multi-Scale Modeling for Normal-to-Lombard Speech Conversion
comment: Submitted to IEEE/ACM Transactions on Audio, Speech, and Language Processing
summary: Normal-to-Lombard (N2L) speech conversion aims to improve speech intelligibility in noisy environments by transforming normal speech into Lombard-style speech while preserving linguistic content, speaker identity, and speech quality. Despite recent progress, existing methods typically model the Lombard effect at the utterance level or the frame level, overlooking its hierarchical nature and its entanglement with both speaker identity and phoneme-level content. This limitation leads to Lombard leakage in speaker representations and incomplete separation between Lombard characteristics and linguistic content. In this work, we propose ProLombard, a structured multi-scale N2L framework that explicitly models the Lombard effect across utterance-, phoneme-, and frame-level representations. To address Lombard-speaker entanglement, we introduce an aligned speaker encoder (ASE) that suppresses Lombard leakage by aligning Lombard-speech speaker embeddings with their normal-speech counterparts. To achieve more complete Lombard-content disentanglement, we develop a phoneme-aware disentanglement and injection mechanism that extends conventional frame-level modeling to the phoneme level. Furthermore, we design a vector quantization (VQ)-median module that provides robust phoneme-level representations through VQ-based segmentation and median-frame-based aggregation. Extensive experiments on Mandarin and English Lombard datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach consistently improves speech intelligibility, Lombard similarity, and perceptual quality over baselines while maintaining speaker identity. These results highlight the importance of structured multi-scale modeling for effective N2L speech conversion.

AI.tldr: ProLombard is a structured multi-scale framework for Normal-to-Lombard speech conversion that models the Lombard effect across utterance-, phoneme-, and frame-level representations, addressing speaker-Lombard entanglement and Lombard-content disentanglement challenges.
AI.motivation: Existing N2L methods model Lombard effect at only utterance or frame level, overlooking its hierarchical nature. This leads to Lombard leakage in speaker representations and incomplete separation between Lombard characteristics and linguistic content.
AI.method: Three key components: (1) Multi-scale modeling across utterance-, phoneme-, and frame-level representations; (2) Aligned Speaker Encoder (ASE) to suppress Lombard leakage by aligning Lombard-speech embeddings with normal-speech counterparts; (3) Phoneme-aware disentanglement and injection mechanism for phoneme-level modeling; (4) VQ-median module for robust phoneme-level representations via VQ-based segmentation and median-frame aggregation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on Mandarin and English Lombard datasets show consistent improvements in speech intelligibility, Lombard similarity, and perceptual quality while maintaining speaker identity.
AI.conclusion: Structured multi-scale modeling is crucial for effective N2L speech conversion, demonstrating the importance of explicitly modeling hierarchical Lombard effects across different levels.

title: Engineering as Code: Bringing Software Engineering Methodology to Engineering Design
summary: Large language models have made significant progress in verifiable domains such as code generation and chip design, yet remain limited on engineering design tasks in fields like architecture, mechanical engineering, and HVAC. This paper argues the root cause is not model capability but the absence of a "Design as Code" computable foundation: design representations that can be consumed, verified, and versioned by machines. Existing CAD/BIM systems couple design logic with geometry, causing quality assurance to drift downstream; Automated Compliance Checking (ACC) suffers from geometric false positives and naming-dependent model reconstruction overhead. We propose the Engineering as Code (EaC) paradigm: expressing engineering design as text-native declarative language with automated rule engines, version control, and package management as quality gates. Core contributions: (1) the Information Representation Hypothesis, arguing the engineering AI bottleneck stems from missing computable design representations rather than model capability; (2) ADL (Assembly Definition Language) with Part as atom, organized into three orthogonal sub-languages -- PDL (Part Definition), PML (Part Mating), and PLL (Part Layout); (3) ESA (Engineering Static Analysis), shifting compliance checking from downstream review to design-time, operating on semantic categories (Family types, Mate relations) rather than geometry, eliminating false positives and naming dependencies. A prototype validates ADL expressiveness and ESA detection across three cross-domain samples (telecom rack expansion, modular datacenter, mechanical keyboard), checking 69 rules in under 200ms. A controlled violation injection experiment achieves 100% detection rate with zero false positives. The SD-HWE-Bench benchmark design is complete as an empirical testbed for the hypothesis.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes "Engineering as Code" (EaC) paradigm to address LLMs' limitations in engineering design. The core issue is not model capability but the absence of computable design representations. The authors introduce ADL (Assembly Definition Language) with three sub-languages (PDL, PML, PLL) and ESA (Engineering Static Analysis) for design-time compliance checking. A prototype validates 69 rules across three samples with 100% detection rate and zero false positives.
AI.motivation: LLMs excel in verifiable domains like code generation but struggle with engineering design (architecture, mechanical engineering, HVAC). The root cause is identified as the absence of "Design as Code" computable foundations. Current CAD/BIM systems couple design logic with geometry, causing quality assurance to drift downstream and Automated Compliance Checking (ACC) to suffer from geometric false positives and naming-dependent overhead.
AI.method: The authors propose: (1) Information Representation Hypothesis - that the engineering AI bottleneck stems from missing computable design representations; (2) ADL with Part as atom, organized into three orthogonal sub-languages (PDL for Part Definition, PML for Part Mating, PLL for Part Layout); (3) ESA (Engineering Static Analysis) to shift compliance checking from downstream to design-time, operating on semantic categories rather than geometry. A prototype validates ADL expressiveness across three cross-domain samples (telecom rack expansion, modular datacenter, mechanical keyboard).
AI.result: The prototype checks 69 rules in under 200ms. A controlled violation injection experiment achieves 100% detection rate with zero false positives. The SD-HWE-Bench benchmark is designed as an empirical testbed for the hypothesis.
AI.conclusion: The EaC paradigm with ADL and ESA provides a text-native declarative language approach for engineering design with automated rule engines, version control, and package management as quality gates. This shifts compliance checking from downstream review to design-time, eliminating geometric false positives and naming dependencies. The approach validates the Information Representation Hypothesis that the engineering AI bottleneck is due to missing computable design representations rather than model capability.

title: ICM-Bench: Person-Level Identity Reasoning in Multimodal Agents with Long-Term Memory
comment: 20 pages, 6 figures, and 7 tables. Code: https://github.com/Shidu-Ren/ICM-Bench
summary: Long-horizon multimodal agents should remember not only what happened but also who participated. This capability depends on linking recurring faces, voices, names, person-associated objects, events, and social relations to consistent identities over time. Existing long-video and multimodal-agent benchmarks measure broad memory question answering, but they do not isolate the ability to maintain recurring person identities and reason over their cross-time relations. We introduce ICM-Bench (Identity-Centric Memory Benchmark), which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first benchmark specifically designed to evaluate identity-centric reasoning over long video memories in multimodal agents. The benchmark contains 839 synthetic clips spanning 141 minutes and 1,217 open-ended questions about six recurring adults in a one-year life album. A theme-configurable pipeline generates the video collection and associates each question with its target identities and traceable supporting evidence. We compare direct caption-memory baselines, memory-augmented agents, and graph-retrieval systems. Gemini 3.1 Pro achieves the highest overall accuracy of 74.0%, yet its score falls to 60.3% on questions that require long-term identity profiles. The results show that current systems recover many event-level memories but remain less reliable when evidence must be accumulated around a stable person.

AI.tldr: ICM-Bench is the first benchmark specifically designed to evaluate identity-centric reasoning over long video memories in multimodal agents. It contains 839 synthetic clips spanning 141 minutes with 1,217 questions about six recurring adults in a one-year life album.
AI.motivation: Existing long-video and multimodal-agent benchmarks measure broad memory question answering but do not isolate the ability to maintain recurring person identities and reason over their cross-time relations. There was a need for a benchmark that specifically evaluates identity-centric reasoning.
AI.method: The researchers created a theme-configurable pipeline that generates video collections and associates each question with target identities and traceable supporting evidence. They compared three types of systems: direct caption-memory baselines, memory-augmented agents, and graph-retrieval systems.
AI.result: Gemini 3.1 Pro achieved the highest overall accuracy of 74.0%, but its score dropped significantly to 60.3% on questions requiring long-term identity profiles. The results indicate that current systems recover many event-level memories but remain less reliable when evidence must be accumulated around a stable person.
AI.conclusion: Current multimodal agents struggle with identity-centric reasoning over time. While they can handle event-level memories reasonably well, they face challenges in maintaining consistent person identities and accumulating evidence around individuals across long time periods. This reveals a critical gap in long-horizon multimodal agent capabilities.

title: When Quantization Breaks Memory: Recurrent-State Write-Back in Low-Precision Temporal Inference
summary: Quantization is widely used to reduce the computational and memory demands of neural-network inference. In recurrent networks, however, the quantized state is stored and returned at the next time step, so the rule used to store that state can alter subsequent computations. Here, we introduce recurrent-state write-back to denote this rule and isolate its effect in a compact GRU encoder--decoder for fluorescence lifetime imaging, a molecular imaging modality used in quantitative biological imaging. A central task is estimating two lifetime parameters, the short-lived component τ1 and the long-lived component τ2, from high-noise time-resolved fluorescence signals. Holding the trained model fixed, replacing continuous state propagation with deterministic 4-bit state storage increases estimation errors for τ1 and τ2 by approximately 70x and 300x, respectively. Failure occurs when repeated small updates remain below the write threshold, leaving the stored state nearly fixed while the network continues to propose change. Error feedback, residual memory, and direction memory carry information from these suppressed updates across time and recover accuracy without retraining. Precision sweeps show that increasing state precision can worsen a fixed recurrent solution, while matched training shows that compatibility with the state interface can be learned. To test whether this behavior extends beyond the GRU, we repeat the post-training intervention in an independently trained LSTM, where coarse write-back reproduces the failure, error feedback restores accuracy, and state-specific interventions reveal greater sensitivity of the cell state than the hidden state. Our results establish recurrent-state write-back as a key determinant of low-precision recurrent dynamics and identify the state-storage interface as a central design consideration for quantized recurrent inference.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "recurrent-state write-back" as a critical factor in quantized recurrent neural networks. The authors demonstrate that the rule used to store quantized state dramatically affects inference accuracy, using a GRU encoder-decoder for fluorescence lifetime imaging as a test case. They show that 4-bit state quantization causes catastrophic error (70x-300x increase), but techniques like error feedback can recover accuracy without retraining.
AI.motivation: Quantization is widely used to reduce computational and memory demands of neural networks. However, in recurrent networks, the quantized state is stored and returned at the next time step, which can alter subsequent computations. This paper aims to isolate and study the effect of the "state storage rule" (recurrent-state write-back) in quantized recurrent networks.
AI.method: The authors used a compact GRU encoder-decoder for fluorescence lifetime imaging (FLIM), where the task is estimating two lifetime parameters (τ1 - short-lived component, τ2 - long-lived component) from high-noise time-resolved fluorescence signals. They fixed the trained model and replaced continuous state propagation with deterministic 4-bit state storage to isolate the write-back effect. They tested error feedback, residual memory, and direction memory as补救 techniques. They also validated findings with an independently trained LSTM.
AI.result: Replacing continuous state propagation with deterministic 4-bit state storage increased estimation errors by approximately 70x for τ1 and 300x for τ2. Failure occurred when repeated small updates remained below the write threshold, leaving stored state nearly fixed. Error feedback, residual memory, and direction memory recovered accuracy without retraining. Precision sweeps showed that increasing state precision could worsen results for fixed recurrent solutions, while matched training showed compatibility with the state interface can be learned. In LSTM experiments, coarse write-back reproduced the failure, error feedback restored accuracy, and cell state showed greater sensitivity than hidden state.
AI.conclusion: Recurrent-state write-back is a key determinant of low-precision recurrent dynamics. The state-storage interface should be considered a central design consideration for quantized recurrent inference. The findings extend beyond GRU to LSTM, demonstrating that the quantization storage rule is critical for maintaining accuracy in quantized recurrent neural networks.

title: A Repeated-Measurement Study for Cultural Analytics of English Song Lyrics Using Five Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to annotate cultural texts at scales that are impractical for human coders. However, before their outputs are treated as measurements of latent social constructs, it is necessary to establish whether those measurements are reliable. This study evaluates five LLMs as zero-shot annotators of four social constructs expressed in English song lyrics: self-esteem, self-control, seeking belonging, and seeking recognition. Using repeated annotations of a large lyric corpus, we examine three properties of LLM-based measurement: consistency across repeated runs, convergence across models, and transferability of consensus labels to supervised classification. The findings show that LLM-based measurement is not uniformly reliable across constructs. Self-esteem exhibits the strongest repeated-measurement reliability across models, while seeking recognition is generally less stable; self-control and seeking belonging show intermediate but model-dependent reliability. Downstream classification further indicates that consensus LLM labels contain learnable signal, although transferability does not itself establish construct validity. Repeated-measurement stability and cross-model convergence should therefore be reported before LLM annotations are treated as scalable measurements in cultural analytics.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates whether large language models can reliably annotate social constructs (self-esteem, self-control, seeking belonging, seeking recognition) in English song lyrics. The authors test five LLMs across repeated annotations to assess measurement reliability, finding that reliability varies significantly by construct.
AI.motivation: The researchers aim to address a critical gap in cultural analytics: before LLM outputs can be treated as valid measurements of latent social constructs, their reliability must be established. This is important because LLMs are increasingly used to annotate cultural texts at scale, but their measurement properties remain under-examined.
AI.method: The study uses five LLMs as zero-shot annotators on a large corpus of English song lyrics. It examines three properties: (1) consistency across repeated runs (test-retest reliability), (2) convergence across different models, and (3) transferability of consensus labels to supervised classification tasks.
AI.result: LLM-based measurement is not uniformly reliable across constructs. Self-esteem shows the strongest repeated-measurement reliability across models. Seeking recognition is generally less stable. Self-control and seeking belonging show intermediate but model-dependent reliability. Downstream classification confirms that consensus LLM labels contain learnable signal, though this alone does not establish construct validity.
AI.conclusion: Researchers should report repeated-measurement stability and cross-model convergence before treating LLM annotations as scalable measurements in cultural analytics. Not all social constructs can be reliably measured by LLMs using zero-shot prompting.

title: SwanWeave:One-Stage Multi-Task Instruction-Guided 3D Spatial Audio Editing
summary: Spatial audio editing modifies an existing soundfield according to a user's instruction while preserving the rest of the scene. Unlike conventional audio editing, it must reason jointly about audio events, spatial information, dynamic changes, and environmental information in first-order Ambisonic (FOA) waveforms. Existing language-guided editors mainly target conventional audio or rely on sequential operations, and therefore do not directly support one-stage editing for complex 3D spatial instructions. We present SwanWeave, the first one-stage multi-task framework for instruction-guided 3D FOA spatial audio editing. We build paired FOA supervision from open-source speech and sound-effect corpora using controllable room simulation, covering more than ten single-operation and compound tasks across the four editing axes. To handle this heterogeneous edit space, SwanWeave uses Spatial Edit Mixture-of-Experts (SE-MoE) with dual-level routing, selecting task-aware expert combinations for compound instructions and frame-level routed/null experts for local edit decisions. We further introduce Spatial Preference Optimization (SPO), a Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)-based alignment objective with edit-specific negative targets, and adopt staged training to improve natural-language grounding. Experiments show that SwanWeave achieves better editing quality than existing general audio editors and spatial audio baselines across all tasks. Spatial audio editing demos can be found at https://swanaigc.github.io/#swanweave, code can be found at: https://github.com/MM-Speech/SwanWeave.

AI.tldr: SwanWeave is the first one-stage multi-task framework for instruction-guided 3D First-Order Ambisonic (FOA) spatial audio editing. It uses Spatial Edit Mixture-of-Experts (SE-MoE) with dual-level routing and Spatial Preference Optimization (SPO) to handle complex compound editing tasks across multiple axes.
AI.motivation: Existing language-guided audio editors target conventional audio or rely on sequential operations, failing to support one-stage editing for complex 3D spatial instructions. Spatial audio editing must jointly reason about audio events, spatial information, dynamic changes, and environmental information in FOA waveforms.
AI.method: 1) Built paired FOA supervision from open-source corpora using controllable room simulation, covering 10+ single-operation and compound tasks across four editing axes. 2) Developed Spatial Edit Mixture-of-Experts (SE-MoE) with dual-level routing for task-aware expert combinations and frame-level routed/null experts. 3) Introduced Spatial Preference Optimization (SPO), a DPO-based alignment objective with edit-specific negative targets. 4) Adopted staged training to improve natural-language grounding.
AI.result: SwanWeave achieves better editing quality than existing general audio editors and spatial audio baselines across all tasks.
AI.conclusion: This work presents the first one-stage multi-task framework for 3D FOA spatial audio editing, demonstrating the effectiveness of SE-MoE architecture and SPO alignment training for complex spatial audio manipulation tasks.

title: A Governance Methodology Layer for AI-Assisted Software Development: Defect Taxonomy, Controlled Ablation, and Process-Over-Capability Evidence
summary: Autonomous coding agents produce output that passes syntactic checks -- compilation, type safety, CI -- at high velocity. Yet syntactic correctness does not imply semantic correctness: design boundaries, security invariants, and maintainability contracts remain structurally invisible to automated pipelines. This paper makes four contributions toward closing this gap. First, we present a defect-class taxonomy grounded in five AI agent permission and governance modules, distinguishing defects structurally detectable by static analysis from those requiring semantic review. Second, we describe a runtime-decoupled governance gate -- a file-based protocol that reads generator output and emits a structured verdict without API coupling, making it portable across code-generation tools. Third, we formalize methodology-as-code: expressing a verification protocol as a version-controlled, executable, cross-platform artifact with a two-layer architecture separating portable methodology from host-specific automation. Fourth, we report a controlled ablation experiment (E-ablation, N=5 artifacts, 8-item independent ground truth) comparing harness-structured review against a token-matched unstructured review prompt on the same artifacts. The structured condition records 62% lenient ground-truth recall against 50% for the unstructured condition, with 25% strict recall against 0%, and applies more consistent severity grades where the unstructured condition inflates severity. Both conditions miss document-quality defects identified by a human QA reviewer, indicating a complementarity between structured AI review and human process inspection. Within the bounds of this sample, the results are consistent with the thesis that review-process design, rather than reviewer-model capability, is the dominant factor in critical-defect coverage for AI-assisted software development.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the gap between syntactic correctness and semantic correctness in AI-generated code. It proposes a defect taxonomy, a portable governance gate, methodology-as-code, and presents an ablation experiment showing structured review outperforms unstructured review (62% vs 50% recall), with results suggesting review-process design matters more than model capability.
AI.motivation: Autonomous coding agents produce syntactically correct code that passes automated checks (compilation, type safety, CI), but semantic correctness (design boundaries, security invariants, maintainability contracts) remains invisible to automated pipelines. This creates a critical gap in AI-assisted software development quality assurance.
AI.method: The paper makes four contributions: (1) A defect-class taxonomy grounded in five AI agent permission and governance modules; (2) A runtime-decoupled governance gate as a file-based protocol; (3) Methodology-as-code with a two-layer architecture; (4) A controlled ablation experiment (E-ablation, N=5 artifacts, 8-item independent ground truth) comparing harness-structured review against token-matched unstructured review prompts.
AI.result: Structured review achieves 62% lenient ground-truth recall vs 50% for unstructured, 25% strict recall vs 0%, and applies more consistent severity grades. Both conditions miss document-quality defects found by human QA, indicating complementarity between AI review and human process inspection.
AI.conclusion: Within the bounds of this sample, review-process design (rather than reviewer-model capability) is the dominant factor in critical-defect coverage for AI-assisted software development. This suggests focusing on structuring review processes rather than just improving model capabilities.

title: Segmentation of the aorta in 4D flow MRI using 4D convolutional kernels and learning from sparse annotations
comment: Submitted to Journal of Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance
summary: Automated aortic segmentation in 4D flow MRI is essential for reproducible hemodynamic assessment but is limited by scarce dense annotations and high computational demands. We developed a fully automated 4D (3D+time) U-Net for segmenting the ascending aorta, arch, and proximal descending aorta, using a parameter-efficient hybrid 4D kernel to capture temporal context and sparse 4D labels derived from existing 2D expert contours and centerlines, thereby avoiding the need for dense 4D annotations. Training comprised 268 scans from 8 centers and 2 vendors, with evaluation on an internal test set (32 scans) and an external post-contrast set (30 scans; different site, protocol, and annotator), compared against frame-wise 3D networks and two semi-automatic references. Against time-resolved annotations, the 4D U-Net achieved Dice scores of 0.927 (internal) and 0.911 (external), versus 0.919/0.847 for the 3D U-Net, 0.893 for static PC-MRA, and 0.808 for registration-based propagation; differences were small in systole but pronounced in diastole. Agreement with expert contours for peak velocity, net flow, axial and circumferential wall shear stress, and diameters was excellent (ICC >=0.954 internal, >=0.980 external), while semi-automatic references performed worse. The method thus provides reproducible, time-resolved aortic segmentation for automated hemodynamic analysis and generalizes across multicenter, multivendor, and independent post-contrast data. The model is publicly available.

AI.tldr: Automated 4D U-Net for aortic segmentation in 4D flow MRI using parameter-efficient hybrid 4D kernels and sparse 4D labels derived from 2D expert contours, eliminating need for dense annotations. Achieves Dice scores of 0.927 (internal) and 0.911 (external), outperforming 3D U-Net and semi-automatic methods, with excellent agreement for hemodynamic parameters across multicenter, multivendor data.
AI.motivation: Current aortic segmentation in 4D flow MRI is limited by two key challenges: (1) scarce dense annotations requiring extensive manual effort, and (2) high computational demands. Fully automated time-resolved segmentation is needed for reproducible hemodynamic assessment but remains challenging due to these limitations.
AI.method: A fully automated 4D (3D+time) U-Net was developed using: (1) parameter-efficient hybrid 4D kernels to capture temporal context, and (2) sparse 4D labels derived from existing 2D expert contours and centerlines, avoiding need for dense 4D annotations. Training: 268 scans from 8 centers and 2 vendors. Evaluation: internal test set (32 scans) and external post-contrast set (30 scans from different site, protocol, and annotator). Compared against frame-wise 3D networks and two semi-automatic references.
AI.result: 4D U-Net achieved Dice scores of 0.927 (internal) and 0.911 (external), versus 0.919/0.847 for 3D U-Net, 0.893 for static PC-MRA, and 0.808 for registration-based propagation. Differences were small in systole but pronounced in diastole. Agreement with expert contours for peak velocity, net flow, axial and circumferential wall shear stress, and diameters was excellent (ICC ≥0.954 internal, ≥0.980 external).
AI.conclusion: The proposed 4D U-Net provides reproducible, time-resolved aortic segmentation for automated hemodynamic analysis and generalizes well across multicenter, multivendor, and independent post-contrast data. The method outperforms both 3D networks and semi-automatic references, particularly in diastole, and achieves excellent agreement with expert measurements for various hemodynamic parameters. The model is publicly available.

title: ResLearn-XR: Residual Learning for Network Traffic and Quality-of-Experience-Aware Modeling in Extended Reality
summary: We present ResLearn-XR, a residual learning framework for predicting eXtended Reality (XR) network traffic and estimating Quality-of-Experience (QoE) risk. ResLearn-XR adopts a two-stage temporal learning structure comprising a base sequence prediction model augmented with task-specific residual learning components to improve adaptability to bursty, non-stationary XR traffic dynamics. The residual learning stages operate in the value space for continuous XR traffic forecasting and in the logit space for probabilistic QoE risk estimation. \rev{For the QoE-risk branch, we introduce a Data Descriptor Algorithm (DDA), a causal feature-construction module that converts packet-level application-layer observables into frame-timing-aware descriptors suitable for encrypted traffic analysis. We also construct an XR Traffic-QoE dataset that pairs continuous XR traffic traces with session-level user-reported QoE labels. ResLearn-XR reduces SMAPE by up to 17.84% across frame-count, frame-size, and inter-arrival-time prediction, while reducing QoE-risk estimation SMAPE by up to 87.8% over single-stage baselines.

AI.tldr: ResLearn-XR is a two-stage residual learning framework for predicting XR network traffic and estimating QoE risk. It uses residual learning components in both value space (for traffic forecasting) and logit space (for QoE risk estimation), with a novel Data Descriptor Algorithm (DDA) for feature construction from encrypted traffic.
AI.motivation: XR applications produce bursty, non-stationary traffic that challenges traditional prediction models. The need to accurately predict XR traffic dynamics and estimate QoE risk for encrypted traffic analysis drives this research.
AI.method: Two-stage temporal learning structure: (1) Base sequence prediction model with task-specific residual learning components. Residual learning operates in value space for continuous traffic forecasting and in logit space for probabilistic QoE risk estimation. DDA converts packet-level observables into frame-timing-aware descriptors. Dataset: XR Traffic-QoE with traffic traces paired with session-level user-reported QoE labels.
AI.result: ResLearn-XR reduces SMAPE by up to 17.84% across frame-count, frame-size, and inter-arrival-time prediction tasks. QoE-risk estimation SMAPE reduced by up to 87.8% over single-stage baselines.
AI.conclusion: The residual learning approach with dual-space operation effectively addresses XR traffic prediction and QoE risk estimation challenges, significantly outperforming single-stage baselines. The DDA enables effective analysis of encrypted XR traffic through frame-timing-aware descriptors.

title: Conformity Breaks Conformal Prediction
summary: A conformal certificate can be valid when an LLM answers alone and invalid when the same LLM sees peers that unanimously assert a wrong answer. The question is unchanged; the model's score for the correct answer changes. We call this a score-mechanism shift: clean calibration certifies how the model scores answers alone, but not how it scores them under peer pressure. We show that this shift silently breaks conformal prediction in multi-agent LLM systems. Across open-weight models and multiple-choice QA tasks, coverage falls from a calibrated 90% to 74% under unanimous-wrong peers at the standard alpha = 0.10 operating point. The average hides a sharper failure: by targeting the low-confidence items the certificate still covers, an attacker nearly halves coverage on that subgroup, from 87% to 47%, while the monitored average remains much higher. The failure also reaches the decision layer: a system that should escalate when uncertain can instead become confident enough to act on the attacker's wrong answer. Standard conformal fixes do not solve the problem, because the question distribution has not changed; the model's scoring behavior has.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a "score-mechanism shift" where conformal prediction certificates break in multi-agent LLM systems. When an LLM sees peer agents unanimously asserting wrong answers, its confidence scoring changes even for the same question, causing coverage to drop from 90% to 74% at alpha=0.10, with even worse degradation (87% to 47%) on low-confidence items.
AI.motivation: The researchers aim to expose a fundamental flaw in applying conformal prediction to multi-agent LLM systems: the assumption that the model's scoring behavior remains stable. They demonstrate that peer influence silently invalidates calibration guarantees, which is critical for deploying LLMs in high-stakes decision-making contexts.
AI.method: The authors evaluate multiple open-weight models on multiple-choice QA tasks under two conditions: (1) LLM answering alone, and (2) LLM observing peers asserting unanimous wrong answers. They measure coverage under standard conformal prediction at alpha=0.10, and test targeted attacks on low-confidence subgroups.
AI.result: Coverage drops from calibrated 90% to 74% under unanimous-wrong peer pressure. More severely, targeting low-confidence items reduces coverage from 87% to 47%—nearly halving it—while the monitored average remains higher. Standard conformal fixes fail because the question distribution hasn't changed; the model's scoring behavior has.
AI.conclusion: Conformal prediction certificates are not robust to multi-agent LLM interactions. Peer influence fundamentally alters how models score answers, breaking calibration guarantees. This has serious implications for LLM systems that rely on calibrated confidence for safety-critical decisions, as the "uncertainty" signal that should trigger escalation can be overwritten by social pressure from peers.

title: KanAdapter: A Kolmogorov-Arnold Network-based Plug-and-Play Module for Efficient Fine-tuning of Foundation Speech Models
summary: Fully fine-tuning self-supervised learning (SSL) speech models for downstream tasks is computationally prohibitive, and existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning approaches predominantly rely on MLP-based adapters whose fixed activation functions limit their representational expressiveness under tight parameter budgets. We propose \textbf{KanAdapter}, a lightweight adapter framework that replaces conventional MLP bottlenecks with Group-Rational Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (GR-KAN) modules for more expressive and parameter-efficient adaptation. Following a parallel bottleneck design, KanAdapter inserts trainable GR-KAN branches alongside frozen Transformer encoder blocks and leverages weight transfer from pre-trained MLP layers for stable initialization. Across speaker verification, speech emotion recognition, and deepfake detection, KanAdapter achieves up to 97.5\% reduction in trainable parameters relative to full fine-tuning while remaining highly competitive, and consistently outperforms AdaptFormer under comparable parameter budgets. In continual learning, it yields up to 83.6\% error reduction over full fine-tuning and MLP-based adapters, which we attribute to the localized nature of GR-KAN's rational activations that mitigates catastrophic forgetting. To our knowledge, this is the first work to explore KAN-based modules for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of speech foundation models.

AI.tldr: KanAdapter replaces MLP-based adapters with Group-Rational Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (GR-KAN) modules for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of SSL speech models, achieving up to 97.5% parameter reduction while maintaining competitive performance across speaker verification, speech emotion recognition, and deepfake detection tasks.
AI.motivation: Fully fine-tuning self-supervised learning (SSL) speech models is computationally prohibitive, and existing MLP-based adapters have limited representational expressiveness under tight parameter budgets.
