AI.method: KanAdapter uses a parallel bottleneck design with trainable GR-KAN branches alongside frozen Transformer encoder blocks, leveraging weight transfer from pre-trained MLP layers for stable initialization. The GR-KAN module replaces conventional MLP bottlenecks with more expressive rational activation functions.
AI.result: KanAdapter achieves up to 97.5% trainable parameter reduction relative to full fine-tuning while remaining highly competitive, consistently outperforming AdaptFormer under comparable parameter budgets. In continual learning, it yields up to 83.6% error reduction over full fine-tuning and MLP-based adapters.
AI.conclusion: This is the first work to explore KAN-based modules for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of speech foundation models. The localized nature of GR-KAN's rational activations mitigates catastrophic forgetting, making it particularly effective for continual learning scenarios.

title: Large Language Models for Fuzz Testing in Microservices: A Systematic Literature Review
summary: Microservice systems (MSS) increasingly rely on heterogeneous APIs whose combinatorial input space and stateful dependencies challenge traditional fuzz testing. Meanwhile, Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently been introduced to enhance fuzzing with semantic reasoning over specifications, inputs, and runtime feedback. This paper presents a systematic literature review (SLR) of LLM-assisted fuzz testing for microservices to synthesise how LLMs are applied, evaluated, and what challenges remain. Following established SLR guidelines, we analyze 20 primary studies published between 2024 and 2026. Results show LLMs are mainly used as semantic input generators in black-box fuzzing, with a growing shift towards agent-based and retrieval-augmented architectures, improving valid input generation and modestly increasing coverage and vulnerability detection. However, evaluation remains heterogeneous, with limited benchmark standardization, scarce cost reporting, and a bias toward single-service experiments, highlighting a gap with real-world multi-service systems. This review provides a taxonomy of LLM roles and integrations, a consolidated view of evaluation practices, and a mapping of open challenges to research directions, supporting the design and deployment of LLM-driven fuzzing in microservices.

AI.tldr: This systematic literature review (SLR) examines 20 primary studies (2024-2026) on LLM-assisted fuzz testing for microservices. It finds LLMs are primarily used as semantic input generators in black-box fuzzing, with emerging agent-based and retrieval-augmented architectures. Evaluation remains heterogeneous with limited benchmark standardization and bias toward single-service experiments.
AI.motivation: Microservice systems (MSS) rely on heterogeneous APIs with combinatorial input space and stateful dependencies that challenge traditional fuzz testing. LLMs have emerged to enhance fuzzing with semantic reasoning, but their application in microservice fuzzing lacks systematic synthesis.
AI.method: Following established SLR guidelines, the authors analyzed 20 primary studies published between 2024 and 2026, examining how LLMs are applied, evaluated, and identifying remaining challenges.
AI.result: LLMs are mainly used as semantic input generators in black-box fuzzing, with growing shift toward agent-based and retrieval-augmented architectures. This improves valid input generation and modestly increases coverage and vulnerability detection. However, evaluation remains heterogeneous with limited benchmark standardization, scarce cost reporting, and bias toward single-service experiments.
AI.conclusion: The review provides a taxonomy of LLM roles and integrations, consolidated evaluation practices, and maps open challenges to research directions. It supports the design and deployment of LLM-driven fuzzing in microservices, highlighting gaps between research and real-world multi-service systems.

title: Topology-Aware Training and Spatial Diagnostics for Fiber Bundle Segmentation in Tracer Histology
summary: Anatomic tracer studies reveal how axon bundles project from an injection site, branch into smaller groups of axons, and course through the brain to reach their destinations. Histological data from such studies provide anatomical reference information for validating diffusion MRI tractography. However, manual annotation of the histological data is very labor-intensive, and although automated segmentation methods have been proposed, they rely mainly on pixel-overlap losses such as BCE and Dice; topology-aware loss functions have not been studied for this task. We compare BCE-Dice, clDice, Betti matching, and Topograph for fiber bundle segmentation in macaque tracer histology using a frozen DINOv3 backbone. To our knowledge, this is the first exploration of foundation-model features for this task. BCE-Dice achieved the highest Dice, while clDice achieved the highest bundle recall but poor mask overlap. Topograph had similar Dice to BCE-Dice, the lowest $β_0$ error, and fewer false positives than BCE-Dice and Betti matching. Fiber bundle segmentation methods are typically evaluated with a permissive rule that counts a bundle as detected given any overlap with the prediction. We show this rule does not capture oversegmentation, and that per-section TPR can be inflated by empty sections assigned perfect recall. To quantify this, we introduce Excess32, a spatial diagnostic measuring predicted pixels outside a 32-pixel tolerance band around annotated bundles. In validation, a Betti-Topograph union raises sparse-bundle TPR from 0.818 to 0.933, but worsens FDR from 0.296 to 0.509, Excess32 from 0.108 to 0.466, and area ratio from 0.94 to 3.34. These results show detection metrics alone are insufficient to characterize segmentation quality.

AI.tldr: This paper compares topology-aware loss functions (BCE-Dice, clDice, Betti matching, Topograph) for fiber bundle segmentation in macaque tracer histology using a frozen DINOv3 backbone. BCE-Dice achieves highest Dice, while Topograph has best topology preservation with lowest β0 error and fewest false positives. The paper introduces Excess32, a spatial diagnostic to detect oversegmentation, and shows that detection metrics alone are insufficient to characterize segmentation quality.
AI.motivation: Manual annotation of histological data for validating diffusion MRI tractography is labor-intensive. While automated segmentation methods exist, they rely mainly on pixel-overlap losses (BCE, Dice) without topology awareness. This work explores foundation-model features and compares topology-aware loss functions for this task.
AI.method: Using a frozen DINOv3 backbone (foundation model) for feature extraction, the authors compare four loss functions: BCE-Dice, clDice, Betti matching, and Topograph for fiber bundle segmentation in macaque tracer histology. They also introduce Excess32, a spatial diagnostic measuring predicted pixels outside a 32-pixel tolerance band around annotated bundles.
AI.result: BCE-Dice achieved the highest Dice score; clDice achieved the highest bundle recall but poor mask overlap; Topograph had similar Dice to BCE-Dice, lowest β0 error, and fewer false positives. A Betti-Topograph union raises sparse-bundle TPR from 0.818 to 0.933 but worsens FDR from 0.296 to 0.509, Excess32 from 0.108 to 0.466, and area ratio from 0.94 to 3.34.
AI.conclusion: Detection metrics alone (like Dice, recall) are insufficient to characterize segmentation quality. The permissive detection rule (any overlap counts as detected) does not capture oversegmentation, and per-section TPR can be inflated by empty sections. The Excess32 metric is essential for revealing oversegmentation issues that traditional metrics miss.

title: Rethinking Indirect Prompt Injection as a Test-Time Search Problem
summary: We formulate indirect prompt injection as a test-time search over a task-dependent attack surface induced by the environment, user task, and injection task. To operationalize this formulation, we introduce an agentic attacker with a dedicated search harness that performs environment reconnaissance, structured reasoning over attack strategies, and adaptive evaluation using victim-agent feedback. Across heterogeneous tasks, we find that increasing attacker test-time compute improves vulnerability discovery and exploitation, while ablations show that explicit strategy management is important for avoiding redundant search and sustaining gains at larger budgets. These results suggest that agentic security evaluations should characterize both the attacker's search procedure and compute budget, rather than treating attack success as a budget-independent property of the victim. More broadly, our findings identify the attacker's adaptive search over the system attack surfaces as an important and underexplored security risk for tool-using agents.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a framework for evaluating indirect prompt injection attacks on AI agents by modeling the attacker as an agentic system that performs test-time search over the attack surface. The approach combines environment reconnaissance, structured reasoning over attack strategies, and adaptive evaluation using victim-agent feedback.
AI.motivation: Current security evaluations of prompt injection treats attack success as a budget-independent property of the victim, ignoring the attacker's search procedure and compute budget. This work addresses this gap by characterizing the attacker's adaptive search as a key security risk factor for tool-using agents.
AI.method: The authors formulate indirect prompt injection as a test-time search problem over a task-dependent attack surface. They introduce an agentic attacker with a dedicated search harness that performs: (1) environment reconnaissance, (2) structured reasoning over attack strategies, and (3) adaptive evaluation using victim-agent feedback. Experiments across heterogeneous tasks evaluate the impact of attacker test-time compute and ablate the importance of explicit strategy management.
AI.result: Increasing attacker test-time compute improves vulnerability discovery and exploitation. Ablations show that explicit strategy management is important for avoiding redundant search and sustaining gains at larger budgets.
AI.conclusion: Agentic security evaluations should characterize both the attacker's search procedure and compute budget, rather than treating attack success as a budget-independent property of the victim. The attacker's adaptive search over system attack surfaces represents an important and underexplored security risk for tool-using agents.

title: When Load-Balancing Goes Too Far: Expert Pruning in Over-Dispersed Mixture-of-Experts Models
summary: Expert pruning reduces the memory and serving cost of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models by removing low-importance experts identified by the router, assuming router probabilities provide a reliable importance signal. We observe that this assumption breaks down under over-dispersed routing, a regime associated with aggressive load-balancing during training, in which tokens are distributed nearly uniformly across experts and importance signals collapse. In this regime, perplexity does not predict downstream task accuracy: on gpt-oss-20B, the lowest-perplexity pruning configuration yields the worst mathematical reasoning, while the highest-perplexity configuration preserves it. This does not occur under standard routing (e.g., Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct), where perplexity and accuracy degrade together. Pruning under over-dispersed routing also exposes a capability trade-off in which no single scoring metric dominates: activation-aware scoring preserves mathematical reasoning but severely degrades knowledge-intensive science (an 18-point gap on GPQA), whereas frequency-based scoring exhibits the reverse. We propose Minimax Expert Score Allocation (MESA), a domain-aware method that iteratively boosts importance scores for experts serving whichever domain is currently worst-affected, minimizing worst-case domain degradation rather than average accuracy. At 25% expert pruning MESA achieves the smallest worst-case degradation across domains, outperforming activation-aware baselines on 7 of 11 benchmarks at a correspondingly reduced memory footprint, and it generalizes to gpt-oss-120B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B, and OLMoE-1B-7B. Our results indicate that over-dispersed routing is a qualitatively distinct pruning regime in which standard assumptions fail, and that recognizing it is a prerequisite for principled expert pruning of load-balanced MoE models.

AI.tldr: This paper examines expert pruning in MoE models under over-dispersed routing (aggressive load-balancing), where standard importance signals collapse. The authors discover that perplexity doesn't predict task accuracy in this regime, and pruning exposes capability trade-offs between domains. They propose MESA, a domain-aware method that minimizes worst-case domain degradation.
AI.motivation: The standard assumption in expert pruning—that router probabilities reliably indicate expert importance—breaks down under over-dispersed routing (aggressive load-balancing). This leads to counterintuitive results where lowest-perplexity pruning yields worst mathematical reasoning, challenging existing pruning methodology for load-balanced MoE models.
AI.method: The authors propose Minimax Expert Score Allocation (MESA), a domain-aware iterative method that boosts importance scores for experts serving whichever domain is currently worst-affected, minimizing worst-case domain degradation rather than average accuracy.
AI.result: At 25% expert pruning, MESA achieves smallest worst-case degradation across domains, outperforming activation-aware baselines on 7 of 11 benchmarks with reduced memory footprint. The method generalizes to gpt-oss-120B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B, and OLMoE-1B-7B. Key findings: (1) perplexity doesn't predict accuracy under over-dispersed routing, (2) capability trade-offs exist where no single scoring metric dominates, (3) activation-aware scoring preserves math reasoning but degrades science tasks (18-point GPQA gap), while frequency-based scoring shows opposite pattern.
AI.conclusion: Over-dispersed routing represents a qualitatively distinct pruning regime where standard assumptions fail. Recognizing this regime is essential for principled expert pruning of load-balanced MoE models. MESA provides a practical solution by minimizing worst-case domain degradation rather than optimizing average performance.

title: Robustness and Trade-offs for Code LLMs on Protected Code
summary: Code large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used on software artifacts that may be intentionally obfuscated for intellectual-property protection, reverse-engineering resistance, or controlled access. In reverse engineering and security analysis, deobfuscation is commonly treated as the preprocessing step before downstream analysis or inference, yet its utility for code LLM pipelines has not been systematically validated across models and protection methods. We present an execution-based study of seven code LLMs on protected-code translation and completion, spanning source programs from C++, Go, Java, and JavaScript, five obfuscation methods, and three inference protocols: plain, obfuscated, and deobfuscated. Our results show that direct inference on obfuscated code often matches or exceeds inference on restored code. In this controlled benchmark, higher-capability models such as GPT-4.1 and Qwen3-Coder-30B retain about 90% Pass@1 on obfuscated translation inputs, indicating that explicit restoration is often unnecessary. Same-model restoration does recover some obfuscation-induced failures, but it also degrades many cases that already succeed, with lower-capability models showing the largest net losses. Across settings, model capability is the primary factor, while source language and obfuscation method have secondary but consistent effects. Overall, our findings support model-aware pipeline design and indicate that protected-code workflows should be evaluated primarily with execution-based metrics rather than static similarity alone.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether code deobfuscation is necessary before using code LLMs on protected software. The study tests 7 code LLMs across 4 programming languages (C++, Go, Java, JavaScript), 5 obfuscation methods, and 3 inference protocols. Results show that direct inference on obfuscated code often matches or exceeds deobfuscated inference, with high-capability models retaining ~90% Pass@1 on obfuscated inputs.
AI.motivation: Deobfuscation is commonly used as a preprocessing step in reverse engineering and security analysis before downstream analysis, but its utility for code LLM pipelines has not been systematically validated across different models and protection methods.
AI.method: Execution-based study of seven code LLMs on protected-code translation and completion tasks. Tested across source programs from C++, Go, Java, and JavaScript, five obfuscation methods, and three inference protocols: plain, obfuscated, and deobfuscated.
AI.result: Direct inference on obfuscated code often matches or exceeds inference on restored code. High-capability models (GPT-4.1, Qwen3-Coder-30B) retain about 90% Pass@1 on obfuscated translation inputs. Same-model restoration recovers some obfuscation-induced failures but degrades many cases that already succeed, with lower-capability models showing the largest net losses. Model capability is the primary factor; source language and obfuscation method have secondary but consistent effects.
AI.conclusion: Explicit code restoration is often unnecessary for code LLMs. Protected-code workflows should be evaluated primarily with execution-based metrics rather than static similarity alone. Model-aware pipeline design is recommended.

title: VISTA: Dense Multi-Label Classroom Coding with Vision-Language Models
comment: DataMFM Workshop @ Computer Vision & Pattern Recognition (CVPR) 2026
summary: Video-language benchmarks are usually constructed by the dataset authors without published reliability statistics, leaving the noise floor of the construct unknown. We argue that multimodal benchmarking benefits from methods taken from research communities that have already invested in strategies to ensure reliability. We illustrate the case with the Classroom Observation Protocol for Undergraduate STEM (COPUS): a 24-code multi-label observation instrument with a decade of peer-reviewed reliability literature. We recast COPUS as a video benchmark for multimodal foundation models, where it provides a dense set of structured labels (a 24-dimensional binary vector every 2 minutes across a 50-90 minute lecture), an externally validated vocabulary, and established literature that provides a per-code reliability target based on human evaluators. Annotations in our evaluation corpus are produced by a 5-person human-evaluator panel whose consensus matrix is our reference. We propose VISTA, a baseline that runs MiniCPM-V-4.5 over a dense sliding window, refines its per-window outputs with a lightweight multi-layer perceptron (MLP) head trained on top of the frozen backbone, and max-pools the resulting predictions onto the 2-minute COPUS grid. On three held-out chemistry lectures, VISTA reaches 80.1% restricted macro accuracy versus 74.9% for the zero-shot variant, with the largest residual errors on visually similar instructor codes and on rare audio-dependent codes. We characterize three systematic failure modes (audio-partial observability, fine-grained group-work discrimination, long-tail recall) and release the benchmark tooling, prompts and baseline code at https://github.com/ajfranck/VISTA.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces VISTA, a benchmark for evaluating multimodal foundation models on classroom observation using the COPUS protocol, achieving 80.1% restricted macro accuracy with a fine-tuned MiniCPM-V-4.5 model.
AI.motivation: Video-language benchmarks lack reliability statistics, making their noise floor unknown. The authors argue that multimodal benchmarking should adopt established reliability methods from other research communities, using COPUS (a 24-code observation instrument with a decade of peer-reviewed reliability literature) as a case study.
AI.method: The authors recast COPUS as a video benchmark providing dense structured labels (24-dimensional binary vector every 2 minutes across 50-90 minute lectures). They propose VISTA, a baseline that runs MiniCPM-V-4.5 over a dense sliding window, refines outputs with a lightweight MLP head trained on the frozen backbone, and max-pools predictions onto the 2-minute COPUS grid. Annotations come from a 5-person human-evaluator panel consensus.
AI.result: VISTA achieves 80.1% restricted macro accuracy versus 74.9% for the zero-shot variant on three held-out chemistry lectures. The largest residual errors occur on visually similar instructor codes and rare audio-dependent codes.
AI.conclusion: The authors identify three systematic failure modes: audio-partial observability, fine-grained group-work discrimination, and long-tail recall. They release benchmark tooling, prompts, and baseline code to enable further research in reliable multimodal benchmarking for video-language models.

title: BioSync: Transformer-Based Cross-Modal Fusion for a Multimodal Physiological Digital Biomarker
summary: Cardiac, neural, behavioral, and speech measurements from wearable and mobile devices provide partial, noise-sensitive views of physiological state. BioSync combines these measurements into the \textbf{BioSync Index (BSI)}, a continuous composite digital biomarker defined under the BEST framework. The model applies multi-head self-attention to modality tokens and adds a linear branch whose hypothesis class includes standard feature concatenation. This architecture is motivated by latent-variable measurement theory and by the possibility that joint observations contain information unavailable from individual modalities. We evaluated BioSync on two literature-informed synthetic cohorts: a four-modality cognitive-decline cohort using HRV, EEG, actigraphy, and speech, and a metabolic-autonomic cohort structured around the public AI-READI wearable schema. In the cognitive cohort, BioSync and concatenation obtained AUCs of 0.928 and 0.926, respectively. In the metabolic cohort, BioSync obtained accuracy/F1 of 0.764/0.766, compared with 0.756/0.758 for concatenation. The BSI correlated with latent severity in both cohorts ($r=0.91$ and $r=0.68$). A pure-attention ablation obtained cognitive-cohort AUC 0.911, locating the increase to 0.928 in the combined wide-and-deep architecture. With matched modality-dropout training, BioSync led concatenation at five of six cognitive-cohort corruption rates and at the highest metabolic-cohort rate. Its cognitive-cohort AUC was also higher than five published digital-biomarker reference values, although differences in datasets and tasks preclude a controlled benchmark claim. Comparison with single-modality, early-fusion, and late-fusion designs across six prespecified criteria identifies the model's computational properties; validation on real cohorts remains necessary.

AI.tldr: BioSync combines cardiac, neural, behavioral, and speech measurements from wearable devices into a composite digital biomarker (BSI) using multi-head self-attention plus a linear branch. Evaluated on two synthetic cohorts, it achieved AUC 0.928 for cognitive decline and accuracy/F1 0.764/0.766 for metabolic-autonomic outcomes, outperforming concatenation and single-modality baselines.
AI.motivation: Wearable and mobile device measurements provide partial, noise-sensitive views of physiological state. Individual modalities may lack information available from joint observations. The study aims to create a unified composite biomarker that integrates multiple modalities more effectively than standard feature concatenation.
AI.method: BioSync applies multi-head self-attention to modality tokens combined with a linear branch (hypothesis class includes standard concatenation). Validated on two synthetic cohorts: (1) four-modality cognitive-decline cohort (HRV, EEG, actigraphy, speech) and (2) metabolic-autonomic cohort based on AI-READI wearable schema. Compared against concatenation, pure-attention ablation, single-modality, early-fusion, and late-fusion designs across six criteria. Tested robustness with modality-dropout training and corruption rates.
AI.conclusion: The combined wide-and-deep architecture (attention + linear branch) effectively fuses multi-modal wearable data into a continuous composite biomarker. BioSync shows improved performance and robustness over concatenation and other fusion methods on synthetic data. Real-cohort validation remains necessary before clinical application.

title: On-board ML for Trace Gas detection in Imaging Spectroscopy data
comment: 2 pages; presented as a short (2 pages) paper at the IEEE HPEC26
summary: Data collected during aerial and spaceborne imaging spectroscopy campaigns enables the detection of transient events such as trace gas emissions. However, current processing pipelines depend on slow, on-the-ground processing, which delays the time to information of each detected event and prohibits immediate follow-up actions. During the Tokyo Field Campaign of March 2026, we explored on-board processing of Imaging Spectroscopy data from the equipped AVIRIS-5 sensor. Due to communication bottlenecks, full datacubes cannot be downlinked immediately during the flight. Instead we downlink the potential events predicted by our efficient and small machine learning model. We show the first on-board detection of methane point source emission with Imaging Spectroscopy data using Edge ML.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates the first on-board detection of methane point source emissions using imaging spectroscopy data (AVIRIS-5 sensor) and Edge ML, addressing delays in traditional ground-based processing pipelines and communication bandwidth limitations.
AI.motivation: Current aerial/spaceborne imaging spectroscopy pipelines rely on slow on-the-ground processing, causing delays in event detection and preventing immediate follow-up actions. Additionally, full datacubes cannot be downlinked immediately due to communication bottlenecks.
AI.method: The study used AVIRIS-5 sensor data during the Tokyo Field Campaign (March 2026). The approach employs an efficient, small machine learning model for on-board processing, enabling only potential events (rather than full datacubes) to be downlinked during flight.
AI.result: The paper reports the first successful on-board detection of methane point source emission using Imaging Spectroscopy data with Edge ML technology.
AI.conclusion: On-board Edge ML processing of imaging spectroscopy data enables real-time detection of transient trace gas events like methane emissions, overcoming traditional pipeline delays and communication constraints.

title: Automated Deployment of Real-Time Tasks for Phased Execution on Scratchpad-Based Multicore Platforms
summary: The increasing throughput demands in real-time systems and the consolidation of functionality on few, high-performance platforms are driving a shift towards parallel architectures. A key challenge for multicore real-time systems is the interference from contention for access to shared memory. Phased execution approaches address this challenge by restricting shared memory access to mutually exclusive memory phases, while computation is limited to memories local to each core. However, the complexity of managing and scheduling said memory phases hinders the adoption of phased execution in real-time applications. To address this challenge, we propose a model-based deployment methodology that automates the process of adapting applications to phased execution. We present an integrated tool-based deployment process that extends the application through the necessary memory phases and provides a runtime environment to orchestrate execution on the target hardware platform. Our approach requires minimal changes to the application implementation since the deployment tool directly extracts the required information from the generated application binaries. We validate our methodology using an avionics case study on a RISC-V multicore system, showcasing its key components and principles of operation.

title: DART: Depth-as-Target Pretraining for Surgical Vision Foundation Models
summary: Vision foundation models (VFMs) are valuable in data-scarce domains such as surgery, where a single pretrained backbone can provide rich representations for many downstream tasks. Yet the dominant self-supervised pretraining paradigm uses only RGB images, leaving readily available complementary signals, such as depth maps, unused. This is a particular missed opportunity in surgery, where natural-image VFMs transfer poorly while the scene geometry is rich and informative. With strong off-the-shelf models now able to produce pseudo-labeled dense depth for any image corpus, we hypothesize that such signals can be folded into pretraining to learn better representations. We present DART, an RGB-D pretraining recipe that builds on DINOv2 with a simple modification: a pixel-space depth reconstruction objective applied to masked iBOT patches, supervised by pseudo-labeled depth. Depth is used only during pretraining, so fine-tuning and inference remain RGB-only. We find that this pixel-level reconstruction head improves representation quality rather than disrupting it. We further show that depth, which encodes scene geometry, is more effective as a target than alternative dense signals such as Canny edges, confirming that the gains stem from depth rather than added supervision alone. Across eight surgical benchmarks spanning segmentation, depth estimation, and image-level recognition, DART outperforms both natural-image and in-domain baselines, including a vanilla DINOv2 trained on identical data, improving dense prediction while also strengthening image-level understanding. More broadly, DART shows that freely available geometric pseudo-labels can strengthen foundation model pretraining without extra labels or added inference cost, pointing toward stronger backbones for surgery.

AI.tldr: DART is an RGB-D pretraining method for vision foundation models that incorporates pseudo-labeled depth maps into masked image modeling (iBOT) on top of DINOv2. It uses a pixel-space depth reconstruction objective during pretraining only, keeping fine-tuning and inference RGB-only. The method outperforms both natural-image and in-domain baselines across eight surgical benchmarks for segmentation, depth estimation, and image-level recognition tasks.
AI.motivation: In data-scarce domains like surgery, self-supervised pretraining typically uses only RGB images, ignoring complementary signals like depth maps. While natural-image VFMs transfer poorly to surgery, the rich scene geometry in surgical images provides valuable information. With strong off-the-shelf models now generating pseudo-labeled dense depth, the authors hypothesize that incorporating depth signals can improve representation learning.
AI.method: DART extends DINOv2 with a pixel-space depth reconstruction objective applied to masked iBOT patches. The method uses pseudo-labeled depth (generated by off-the-shelf models) as supervision. Depth is used only during pretraining; fine-tuning and inference remain RGB-only. The approach was evaluated against alternatives like Canny edges to confirm gains stem specifically from depth information.
AI.result: DART outperforms both natural-image and in-domain baselines across eight surgical benchmarks spanning segmentation, depth estimation, and image-level recognition. It improves dense prediction while also strengthening image-level understanding compared to vanilla DINOv2 trained on identical data. Depth (scene geometry) proves more effective as a target than alternative dense signals like Canny edges.
AI.conclusion: Freely available geometric pseudo-labels can strengthen foundation model pretraining without extra labels or added inference cost. This points toward developing stronger backbones for surgery and similar domains where depth information is available but underutilized.

title: What Does Multi-Harness RL Learn? Credit Assignment and Portability in Coding Agents
summary: Agent reinforcement learning (RL) increasingly runs through full execution harnesses, and a multi-harness recipe mixes two choices: exposing the policy to several harnesses, and comparing their rewards inside one relative-advantage group. We isolate the second choice in repository-level coding. From one Qwen3-8B supervised warm start we replay the same frozen task-harness records from Aider, OpenHands, Qwen Code, and SWE-agent, with the same number of updates, under two rules for group-relative policy optimization (GRPO), Within (one group per task-harness pair) and Cross (harnesses pooled within a task), and score every checkpoint with a sealed SWE-bench Verified oracle on four source harnesses and a minimal harness held out of training. The evaluation harness is the dominant variable: across 24,000 sealed evaluations it moves the mean solve rate from 2.14\% to 9.27\%, a factor of 4.3, where the training recipe moves it by 1.16. The grouping rule is not. On the held-out harness, Cross minus Within is +0.25 pp, 95\% confidence interval [-0.48, +1.02], at eight attempts per task, and +0.16 [-0.41, +0.72] pooled over three training seeds whose individual estimates change sign. Each rule's own seed range, 0.42 to 0.45 pp, exceeds the difference between them. Both rules place their largest gains on the same source harness. The pooled advantage carries the harness: an out-of-fold classifier recovers the generating harness from Cross's advantage +4.48 pp above the shuffled-label baseline and from Within's not at all, and the two rules still reach the same held-out score and action distribution inside each harness. Re-collecting half the training data on-policy does not change this. Cross-harness credit yields configuration adaptation and no more portable capability than within-harness credit. Multi-harness RL reports should state the grouping boundary and test under an unseen harness.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether grouping harnesses differently (Within vs Cross) during multi-harness reinforcement learning affects software engineering agent performance. Using Qwen3-8B on SWE-bench Verified, they find the evaluation harness is the dominant variable (4.3x impact), while the grouping rule has negligible effect. Cross-harness credit yields no more portable capability than within-harness credit.
AI.motivation: Multi-harness RL is becoming common for training software engineering agents, but it's unclear how to group different evaluation harnesses during training. The authors wanted to isolate whether comparing rewards across harnesses (Cross) versus within each harness (Within) affects generalization to unseen harnesses.
AI.method: They used Qwen3-8B as a supervised warm start, replayed frozen task-harness records from 4 different agents (Aider, OpenHands, Qwen Code, SWE-agent), and trained with GRPO under two grouping rules. They evaluated 24,000 checkpoints using a sealed SWE-bench Verified oracle across 4 source harnesses and 1 held-out harness.
AI.result: The evaluation harness is the dominant variable (2.14% to 9.27% solve rate, 4.3x factor), while the grouping rule has minimal effect. On the held-out harness, Cross minus Within is +0.25 pp with 95% CI [-0.48, +1.02]. The difference between grouping rules is smaller than the variance across training seeds (0.42-0.45 pp). An out-of-fold classifier can recover the generating harness from Cross's advantage but not from Within's.
AI.conclusion: The grouping rule (Within vs Cross) does not significantly affect held-out performance. Cross-harness credit yields configuration adaptation but no more portable capability than within-harness credit. The authors recommend that multi-harness RL papers should state the grouping boundary and test under an unseen harness.

title: Nested Inductive Bias Framework for SPD Manifold Learning
summary: In Geometric Deep Learning, inductive biases serve two primary functions: enforcing manifold constraints and embedding relational priors. Currently, representation learning on SPD manifolds frequently relies on pullback Euclidean metrics, such as the Log-Euclidean Metric, to satisfy the former. While computationally efficient in avoiding domain boundary violations, these metrics induce a flat geometry that may fail to capture the intrinsic relational priors of datasets. While metrics such as the Poincaré metric are widely utilized to induce domain-aligned relational priors, generalizing them from standard vector representations to the SPD manifold has remained a challenge. To bridge this gap, we introduce a Nested Inductive Bias framework that utilizes a two-stage diffeomorphic composition to formally pull back non-Euclidean target geometries onto the SPD manifold. This framework enables the construction of curvature-aligned Riemannian classifiers that simultaneously respect matrix constraints and the latent relational geometry of the data. Empirical evaluations on kinematic and signal processing benchmarks, together with synthetic experiments, demonstrate that deep manifold networks experience degradation in class separability unless the metric curvature aligns with the intrinsic data distribution. Furthermore, for standard vectorized architectures, we propose the Rational Conformal Metric (RCM), designed to establish state-of-the-art geometric robustness against outliers by bounding the representation space.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses representation learning on SPD (Symmetric Positive Definite) manifolds in Geometric Deep Learning. The authors propose a Nested Inductive Bias framework that uses two-stage diffeomorphic composition to pull back non-Euclidean geometries (like Poincaré metric) onto SPD manifolds, enabling curvature-aligned Riemannian classifiers. They also introduce Rational Conformal Metric (RCM) for standard vectorized architectures to achieve geometric robustness against outliers.
AI.motivation: Current SPD manifold representation learning relies on pullback Euclidean metrics (e.g., Log-Euclidean Metric) which are computationally efficient but induce flat geometry that fails to capture intrinsic relational priors of datasets. While Poincaré metric can induce domain-aligned relational priors, generalizing it from vector representations to SPD manifolds has remained challenging.
AI.method: The authors propose a Nested Inductive Bias framework using two-stage diffeomorphic composition to formally pull back non-Euclidean target geometries onto the SPD manifold. For standard vectorized architectures, they propose the Rational Conformal Metric (RCM) designed to establish geometric robustness against outliers by bounding the representation space.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations on kinematic and signal processing benchmarks, together with synthetic experiments, demonstrate that deep manifold networks experience degradation in class separability unless the metric curvature aligns with the intrinsic data distribution. RCM achieves state-of-the-art geometric robustness against outliers.
AI.conclusion: The Nested Inductive Bias framework successfully enables the construction of curvature-aligned Riemannian classifiers that simultaneously respect matrix constraints and the latent relational geometry of data. The proposed RCM provides effective geometric robustness for standard vectorized architectures.

title: Physics-Direct FPGA Tooth-Contact Computation for Deterministic Gear Digital Twins
summary: Gear digital twins, hardware-in-the-loop rigs, and active vibration control close a loop around the instantaneous tooth-contact state, demanding a solver that is real-time, deterministic, and embeddable -- properties that loaded tooth contact analysis (LTCA), a data-dependent linear complementarity problem (LCP) costing seconds per mesh phase in fp64, structurally lacks; learned surrogates infer fast but spend one full LTCA solve per training sample and offer no guarantee beyond their training envelope. We instead compress the closed-form contact physics -- contact-point localization, principal-curvature extraction, and the elliptical Hertz solution -- directly into a branch-free fixed-point FPGA datapath, termed physics-direct, realized through the fully open-source openXC7 flow (no vendor tools, no floating-point IP) and validated on retired XC7K480T silicon. Four SoCs -- geometry, Hertz, and two fused paths -- pass bit-exact JTAG readback against a golden model. The on-chip preview tracks LCP body pressure to within -22% and loaded transmission error (LTE) peak-to-peak to -19%, preserving the exact $W^{1/3}$ law; with zero training it extrapolates in load more accurately than a trained network (18.9% versus 20.3%). Latency is a compile-time constant ($σ= 0$ jitter), and the DSP-bound geometry kernel saturates the fabric near 63 lanes. Physics-direct is an interpretable, deterministic alternative to neural surrogacy for embedded tooth-contact estimation.

title: Dual-Part Multi-Lateral Branched Network for Multi-Class Segmentation in Cardiovascular Catheterization Angiograms
summary: Catheterisation image processing requires segmentation models that are fast, accurate and explainable. While most of the existing studies usually focus on binary segmentation, there is a recent demand for simultaneous segmentation of multiple structures found in catheterization scenes. In this study, a dual-part MLBNet architecture is designed with multi-lateral encoder blocks and multi-head decoder branches for class-aware segmentation in cardiovascular catheterization scenes. Lateral branches in the encoder enables repeated feature extraction to learn diverse shared representations, while multiple decoder heads are used to introduce class-skewed branches that specialize in different structural properties in catheterization scenes. To analyze the performances of the dual-part MLBNet architecture, several multi-class segmentation angiogram data obtained during cardiovascular catheterization in phantom models, synthetic human-simulated aorta, and animal model are used for model training and evaluation. Results obtained showed the dual-part models could effectively separate guidewire, catheter, vessels and background pixels to their classes of memberships with high probability. The results demonstrate that all models were able to distinguish the dominant background class from foreground structures with high overall accuracy.

AI.tldr: MLBNet is a dual-part deep learning architecture for multi-class segmentation in cardiovascular catheterization images, combining multi-lateral encoder blocks with multi-head decoder branches to simultaneously segment guidewire, catheter, vessels, and background.
AI.motivation: Current catheterisation image processing lacks fast, accurate, and explainable segmentation models. Existing studies focus on binary segmentation, but there is a growing need for simultaneous segmentation of multiple structures in catheterization scenes.
AI.method: Dual-part MLBNet architecture with: (1) Multi-lateral encoder blocks enabling repeated feature extraction for diverse shared representations; (2) Multi-head decoder branches introducing class-skewed branches that specialize in different structural properties. Training and evaluation performed on multi-class segmentation angiogram data from phantom models, synthetic human-simulated aorta, and animal models.
AI.result: The dual-part models effectively separated guidewire, catheter, vessels, and background pixels into their respective classes with high probability. All models achieved high overall accuracy in distinguishing the dominant background class from foreground structures.
AI.conclusion: The MLBNet architecture demonstrates promising performance for multi-class semantic segmentation in cardiovascular catheterization, successfully handling multiple structures simultaneously with high accuracy.

title: MaxKernel: Agentic Kernel Generation for TPUs
summary: Designing and authoring high-performance custom kernels for accelerators is a complex task that requires deep hardware-level expertise. Large Language Models (LLM) can be leveraged together with real-time compiler feedback to build agentic systems for kernel generation. In this work, we present MaxKernel, a multi-agent system that implements three distinct paradigms for TPU kernel development: (1) a Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) agent for collaborative, step-by-step design; (2) an Autonomous (Auto) agent that executes a fully automated, metric/trace-driven optimization loop; and (3) a Graph-Based Autonomous Search that scales the Auto agent for global exploration of the design space. All three paradigms leverage a shared pool of specialized sub-agents to handle planning, implementation, self-debugging, testing, and hardware profiling. We evaluate MaxKernel on JaxBench, a comprehensive suite of 50 diverse kernel tasks for TPUs, alongside complex, real-world workloads from state-of-the-art open-source models. We demonstrate that MaxKernel consistently generates highly optimized implementations, matching expert hand-tuned baselines and delivering significant performance across the benchmark. Our agent is open-sourced and available https://github.com/AI-Hypercomputer/accelerator-agents/tree/main/MaxKernel.

AI.tldr: MaxKernel is a multi-agent system that leverages Large Language Models with real-time compiler feedback to generate high-performance TPU kernels. It implements three paradigms: Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) for collaborative design, Autonomous (Auto) for automated metric/trace-driven optimization, and Graph-Based Autonomous Search for scalable global design space exploration.
AI.motivation: Designing and authoring high-performance custom kernels for accelerators (like TPUs) requires deep hardware-level expertise, which is a significant barrier. This work aims to leverage LLMs together with compiler feedback to automate and simplify the kernel generation process.
AI.method: MaxKernel uses a shared pool of specialized sub-agents for planning, implementation, self-debugging, testing, and hardware profiling. It implements three paradigms: (1) Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) for collaborative step-by-step design; (2) Autonomous (Auto) agent for fully automated metric/trace-driven optimization; (3) Graph-Based Autonomous Search that scales the Auto agent for global design space exploration. Evaluation was performed on JaxBench (50 diverse TPU kernel tasks) and real-world workloads from state-of-the-art open-source models.
AI.result: MaxKernel consistently generates highly optimized implementations that match expert hand-tuned baselines and deliver significant performance improvements across the benchmark. The system is open-sourced.
AI.conclusion: MaxKernel demonstrates that LLM-based multi-agent systems can effectively automate TPU kernel generation, achieving performance comparable to expert hand-tuned implementations. The approach successfully combines human collaboration with automated optimization and scalable graph-based exploration.

title: Hakken: Predicting future discoveries to fill the gaps in today's knowledge
summary: We present Hakken, a domain-agnostic prediction and explanation system performing knowledge prediction, i.e., growing scientific knowledge by establishing novel relationships, ones that are not limited to the deductive hull of previous knowledge. Hakken uses a transformer-based prediction model built on temporal sequences of knowledge graphs extracted from vast bodies of research publications, fused with an LLM's semantic knowledge, to predict the presence and define the type of as-yet undocumented relationships between scientific concepts. It then calls a model-agnostic explanation framework to provide accompanying information for each prediction that allows scientists to evaluate the suggested new relationship. While general purpose, we demonstrate Hakken's practical capabilities by applying it to the biomedical domain. There, Hakken's prediction model establishes a new benchmark for time-aware multi-label relation prediction, and we show that the model's output stays coherent and informative over extended time spans in historic data. In addition, we scored 1.5 million above-confidence-threshold hypotheses related to aging, qualitatively validated batches of these predictions with biologists and progressed three of them for empirical validation in wet-lab. Two predictions with potentially significant impact in the context of drug discovery and repurposing were confirmed, introducing previously undocumented interactions between TP53 and BAMBI, and between RAF1 and TNF, to biomedical science.

AI.tldr: Hakken is a domain-agnostic prediction and explanation system that uses transformer-based models on temporal knowledge graphs combined with LLM semantic knowledge to predict novel scientific relationships beyond existing knowledge, demonstrated in the biomedical domain with experimentally validated predictions.
AI.motivation: Growing scientific knowledge by establishing novel relationships that are not limited to the deductive hull of previous knowledge - predicting as-yet undocumented relationships between scientific concepts.
AI.method: Transformer-based prediction model built on temporal sequences of knowledge graphs extracted from research publications, fused with LLM's semantic knowledge, combined with a model-agnostic explanation framework to provide accompanying information for each prediction.
AI.result: Establishes new benchmark for time-aware multi-label relation prediction in biomedical domain; scored 1.5 million above-confidence-threshold hypotheses related to aging; qualitatively validated predictions with biologists; progressed 3 predictions for empirical wet-lab validation; confirmed two previously undocumented interactions: TP53-BAMBI and RAF1-TNF (relevant to drug discovery and repurposing).
AI.conclusion: Hakken demonstrates practical capabilities for knowledge prediction and discovery, successfully predicting and experimentally validating novel scientific relationships that contribute to biomedical knowledge.

title: Sound-based Multi-Person 3D Pose Estimation
comment: Accepted at ECCV 2026, Project Page: https://oumi03.github.io/sound-mhpe/
summary: Can we recover the 3D poses of multiple people using only sound? This paper presents the first attempt to estimate multi-person 3D poses solely from acoustic signals. Estimating the poses of multiple individuals using acoustic signals is inherently challenging due to the superposition of motion-dependent signal variations. Unlike single-person scenarios, the presence of multiple subjects leads to overlapping acoustic signatures, making it difficult to attribute specific signal changes to an individual's pose. Furthermore, the complexity is compounded by inter-person reflections, which introduce intricate propagation delays that obscure the temporal motion-acoustic relationship. To address these issues, we propose SoundMHPE (Sound-based Multi-person Human Pose Estimator), a novel encoder-decoder framework consisting of two key components. First, the Acoustic Multi-scale Encoder captures diverse temporal and fine-grained frequency features to isolate subtle acoustic signatures from complex, overlapping signals. Second, the Temporal Pose Decoder employs an attention mechanism to disentangle multi-person information across successive frames. By jointly accounting for temporal dynamics and inter-person dependencies, this component precisely reconstructs frame-wise individual poses. To validate our approach, we constructed the 6-hour Acoustic Multi-person Pose (AMP) dataset consisting of 432K synchronized frames of multi-person pose and acoustic data, and demonstrated that our SoundMHPE outperforms baseline models. Project page: https://oumi03.github.io/sound-mhpe/

AI.tldr: This paper presents SoundMHPE, the first framework to estimate multi-person 3D poses from acoustic signals alone. It addresses the challenge of overlapping acoustic signatures from multiple individuals and inter-person reflections that obscure motion-acoustic relationships.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to explore whether 3D poses of multiple people can be recovered using only sound, which is inherently challenging due to signal superposition from multiple subjects, overlapping acoustic signatures, and inter-person reflections causing propagation delays that obscure temporal motion-acoustic relationships.
AI.method: SoundMHPE uses an encoder-decoder framework with two key components: (1) Acoustic Multi-scale Encoder to capture diverse temporal and fine-grained frequency features from complex overlapping signals; (2) Temporal Pose Decoder with attention mechanism to disentangle multi-person information across successive frames, accounting for temporal dynamics and inter-person dependencies.
AI.result: The approach was validated on the AMP dataset (6 hours, 432K synchronized frames of multi-person pose and acoustic data), demonstrating that SoundMHPE outperforms baseline models.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes the feasibility of multi-person 3D pose estimation from acoustic signals alone, opening new research directions in acoustic-based perception.

title: Reviewer Capability Governs Rejection Targeting, Not Repair Skill: Evidence from LLM Execute-Review-Revise Pipelines
summary:
Multi-agent LLM pipelines increasingly assign roles, including execution and verification, to models of different capability tiers. This is done because running a flagship model at every stage is expensive. Previous literature has established that verification stages are not always beneficial, but holds reviewer capability roughly fixed relative to the executor. We vary it. We replace the reviewer with models spanning a capability range down to one that cannot solve the problems at all, and measure the outcome of every individual rejection. This is done across a constant set of 100 olympiad mathematics problems.
  A cross-family mid-tier reviewer improves final accuracy by 12 percentage points, from 52 to 64 percent (p = 0.0005), with zero damaged answers. Same-model self-review attains the highest error-detection rate of any condition (0.85 recall) yet yields no significant gain: it rejects 2.1 times as often for a third the repair rate (15 against 43 percent, p = 0.0074) and falsely rejects 35 percent of its own correct answers against 2 percent for the cross-family reviewer (paired p = 0.000015). The low damage rate of self-review proves to be an artifact of revision inertia rather than reviewer quality: of 18 falsely rejected correct answers, the three where the executor complied all became wrong, while the fifteen it ignored survived unchanged. Below a capability floor the role becomes inert: our weakest reviewer changed zero of 100 final answers while doubling token cost. These findings describe a single executor-reviewer configuration on 100 problems and should be read as a controlled pilot rather than a general claim about verification stages.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the effectiveness of different capability reviewers in multi-agent LLM pipelines for solving olympiad mathematics problems. The study finds that a cross-family mid-tier reviewer improves accuracy by 12 percentage points (52% to 64%), while same-model self-review, despite having the highest error-detection rate (0.85 recall), provides no significant gain due to excessive false rejections. The weakest reviewer tested proved inert, changing zero answers while doubling token cost.
AI.motivation: Previous literature established that verification stages are not always beneficial in multi-agent LLM pipelines, but held reviewer capability fixed relative to the executor. This study aims to fill that gap by varying reviewer capability across a range, including models that cannot solve the problems at all, to understand when and how verification stages add value.
AI.method: The researchers tested a single executor-reviewer configuration across 100 olympiad mathematics problems. They replaced the reviewer with models spanning a capability range—from flagship models down to one that cannot solve the problems at all—and measured the outcome of every individual rejection. They compared cross-family mid-tier review, same-model self-review, and weak reviewer conditions.
AI.result: A cross-family mid-tier reviewer improved final accuracy by 12 percentage points (from 52% to 64%, p=0.0005) with zero damaged answers. Same-model self-review achieved the highest error-detection rate (0.85 recall) but yielded no significant gain: it rejected 2.1 times as often for only a 15% repair rate versus 43% for cross-family review (p=0.0074). Self-review falsely rejected 35% of its own correct answers versus 2% for cross-family reviewer (paired p=0.000015). Of 18 falsely rejected correct answers, the 3 where the executor complied all became wrong, while the 15 ignored survived unchanged. The weakest reviewer changed zero of 100 final answers while doubling token cost.
AI.conclusion: Self-review's low damage rate is an artifact of revision inertia rather than reviewer quality—when executors comply with false rejections, answers become wrong. Below a capability floor, the reviewer role becomes inert. The authors note these findings describe a single executor-reviewer configuration on 100 problems and should be read as a controlled pilot rather than a general claim about verification stages.

title: Hidden In Plain Gaze: Gaze Representations as Privacy Controls for Utility and Re-identification Risk in XR
summary: Intelligent extended reality (XR) systems increasingly use eye and head tracking to infer user intent, task, and attention, but the same signals can also reveal biometric identity. We study whether gaze data representation choice can serve as a lightweight privacy control at feature extraction, before adding perturbation or formal privacy mechanisms. Using the egocentric HoloAssist dataset, we compare three gaze representations under matched model capacity: raw gaze, spatial attention heatmaps, and engineered eye-movement features. We evaluate each representation on action recognition as task utility and closed-set user re-identification as privacy leakage. Representation choice substantially changes the privacy-utility tradeoff. Engineered features retain roughly 85% of raw gaze's action-recognition accuracy while reducing re-identification by about an order of magnitude, to roughly four times the chance rate across 206 identities. This reduction attenuates rather than eliminates identity leakage, and the differences across representations show that abstraction alone does not guarantee privacy. Engineered features expose interpretable and auditable structure, giving designers a transparent privacy lever that complements mechanisms such as differential privacy.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether different gaze data representations can serve as a lightweight privacy control in intelligent XR systems, comparing raw gaze, spatial attention heatmaps, and engineered eye-movement features for their privacy-utility tradeoff using the HoloAssist dataset.
AI.motivation: Eye and head tracking in XR systems can reveal user identity (biometric) while also inferring user intent and attention. The study explores if representation choice at feature extraction can provide privacy before adding perturbation or formal privacy mechanisms.
AI.method: Using the egocentric HoloAssist dataset, three gaze representations (raw gaze, spatial attention heatmaps, engineered eye-movement features) were compared under matched model capacity. Each was evaluated on action recognition (task utility) and closed-set user re-identification (privacy leakage).
AI.result: Representation choice substantially changes the privacy-utility tradeoff. Engineered features retain ~85% of raw gaze's action-recognition accuracy while reducing re-identification by about an order of magnitude (to ~4x chance rate across 206 identities).
AI.conclusion: Abstraction alone does not guarantee privacy; engineered features reduce but don't eliminate identity leakage. This approach provides a transparent, auditable privacy lever that complements mechanisms like differential privacy.

title: Towards a universal language of concepts: A survey
comment: Originally completed as an M.S. capstone project at UCLA in 2022
summary: Humans can learn and generalize novel concepts from sparse data because they express knowledge in rich structural formats. In this paper, we propose that programs are a strong candidate for universal representation of concepts. We review computational models of concept learning that use programs as their concept representation and evaluate their contribution toward a universal representational language.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes programs as a universal representation for concepts, arguing that their rich structural format enables humans to learn and generalize from sparse data. The authors review computational models of concept learning that use programs as their concept representation and evaluate their contribution toward developing a universal representational language.
AI.motivation: Humans can learn and generalize novel concepts from sparse data because they express knowledge in rich structural formats. This paper investigates programs as a strong candidate for universal representation of concepts, addressing the need for a representational language that can capture the expressive power of human knowledge.
AI.method: The paper employs a review methodology, examining computational models of concept learning that utilize programs as their concept representation. It evaluates these models against criteria for universal representation.
AI.result: The paper evaluates the contribution of program-based computational models toward establishing a universal representational language, though specific findings are not detailed in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The abstract suggests that program-based representations show promise as a universal concept representation, though the full conclusion requires access to the complete paper.

title: An Energy-Based Conservative-Dissipative Latent Neural Evolution Operator for Magnetization Dynamics
summary: We develop an energy-based reduced-order model for micromagnetic magnetization dynamics that couples a convolutional autoencoder to a structured latent neural ordinary differential equation. Motivated by the precessional-dissipative structure of the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation, the latent vector field is generated from the gradient of a learned scalar potential through an antisymmetric operator and a symmetric positive-semidefinite dissipative operator. This potential is learned in nonunique latent coordinates and is not identified with the Gibbs free energy, but decreases monotonically along autonomous continuous-time solutions, while the antisymmetric component permits motion along its level sets. The encoder, decoder, latent energy, and operators are trained jointly on short trajectory windows using latent and decoded-rollout losses alone, without time-derivative supervision, physical-energy labels, or dissipation penalties. At inference, an initial state is encoded once, evolved in latent space, and decoded only at the requested output times, enabling substantially cheaper trajectory prediction than the micromagnetic solver used to generate the training data. We compare quadratic, deep, and additive deep-quadratic latent energies on two datasets parameterized by field amplitude and generated for the two applied-field directions of the NIST $μ$MAG Standard Problem 4. Dissipative-only and antisymmetric-dissipative models achieve comparable accuracy on short training-style windows but differ substantially on uninterrupted rollouts, for which the antisymmetric-dissipative models provide markedly more accurate trajectory predictions. The deep-quadratic energy gives the best overall accuracy for both field directions and exhibits slower error growth when rollouts are extended to twice the training horizon.

AI.tldr: This paper develops an energy-based reduced-order model for micromagnetic magnetization dynamics using a convolutional autoencoder coupled with a structured latent neural ODE. The model learns a scalar potential in latent space with antisymmetric (precessional) and symmetric positive-semidefinite (dissipative) operators, trained via latent and decoded-rollout losses without physical supervision.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to create a computationally efficient reduced-order model for micromagnetic magnetization dynamics that captures the precessional-dissipative structure of the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation while being substantially cheaper than full micromagnetic solvers at inference time.
AI.method: The method combines a convolutional autoencoder with a structured latent neural ODE. The latent vector field is generated from the gradient of a learned scalar potential through an antisymmetric operator and a symmetric positive-semidefinite dissipative operator. The model is trained jointly on short trajectory windows using latent and decoded-rollout losses alone, without time-derivative supervision, physical-energy labels, or dissipation penalties. Three latent energy architectures are compared: quadratic, deep, and additive deep-quadratic.
AI.result: The antisymmetric-dissipative models provide markedly more accurate trajectory predictions on uninterrupted rollouts compared to dissipative-only models. The deep-quadratic energy gives the best overall accuracy for both field directions in NIST μMAG Standard Problem 4 and exhibits slower error growth when rollouts are extended to twice the training horizon.
AI.conclusion: The proposed energy-based reduced-order model successfully captures micromagnetic dynamics with significantly reduced computational cost compared to full micromagnetic solvers. The inclusion of both antisymmetric and dissipative components is essential for accurate long-horizon predictions, with the deep-quadratic energy architecture providing the best performance.

title: Integrating Crash Report Mining and LLMs for Bug Localization and Repair: An Industrial Report
summary: Analyzing crash-report bugs in large-scale industrial software systems requires substantial maintenance effort, particularly in production environments where developers must handle large volumes of crash reports and source code artifacts to localize and fix their root causes. While recent studies have shown that Large Language Models (LLMs) can assist with maintenance tasks, little is known about their effectiveness in supporting developers in analyzing crash-report bugs and repairing bugs associated with groups of crash reports in industrial settings. To address this gap, we investigate whether integrating crash report mining techniques---specifically stack trace clustering and suspicious file and method ranking---with LLMs can support crash localization and repair in production environments. We conduct a retrospective evaluation of five LLMs under four prompt configurations. After that, we chose the best model to run on 38 crash bugs collected from two large Java enterprise systems. We further analyze the structural characteristics and explanatory patterns of LLM-generated responses and assess localization and repair effectiveness through manual validation. Our results show that the best-performing configuration localizes up to 71% and correctly repairs 52% of crash bugs on the full dataset. These findings provide empirical evidence that combining crash report mining with LLM-based repair can effectively support debugging activities in industrial maintenance workflows.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the integration of crash report mining techniques (stack trace clustering, suspicious file/method ranking) with Large Language Models (LLMs) to support crash localization and repair in large-scale industrial Java systems. The study evaluates five LLMs under four prompt configurations on 38 crash bugs from two Java enterprise systems, achieving up to 71% localization accuracy and 52% correct repair rate.
AI.motivation: Crash-report bug analysis in large-scale industrial software systems requires substantial maintenance effort. Developers must handle large volumes of crash reports and source code artifacts to localize and fix root causes. While LLMs have shown promise in maintenance tasks, their effectiveness for crash-report bug analysis and repair in industrial settings remains underexplored.
AI.method: The researchers conducted a retrospective evaluation of five LLMs under four prompt configurations. They selected the best-performing model and evaluated it on 38 crash bugs collected from two large Java enterprise systems. They analyzed the structural characteristics and explanatory patterns of LLM-generated responses and assessed localization and repair effectiveness through manual validation.
AI.result: The best-performing configuration achieved up to 71% crash localization accuracy and correctly repaired 52% of crash bugs on the full dataset.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide empirical evidence that combining crash report mining with LLM-based repair can effectively support debugging activities in industrial maintenance workflows. This approach offers a promising solution for reducing maintenance effort in production environments.

title: An Evaluation Framework for Generating Multi-View Images of a Person in a Scene
summary: Recent generative image-editing Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) demonstrate impressive semantic editing capabilities but still struggle with spatially consistent camera angle changes. A primary bottleneck in training foundation models to execute free-form, promptable camera angle changes is the lack of specialized training data. While multi-view datasets exist for generic 3D environments and objects, there remains an absence of paired, multi-view datasets featuring human subjects at fixed locations in natural scenes, including frontal and side-profile views. Capturing such multi-camera data in unconstrained environments is logistically challenging and unscalable. In this paper, we first experiment with multiple state-of-the-art image editing models to create this data synthetically, but find that the outputs are frequently prone to hallucinations involving how much the subject's head turns relative to the background, often producing inconsistent environments. To address this issue, we propose the Head Scene Rotation Difference (HSRD) metric to quantitatively evaluate camera movements around a person. The proposed metric operates by decoupling camera movement from localized head pose manipulation. As demonstrated by the extensive experimentation, HSRD provides the pipeline necessary to evaluate 3D spatial parallax for a person in a scene, paving the way to reliably construct high-quality multi-view synthetic datasets.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the lack of training data for Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) to perform free-form, promptable camera angle changes around human subjects. The authors propose a Head Scene Rotation Difference (HSRD) metric to evaluate camera movements by decoupling camera movement from head pose, enabling reliable construction of synthetic multi-view datasets.
AI.motivation: Current generative image-editing Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) struggle with spatially consistent camera angle changes. The primary bottleneck is the lack of specialized training data - specifically paired, multi-view datasets featuring human subjects at fixed locations in natural scenes (including frontal and side-profile views). Existing multi-view datasets cover generic 3D environments/objects but not human subjects in this manner.
AI.method: The authors first experimented with multiple state-of-the-art image editing models to create synthetic multi-view data. However, outputs suffered from hallucinations regarding head turning relative to background and inconsistent environments. To address evaluation challenges, they proposed the Head Scene Rotation Difference (HSRD) metric, which operates by decoupling camera movement from localized head pose manipulation.
AI.result: The proposed HSRD metric provides the pipeline necessary to evaluate 3D spatial parallax for a person in a scene. This enables reliable construction of high-quality multi-view synthetic datasets for training foundation models on camera angle changes.
AI.conclusion: The HSRD metric addresses a critical evaluation gap in synthesizing multi-view human datasets, paving the way for training DiTs to execute free-form, promptable camera angle changes around human subjects in natural scenes.

title: Data-Driven Discovery of Composition-Dependent Constitutive Models for Hyperelasticity and Viscoelasticity of Digital Materials
comment: 40 pages including references, 9 figures in the main manuscript. Supplementary material is available upon request from the corresponding author
summary: Digital materials fabricated by multi-material 3D printing are designed as controlled mixtures of stiff and compliant constituents, yielding effective responses that span more than an order of magnitude in apparent stiffness and exhibit strongly nonlinear, composition-dependent, and rate-dependent dissipative behavior. Classical finite-strain viscoelastic models represent such behavior with closed-form strain energy functions for equilibrium and non-equilibrium stresses as well as evolution of internal variables, which may limit flexibility when a single constitutive model is expected to generalize across materials and loading rates. Here, we present a data-driven multi-material constitutive modeling framework that generalizes a formulation by Bergström and Boyce. The proposed framework retains the structure of the classical model, namely multiplicative kinematics, invariant-based strain-energy functions, and a scalar dissipative evolution law directed along the normalized nonequilibrium deviatoric stress. For the equilibrium branch, the data-driven discovery framework either directly predicts closed-form model parameters as functions of composition or automatically constructs a polyconvex strain-energy function using neural ordinary differential equations (NODEs). The nonequilibrium branch kinetics are learned similarly, either by directly identifying closed-form parameters across compositions or by using appropriately constrained artificial neural networks. Using multi-rate uniaxial compression data across multiple material compositions, we show that the proposed formulation captures rate-dependent stiffness and hysteresis across compositions while preserving thermodynamic consistency.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a data-driven multi-material constitutive modeling framework for digital materials fabricated by multi-material 3D printing. The framework generalizes Bergström and Boyce's classical viscoelastic model by using neural ordinary differential equations (NODEs) to automatically construct polyconvex strain-energy functions and learn nonequilibrium branch kinetics, enabling prediction of rate-dependent stiffness and hysteresis across different material compositions while maintaining thermodynamic consistency.
AI.motivation: Classical finite-strain viscoelastic models with closed-form strain energy functions may lack flexibility when a single constitutive model needs to generalize across different materials and loading rates. The goal is to develop a more adaptable framework that can capture the complex behavior of digital materials spanning more than an order of magnitude in apparent stiffness with strongly nonlinear, composition-dependent, and rate-dependent dissipative behavior.
AI.method: The proposed framework retains the structure of the classical Bergström-Boyce model (multiplicative kinematics, invariant-based strain-energy functions, and scalar dissipative evolution law). For the equilibrium branch, the data-driven discovery framework either directly predicts closed-form model parameters as functions of composition or automatically constructs a polyconvex strain-energy function using neural ordinary differential equations (NODEs). The nonequilibrium branch kinetics are learned similarly, either by directly identifying closed-form parameters across compositions or by using appropriately constrained artificial neural networks. Validation is performed using multi-rate uniaxial compression data across multiple material compositions.
AI.result: The proposed formulation captures rate-dependent stiffness and hysteresis across compositions while preserving thermodynamic consistency.
AI.conclusion: The data-driven multi-material constitutive modeling framework successfully generalizes the classical Bergström-Boyce model by incorporating neural network-based approaches (NODEs), enabling accurate prediction of complex material behavior across different compositions and loading rates while maintaining thermodynamic consistency.

title: Distilled Continuous Diffusion Language Models Can Write Code in Few Steps---or One
summary: Language generation is almost universally treated as a sequential process: autoregressive models emit one token at a time, while diffusion language models replace token-level seriality with a long trajectory of iterative refinement. In this work, we introduce PlaidQ, a 0.7B continuous diffusion language model for code generation, and show that its trajectory can be aggressively distilled into only a few denoising steps---or even one, enabling efficient code generation. PlaidQ repurposes a pretrained autoregressive model as a bidirectional denoiser over continuous token embeddings. We distill PlaidQ with distribution matching for few-step generation and paired-trajectory supervision for one-step generation. At matched model scale, PlaidQ is competitive with discrete diffusion language models on code generation. Distillation then shifts the quality--compute frontier: a 16-step student reaches 31.78 and 40.49 pass@10 on HumanEval and MBPP+, surpassing the same PlaidQ teacher sampled for 512 steps. At the extreme, paired-trajectory distillation achieves 7.07 pass@1 on HumanEval with a single denoising step, producing functionally correct programs. Together, these results establish continuous diffusion as a viable path to few-step and one-step code generation. Broadly, continuous diffusion is not merely another representation for language: it provides an interface through which language models can inherit the acceleration and distillation machinery of continuous diffusion modeling. Training and inference code and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/pengzhangzhi/plaidq.

AI.tldr: PlaidQ is a 0.7B continuous diffusion language model for code generation that can be distilled into very few denoising steps (even one), achieving competitive performance with significantly reduced computational cost.
AI.motivation: Language generation is typically sequential (autoregressive) or requires many iterative refinement steps (diffusion). The goal is to enable efficient few-step or one-step code generation while maintaining quality.
