AI.method: PlaidQ repurposes a pretrained autoregressive model as a bidirectional denoiser over continuous token embeddings. It uses two distillation techniques: (1) distribution matching for few-step generation, and (2) paired-trajectory supervision for one-step generation.
AI.result: A 16-step distilled student achieves 31.78 pass@1 on HumanEval and 40.49 pass@10 on MBPP+, surpassing the same teacher sampled for 512 steps. With a single denoising step, paired-trajectory distillation achieves 7.07 pass@1 on HumanEval.
AI.conclusion: Continuous diffusion is a viable path to few-step and one-step code generation, providing an interface through which language models can inherit the acceleration and distillation machinery of continuous diffusion modeling.

title: An Empirical Analysis of CodeQL False Positives and Query Refinements for Java Vulnerabilities
summary:
Static application security testing (SAST) tools help developers find vulnerabilities before deployment, but false positives create substantial triage effort. We study whether CodeQL false positives in Java security analysis form recurring, explainable patterns that can be reduced by refining the analysis. We run CodeQL's Java security query suite on 167 CVE instances from 110 projects, focusing on the ten queries with the highest false positive rates. We manually review 500 sampled false positive paths and locations and construct a source-level taxonomy. The five categories are Missed Path Constraint or Sanitization (36.6%), Benign Execution Context (29.4%), Missing Trust Boundary Modeling (27.6%), Imprecise Concurrency Modeling (5%), and Imprecise Sink Modeling (1.4%).
  Guided by these findings, we implement CodeQL refinements that detect and filter recurring false positive patterns at the query level. The refinements remove 81.8% of reviewed false positives. Across the full selected-query dataset, they remove 15.8% of reported paths and locations while retaining 7 of 8 true positives. This shows that many false positives can be reduced in the analysis, although fixed refinements often depend on project-specific context. To address this generalization gap, we evaluate whether agentic coding tools can adapt refinement patterns to new projects. Given our patterns as templates, the two tools succeed on 56% and 62% of tasks, with query compile-pass rates above 90%. Without this guidance, both succeed on only 28%, while compile rates fall to 30-36%. These results support a refinement-oriented SAST workflow in which recurring false positives are modeled in CodeQL queries and automatically adapted to different project contexts, reducing repeated triage.

AI.tldr: This paper studies CodeQL false positives in Java security analysis, identifying five recurring patterns through manual review of 500 cases. The researchers implemented query-level refinements that eliminate 81.8% of reviewed false positives and evaluated whether agentic coding tools can adapt these patterns to new projects.
AI.motivation: Static application security testing (SAST) tools like CodeQL help developers find vulnerabilities before deployment, but false positives create substantial triage effort. This study investigates whether CodeQL false positives form recurring, explainable patterns that can be reduced through analysis refinements.
AI.method: The researchers ran CodeQL's Java security query suite on 167 CVE instances from 110 projects, focusing on the ten queries with the highest false positive rates. They manually reviewed 500 sampled false positive paths and locations to construct a source-level taxonomy. Guided by findings, they implemented CodeQL refinements to detect and filter recurring false positive patterns at the query level. They also evaluated whether agentic coding tools could adapt refinement patterns to new projects.
AI.result: The taxonomy identified five categories: Missed Path Constraint or Sanitization (36.6%), Benign Execution Context (29.4%), Missing Trust Boundary Modeling (27.6%), Imprecise Concurrency Modeling (5%), and Imprecise Sink Modeling (1.4%). Refinements removed 81.8% of reviewed false positives. Across the full dataset, they removed 15.8% of reported paths/locations while retaining 7 of 8 true positives. With pattern guidance, agentic tools succeeded on 56% and 62% of tasks with >90% compile rates; without guidance, only 28% success with 30-36% compile rates.
AI.conclusion: Many false positives can be reduced through analysis refinements, although fixed refinements often depend on project-specific context. Agentic coding tools can effectively adapt refinement patterns to new projects when given templates, supporting a refinement-oriented SAST workflow that reduces repeated triage effort.

title: Importance-Aware Low-Rank Distillation of Diffusion Transformers
summary:
Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have emerged as a dominant architecture for high-quality text-to-image generation, yet their scale poses challenges for efficient deployment. While truncated singular value decomposition (SVD) is a principled tool for parameter reduction, evidence from large language models (LLMs) suggests that naive low-rank approximation can cause catastrophic failure. In contrast, we find that truncated SVD in DiTs produces smooth degradation even under substantial global compression, with redundancy distributed across projection matrices throughout the whole network rather than concentrated in a few transformer blocks. Building on these insights, we introduce SVDtrunc, a two-step block-level compression scheme, first allocating ranks across blocks and compressing the least important ones via truncated SVD under a global parameter budget, and then fine-tuning all blocks with modular knowledge distillation and a rectified-flow objective. We apply SVDtrunc to FLUX.dev across compression levels ranging from 40-90% of the original parameter count. Across three benchmarks, GenEval, HPSv2, and DPG, we outperform all competing approaches. Notably, and in contrast to prior work, we retain near-full performance at 68% and remain competitive even at 57% of the original parameter budget. Furthermore, we show that SVDtrunc complements step distillation and achieves strong results even without fine-tuning, positioning it as a practical continuation of efficiency improvements beyond diffusion step reduction for large-scale generative models.
  Project page: https://vislearn.github.io/SVDtrunc/

AI.tldr: SVDtrunc is a two-step block-level compression method for Diffusion Transformers that allocates ranks across blocks, compresses the least important ones via truncated SVD under a global parameter budget, and then fine-tunes with modular knowledge distillation. It achieves near-full performance at 68% and competitiveness at 57% of original parameters, outperforming all competing approaches on FLUX.dev across three benchmarks (GenEval, HPSv2, and DPG).
AI.motivation: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have become dominant for high-quality text-to-image generation but pose challenges for efficient deployment due to their large scale. While truncated SVD is a principled tool for parameter reduction, it was important to understand how it behaves in DiTs compared to LLMs where naive low-rank approximation causes catastrophic failure.
AI.method: The method has two steps: 1) Rank allocation across transformer blocks based on importance, with compression of least important blocks via truncated SVD under a global parameter budget; 2) Fine-tuning all blocks using modular knowledge distillation with a rectified-flow objective. The key insight is that redundancy in DiTs is distributed across projection matrices throughout the whole network, not concentrated in a few blocks.
AI.result: Applied to FLUX.dev across compression levels of 40-90% original parameters, SVDtrunc outperforms all competing approaches on GenEval, HPSv2, and DPG benchmarks. It retains near-full performance at 68% and remains competitive even at 57% of original parameters. It also complements step distillation and achieves strong results even without fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: SVDtrunc provides a practical approach for compressing large-scale generative models beyond diffusion step reduction, with smooth degradation under substantial compression instead of catastrophic failure. The method demonstrates that DiTs have distributed redundancy across projection matrices, enabling effective block-level compression.

title: From Answers to Interpretations: Rethinking Ambiguity-Induced Aleatoric Uncertainty Estimation in LLMs
summary: A key challenge in reliable LLM deployment is recognizing when uncertainty reflects irreducible variability in the task rather than limitations in the model's knowledge. In language tasks, a central source of such aleatoric uncertainty is input ambiguity or underspecification, where multiple interpretations remain plausible. Existing decomposition methods estimate aleatoric uncertainty by generating multiple clarifications of the input, querying the model for an answer under each clarification, and comparing the resulting answers. We argue that answers are not necessary for identifying ambiguity: they are often redundant, add avoidable cost, and can mislead through epistemic leakage. We support this claim theoretically, and propose a clarification-only approach that estimates this ambiguity-induced component directly from the space of plausible interpretations, without answers to the clarified inputs. Using ambiguity detection as an operational evaluation across three benchmarks, this direct approach improves AUROC (63.34 vs. 60.85), reduces computational cost by 4-26x in output tokens and 2.2-3.5x in API calls, and yields estimates with substantially lower correlation with epistemic uncertainty. Overall, our results suggest that ambiguity-induced aleatoric uncertainty is better estimated from the interpretation space than from the response space.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses a key challenge in LLM deployment: distinguishing aleatoric uncertainty (irreducible task variability) from epistemic uncertainty (model knowledge limitations). The authors propose a "clarification-only" approach that estimates ambiguity-induced aleatoric uncertainty directly from the space of plausible interpretations, without requiring answers to clarified inputs.
AI.motivation: Existing methods estimate aleatoric uncertainty by generating multiple clarifications, querying the model for answers under each, and comparing results. However, answers are often redundant, add cost, and can mislead through "epistemic leakage." The authors argue that answers are unnecessary for identifying ambiguity.
AI.method: The proposed clarification-only approach estimates ambiguity-induced uncertainty directly from the interpretation space, bypassing the response space. This was evaluated using ambiguity detection as a test case across three benchmarks.
AI.result: The direct approach improves AUROC (63.34 vs. 60.85), reduces computational cost by 4-26x in output tokens and 2.2-3.5x in API calls, and yields estimates with substantially lower correlation with epistemic uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: Ambiguity-induced aleatoric uncertainty is better estimated from the interpretation space than from the response space, offering both improved accuracy and significant computational efficiency.

title: Mitra-v2 Technical Report
comment: 38 pages. Model weights, inference and fine-tuning code, and evaluation results: https://huggingface.co/autogluon/mitra-finetune
summary: We introduce Mitra-v2, a tabular foundation model that delivers state-of-the-art performance on real-world classification and regression problems, from credit-risk scoring and clinical prediction to equipment-failure detection and house-price estimation. Mitra-v2 is trained only on synthetic data, with a pretraining distribution that is much larger and more diverse than Mitra-v1's. Built on a small 2D Transformer backbone, Mitra-v2 supports longer contexts and larger feature spaces. Improved optimization lets it learn from this larger task distribution. We evaluate Mitra-v2 on the TabArena and TALENT benchmarks, comprising more than 300 real-world datasets under two evaluation protocols. On the full TabArena benchmark, Mitra-v2 delivers state-of-the-art performance at the level of the industry-scale TabFM and EXAONE Tabular models, while surpassing TabPFN-3 by a wide margin in both classification and regression. Mitra-v2 matches the 1.6B-parameter TabFM with only 5% of its size (77M parameters), delivering frontier performance at a fraction of the cost. On TALENT, Mitra-v2 remains among the leading models, clearly outperforming TabPFN-3 and TabICLv2. It also ranks first on classification tasks with more than ten classes, even though it was pretrained only on tasks with at most ten classes. These results make Mitra-v2 one of the strongest and most broadly applicable open tabular foundation models released to date. We release the model weights, the inference and fine-tuning code, and our evaluation results under the Apache-2.0 license.

AI.tldr: Mitra-v2 is a tabular foundation model trained on synthetic data that achieves state-of-the-art performance on real-world tabular data tasks (classification and regression), competing with industry-scale models while using only 5% of their size (77M parameters).
AI.motivation: To create a more powerful and broadly applicable open tabular foundation model that can handle diverse real-world problems (credit-risk scoring, clinical prediction, equipment-failure detection, house-price estimation) with improved performance over predecessor Mitra-v1.
AI.method: Trained on synthetic data with a larger and more diverse pretraining distribution than Mitra-v1, using a small 2D Transformer backbone with longer context support and larger feature spaces, combined with improved optimization techniques.
AI.result: Mitra-v2 delivers state-of-the-art performance on TabArena benchmark, matching the 1.6B-parameter TabFM with only 77M parameters (5% of its size), surpassing TabPFN-3 in both classification and regression, and performing well on TALENT benchmark. It excels at classification tasks with more than 10 classes despite being pretrained on tasks with at most 10 classes.
AI.conclusion: Mitra-v2 is one of the strongest and most broadly applicable open tabular foundation models released to date, achieving frontier performance at a fraction of the cost compared to industry-scale models.

title: Dynamic Adaptation of the LLM Context for Generating Routines with Coupled Semantics
summary: LLM-based code generation fails when correctness depends on execution-dependent coupling: the meaning of one routine is defined by the runtime behavior of another, a relationship that cannot be resolved from textual descriptions alone. This limitation, which we call static binding, is not confined to explicitly coupled problems; it appears to varying degrees whenever correctness depends on joint execution behavior across components, from explicit cross-coupled optimizers to subtler joint constraints in packing, routing, and symbolic search. This paper proposes dynamic context adaptation, a sample-efficient validation-generation loop designed for this setting. A validation agent extracts structured diagnostic information from execution traces, providing gradient-like guidance to a generation agent that proposes multiple candidates per iteration. A knowledge graph derived from the problem description supplies semantic constraints to the generation agent. Simulated annealing selects among candidates to avoid greedy collapse. Our method outperforms zero-shot, Reflexion, and OpenEvolve on seven of eight problems at both 300 and 600 evaluations (p < 0.01), a regime where population-based search has not yet accumulated sufficient diversity to compete. Notably, on the primary motivating problem (cross-coupled optimization), our method also achieves the best score at 1000 evaluations, consistent with the hypothesis that structured execution feedback is most beneficial when correctness depends on runtime coupling. Ablation results confirm that structured execution feedback is the primary driver.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses a key limitation in LLM-based code generation: static binding, where correctness depends on execution-dependent coupling between routines that cannot be resolved from textual descriptions alone. The authors propose dynamic context adaptation, a validation-generation loop using a validation agent to extract structured diagnostic information from execution traces, a generation agent with knowledge graph constraints, and simulated annealing for candidate selection.
AI.motivation: LLM-based code generation fails when the meaning of one routine depends on the runtime behavior of another (execution-dependent coupling). This limitation, called static binding, appears in various problems from cross-coupled optimizers to packing, routing, and symbolic search. Existing methods struggle in this regime where correctness depends on joint execution behavior across components.
AI.method: The proposed dynamic context adaptation framework includes: (1) a validation agent that extracts structured diagnostic information from execution traces, providing gradient-like guidance to (2) a generation agent that proposes multiple candidates per iteration, (3) a knowledge graph derived from problem descriptions for semantic constraints, and (4) simulated annealing for candidate selection to avoid greedy collapse.
AI.result: The method outperforms zero-shot, Reflexion, and OpenEvolve on seven of eight problems at both 300 and 600 evaluations (p < 0.01). Notably, on the primary motivating problem (cross-coupled optimization), it achieves the best score at 1000 evaluations. Ablation results confirm that structured execution feedback is the primary driver of performance.
AI.conclusion: Structured execution feedback is most beneficial when correctness depends on runtime coupling. The dynamic context adaptation approach provides a sample-efficient solution for LLM-based code generation in execution-dependent coupling scenarios, outperforming existing methods in low-evaluation regimes where population-based search lacks diversity.

title: ReaDiT Guidance: Control for Image and Video Generation using Diffusion Transformer Features
summary: We present DiT Readout (ReaDiT) Guidance, a lightweight framework for controlling generation with Diffusion Transformer (DiT) models via their internal feature representations. ReaDiT Guidance uses features from a single DiT block to steer the generative process according to spatial targets - like depth, pose, or edge maps - provided at test time. Furthermore, since modern text-to-video models are largely built on DiT backbones, ReaDiT Guidance naturally extends to video generation, enabling camera and motion control. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves competitive or improved results compared to existing feature-based and off-the-shelf adapter-based approaches while requiring fewer parameters.

AI.tldr: DiT Readout (ReaDiT) Guidance is a lightweight method for controlling Diffusion Transformer (DiT) models using their internal feature representations. It uses features from a single DiT block to steer generation based on spatial targets like depth, pose, or edge maps, and extends to video generation for camera and motion control.
AI.motivation: Control generation in Diffusion Transformer models (DiT) using their internal features, enabling spatial control (depth, pose, edge maps) and video generation control (camera, motion) without heavy adapter-based approaches.
AI.method: ReaDiT Guidance uses features from a single DiT block to steer the generative process according to spatial targets provided at test time. It is a lightweight framework that works with DiT-based text-to-video models.
AI.result: Achieves competitive or improved results compared to existing feature-based and adapter-based approaches while requiring fewer parameters.
AI.conclusion: ReaDiT Guidance provides an efficient and effective method for controlling DiT-based generation with minimal parameters, applicable to both image and video generation tasks.

title: IPGeoAI: Transformer-Based Geolocation with LLM Semantic Fusion
summary: Accurate city-level IP Geolocation is an important enabler for the modern digital ecosystem, underpinning services ranging from local content delivery and targeting to digital rights enforcement. However, traditional heuristic and database-driven methods often struggle to resolve the complex, non-linear allocation patterns of modern network infrastructures, particularly within the exploding IPv6 address space and transient mobile networks. In this paper, we introduce IPGeoAI, a novel deep learning model architecture that reframes geolocation from a static lookup problem to a sequential modeling task. Our approach utilizes the Transformer Encoder to capture hierarchical dependencies inherent in IP subnet structures. We propose a method to resolve geographic ambiguity by integrating unstructured semantic context via a Zero-Shot LLM Feature Extraction pipeline. We utilize Large Language Models to transform raw, noisy Autonomous Systems (AS) descriptions into structured, domain-specific metadata (such as 'University' vs. 'ISP' or 'Global' vs. 'Local') via an offline pre-computation process. By fusing these semantic signals into the network via a Multi-Head Cross-Attention module, we bridge the gap between numerical network topology and real-world semantic identity. Extensive offline evaluation on a proprietary dataset spanning 200,000 cities demonstrates that IPGeoAI significantly outperforms a leading external vendor in city-level granularity. By adopting a hierarchical inference strategy that refines coarse-grained country signals, our model achieves a 6% improvement in city-level accuracy while extending coverage to 100% of the traffic. Furthermore, in large-scale online production tests, the model drove a statistically significant +0.35% improvement in our 1st-tier downstream use cases metric.

AI.tldr: IPGeoAI is a novel deep learning model that transforms IP geolocation from a static lookup problem into a sequential modeling task using Transformer Encoder architecture, achieving 6% improvement in city-level accuracy by integrating LLM-extracted semantic features from Autonomous Systems descriptions via Multi-Head Cross-Attention modules.
AI.motivation: Traditional heuristic and database-driven IP geolocation methods struggle with complex, non-linear allocation patterns in modern network infrastructures, especially in IPv6 address space and transient mobile networks. There is a need for more accurate city-level geolocation to support local content delivery, targeting, and digital rights enforcement.
AI.method: 1) Transformer Encoder to capture hierarchical dependencies in IP subnet structures; 2) Zero-Shot LLM Feature Extraction pipeline to transform raw AS descriptions into structured metadata (e.g., 'University' vs. 'ISP'); 3) Multi-Head Cross-Attention module to fuse semantic signals with network topology; 4) Hierarchical inference strategy refining coarse-grained country signals to city-level
AI.result: 6% improvement in city-level accuracy over a leading external vendor; 100% traffic coverage; +0.35% improvement in 1st-tier downstream use cases in online production tests
AI.conclusion: IPGeoAI successfully reframes geolocation as a sequential modeling problem, demonstrating that integrating LLM-derived semantic context with network topology significantly improves city-level IP geolocation accuracy and coverage in both offline evaluations and real-world production environments.

title: Fast Surrogate Modeling of Excitable and Oscillatory FitzHugh-Nagumo Dynamics with Parametric Neural Operators
comment: Human Brain & AI @ International Joint Conferences on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI) 2026
summary: The FitzHugh-Nagumo (FHN) system serves as a simplified model of neuronal voltage dynamics, capturing the activator-inhibitor structure behind both isolated action potentials and the rhythmic spiking seen across the brain. Exploring its 5D physiological parameter space is important for neuromodulation and mapping voltage recordings back to biophysics, yet classical finite-difference solvers make rapid parameter sweeps expensive. We train parameter-conditioned Fourier Neural Operators (FNOs) as fast, differentiable surrogates for the FHN voltage and recovery fields on a one-dimensional spatial domain, conditioning each Fourier layer on the parameter vector $λ= (D_u, D_v, a, b, τ)$ via feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM). We apply a single bifurcation analysis that delimits the two distinct regimes the model spans, oscillatory (tonic firing) and excitable (action-potential propagation), and we train one operator in each. In the oscillatory regime the surrogate attains sub-$0.1\%$ relative $L^2$ error on both fields, runs nearly three orders of magnitude faster than the finite-difference baseline, generalizes uniformly across the parameter space, and extrapolates to low single-digit percentage errors outside of the training bounds. In the excitable regime the same operator accurately reproduces the firing threshold and the $c \propto \sqrt{D_u}$ conduction-velocity law and replicates full traveling pulses, fully capturing the excitable bifurcation structure rather than just smoothly interpolating fields.

AI.tldr: The paper trains Fourier Neural Operators (FNOs) as fast surrogates for the FitzHugh-Nagumo neuronal model, using FiLM conditioning on 5 parameters. Two operators are trained for oscillatory and excitable regimes, achieving sub-0.1% error and 1000x speedup.
AI.motivation: Classical finite-difference solvers make rapid parameter sweeps expensive when exploring the 5D physiological parameter space of the FHN system, which is important for neuromodulation and mapping voltage recordings back to biophysics.
AI.method: Train parameter-conditioned FNOs as differentiable surrogates for FHN voltage and recovery fields on a 1D domain, conditioning each Fourier layer via FiLM on parameter vector λ = (D_u, D_v, a, b, τ). Apply bifurcation analysis to delimit oscillatory (tonic firing) and excitable (action-potential propagation) regimes, training one operator in each.
AI.result: In oscillatory regime: sub-0.1% relative L2 error on both fields, ~1000x faster than finite-difference baseline, generalizes uniformly across parameter space, extrapolates to low single-digit percentage errors outside training bounds. In excitable regime: accurately reproduces firing threshold and c ∝ √D_u conduction-velocity law, replicates full traveling pulses, capturing excitable bifurcation structure.
AI.conclusion: FiLM-conditioned FNOs serve as effective fast surrogates for FHN dynamics, enabling rapid parameter exploration while preserving critical biophysical phenomena like action potential propagation and conduction velocity scaling across both oscillatory and excitable regimes.

title: Software Engineering in the Agent Era From Trustworthy Change to Human Agent Software Organizations
summary:
Software agents make digital execution elastic: repository analysis, code generation, testing, migration, tool use, and operations can be replicated and parallelized without proportional human headcount. Problem framing, semantic commitment, verification, integration, attention, and residual-risk acceptance remain bounded by human cognition, organizational authority, and economic capacity. How should scalable execution be governed so organizations can accept and sustain its changes?
  Our testable framework has two constructs and one execution abstraction. Trustworthy Change (TC) is the engineering object moving from intent through delegated execution, verification, integration, acceptance, and operation. Responsibility Topology classifies organizations by the distribution of independent residual-risk acceptance authority. A single-center topology has one final baseline responsibility anchor; a multi-anchor topology requires joint acceptance across independently governed domains. The Human-Agent Cell (HAC) produces candidates, proposals, and evidence; execution grants no acceptance authority. As execution and authority scale differently, distributed HACs create context-coherence and invalidation pressures, while multi-anchor governance adds joint acceptance and explicit responsibility closure.
  Responsibility, accountability, change management, specification, verification, and human oversight predate this work; our claim is only that agent-scaled execution changes how they fit together. We make that authority an explicit classification axis and derive consequences for change state, shared engineering facts, verification, and flow control. Progressive Specification and bounded-capacity analysis remain hypotheses to test, not laws. We contribute theory construction and operationalization; empirical validity remains open to controlled, longitudinal, and field studies.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a governance framework for agent-scaled software execution, addressing how organizations can accept and sustain changes driven by AI agents that handle digital tasks while humans retain responsibility for verification, integration, and risk acceptance.
AI.motivation: Software agents enable elastic digital execution (code generation, testing, migration, operations) without proportional human headcount, but human cognition, organizational authority, and economic capacity remain bottlenecks. The problem is how to govern scalable execution so organizations can accept and sustain its changes.
AI.method: The paper proposes a testable framework with two constructs and one execution abstraction: (1) Trustworthy Change (TC) - an engineering object moving through intent, delegated execution, verification, integration, acceptance, and operation; (2) Responsibility Topology - classifies organizations by distribution of residual-risk acceptance authority (single-center vs. multi-anchor); (3) Human-Agent Cell (HAC) - produces candidates/proposals but grants no acceptance authority.
AI.result: The framework makes authority an explicit classification axis and derives consequences for change state, shared engineering facts, verification, and flow control. Distributed HACs create context-coherence and invalidation pressures; multi-anchor governance adds joint acceptance and explicit responsibility closure.
AI.conclusion: The contribution is theory construction and operationalization, not new concepts. Progressive Specification and bounded-capacity analysis remain hypotheses to test. Empirical validity remains open to controlled, longitudinal, and field studies.

title: Retinal OCTA Phenotyping with LLM Reporting for Alzheimer's Disease
comment: 4th IEE International Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Blockchain, and Internet of Things, (AIBThings)
summary: Early identification of Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains challenging because established assessment methods can be costly, resource-intensive, or unsuitable for population-scale screening. Optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) provides non-invasive visualization of retinal microvasculature, but existing approaches often require diagnostic labels and provide limited measurement-level interpretation. We present an explainable OCTA pipeline that integrates annotation-aware vessel segmentation, layer-specific vascular biomarker extraction, label-free phenotyping, and measurement-grounded LLM reporting. Using 117 ROSE-1 images from 39 subjects, we apply annotation-matched segmentation models to superficial vascular complex (SVC), deep vascular complex (DVC), and combined SVC+DVC representations. The models achieve ROC-AUC values of 0.916-0.970 and Dice scores of 0.695-0.781. Six density and fractal-dimension biomarkers form subject-level profiles for exploratory clustering. Analysis of nine held-out subjects identifies an internally consistent lower-density, lower-fractal-dimension phenotype, although the absence of diagnostic labels prevents clinical interpretation. Reports generated using GPT, Gemini, and Llama are evaluated for measurement grounding, citation faithfulness, and diagnostic caution. Overall, the framework provides a transparent, non-diagnostic connection between retinal vascular measurements, exploratory phenotyping, and evidence-linked interpretation for Alzheimer's research.

AI.tldr: An explainable OCTA pipeline is proposed for Alzheimer's disease research, integrating annotation-aware vessel segmentation, layer-specific biomarker extraction, label-free phenotyping, and LLM-based reporting. Using 117 ROSE-1 images, models achieve 0.916-0.970 ROC-AUC and 0.695-0.781 Dice scores, identifying a lower-density phenotype in nine held-out subjects.
AI.motivation: Early identification of AD remains challenging due to costly, resource-intensive assessment methods unsuitable for population-scale screening. OCTA provides non-invasive retinal microvasculature visualization, but existing approaches require diagnostic labels and offer limited measurement-level interpretation.
AI.method: 117 ROSE-1 images from 39 subjects were analyzed using an explainable OCTA pipeline featuring: (1) annotation-matched segmentation models for SVC, DVC, and combined SVC+DVC; (2) six density and fractal-dimension biomarkers for subject-level profiles; (3) exploratory clustering for phenotyping; (4) GPT, Gemini, and Llama for measurement-grounded report generation. Nine subjects were held out for validation.
AI.result: Models achieved ROC-AUC of 0.916-0.970 and Dice scores of 0.695-0.781. Analysis of nine held-out subjects identified an internally consistent lower-density, lower-fractal-dimension phenotype, though absence of diagnostic labels prevents clinical interpretation. LLM reports were evaluated for measurement grounding, citation faithfulness, and diagnostic caution.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a transparent, non-diagnostic connection between retinal vascular measurements, exploratory phenotyping, and evidence-linked interpretation for Alzheimer's research. It demonstrates the potential of OCTA-based biomarkers for AD screening while emphasizing that the approach is for research purposes only.

title: Reducing Hallucinated Transcripts in Whisper via Hallucination Space Projection
summary:
Whisper is a widely used foundation model for automatic speech recognition (ASR), but its generative decoder can produce fluent hallucinated transcripts for inputs containing little or no speech. We propose a training-free, inference-time method to reduce these hallucinations using low-rank projection of decoder activations. A compact hallucination-associated subspace is estimated from non-speech calibration data, and decoder hidden states are projected away from this subspace during inference.
  We evaluate two variants: always-on, which applies projection to all inputs, and gated, which applies it only when Whisper predicts that an input is likely non-speech. Across non-speech benchmarks, always-on projection reduces average hallucination rate (HR) from 31.31% to 2.44%, a 92.21% relative reduction, while gated projection reduces HR to 3.74%, an 88.05% relative reduction, with lower false rejection of genuine speech. On LibriSpeech, gated projection increases absolute word error rate (WER) by 0.33-4.39 percentage points and yields false-rejection rates (FRR) of 0.41--9.97% across model and split settings.
  These results show that low-rank activation projection can substantially suppress Whisper hallucinations without retraining, while providing a controllable trade-off between hallucination suppression and speech recognition performance.

AI.tldr: A training-free inference-time method using low-rank projection of Whisper's decoder activations to reduce hallucinated transcripts for non-speech inputs. The method projects decoder hidden states away from a hallucination-associated subspace estimated from non-speech calibration data.
AI.motivation: Whisper, a widely used ASR foundation model, generates fluent hallucinated transcripts when input contains little or no speech, which is a significant reliability issue in practical deployments.
AI.method: Two variants: (1) Always-on projection applies to all inputs; (2) Gated projection applies only when Whisper predicts non-speech. Both estimate a compact hallucination-associated subspace from non-speech calibration data and project decoder hidden states away from this subspace during inference.
AI.result: On non-speech benchmarks, always-on reduces hallucination rate (HR) from 31.31% to 2.44% (92.21% relative reduction), while gated reduces HR to 3.74% (88.05% relative reduction). On LibriSpeech, gated increases WER by 0.33-4.39 percentage points with FRR of 0.41-9.97%.
AI.conclusion: Low-rank activation projection can substantially suppress Whisper hallucinations without retraining, offering a controllable trade-off between hallucination suppression and speech recognition performance.

title: Training-Free Halving of Activated Experts in Fine-Grained Mixture-of-Experts Models
summary: Modern fine-grained Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models route each token to a small number of experts and renormalize their router probabilities. We show that this renormalization implicitly calibrates expert output gain to the training top-$k$: reducing $k$ at inference changes not only which experts are used but also the strength of the expert branch. We separate these effects by activating the top $k_1$ experts while normalizing by the probability mass of the top $k_2$ experts, introducing one integer with no parameters, training, or measurable compute overhead. On Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, reducing from 8 to 4 experts causes a 4.65-point MMLU drop under standard renormalization but only 0.35 points with $k_2=16$, while halving routed-expert compute. The result replicates on the $11\times$ larger Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, where reducing from 10 to 5 experts loses only 0.55 points with an appropriate reference set. Removing renormalization entirely is catastrophic, showing that preserving a suitable reference mass is crucial. We further find that perplexity and downstream accuracy favor different $k_2$, cautioning against selecting MoE compression settings using unlabeled text alone. Analyses also show that expert identity matters substantially more than expert weighting, while balanced and domain-specialized routing leaves limited room for expert pruning.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses a key limitation in fine-grained Mixture-of-Experts models: the renormalization of router probabilities is coupled to the training top-k, making inference-time reduction in active experts harmful. The authors propose a simple fix using two separate k values (k1 for activation, k2 for normalization) with no additional parameters.
AI.motivation: Modern fine-grained MoE models route each token to a small number of experts and renormalize their router probabilities. However, this renormalization implicitly calibrates expert output gain to the training top-k. Reducing k at inference not only changes which experts are used but also alters the strength of the expert branch, causing performance degradation.
AI.method: The authors propose separating these two effects by activating the top k1 experts while normalizing by the probability mass of the top k2 experts. This introduces one integer hyperparameter with no parameters, training, or measurable compute overhead. They experiment with different k1 (active experts) and k2 (normalization reference) values on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B models.
AI.result: On Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, reducing from 8 to 4 experts causes a 4.65-point MMLU drop under standard renormalization but only 0.35 points with k2=16, while halving routed-expert compute. On the 11x larger Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, reducing from 10 to 5 experts loses only 0.55 points with appropriate k2. Removing renormalization entirely is catastrophic, demonstrating preserving suitable reference mass is crucial. Further analysis shows: (1) expert identity matters substantially more than expert weighting, (2) balanced and domain-specialized routing leaves limited room for expert pruning.
AI.conclusion: The key insight is that MoE compression should preserve a large reference mass (k2) while reducing active experts (k1). Perplexity and downstream accuracy favor different k2 values, cautioning against selecting MoE compression settings using unlabeled text alone. The proposed method enables efficient MoE compression without significant performance loss.

title: How Developers Discuss Generative AI: A Longitudinal Study of the Visual Studio Code Community
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables. Accepted at 34th IEEE/ACIS SNPD 2026
summary: Generative AI tools such as GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT, and coding agents have rapidly become part of everyday software development, yet little is known about how mainstream open source communities discuss them in practice. This paper presents a longitudinal analysis of generative-AI-related discussions in the Visual Studio Code (VS Code) GitHub repository, using 43,806 candidate issues created between January 2021 and June 2026. To improve corpus quality, we combined keyword retrieval with semantic relevance filtering, yielding a filtered corpus of 25,227 AI-related issues. We applied BERTopic to the retrieved corpus to identify discussion topics, using the filtered corpus for theme validation and a robustness re-clustering, and analyzed their evolution over time using monthly prevalence and Mann-Kendall trend tests. The results show that developer discussions are dominated by practical concerns regarding the operation of AI-assisted development environments, including agent management, configuration, reliability, authentication, and billing, whereas risks frequently emphasized in survey-based studies, such as hallucination and licensing, rarely surface in this venue. This suggests that discussions of generative AI in the VS Code issue tracker primarily focus on operational aspects of AI-assisted software development. Furthermore, discussions evolved from AI-assisted code completion toward conversational and agent-based development, reflecting the increasing integration of generative AI into software development workflows. These findings suggest that GitHub Issues provide a practical, workflow-oriented perspective on generative AI that complements survey-based studies of developer perceptions.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes generative AI discussions in the VS Code GitHub repository using 25,227 filtered issues from 43,806 candidates. Developer discussions primarily focus on operational concerns (agent management, configuration, reliability, authentication, billing) rather than risks like hallucination or licensing. Discussions evolved from code completion toward conversational and agent-based development, providing a practical perspective that complements survey-based studies.
AI.motivation: While generative AI tools like GitHub Copilot and ChatGPT have become widespread in software development, there is limited understanding of how mainstream open source communities discuss these tools in practice. Survey-based studies dominate the literature, but real-world issue discussions may reveal different concerns.
AI.method: Longitudinal analysis of VS Code GitHub repository issues (Jan 2021 - Jun 2026). Combined keyword retrieval with semantic relevance filtering to improve corpus quality (25,227 AI-related issues from 43,806 candidates). Applied BERTopic for topic identification, with theme validation and robustness re-clustering using the filtered corpus. Analyzed topic evolution using monthly prevalence and Mann-Kendall trend tests.
AI.result: Developer discussions are dominated by practical operational concerns: agent management, configuration, reliability, authentication, and billing. Risks frequently emphasized in survey studies (hallucination, licensing) rarely surface. Discussions evolved from AI-assisted code completion toward conversational and agent-based development, reflecting increasing integration of generative AI into software development workflows.
AI.conclusion: GitHub Issues provide a practical, workflow-oriented perspective on generative AI that complements survey-based studies of developer perceptions. The real-world discussion patterns differ significantly from survey-based perceptions, highlighting the importance of analyzing actual usage contexts rather than self-reported attitudes.

title: Enhancing Multimodal Emotion Recognition via Multi-Feature Encoding and Attention-Based Fusion
comment: 15 pages, 6 figures, 6 tables. Pre-peer-review version. The final published version appears in ICONIP 2025, Lecture Notes in Computer Science, vol. 16312, pp. 142-157 (2026)
summary: Multimodal emotion recognition has attracted growing interest due to its importance in human-computer interaction, remote education, and healthcare. This paper proposes a novel multimodal emotion recognition framework that integrates rich audio and visual feature extraction with an attention-based fusion strategy. For audio, we extract three complementary feature types: semantic embeddings from Wav2Vec2, MFCC features, and statistical acoustic descriptors such as pitch, energy, and rhythm. These are aligned and fused via a BiLSTM to capture temporal dependencies. For video, we propose a ResNet50-BiLSTM architecture that combines deep residual learning and sequential modeling to extract expressive spatiotemporal features from facial sequences. To enhance multimodal synergy, we introduce a feature-level fusion mechanism based on multi-head attention, allowing the model to adaptively weigh contributions across modalities. Experiments conducted on the MELD and IEMOCAP datasets demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms baselines in both accuracy and robustness. Furthermore, ablation studies show that the attention-based fusion strategy significantly improves performance in unbalanced data settings. Our findings suggest that the proposed framework effectively captures diverse emotional cues from speech and visual expressions, and offers a practical and generalizable approach for real-world multimodal emotion recognition tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel multimodal emotion recognition framework that combines audio features (Wav2Vec2, MFCC, statistical descriptors) using BiLSTM with visual features (ResNet50-BiLSTM) through a multi-head attention-based fusion mechanism. The approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on MELD and IEMOCAP datasets, particularly showing robustness in unbalanced data settings.
AI.motivation: Multimodal emotion recognition is important for human-computer interaction, remote education, and healthcare applications. The motivation is to develop a framework that effectively captures diverse emotional cues from both speech and visual expressions, addressing limitations in existing approaches that may not adequately leverage complementary multimodal information or handle data imbalance.
AI.method: The proposed framework uses: (1) Audio features - semantic embeddings from Wav2Vec2, MFCC features, and statistical acoustic descriptors (pitch, energy, rhythm) processed through BiLSTM for temporal modeling; (2) Video features - ResNet50 combined with BiLSTM for spatiotemporal feature extraction from facial sequences; (3) Feature-level fusion via multi-head attention that adaptively weighs contributions across modalities. The model is evaluated on MELD and IEMOCAP datasets.
AI.result: The model significantly outperforms baseline methods in both accuracy and robustness. Ablation studies demonstrate that the attention-based fusion strategy substantially improves performance in unbalanced data settings, suggesting effective handling of class imbalance common in emotion recognition tasks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively captures diverse emotional cues from speech and visual expressions through complementary audio-visual features and adaptive attention-based fusion. It offers a practical and generalizable approach for real-world multimodal emotion recognition tasks, with particular strengths in robustness and handling data imbalance.

title: La Agente Óptima: Towards Agentic Self-Driving Laboratories
summary: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) combine automated experimentation with adaptive decision-making to accelerate scientific discovery. Their operation nevertheless often depends on human specialists who translate scientific objectives into executable closed-loop campaigns. Specialists adjust them as data and operating conditions change. Here, we present La Agente Óptima, an agentic framework that constructs and supervises Bayesian optimization campaigns across computational and experimental systems while maintaining a persistent optimization state. By separating large language model (LLM) reasoning from executed campaigns, Óptima runs repetitive optimization loops consistently, returns control to the agent only when progress requires interpretation or campaign revision, and keeps every decision auditable. We evaluate Óptima across ablation studies, five digital discovery tasks, and two physical platforms. Throughout, Óptima maintained executable campaigns as both the scientific problem and execution environment evolved. In a closed-loop contact angle optimization campaign, Óptima identified and corrected a mid-run measurement failure, bringing the contact angle from 71.4 to 67.8 degrees, just above the 64-66 degree range. From this result, Óptima correctly inferred that the target was likely unattainable with the available reagents and recommended changing the formulation. In a five-day multi-objective flow-chemistry campaign, Óptima increased the yield from 30% to 59% over 23 experiments. Despite substantial inference costs, it cost less and used substantially less starting material than a human-directed campaign, while selecting a more mass-efficient operating point. These results show that LLM-based agents can make rigorous, long-running optimization campaigns accessible to domain scientists without specialist setup, expanding the scope of SDLs.

AI.tldr: La Agente Óptima is an LLM-powered agentic framework that autonomously constructs and supervises Bayesian optimization campaigns across computational and experimental systems, maintaining persistent optimization state and enabling domain scientists to run complex optimization campaigns without specialist intervention.
AI.motivation: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) currently depend on human specialists to translate scientific objectives into executable campaigns and adjust them as conditions change. This creates a bottleneck requiring expert knowledge. The goal is to make rigorous, long-running optimization campaigns accessible to domain scientists without specialist setup.
AI.method: The framework separates LLM reasoning from executed campaigns, allowing repetitive optimization loops to run consistently while returning control to the agent only when progress requires interpretation or campaign revision. It maintains executable campaigns as both the scientific problem and execution environment evolve, keeping every decision auditable.
AI.result: In ablation studies and five digital discovery tasks, Óptima maintained executable campaigns during problem and environment evolution. In a closed-loop contact angle optimization campaign, it identified and corrected a mid-run measurement failure (71.4° to 67.8°, near target 64-66°), inferred the target was likely unattainable, and recommended formulation changes. In a five-day multi-objective flow-chemistry campaign, it increased yield from 30% to 59% over 23 experiments, costing less and using less starting material than human-directed campaigns while selecting a more mass-efficient operating point.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based agents can make rigorous, long-running optimization campaigns accessible to domain scientists without specialist setup, significantly expanding the scope of self-driving laboratories.

title: Optimizer Memory Schedules for Outscaling the Overtraining Axis
summary: We investigate how optimizers scale across the overtraining axis and show that relative optimizer performance and optimal hyperparameters change substantially with training horizon. In particular, we study how matrix-preconditioned methods (Muon and SOAP) and a momentum-scheduled method (ADANA) scale relative to AdamW. We compare these four optimizers across models from 51M to 253M parameters and overtraining (OT) factors from 1x to 256x, sweeping the base learning rate at every setting. The preferred learning rate schedule can reverse across the overtraining axis, the best weight decay coefficient scales approximately as sqrt(OT), and longer horizons generally favor longer fixed memory. ADANA's scaling advantage over AdamW persists after tuning AdamW's fixed memory separately at each horizon. Log-time weight decay and momentum cooldown provide substantial gains for ADANA that compound as training increases. With this treatment, ADANA outscales AdamW with an exponent advantage close to that predicted by DANA theory on power-law random features. Muon and SOAP instead provide roughly constant token-efficiency advantages over AdamW across most of the measured range, although SOAP may gain further at the highest overtraining factors. ADANA begins behind both matrix-preconditioned optimizers but closes the gaps as training increases, surpassing Muon and becoming competitive with SOAP at our highest OT factors. These results establish training horizon as an essential axis for optimizer evaluation and design.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that optimizer performance rankings and optimal hyperparameters (learning rate schedules, weight decay) significantly change with training duration. ADANA outperforms AdamW at scale with theoretical exponent advantage, while Muon and SOAP maintain constant token-efficiency advantages. Training horizon should be a standard evaluation axis for optimizers.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses a critical gap in optimizer evaluation: how optimizer performance changes across different training horizons (overtraining factors). Most prior work evaluates optimizers at a single training duration, but the authors argue that relative performance and optimal hyperparameters can change substantially with extended training.
AI.method: The authors compared four optimizers (AdamW, Muon, SOAP, and ADANA) across models ranging from 51M to 253M parameters, with overtraining factors from 1x to 256x. They swept the base learning rate at every setting and investigated learning rate schedules, weight decay scaling, and memory allocation strategies across the overtraining axis.
AI.result: Key findings include: (1) Relative optimizer performance and optimal hyperparameters change substantially with training horizon; (2) Preferred learning rate schedule reverses across the overtraining axis; (3) Best weight decay scales approximately as sqrt(OT); (4) ADANA's scaling advantage over AdamW persists after separate tuning at each horizon; (5) Log-time weight decay and momentum cooldown provide compounding gains for ADANA; (6) Muon and SOAP provide roughly constant token-efficiency advantages over AdamW; (7) ADANA starts behind Muon and SOAP but closes gaps at highest OT factors.
AI.conclusion: Training horizon is an essential axis for optimizer evaluation and design. ADANA achieves exponent advantage close to DANA theory predictions on power-law random features, while matrix-preconditioned methods (Muon, SOAP) provide constant advantages that may grow at highest OT factors.

title: Beyond Code Generation: Reliability, Verification, and Cost Economics in the Agentic Software Development Lifecycle
comment: 18 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables. Systems synthesis and research agenda on agentic software engineering, code review, testing, reliability, and AI cost. No new experimental measurements are claimed; empirical and company-reported results are attributed to the cited sources
summary:
AI coding systems are moving from autocomplete and chat toward agents that can inspect repositories, edit multiple files, run tools, write tests, open pull requests, and work for long periods with limited supervision. This capability changes the bottleneck in software delivery. Recent field studies show meaningful gains in coding activity, but newer evidence also shows that those gains attenuate sharply between writing code and shipping reliable software. Review, integration, testing, security, deployment, and production operations remain constraining stages, while the economics are shifting from predictable per-seat licensing toward variable token, tool, sandbox, CI, and rework costs.
  This paper synthesizes peer-reviewed software-engineering research, university studies, benchmark audits, production reports from major technology companies, developer telemetry, and cost-management evidence released primarily from 2024 through September 2026. No new model experiment is claimed; numerical findings remain attributed to their original studies. The synthesis proposes four engineering concepts: the Agentic SDLC Throughput Paradox, Production-Qualified Change (PQC), the Verification Tax, and an Agentic SDLC Control Plane that allocates autonomy subject to cost, reliability, and human-attention budgets. An evidence-based horizon then maps today's supervised agents to future policy-bounded software factories. The central research question shifts from how much code an agent can generate to how much production-qualified value an engineering system can deliver per dollar, per reviewer-hour, and per unit of operational risk.

AI.tldr: This paper examines the evolution of AI coding systems from simple autocomplete to autonomous agents, and identifies a critical bottleneck shift: while code generation has improved, the bottleneck has moved to later stages (review, integration, testing, security, deployment, operations). The paper proposes four new engineering concepts and reframes the research question from code quantity to production-qualified value delivery per dollar, reviewer-hour, and operational risk.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address a gap in understanding AI's impact on software delivery. While AI coding tools show productivity gains in writing code, these gains attenuate sharply when shipping reliable software. The economics are also shifting from predictable licensing to variable costs. The paper aims to synthesize evidence to understand the true impact of AI agents on software engineering.
AI.method: The paper synthesizes peer-reviewed software-engineering research, university studies, benchmark audits, production reports from major tech companies, developer telemetry, and cost-management evidence from 2024 through September 2026. No new model experiments are conducted; numerical findings are attributed to original studies.
AI.result: The synthesis proposes four engineering concepts: (1) Agentic SDLC Throughput Paradox - the phenomenon where increased code generation doesn't proportionally increase shipped software; (2) Production-Qualified Change (PQC) - a metric for changes that successfully reach production; (3) Verification Tax - the cost overhead for verifying AI-generated code; (4) Agentic SDLC Control Plane - a framework for allocating autonomy subject to cost, reliability, and human-attention budgets.
AI.conclusion: The central research question shifts from "how much code can an agent generate" to "how much production-qualified value can an engineering system deliver per dollar, per reviewer-hour, and per unit of operational risk." The paper maps today's supervised agents to future policy-bounded software factories, suggesting a need to focus on the entire software delivery value chain rather than just code generation.

title: LookThere! Sparse Vision by Reinforced Selection
summary: Vision transformers typically treat every image token as equally important, yet for most tasks in computer vision only a fraction are needed. Adaptive computation methods accelerate inference by choosing which tokens to process, but existing methods struggle at extreme sparsity and require heuristics that may not generalize like token diversity and attention scores. We address these limitations with LookThere, achieving a new pareto frontier in performance-compute trade-offs through an end-to-end reinforcement learning framework that jointly trains a shallow input selector and a deep representation extractor. The selector learns where to look and the extractor learns what to see, together saving computation by selecting only what is worth processing for a given task without relying on auxiliary signals. We show that LookThere only selects the task-specific input, excelling at sparse recognition in high-resolution settings (traffic signs, billiards), and maintaining accuracy with as little as 0.2% of the input. It generalizes across tasks and models, including global recognition (ImageNet classification), local recognition (ADE20K segmentation), zero-shot classification (by distillation), and regression (counting). Across all settings, LookThere surpasses state-of-the-art selection to provide a general and scalable framework for specialized and efficient adaptive computation.

AI.tldr: LookThere is an end-to-end reinforcement learning framework for adaptive computation in vision transformers that jointly trains a shallow input selector and a deep representation extractor, achieving state-of-the-art performance-compute trade-offs by learning to select only task-relevant tokens without relying on auxiliary heuristics.
AI.motivation: Vision transformers treat every image token as equally important, but for most computer vision tasks only a fraction of tokens are needed. Existing adaptive computation methods struggle at extreme sparsity and rely on heuristics (token diversity, attention scores) that may not generalize well across tasks.
AI.method: End-to-end reinforcement learning framework with two components: (1) a shallow input selector that learns where to look, and (2) a deep representation extractor that learns what to see. The selector and extractor are jointly trained to save computation by selecting only task-relevant input without relying on auxiliary signals.
AI.result: LookThere achieves extreme sparsity (using only 0.2% of input) while maintaining accuracy, excels at sparse recognition in high-resolution settings (traffic signs, billiards), and generalizes across diverse tasks including ImageNet classification, ADE20K segmentation, zero-shot classification via distillation, and regression (counting). It surpasses existing selection methods across all settings.
AI.conclusion: LookThere provides a general and scalable framework for specialized and efficient adaptive computation in vision transformers, achieving a new pareto frontier in performance-compute trade-offs without relying on heuristic auxiliary signals.

title: Extremely Sparse Supervision Incentivizes Reasoning Ability
summary: Large language models demonstrate increasingly strong reasoning capabilities through effective post-training. Yet, prevailing post-training methods optimize over massive numbers of tokens, implicitly assuming that effective learning must be token-intensive. We revisit this assumption in the on-policy distillation (OPD) setting, which naturally admits dense teacher supervision at every generated token. Using the Qwen3 family, we discover a counter-intuitive phenomenon: reasoning can be effectively incentivized by an extremely small fraction of generated tokens--as few as one or two tokens per reasoning trajectory, corresponding to only 0.05% of all tokens. Surprisingly, this sparse supervision in most cases matches or surpasses full-token training in improving reasoning ability, despite excluding the vast majority of generated tokens from the training objective. This phenomenon is consistently observed across nine teacher--student configurations spanning different model scales on mathematical reasoning tasks, and is further validated on coding reasoning, Llama models and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)-based reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR). Interestingly, such extremely sparse supervision may be closer to the natural learning process: rather than correcting every step word by word, one reflects on a few critical reasoning steps, updates prior understanding, and continues the trial-and-error, avoiding micro-level corrections while remaining remarkably effective. Overall, our results challenge the assumption that effective post-training must be token-intensive and point to a new direction for understanding and designing more efficient post-training algorithms.

AI.tldr: The paper challenges the prevailing assumption that effective post-training for large language models requires token-intensive learning. Through on-policy distillation (OPD) experiments with the Qwen3 family, the authors discover that reasoning can be effectively learned using only 0.05% of generated tokens (1-2 tokens per trajectory), matching or exceeding full-token training performance.
AI.motivation: Prevailing post-training methods assume effective learning must be token-intensive, optimizing over massive numbers of tokens. This work questions that assumption by exploring sparse supervision in on-policy distillation, where dense teacher supervision is available at every generated token.
AI.method: The authors conduct experiments across nine teacher-student configurations using the Qwen3 family, testing mathematical reasoning tasks. They validate findings on coding reasoning, Llama models, and PPO-based reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR). They systematically vary the sparsity of supervision from full-token training to extremely sparse (0.05% of tokens).
AI.result: Sparse supervision with just 1-2 tokens per reasoning trajectory (0.05% of all tokens) matches or surpasses full-token training in improving reasoning ability. This counter-intuitive phenomenon is consistently observed across diverse model scales, reasoning domains, and training paradigms (OPD and PPO-RLVR).
AI.conclusion: Effective post-training does not require token-intensive optimization. The authors propose that sparse supervision may better reflect natural learning processes - reflecting on critical reasoning steps rather than correcting every token. This opens a new direction for designing more efficient post-training algorithms and understanding the mechanisms of LLM reasoning development.

title: Representation Redundancy and Structural Complexity in Finite-Field Inversion
summary: The representation chosen for a mathematical operation can affect both its algebraic form and its empirical learning difficulty. We study this phenomenon for inversion over \(\mathbb F_{2^n}\), with field elements expressed in varying ordered \(\mathbb F_2\)-bases. We prove that two ordered bases induce the same coordinate inversion map if and only if they belong to the same Galois orbit. Since every orbit has size \(n\), the correspondence between ordered bases and distinct inversion maps is exactly \(n\)-to-one. We then analyze three Boolean formulations of inversion. The reference formulation has algebraic degree \(n-1\) and joint ANF leap \(1\), the mixed representation formulation has degree \(2(n-1)\) and joint ANF leap \(2\), and the complete raw formulation has degree at most \(3(n-1)\) and joint ANF leap at least \(n\). Exhaustive computations agree with the theoretical results and bounds in the cases considered. Controlled experiments with multilayer perceptrons show the same ordering in learning difficulty, while Galois orbit redundancy provides only a limited generalization benefit under the tested conditions. These results show that exact redundancy among representations can coexist with changes in Boolean structure and learning behavior when the representation is exposed as part of the input.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how different representations of finite field inversion (over F_{2^n}) affect algebraic complexity and machine learning difficulty. The key finding is that representations belonging to the same Galois orbit produce identical inversion maps (n-to-one correspondence), but their Boolean formulations vary significantly in algebraic degree and ANF leap. Experiments with multilayer perceptrons confirm that more complex Boolean representations are harder to learn.
AI.motivation: Understanding how mathematical representation choices impact both algebraic structure and learning difficulty is crucial for fields like cryptanalysis, circuit design, and machine learning. The specific case of finite field inversion provides a well-defined setting to study this phenomenon.
AI.method: The study combines theoretical analysis (group theory, Galois theory) with empirical validation (exhaustive computations and neural network experiments). Three Boolean formulations of inversion were analyzed: reference, mixed representation, and complete raw formulations.
AI.result: Key results: (1) Ordered bases induce the same coordinate inversion map iff they belong to the same Galois orbit (n-to-one correspondence); (2) Reference formulation has degree n-1 and joint ANF leap 1; (3) Mixed representation has degree 2(n-1) and joint ANF leap 2; (4) Complete raw formulation has degree ≤3(n-1) and joint ANF leap ≥ n; (5) Learning difficulty increases with Boolean complexity; (6) Galois orbit redundancy provides only limited generalization benefit.
AI.conclusion: Exact redundancy among representations (Galois orbits) can coexist with significant changes in Boolean structure and learning behavior when the representation is exposed as part of the input. This demonstrates that representation choices have concrete implications for both algebraic complexity and empirical learning difficulty.

title: Building a research-software catalog with a coding agent: from hackathon prototype to public deployment
summary: Generative AI and coding agents can accelerate research software development, but they also increase the need for efficient software discovery and maintenance. We developed a repository catalog during a three-day hackathon and subsequently examined the engineering required to make it suitable for public deployment, including adversarial review, data-quality checks, browser-level validation, and publication safeguards. We then explored whether the lessons learned from this prototype could be transferred to a much larger, human-curated portal, through a retrieval agent under development for MateriApps that combines curated portal metadata, external documentation, vector search, and local language-model generation. Implementation with coding agents was rapid, but achieving reliable operation required substantial additional engineering: the most consequential problems were not crashes but silent failures that produced plausible yet incomplete or incorrect outputs, arising from incomplete data acquisition, misleading assessments, and retrieval or preprocessing failures. These observations suggest that AI-assisted software portals require explicit validation, monitoring, and repeated review, and that curated metadata and maintained documentation remain essential. The MateriApps work is exploratory and remains under active development, so the observations reported for it are preliminary; a comparable combination of curated metadata, automatically collected documentation, and retrieval-based assistance may nevertheless be useful for extending other research-software portals.

AI.tldr: The paper explores using generative AI and coding agents to accelerate research software development, specifically for software discovery and maintenance. The authors developed a repository catalog prototype and then attempted to transfer lessons to a larger portal (MateriApps). They found that while AI-assisted implementation was rapid, achieving reliable operation required substantial additional engineering due to silent failures producing plausible but incorrect outputs.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address the increased need for efficient software discovery and maintenance in research software development, brought about by generative AI and coding agents that accelerate development but also create new challenges.
AI.method: The authors developed a repository catalog during a three-day hackathon, then examined engineering requirements for public deployment including adversarial review, data-quality checks, browser-level validation, and publication safeguards. They also explored transferring lessons to a larger portal (MateriApps) through a retrieval agent combining curated metadata, external documentation, vector search, and local language-model generation.
AI.result: Implementation with coding agents was rapid, but achieving reliable operation required substantial additional engineering. The most consequential problems were not crashes but silent failures producing plausible yet incomplete or incorrect outputs, arising from incomplete data acquisition, misleading assessments, and retrieval or preprocessing failures.
AI.conclusion: AI-assisted software portals require explicit validation, monitoring, and repeated review. Curated metadata and maintained documentation remain essential. The MateriApps work is exploratory and preliminary, but the approach of combining curated metadata, automatically collected documentation, and retrieval-based assistance may be useful for extending other research-software portals.

title: AngelFingerprint: A Traceable, Explainable, and White-Box Stealthy Watermark for Text-Guided Image Editing
summary: Text-guided diffusion editing raises disinformation concerns, making reliable image provenance essential. While watermarks are commonly used for this purpose, most methods carry a fixed ID that cannot explain what was changed and which prompt produced it. Furthermore, under open-source white-box access, attackers can easily locate and remove watermarks added as separate modules. Targeting this setting, we propose AngelFingerprint, a novel watermarking framework ensuring edit traceability, explainability, and white-box stealthiness. It integrates a LoRA into the diffusion model to embed the editing prompt's CLIP text embedding directly into the model's weights. An extractor then recovers this embedding from the image pixels alone. This semantic payload explains the edit, while the weight-integrated design makes it hard to detect and isolate even under full white-box access. Two techniques make this possible: a velocity-alignment anchor that preserves edit quality, and a specially designed frequency filter that keeps the watermark imperceptible yet recoverable and robust. On the MagicBrush dataset, our extractor achieves $86\%$ top-1 accuracy in a 200-way prompt retrieval, versus $20\%$ for prompt inversion.

AI.tldr: AngelFingerprint is a novel watermarking framework for text-guided diffusion editing that embeds the editing prompt's CLIP text embedding directly into the diffusion model's weights using LoRA, enabling edit traceability, explainability, and white-box stealthiness through a velocity-alignment anchor and frequency filter.
AI.motivation: Text-guided diffusion editing raises disinformation concerns, but existing watermarks cannot explain what was changed and which prompt produced it. Additionally, under open-source white-box access, attackers can easily locate and remove watermarks added as separate modules.
AI.method: The framework integrates a LoRA into the diffusion model to embed the editing prompt's CLIP text embedding directly into the model's weights. An extractor recovers this embedding from image pixels alone. Two key techniques enable this: (1) velocity-alignment anchor that preserves edit quality, and (2) a specially designed frequency filter that keeps the watermark imperceptible yet recoverable and robust.
AI.result: On the MagicBrush dataset, the extractor achieves 86% top-1 accuracy in a 200-way prompt retrieval, compared to 20% for prompt inversion.
AI.conclusion: AngelFingerprint successfully provides edit traceability, explainability, and white-box stealthiness for AI-generated images, significantly outperforming prior approaches like prompt inversion in prompt retrieval tasks.

title: Does the Selected Object Reach the Reader? Auditing Identity Handoffs in Grounded Language-Model Pipelines
comment: 15 pages, 1 figure, 23 tables. Accepted to the GroundLM Workshop (Grounding Language Models: Learning Faithfully and Efficiently) at EMNLP 2026
summary: Grounded language-model pipelines can be divided into three stages: selecting an object, retrieving passages for it, and using that evidence to answer. If the selected object must reach the reader, losing it breaks the handoff. Benchmark recall checks the dataset-linked object, which can differ. We audit 600 HybridQA questions across three selector families. On 1,463 resolvable records where the selected object matches the dataset-traced passage, exact key lookup and exact title matching return the object every time. With every ranked rule given the same decoded selected title, body-only BM25 omits it on 389 records (26.6%) at cutoff five, while hybrid retrieval with reranking omits it on 14 (1.0%). The two identities differ on 329 of 1,792 resolvable records. With original-question rankings, their top-five checks disagree on 106 records (5.9%). Frozen reader comparisons associate the aligned object's presence with 28.6 to 31.0 points higher exact match. In a deliberately selected 64-item cohort, removing that passage sharply lowers exact match, while removing a similar-length comparison passage does not reproduce the drop. We release the Returned-Object Profile (ROP), an executable record of the target, returned-ID field, cutoff, membership rule, and complete expected population, with data and an offline replay.

AI.tldr: This paper audits grounded language-model pipelines in HybridQA, examining whether selected objects (passages) are actually retrieved and how retrieval failures impact question answering accuracy. The study analyzes 600 questions across three selector families, comparing exact key lookup, exact title matching, body-only BM25, and hybrid retrieval with reranking.
AI.motivation: Grounded language-model pipelines have three stages: object selection, passage retrieval, and evidence-based answering. The critical issue is that if the selected object fails to be retrieved (broken "handoff"), the entire pipeline fails. Existing benchmarks check dataset-linked objects rather than the actual objects selected by the system, creating a gap in evaluation.
AI.method: The authors audited 600 HybridQA questions across three selector families. They examined 1,463 resolvable records where the selected object matched the dataset-traced passage, comparing exact key lookup, exact title matching, body-only BM25 (cutoff five), and hybrid retrieval with reranking. They also conducted a 64-item cohort experiment removing specific passages to test their impact on exact match.
AI.result: Exact key lookup and exact title matching returned the object 100% of the time. Body-only BM25 omitted the object on 389 records (26.6%) at cutoff five, while hybrid retrieval with reranking omitted it on only 14 records (1.0%). The two retrieval identities differed on 329 of 1,792 resolvable records. With original-question rankings, top-five checks disagreed on 106 records (5.9%). Frozen reader comparisons showed 28.6 to 31.0 points higher exact match when the aligned object was present.
