In the 64-item cohort, removing the target passage sharply lowered exact match, while removing a comparison passage did not reproduce the drop.
AI.conclusion: The study reveals significant handoff failures in retrieval systems, with body-only BM25 failing to retrieve selected objects in over a quarter of cases. Hybrid retrieval with reranking performs substantially better. The aligned object's presence strongly correlates with answer accuracy. The authors release the Returned-Object Profile (ROP) as an executable record for reproducibility.

title: GNN-Guided Graph Coarsening and Adaptive QUBO Penalties for the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows on a Quantum Annealer
summary:
Graph coarsening reduces the large Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) formulations arising when vehicle-routing problems are solved by quantum annealing. Nearby customers with compatible time windows are merged into super-nodes, the reduced problem is solved, and the solution is expanded to the original graph. For the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows (CVRPTW), existing coarsening heuristics require family-specific tuning and remain unreliable on random instances. We address these limitations on the Solomon benchmark using simulated annealing and a D-Wave Advantage2 processor.
  We first introduce adaptive penalty calibration. Uniform penalty scaling has little effect, whereas controlling the internal coefficient range substantially improves raw samples. Removing non-binding constraints, normalising binding ones, and scaling the remaining penalties reduces mean raw constraint violations from 33.0 to 0.06 at the same solver budget (p=3.7e-11, n=56). A variable-count-preserving control attributes this gain to conditioning rather than problem size.
  Second, we replace the hand-tuned merge score with a graph neural network (GNN) using one configuration across all families. At N=10, it achieves 100% feasibility across all Solomon families, including R-type (100% vs. 80% for the tuned heuristic). Across N=10,...,100, feasibility is 83% vs. 69%, with the GNN better or tied on 85/90 instance-size pairs. At N=80,100, the difference is significant (p=0.002; 25/25 pairs), while the QUBO remains approximately 5-6 times smaller.
  Finally, hardware experiments reproduce the conditioning effect at fixed logical variable count: feasible samples increase from 0.02% to 39% across 13 instances. Classical repair with local search remains a reference bound for end-to-end solution cost.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses limitations in graph coarsening for solving CVRPTW via quantum annealing. The authors propose adaptive penalty calibration and a GNN-based merge score, demonstrating significant improvements in feasibility and solution quality on the Solomon benchmark using both simulated annealing and D-Wave Advantage2 hardware.
AI.motivation: Existing graph coarsening heuristics for CVPTW require family-specific tuning and perform unreliably on random instances. The goal is to improve the coarsening process and penalty calibration to achieve better feasibility and solution quality when using quantum annealing.
AI.method: Three main approaches: (1) Adaptive penalty calibration by removing non-binding constraints, normalizing binding ones, and scaling remaining penalties; (2) Replacing hand-tuned merge score with a graph neural network (GNN) using one configuration across all families; (3) Hardware experiments on D-Wave Advantage2 processor.
AI.result: Adaptive calibration reduced mean raw constraint violations from 33.0 to 0.06 (p=3.7e-11). GNN achieved 100% feasibility at N=10 across all Solomon families (vs 80% for tuned heuristic on R-type). Across N=10-100, feasibility was 83% vs 69%, with GNN better/tied on 85/90 instance-size pairs. At N=80,100, difference was significant (p=0.002). Hardware experiments showed feasible samples increasing from 0.02% to 39% across 13 instances.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive penalty calibration and GNN-based merge scoring significantly improve graph coarsening for quantum annealing solvers, achieving high feasibility across all Solomon families while maintaining 5-6x QUBO size reduction. Classical repair with local search remains the best bound for end-to-end solution cost.

title: Same Request, Different Answer: Quantization Amplifies Cache-Induced Divergence in LLM Serving
summary: Prefix caching, in which a serving engine reuses the key and value tensors of a shared prompt prefix across requests, is enabled by default in the major open-source stacks and treated as a transparent optimization. We measure what it costs in reproducibility, and find that the cost rises sharply with weight quantization. Holding the model, decoding parameters, seed, and request order fixed, and issuing every request serially at batch size one, we ran an eighty-episode multi-turn agentic tool-use workload with caching enabled and disabled across two engines and four weight formats. Enabling the cache changed the agent's trajectory on 36.2 percent of episodes at 16-bit precision and on 75.0 percent at four-bit, a gradient that survives re-measurement under a controlled cache configuration. With caching disabled, repeated execution was bit-identical in every configuration, 0 of 800 episodes, which bounds other sources of nondeterminism at 0.5 percent. Repeated cache-enabled runs did diverge, and three experiments locate the cause: a single server-level prompt-cache setting moves run-to-run divergence by 37.5 percentage points, execution order acts only while that setting is active, and restoring cache state makes the cached and recompute paths each reproduce on 40 of 40 items while still differing from each other on 14. Cached serving is deterministic given cache state, and irreproducible in practice because that state is absent from the request and never reset by default. A single-turn bridge shows the divergence reaching task outcomes without shifting aggregate accuracy. We release the harness, logs, and analysis pipeline.

AI.tldr: Prefix caching in LLM serving systems, enabled by default in major open-source stacks, causes significant reproducibility issues that worsen with weight quantization. The study found that caching changed agent trajectories in 36.2% of episodes at 16-bit precision and 75.0% at 4-bit precision, while disabling caching resulted in 0% divergence across 800 episodes.
AI.motivation: To investigate the reproducibility costs of prefix caching in LLM serving systems, which is treated as a transparent optimization but may have hidden consequences for deterministic execution.
AI.method: Controlled experiments across two engines and four weight formats using an eighty-episode multi-turn agentic tool-use workload. The study fixed model, decoding parameters, seed, and request order while issuing requests serially at batch size one. They compared results with caching enabled vs. disabled, tested a server-level prompt-cache setting, and performed cache state restoration experiments.
AI.result: With caching enabled, 36.2% of episodes had altered agent trajectories at 16-bit precision, rising to 75.0% at 4-bit precision. With caching disabled, 0 of 800 episodes showed divergence (bounding nondeterminism at 0.5%). A single server-level prompt-cache setting shifted run-to-run divergence by 37.5 percentage points. Restoring cache state made both cached and recompute paths reproducible (40/40 items each) but still different from each other on 14 items.
AI.conclusion: Cached serving is deterministic given cache state, but irreproducible in practice because cache state is absent from requests and never reset by default. The divergence reaches task outcomes without necessarily shifting aggregate accuracy. This represents a significant hidden cost of prefix caching that practitioners should be aware of.

title: Counting Beyond Instances: A Benchmark for Group-Individual Object Counting
summary: Visual counting is commonly formulated at the instance level, aiming to estimate how many objects of a queried category appear in an image. However, real-world counting often involves higher-level semantic units formed by multiple instances, such as a bunch of grapes, a stack of plates, or a pair of shoes. This exposes a key limitation of existing counting formulations, which mainly focus on what to count, while largely overlooking at which semantic unit to count. We introduce Group-Individual Object Counting (GIC), a new setting that requires models to count both individual objects and semantic groups within a unified framework. To support this new task, we present BunchCount, a real-world benchmark with 1,330 images, 89,254 individual annotations, and 11,065 group annotations. BunchCount provides paired individual-group annotations within the same image and explicitly records containment relations between each group and its constituent individuals. Experiments on BunchCount show that current advanced counting models perform well on individual instances but fail to count semantic groups more accurately. To mitigate semantic granularity conflict, we propose a counting-unit guided relational counting framework, which exploits group-individual containment relations to regularize cross-granularity representations during training. Our method substantially improves group-level counting while better preserving individual-level counting ability, establishing a strong baseline for counting beyond instances.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Group-Individual Object Counting (GIC), a new counting task that requires counting both individual objects and semantic groups (e.g., bunch of grapes, stack of plates) within a unified framework. The authors present BunchCount, a benchmark dataset with 1,330 images containing 89,254 individual and 11,065 group annotations with explicit containment relations.
AI.motivation: Existing visual counting formulations focus on instance-level counting (counting individual objects), but real-world counting often involves higher-level semantic units formed by multiple instances. This semantic granularity conflict—counting at different semantic levels—has been overlooked in prior work.
AI.method: The authors propose a counting-unit guided relational counting framework that exploits group-individual containment relations to regularize cross-granularity representations during training. This approach addresses the semantic granularity conflict by using containment relations as supervision signals.
AI.result: Experiments on BunchCount show that current advanced counting models perform well on individual instances but struggle with semantic group counting. The proposed method substantially improves group-level counting while better preserving individual-level counting ability, establishing a strong baseline for the new task.
AI.conclusion: This work opens a new research direction for counting beyond instances by introducing the GIC task and a corresponding dataset. The proposed framework effectively bridges the gap between individual and group-level counting, demonstrating the importance of considering semantic granularity in visual counting tasks.

title: $τ^τ$-Bench: An Environment for End-To-End, Realistic Agent Construction
summary: LLM agents are rapidly becoming production software, deployed to handle customer service, adjudicate disputes, and operate internal systems. Notably, the work of building them is increasingly handed to coding agents, yet existing benchmarks say little about whether an AI system can deliver one under the conditions of a real client engagement. We introduce $τ^τ$-bench (pronounced hyper-tau-bench), a benchmark that makes agent construction the task. A developer agent is given the records a business actually keeps, a client who holds requirements, a production API that operations must run through, a codebase to inherit, and limits on serving cost and models: the same starting point a real engagement provides. From these it must deliver a complete customer-service agent, scored by deploying that agent against held-out simulated users. Across 53 tasks spanning four domains, the strongest configuration, Claude Opus 5 under Claude Code, passes just 23.9% of evaluation simulations. Meanwhile, an expert-authored reference ceiling scores 82.2%. The failures mirror ones human agent developers see: models issue shallow queries in place of deep comprehension of the records, communicate almost nothing to the client, and experiment too little with agent architecture and serving spend, shipping the first design that runs. We aim for $τ^τ$-bench to turn the work of cooperative agent building into a measurable target for coding agents.

AI.tldr: ττ-bench (hyper-tau-bench) is a benchmark that evaluates AI systems' ability to build production LLM agents under realistic client engagement conditions, rather than testing agent performance directly. Given realistic inputs (business records, client requirements, production API, codebase, cost limits), the AI must deliver a complete customer-service agent scored by deployment against simulated users.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are increasingly deployed in production (customer service, dispute adjudication, internal systems), yet existing benchmarks only evaluate agent performance, not the ability to build agents. Additionally, AI coding agents are increasingly tasked with building these systems, but there's no way to measure whether they can do so under real-world engagement conditions.
AI.method: The benchmark provides AI developers with: (1) actual business records, (2) client requirements, (3) a production API, (4) an inherited codebase, and (5) cost/model constraints. The AI must deliver a complete customer-service agent, which is then evaluated by deploying it against held-out simulated users across 53 tasks in four domains.
AI.result: Claude Opus 5 under Claude Code (strongest configuration) passes only 23.9% of evaluation simulations. An expert-authored reference ceiling scores 82.2%. Common failure modes include: issuing shallow queries instead of deep record comprehension, poor communication with clients, and insufficient experimentation with agent architecture and cost optimization—shipping the first working design rather than iterating.
AI.conclusion: ττ-bench reveals a significant gap between current AI capabilities and expert human developers in building production LLM agents. The benchmark aims to make cooperative agent building a measurable target for coding agents, addressing the growing need for AI systems that can deliver real production software under authentic client engagement conditions.

title: Too Rare to Learn: Prescribed Cyclone Tracks Degrade a Bay of Bengal Ocean Emulator
comment: 11 pages, 7 figures. In review at the NeurIPS 2026 Tackling Climate Change with Machine Learning workshop
summary: Neural ocean emulators are being proposed for regional forecasting in cyclone-exposed coastal seas, and a natural design choice is to hand the network the cyclone as a prescribed input. We test that choice in the Bay of Bengal and find it harmful. We withhold 15 whole cyclones spanning 65 to 150 kt from GLORYS12 reanalysis and compare two U-Nets that are identical except for four prescribed cyclone-track channels. Across three seeds the ocean-only model beats persistence in every run and the storm-conditioned model loses to it in every run, with the two skill ranges disjoint (p = 3.1e-5, paired across storms). The cause is exposure frequency rather than signal content: the channels are non-zero on only 7.9% of training days, so they are out of distribution the moment they activate. The extra error falls inside the prescribed storm footprint, and replacing the real cyclone map with a no-storm map at inference improves held-out storm forecasts by 7.5 to 16.4% in every seed. The conditioned network has learned a response to a rare signal that is confidently wrong.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether providing cyclone track information as input to neural ocean emulators improves regional forecasting in the Bay of Bengal. The authors find that this "storm-conditioned" approach actually degrades forecast performance compared to both persistence baselines and ocean-only models, because cyclone tracks are too rare (7.9% of training days) for the network to learn reliable responses.
AI.motivation: Neural ocean emulators are being proposed for regional forecasting in cyclone-exposed coastal seas. A natural design choice is to provide the cyclone track as a prescribed input to the network. This paper questions whether this choice is actually beneficial.
AI.method: The authors withheld 15 whole cyclones (spanning 65 to 150 kt) from GLORYS12 reanalysis and compared two U-Net architectures that are identical except that one includes four prescribed cyclone-track channels. They tested across three random seeds and evaluated against persistence baseline.
AI.result: The ocean-only model beats persistence in every run, while the storm-conditioned model loses to persistence in every run. The skill ranges are statistically disjoint (p = 3.1e-5, paired across storms). The cause is exposure frequency rather than signal content: cyclone channels are non-zero on only 7.9% of training days. Replacing the real cyclone map with a no-storm map at inference improves held-out storm forecasts by 7.5 to 16.4% in every seed.
AI.conclusion: The storm-conditioned network learns a response to a rare signal that is confidently wrong. The key insight is that providing rare event information as input to neural networks can actually harm predictions because the network cannot reliably learn from insufficient exposure. This challenges the intuition that providing more information (cyclone tracks) should improve forecasts.

title: Better Understanding, Better Fixes? A Study of Hallucination in LLM-based Automated Program Repair
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have significantly advanced automated program repair (APR), yet existing evaluations remain largely result-centric and provide limited insight into hallucination during repair. In APR, hallucination may arise not only in final patches but also in the intermediate artifacts that guide patch generation. To address this gap, we perform a multi-layered analysis of hallucination throughout the APR process. Specifically, we characterize hallucination as the production of patches or intermediate artifacts that are not faithfully grounded in the available repair evidence. We examine repair hallucination in final patches and understanding hallucination in intermediate artifacts through three tasks, namely triggering testcase identification, line coverage prediction, and additional testcase generation.We then evaluate three representative LLMs on 832 Defects4J bugs through automatic evaluation and manual analysis. Our results show that both repair and understanding hallucinations remain prevalent. Across models and settings, only 21.0%-55.9% of generated patches pass the developer-written test suite. Moreover, although more accurate intermediate artifacts are generally associated with successful repairs, this relationship does not always hold. Manual analysis of 812 sampled repairs identifies repair hallucinations in 72.7% of cases, including patches that pass all available tests; incorrect causal localization and incorrect repair strategies account for 45.9% and 18.5% of these hallucinations, respectively. Meanwhile, models frequently misidentify triggering testcases, mispredict line coverage involving branching control flow, and generate additional testcases with missing bug-triggering conditions or incorrect expected behavior.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates hallucination in large language models (LLMs) for automated program repair (APR). The authors perform a multi-layered analysis examining hallucination not only in final patches but also in intermediate artifacts (triggering testcase identification, line coverage prediction, and additional testcase generation). Evaluation on 832 Defects4J bugs reveals that only 21.0%-55.9% of generated patches pass tests, with manual analysis showing 72.7% of repairs contain hallucination, including patches that pass all available tests.
AI.motivation: Existing APR evaluations are result-centric and provide limited insight into hallucination during repair. Hallucination can occur in both final patches and intermediate artifacts that guide patch generation, which is a gap the authors aim to address.
AI.method: The authors characterize hallucination as production of patches or intermediate artifacts not faithfully grounded in available repair evidence. They examine repair hallucination in final patches and understanding hallucination in intermediate artifacts through three tasks: triggering testcase identification, line coverage prediction, and additional testcase generation. Three representative LLMs are evaluated on 832 Defects4J bugs through automatic evaluation and manual analysis.
AI.result: Only 21.0%-55.9% of generated patches pass the developer-written test suite. 72.7% of sampled repairs contain hallucination, including patches that pass all tests. Incorrect causal localization accounts for 45.9% and incorrect repair strategies for 18.5% of hallucinations. Models frequently misidentify triggering testcases, mispredict line coverage involving branching control flow, and generate additional testcases with missing bug-triggering conditions or incorrect expected behavior.
AI.conclusion: Both repair and understanding hallucinations remain prevalent in LLM-based APR. While more accurate intermediate artifacts are generally associated with successful repairs, this relationship does not always hold. The study highlights the need to address hallucination at all levels of the APR process.

title: HiSfM: Disambiguating Structure-from-Motion via Scaffold-Anchored Hierarchical Reconstruction
summary: Structure-from-Motion (SfM) is a fundamental tool for sparse 3D reconstruction with broad impact in robotics and vision, supporting mapping, localization, and large-scale scene modeling. However, conventional pipelines often fail under hard visual ambiguity caused by repeated or symmetric structures, and incur heavy computational cost due to redundant cameras and constraints. We present HiSfM, a hierarchical coarse-to-fine SfM framework that improves robustness and efficiency through scaffold construction. HiSfM first forms strong local communities using geometrical induced heuristics, then connects communities with a compact yet strong skeleton by packing edge-disjoint spanning trees (EDST) while verifying skeletal edges with a two-view disambiguator. We reconstruct a stable scaffold on this verified skeleton, serving as an anchor to capture the essence of the scene, and subsequently absorb remaining images via efficient registration and triangulation for further refinements. Experiments on ambiguity-focused benchmarks and general datasets show that HiSfM prevents ambiguity-induced failures while substantially reducing runtime compared to previous methods, and improves completeness over aggressive sparsification methods. Code is available at https://github.com/3dv-casia/HiSfM.

AI.tldr: HiSfM is a hierarchical coarse-to-fine Structure-from-Motion framework that improves robustness against visual ambiguity (repeated/symmetric structures) and reduces computational cost through scaffold construction, using edge-disjoint spanning trees and a two-view disambiguator for verification.
AI.motivation: Conventional SfM pipelines fail under hard visual ambiguity caused by repeated or symmetric structures, and incur heavy computational cost due to redundant cameras and constraints. There is a need for a more robust and efficient approach.
AI.method: HiSfM forms strong local communities using geometrical induced heuristics, then connects communities with a compact skeleton by packing edge-disjoint spanning trees (EDST) while verifying skeletal edges with a two-view disambiguator. A stable scaffold is reconstructed on this verified skeleton, serving as an anchor to capture the scene's essence. Remaining images are absorbed via efficient registration and triangulation for further refinements.
AI.result: Experiments on ambiguity-focused benchmarks and general datasets show that HiSfM prevents ambiguity-induced failures while substantially reducing runtime compared to previous methods, and improves completeness over aggressive sparsification methods.
AI.conclusion: HiSfM successfully addresses both robustness and efficiency challenges in SfM through its hierarchical scaffold-based approach, demonstrating improved performance on ambiguous scenes and reduced computational cost.

title: Leveraging Imperfect Restoration for Data Availability Attack
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2024. Equal contribution by Yi Huang, Jeremy Styborski, Mingzhi Lyu - cite in any order
summary: The abundance of online data is at risk of unauthorized usage in training deep learning models. To counter this, various Data Availability Attacks (DAAs) have been devised to make data unlearnable for such models by subtly perturbing the training data. However, existing attacks often excel against either Supervised Learning (SL) or Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) scenarios. Among these, a model-free approach that generates a Convolution-based Unlearnable Dataset (CUDA) stands out as the most robust DAA across both SSL and SL. Nonetheless, CUDA's effectiveness against SSL is underwhelming and it faces a severe trade-off between image quality and its poisoning effect. In this paper, we conduct a theoretical analysis of CUDA, uncovering the sub-optimal gradients it introduces and elucidating the strategy it employs to induce class-wise bias for data poisoning. Building on this, we propose a novel poisoning method named Imperfect Restoration Poisoning (IRP), aiming to preserve high image quality while achieving strong poisoning effects. Through extensive comparisons of IRP with eight baselines across SL and SSL, coupled with evaluations alongside five representative defense methods, we showcase the superiority of IRP. Code: https://github.com/lyumingzhi/IRP

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the problem of unauthorized use of online data in training deep learning models by proposing Imperfect Restoration Poisoning (IRP), a novel Data Availability Attack (DAA) that achieves strong poisoning effects while preserving high image quality. The method builds on a theoretical analysis of the existing CUDA approach, which reveals its sub-optimal gradients and class-wise bias strategy.
AI.motivation: The abundance of online data is at risk of unauthorized usage in training deep learning models. Existing Data Availability Attacks (DAAs) excel against either Supervised Learning (SL) or Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) but not both. The state-of-the-art CUDA approach, while robust across both scenarios, suffers from underwhelming effectiveness against SSL and a severe trade-off between image quality and poisoning effect.
AI.method: The paper conducts a theoretical analysis of CUDA to uncover its sub-optimal gradients and class-wise bias strategy for data poisoning. Based on this analysis, a novel poisoning method called Imperfect Restoration Poisoning (IRP) is proposed, which aims to preserve high image quality while achieving strong poisoning effects. The method is evaluated through extensive comparisons with eight baselines across SL and SSL, and alongside five representative defense methods.
AI.result: The proposed IRP method demonstrates superiority over eight baseline methods across both SL and SSL scenarios, while also showing effectiveness against five representative defense methods. The method successfully achieves a better balance between image quality and poisoning effect compared to the existing CUDA approach.
AI.conclusion: The proposed IRP method successfully addresses the limitations of existing DAAs by providing strong poisoning effects against both SL and SSL while preserving high image quality. The theoretical analysis of CUDA provides valuable insights into the mechanisms of data poisoning, which informed the design of IRP. This work contributes to the field of data protection against unauthorized model training.

title: SMILE: Bridging Continuous Optimization and Discrete Symbolic Recovery
summary: Symbolic regression (SR) discovers closed-form mathematical expressions from data, offering interpretability beyond black-box models. Existing methods suffer from slow convergence in combinatorial search spaces and lack mechanisms to exploit compositional structure in the data. We introduce SMILE (Sine, Multiplication, Identity, Logarithm, Exponential), a hybrid framework that unifies continuous gradient-based optimization with discrete symbolic recovery through three stages: structural analysis of the data to identify the compositional hierarchy of the target expression, continuous optimization to learn parameters of a network that encodes the target expression using interpretable activations, and symbolic recovery through structured pruning, coefficient optimization, and rounding. This final stage distills the learned network into a compact expression with exact symbolic constants. We evaluate SMILE on SRBench across ground-truth and black-box datasets, with ablation studies validating each component. SMILE achieves the highest symbolic solution rate at the largest noise levels, demonstrating strong robustness where competing methods degrade substantially. It consistently lies on the Pareto front of accuracy versus complexity, recovering significantly simpler expressions in a fraction of the time required by the competing methods.

AI.tldr: SMILE is a hybrid symbolic regression framework that combines continuous gradient-based optimization with discrete symbolic recovery through three stages: structural analysis, continuous optimization using interpretable activations, and symbolic recovery via pruning and rounding. It achieves highest symbolic solution rates at high noise levels and lies on the Pareto front of accuracy vs complexity.
AI.motivation: Existing symbolic regression methods suffer from slow convergence in combinatorial search spaces and lack mechanisms to exploit compositional structure in data.
AI.method: Three-stage hybrid framework: (1) Structural analysis to identify compositional hierarchy, (2) Continuous optimization with interpretable activation network, (3) Symbolic recovery through structured pruning, coefficient optimization, and rounding.
AI.result: SMILE achieves highest symbolic solution rate at largest noise levels with strong robustness. It consistently lies on Pareto front of accuracy vs complexity, recovering simpler expressions faster than competitors.
AI.conclusion: SMILE successfully unifies gradient-based optimization with discrete symbolic recovery, demonstrating superior robustness to noise and better accuracy-complexity trade-offs compared to existing SR methods on SRBench.

title: ARIA - An Agentic Framework for Autonomous Testing of Infotainment Systems
summary: Automotive infotainment validation still relies on manual testing, slow, costly, and incompatible with agile releases and OTA updates. Scripted automation only partly helps: it couples test logic to implementation, yielding brittle, high-maintenance suites. Existing LLM-driven frameworks mostly target web/mobile apps, using single- or dual-agent setups that overload one or two models with perception, planning, action selection, and validation at once, prone to hallucinations and unproductive exploration loops given infotainment complexity. We present ARIA (Autonomous Real-time Infotainment Assessment), a multi-agent LLM framework that autonomously runs end-to-end tests on Android infotainment systems via visual interaction, using a closed-loop pipeline of four specialized agents per step plus a report stage. From single-sentence scenarios (path, action, expected outcome), ARIA runs the interactions and produces reports, reproducible scripts, and visual evidence per step. Evaluated on a manufacturer's physical Android infotainment system across 30 scenarios, ARIA completed 28 (93.3%) with a verdict (2 errored), 20 of which (71.4%) matched ground truth. It caught all 5 known defects, no fault passed as working; its 8 false positives stem from navigation/image limits and unsupported gestures, showing multi-agent LLMs can run infotainment tests industrially while exposing the cost of a low false-positive tolerance. A single-agent baseline confirms the multi-agent design's value: on the first pass, before stronger-model revisitation narrows the gap, it shows a far higher false-positive rate (72.0% vs. 52.6%), conflating navigational difficulty with system failure. We report first-pass/post-revisitation results, token/call/cost per scenario, and show via repeated runs that stability tracks complexity, with fault detection perfectly consistent, pointing to CI integration of visual testing.

AI.tldr: ARIA is a multi-agent LLM framework that autonomously runs end-to-end tests on Android infotainment systems via visual interaction. Using a closed-loop pipeline of four specialized agents plus a report stage, it completed 93.3% of scenarios with 71.4% ground truth match, detected all 5 known defects, and significantly outperformed a single-agent baseline (52.6% vs 72.0% false positive rate).
AI.motivation: Automotive infotainment validation currently relies on manual testing, which is slow, costly, and incompatible with agile releases and OTA updates. Scripted automation couples test logic to implementation, creating brittle, high-maintenance test suites. Existing LLM-driven frameworks target web/mobile apps with single- or dual-agent setups that overload models with multiple tasks, leading to hallucinations and unproductive exploration loops given infotainment complexity.
AI.method: ARIA uses a closed-loop pipeline with four specialized agents per step plus a report stage. The system takes single-sentence scenarios (path, action, expected outcome) and runs interactions autonomously, producing reports, reproducible scripts, and visual evidence per step. Evaluation was performed on a physical Android infotainment system across 30 scenarios, with comparison to a single-agent baseline.
AI.result: ARIA completed 28 of 30 scenarios (93.3%) with a verdict. 20 scenarios (71.4%) matched ground truth. It detected all 5 known defects with zero faults passing as working. 8 false positives stemmed from navigation/image limits and unsupported gestures. Compared to single-agent baseline: first-pass false positive rate was 72.0% vs 52.6% (multi-agent). Post-revisitation narrowed this gap. Fault detection was perfectly consistent across repeated runs.
AI.conclusion: ARIA demonstrates that multi-agent LLM frameworks can autonomously run end-to-end tests on Android infotainment systems with high accuracy. The system achieved 93.3% completion rate (28/30 scenarios), with 71.4% ground truth match. It detected all 5 known defects with zero missed faults. The multi-agent design significantly outperforms single-agent baselines (52.6% vs 72.0% false positive rate), and stability correlates with task complexity. The approach enables CI integration of visual testing for automotive infotainment validation.

title: Bridging Modalities and Tasks: A Unified Hierarchical ViT for SAR-to-Optical Translation and Semantic Segmentation
summary: Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) images have all-weather, day-and-night observation capabilities. However, compared with optical images, their speckle noise and non-intuitive scattering mechanism limit the interpretability of the images. Generative models for SAR-to-optical (S2O) conversion can improve visual interpretability, but existing methods often ignore the constraints on semantic structure, which are necessary for downstream tasks, for the sake of visual effects. We propose a unified collaborative dual-task learning framework, termed BMT (Bridging Modalities and Tasks), that jointly optimizes S2O image translation and semantic segmentation through a shared hierarchical Vision Transformer. The framework integrates: (1) a LocalViTBlock that fuses global self-attention with spatial depthwise convolution through a learnable gating mechanism; (2) an enhanced output module combining multi-scale refinement processing, color correction and anti-aliasing, which calibrates channel-level color statistics through feature fusion; (3) a ControlNet-style conditional injection mechanism that encodes SAR wavelet features and segmentation labels into a multi-scale feature pyramid and injects them at each encoder layer through zero-initialized convolution; (4) a bounded Kendall uncertainty weighting scheme that prevents either task from dominating the shared representation. We evaluate the framework under both paired and unpaired translation settings, on the public WHU-OPT-SAR paired dataset and a self-constructed unpaired ship dataset built from HRSID and DIOR, respectively. The experimental results show that the proposed method achieves competitive S2O translation quality and semantic segmentation performance. The dataset and source code have been publicly released at https://github.com/Lewisyuaner/BMT-S2O-main.

AI.tldr: BMT (Bridging Modalities and Tasks) is a unified dual-task learning framework that jointly optimizes SAR-to-optical image translation and semantic segmentation using a shared hierarchical Vision Transformer, addressing the interpretability limitations of SAR images while preserving semantic structure for downstream tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing SAR-to-optical conversion methods focus on visual quality but ignore semantic structure constraints needed for downstream tasks. SAR images have inherent limitations including speckle noise and non-intuitive scattering mechanisms that reduce interpretability compared to optical images.
AI.method: The framework uses a shared hierarchical Vision Transformer with four key components: (1) LocalViTBlock fusing global self-attention with spatial depthwise convolution via learnable gating; (2) Enhanced output module with multi-scale refinement, color correction, and anti-aliasing; (3) ControlNet-style conditional injection encoding SAR wavelet features and segmentation labels into a multi-scale feature pyramid injected at each encoder layer through zero-initialized convolution; (4) Bounded Kendall uncertainty weighting to prevent task domination in shared representation.
AI.result: The method achieves competitive S2O translation quality and semantic segmentation performance on both the paired WHU-OPT-SAR dataset and a self-constructed unpaired ship dataset (from HRSID and DIOR).
AI.conclusion: The BMT framework successfully bridges modalities and tasks by jointly optimizing SAR-to-optical translation and semantic segmentation, providing improved visual interpretability while maintaining structural constraints necessary for downstream applications.

title: SiLR: Structure-Preserving Admission and Process Reward for LLM Tool Agents
comment: 13 pages, 8 figures, 6 tables. Appendix includes full proofs, attack-family constructions, and the extended process-reward study
summary: A runtime gate for an LLM tool agent is usually cast as a filter. In a ReAct loop a rejected proposal is followed by another at the same state, so the gate is a search operator over the proposal stream whose admission criterion shapes which trajectories are reachable. We study post-violation recovery admission, where progress must be admitted while the system is still in violation, and identify the scalar projection trap: an aggregate-score gate accepts a locally improving proposal and commits the trajectory to a plateau. SiLR instead shadow-executes each proposal and admits it under a product order over the branch-level violation state (overloaded-branch support and per-branch severity). We prove that no scalar surrogate is sound for this order, so the failure is representational, not a matter of threshold tuning. On mined Gym-ANM scenarios, SiLR recovers 21/21 multi-action episodes against 0/21 for terminal and 9/21 for the best scalar gate, significant across the full 24-scenario benchmark. The terminal-versus-structured dichotomy holds across three model families and in CityLearn. Because admission rests on deterministic simulation, the LLM lies outside the trust boundary: a magnitude-redistribution attack that defeats both scalar and support-only baselines is contained only by the full per-branch predicate. With two constraint families active, every tested scalar projection admits physically unsafe actions; support-only admits the largest fraction (63.2% of 42,410; product order 0). In the hardest dual-family traces, scalar gates recover only through that unsafe class. Reused as a GRPO process reward, it outperforms its count projection in every mined scenario and is the only tested reward whose ungated policy exceeds the untrained base (0.844 vs. 0.778). Scalar projection loses the violation geometry at both design points; only the full product order is structurally sufficient.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SiLR, a runtime gate mechanism for LLM tool agents that uses shadow-execution with a product order over branch-level violation state (overloaded-branch support and per-branch severity) to handle post-violation recovery admission. The key insight is that scalar projection gates fail due to a representational problem (not threshold tuning), as they trap trajectories in plateaus by accepting locally improving proposals. SiLR achieves 21/21 multi-action episode recoveries in Gym-ANM scenarios versus 0/21 for terminal gates and 9/21 for the best scalar gate, and contains magnitude-redistribution attacks that defeat both scalar and support-only baselines.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address a fundamental limitation in LLM tool agents: when a runtime gate rejects a proposal in a ReAct loop, the system attempts another proposal at the same state. Existing scalar aggregate-score gates suffer from the "scalar projection trap" - they accept locally improving proposals that commit trajectories to plateaus, failing to recover from violations while still in violation state. The authors seek a gate mechanism that can admit progress while the system remains in violation, without sacrificing safety.
AI.method: The proposed method SiLR uses shadow-execution of each proposal and admits it under a product order over the branch-level violation state, which combines overloaded-branch support and per-branch severity. This is fundamentally different from scalar projection gates that use aggregate scores. The key theoretical contribution is proving that no scalar surrogate is sound for this product order - the failure is representational, not a matter of tuning thresholds.
AI.result: SiLR recovers 21/21 multi-action episodes in mined Gym-ANM scenarios, compared to 0/21 for terminal gates and 9/21 for the best scalar gate (statistically significant across the 24-scenario benchmark). This terminal-versus-structured dichotomy holds across three model families and in CityLearn. With two constraint families active, every tested scalar projection admits physically unsafe actions (63.2% of 42,410 cases for support-only, 0% for product order). The full per-branch predicate contains magnitude-redistribution attacks that defeat both scalar and support-only baselines. When reused as a GRPO process reward, it outperforms count projection in every mined scenario and is the only tested reward whose ungated policy exceeds the untrained base (0.844 vs. 0.778).
AI.conclusion: Scalar projection loses the violation geometry at both design points - it fails both as a simple aggregate and even with support-only modifications. Only the full product order over branch-level violation state is structurally sufficient for post-violation recovery in LLM tool agents. This represents a fundamental architectural insight: the LLM lies outside the trust boundary because admission rests on deterministic simulation, and safe recovery requires per-branch predicates rather than any scalar approximation.

title: Interpretability for Turing Machines
comment: 75 pages, 31 figures, 3 tables. Interactive companion: https://tminterp.timaeus.co. Code and data: doi:10.5281/zenodo.22205895
summary: We show that susceptibilities, an interpretability technique developed for neural networks, can identify the presence of algorithmic structure in Turing machines by probing the local loss landscape of a learning problem for noisy Turing machines introduced by Murfet and Troiani (arXiv:2504.08075). We prove that symmetries and path separation in the algorithm implemented by a Turing machine induce permutation symmetries and low-rank blocks in its susceptibility matrix. We study this empirically on a set of deterministic finite automata (DFAs) and demonstrate that algorithmic features can be recovered by principal component analysis and clustering methods in susceptibility space.

AI.tldr: This paper applies susceptibilities, an interpretability technique from neural networks, to identify algorithmic structure in Turing machines by analyzing the local loss landscape of noisy Turing machines. The authors prove that algorithmic symmetries and path separation manifest as specific matrix structures, and demonstrate empirically on DFAs that PCA and clustering can recover algorithmic features from susceptibility data.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to bridge interpretability techniques from deep learning with formal language theory. Specifically, the authors aim to show that susceptibilities—a technique developed for analyzing neural networks—can effectively identify and recover algorithmic structure in computational models like Turing machines and finite automata.
AI.method: The methodology involves: (1) Probing the local loss landscape of a learning problem for noisy Turing machines (building on Murfet and Troiani's work); (2) Proving that symmetries and path separation in algorithms induce permutation symmetries and low-rank blocks in susceptibility matrices; (3) Empirical validation on deterministic finite automata (DFAs) using principal component analysis (PCA) and clustering methods to recover algorithmic features from susceptibility space.
AI.result: The authors demonstrate that algorithmic features can be successfully recovered through PCA and clustering in susceptibility space. The theoretical analysis establishes that specific algorithmic properties (symmetries, path separation) directly correspond to structural patterns in the susceptibility matrix.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a connection between neural network interpretability and formal language theory, showing that susceptibility analysis can serve as a tool for detecting and recovering algorithmic structure in computational models.

title: An Empirical Study on Learning Paths and Gender Dynamics in Scrum Master Roles
summary:
Context: Agile development methodology has been widely adopted by industry and the demand for experienced professionals in Agile-related roles is persistently high. Objectives: We focus on the learning path for a Scrum Master role in multicultural software companies and investigate the role in relation to team size, together with the learning process for a career path, and how companies monitor soft skills development. Method: We conducted our study in two phases, two qualitative surveys (interview studies) and performed a qualitative and quantitative data analysis of the results. Conclusions: Our results identified that the need for a Scrum Master (SM) depends on the size of the team, with our study indicating a six-member limit. There is no overall standardized process for soft skills learning or metrics to measure progress. Some companies measure soft skills based on feedback received from the client or from the team, and other companies are taking both types of feedback into consideration. Many learning initiatives, especially on soft skills for an SM role, were based on actions of the employees.
  The version of Record of this contribution is published in Software Engineering and Advanced Applications. SEAA 2025. Lecture Notes in Computer Science, vol 16083. Springer, Cham. and available online at: check DOI.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the Scrum Master role in multicultural software companies, focusing on learning paths, team size implications, career development, and soft skills monitoring. Study findings indicate a six-member team limit for SM necessity, lack of standardized soft skills learning processes, and varied feedback-based measurement approaches.
AI.motivation: The demand for experienced Agile professionals, particularly Scrum Masters, remains high in the industry. However, there is limited research on how Scrum Masters should be trained, how their role varies with team size, and how companies track soft skills development - especially in multicultural settings.
AI.method: Two-phase study consisting of two qualitative surveys (interview studies) with qualitative and quantitative data analysis of the results.
AI.result: The study found that the need for a Scrum Master depends on team size, with a six-member limit identified. No standardized process exists for soft skills learning or progress metrics. Companies measure soft skills through client feedback, team feedback, or both. Learning initiatives for SM roles, particularly in soft skills, are often employee-driven.
AI.conclusion: Team size is a critical factor in determining Scrum Master necessity (six-member threshold). The industry lacks standardized soft skills development frameworks for SM roles, with measurement approaches varying across organizations. Professional development in this area is largely self-directed rather than systematically managed by companies.

title: Where to Look Matters: Learning Influential Views for VLM-based 3D Visual Grounding
summary: Recent zero-shot 3D visual grounding methods leverage vision-language models (VLMs) to localize objects in 3D scenes from natural language queries. However, these methods typically rely on heuristic rules to select which camera views are provided to the VLM, often prioritizing object visibility rather than grounding relevance. We present IVSGround, a framework that learns Influential View Selection for VLM-based 3D visual grounding. Instead of using fixed heuristics, a lightweight view selector is trained to identify views that provide discriminative evidence for grounding. To obtain supervision signals, we generate training signals using feedback from a reasoning VLM through a two-stage rejection sampling process. During inference, the learned selector predicts query-conditioned influential views for each candidate object, which are then evaluated by a frozen reasoning VLM through comparative grounding. Experiments on ScanRefer and NR3D show that IVSGround consistently improves grounding accuracy over existing zero-shot pipelines, demonstrating that selecting where to look is crucial for effective 3D visual grounding. Project page: https://ivsground.github.io/

AI.tldr: IVSGround is a novel framework that learns to select influential views for VLM-based zero-shot 3D visual grounding, replacing heuristic view selection with a learned selector that identifies discriminative views guided by feedback from a reasoning VLM.
AI.motivation: Zero-shot 3D visual grounding methods using VLMs typically rely on heuristic rules to select camera views, prioritizing object visibility rather than grounding relevance. This suboptimal view selection limits grounding accuracy.
AI.method: 1) Train a lightweight view selector to identify discriminative views for grounding instead of using fixed heuristics. 2) Generate training signals using feedback from a reasoning VLM through a two-stage rejection sampling process. 3) During inference, the learned selector predicts query-conditioned influential views for each candidate object. 4) A frozen reasoning VLM evaluates these views through comparative grounding.
AI.result: IVSGround consistently improves grounding accuracy over existing zero-shot pipelines on both ScanRefer and NR3D benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Selecting where to look is crucial for effective 3D visual grounding. The learned view selection approach outperforms heuristic-based methods, demonstrating the importance of query-conditioned influential view selection.

title: A Cost-Aware Agentic Architecture for NL-to-SQL over Nested Enterprise Schemas, with a New Benchmark
summary: Natural-language-to-SQL systems have ad- vanced rapidly on academic benchmarks, yet production enterprise schemas exhibit graph- like, semi-structured, deeply nested structure that current benchmarks do not measure. We make two complementary contributions. First, we introduce the DevRev NL2SQL bench- mark: 900 execution-verified queries with nested-type and link-graph structure, accom- panied by the Semantic Depth Score (SDS), a schema-agnostic rubric for analytical reasoning depth. Second, we present a cost-aware single- generation agentic architecture whose schema- selection, metadata-retrieval, and error-repair components are designed for the requirements this regime imposes. On the DevRev NL2SQL benchmark the system attains 91.7% answer correctness, a margin of 54.6 percentage points over the next-best baseline; on the Spider 2.0 Snowflake public dataset, it is competitive with leading systems at a single-generation operating point.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the gap between NL2SQL performance on academic benchmarks vs. real-world enterprise schemas with complex graph-like, nested structures. The authors introduce a new benchmark (DevRev NL2SQL with 900 queries) and a cost-aware agentic architecture that achieves 91.7% accuracy, significantly outperforming baselines.
AI.motivation: Current NL2SQL systems perform well on academic benchmarks but fail on production enterprise schemas that have graph-like, semi-structured, deeply nested structures - existing benchmarks don't capture this complexity.
AI.method: Two complementary contributions: (1) DevRev NL2SQL benchmark with 900 execution-verified queries featuring nested-type and link-graph structure, accompanied by Semantic Depth Score (SDS) for measuring analytical reasoning depth; (2) Cost-aware single-generation agentic architecture with schema-selection, metadata-retrieval, and error-repair components designed for complex schemas.
AI.result: The system achieves 91.7% answer correctness on DevRev NL2SQL benchmark, a margin of 54.6 percentage points over the next-best baseline. On Spider 2.0 Snowflake public dataset, it is competitive with leading systems at a single-generation operating point.
AI.conclusion: The proposed architecture successfully handles complex enterprise schemas with nested and graph-like structures, significantly outperforming existing approaches. The new benchmark and SDS metric provide better evaluation for real-world NL2SQL challenges.

title: WEECFP-SuRGE: Wide Embedded Extended Connectivity Fingerprint with Substructure Rotary Graph-distance Encoding
summary: We introduce WEECFP, a parameter-free 1024-dimensional continuous molecular fingerprint that scatters each Morgan substructure across roughly thirty-two signed positions of a single vector, and WEECFP-SuRGE, a transformer architecture whose self-attention applies SuRGE (Substructure Rotary Graph-distance Encoding) -- a RoPE-like rotation parameterized by molecular shortest-path graph distance -- to WEECFP substructure tokens. A 7-model blend of this architecture (the WEECFP-SuRGE Blend) achieves the lowest average regression rank on the TDC ADMET leaderboard; is #2 overall on the TDC ADMET leaderboard (behind only pretrained MapLight+GNN), and is #1 overall among methods that use no external pretraining; takes leaderboard #1 finishes on Pgp, Lipophilicity, CYP2D6 Substrate, Clearance Microsome, and LD50 (with the WEECFP-NoSuRGE Blend separately reaching #1 on HIA) across the full 22-benchmark suite -- without any external pretraining. On MoleculeNet, WEECFP-SuRGE beats every classical-fingerprint baseline on 3 of 4 regression tasks (ESOL, Lipophilicity, QM9). We further show that WEECFP tokenization is near-lossless: a greedy overlap reconstruction recovers the exact canonical SMILES of 99.9% of in-distribution molecules across 9 MoleculeNet datasets and 98.93% of molecules in a cross-dataset holdout (HIV->Lipophilicity), and that a three-reference farthest-first encoding of graph distance correlates at Pearson r = 0.901 with the true pairwise distance, enabling O(S) positional memory at matching accuracy.

AI.tldr: WEECFP is a parameter-free 1024-dimensional continuous molecular fingerprint that scatters Morgan substructures across ~32 signed positions. WEECFP-SuRGE is a transformer architecture using SuRGE (a RoPE-like rotation based on molecular graph distance) for substructure tokens. The 7-model blend achieves state-of-the-art results on TDC ADMET leaderboard (#2 overall, #1 among non-pretrained methods) and MoleculeNet regression tasks, with near-lossless tokenization (99.9% reconstruction accuracy).
AI.motivation: Molecular fingerprints are fundamental to computational chemistry, but existing methods either lack parameter efficiency, fail to capture graph distance information, or require extensive pretraining. This work aims to develop a parameter-free fingerprint that preserves substructure information while incorporating positional encoding based on molecular graph topology, without relying on external pretraining.
AI.method: WEECFP generates 1024-dimensional continuous fingerprints by scattering Morgan substructures across ~32 signed positions. WEECFP-SuRGE uses a transformer architecture with self-attention applying SuRGE (Substructure Rotary Graph-distance Encoding) - a RoPE-like rotation parameterized by molecular shortest-path graph distance - to WEECFP substructure tokens. A 7-model blend is used for ensemble predictions.
AI.result: The WEECFP-SuRGE Blend achieves: (1) Lowest average regression rank on TDC ADMET leaderboard; (2) #2 overall (behind pretrained MapLight+GNN); (3) #1 among non-pretrained methods; (4) Leaderboard #1 on Pgp, Lipophilicity, CYP2D6 Substrate, Clearance Microsome, and LD50; (5) Beats classical fingerprints on 3/4 MoleculeNet regression tasks (ESOL, Lipophilicity, QM9). Tokenization achieves 99.9% exact SMILES reconstruction for in-distribution and 98.93% for cross-dataset holdout. Graph distance encoding correlates at Pearson r = 0.901 with true pairwise distances.
AI.conclusion: WEECFP-SuRGE demonstrates that a well-designed parameter-free fingerprint combined with graph-distance-based positional encoding can achieve state-of-the-art performance on ADMET prediction tasks without any external pretraining, rivaling even pretrained GNN methods. The near-lossless tokenization and effective graph distance encoding (O(S) positional memory) are key technical innovations enabling this performance.

title: T(r)opical Islands: Visualizing & Understanding Socio-Technical Artifacts
comment: 12 pages, 11 figures, 1 table, accepted at ICSME 2026
summary:
Projects hosted on collaborative software development platforms, such as GitHub, include many non-code artifacts documenting the project's lifecycle, with its challenges, plans, design, and even community. These socio-technical artifacts include, for example, bug reports, feature requests, and forum posts, offering a useful prospect on the project's evolution. However, these artifacts are dispersed over multiple communication channels and written in natural language, making their analysis difficult, as they are fragmented and with considerable noise.
  We present a 3D visualization approach mapping topics found across a project's socio-technical artifacts onto vegetation-covered islands, where the individual artifacts are depicted as trees of various types. The topic islands rise out of the ocean as they become discussed, to sink again when they are no longer so. We built a prototype implementing the entire visualization pipeline, from data mining to interactive rendering, leveraging machine learning techniques to cluster the artifacts and extract their topics. We present, through several case studies, the insights that our approach elicits about discussions of development topics throughout a project's history. The user study we conducted (N=34) further strengthens our conclusions about its suitability for understanding socio-technical artifacts and their evolution.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a 3D visualization approach that maps topics from socio-technical artifacts (bug reports, feature requests, forum posts) in software projects onto vegetation-covered islands, with artifacts depicted as trees. The visualization shows topics rising when discussed and sinking when abandoned.
AI.motivation: Software projects on platforms like GitHub contain numerous non-code artifacts documenting their lifecycle, but these are dispersed across multiple communication channels and written in natural language, making analysis difficult due to fragmentation and noise.
AI.method: Built a prototype implementing the full visualization pipeline from data mining to interactive rendering, using machine learning techniques to cluster artifacts and extract topics. Evaluated through case studies and a user study with 34 participants.
AI.result: The approach provides insights into discussions of development topics throughout a project's history. The user study (N=34) validated the suitability of the visualization for understanding socio-technical artifacts and their evolution.
AI.conclusion: The 3D island-based visualization effectively helps stakeholders understand socio-technical artifacts and track how topics emerge, evolve, and fade over a project's lifetime.

title: SeamFlow: Structure-Aware Flow Matching on Edge Probabilities for Artist-Like UV Unwrapping
summary: 3D surface cutting and UV unwrapping are fundamental problems in computer graphics. Traditional geometric optimization methods mainly focus on reducing parameterization distortion, but they often overlook visual semantic coherence in seam layouts. Recent autoregressive generative methods improve semantic coherence, yet limited perception of mesh topology often causes inaccurate local cuts. To address these limitations, we introduce SeamFlow, a novel generative framework for 3D surface cutting. We reformulate the discrete mesh-cutting problem as continuous flow matching in a high-dimensional edge-probability space. Through continuous relaxation, SeamFlow learns a deterministic mapping from a Gaussian prior to a target seam-probability distribution. An evolution network couples local topological tokens with global shape priors and guides smooth probability flow through Ordinary Differential Equation solving. Compared with existing autoregressive generative frameworks, SeamFlow improves topology awareness through edge tokenization while eliminating both 3D spatial projection errors and artificial sequential-order bias. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SeamFlow achieves exceptional semantic coherence and remarkably low parameterization distortion. The project page is https://meshy-dev.github.io/seamflow.

AI.tldr: SeamFlow is a novel generative framework for 3D surface cutting and UV unwrapping that reformulates the discrete mesh-cutting problem as continuous flow matching in high-dimensional edge-probability space, improving upon traditional geometric optimization and autoregressive generative methods.
AI.motivation: Traditional geometric optimization methods focus on reducing parameterization distortion but overlook visual semantic coherence in seam layouts. Autoregressive generative methods improve semantic coherence but have limited perception of mesh topology, causing inaccurate local cuts.
AI.method: SeamFlow learns a deterministic mapping from a Gaussian prior to a target seam-probability distribution through continuous relaxation. An evolution network couples local topological tokens with global shape priors and guides probability flow via Ordinary Differential Equation solving. The method uses edge tokenization to improve topology awareness.
AI.result: SeamFlow achieves exceptional semantic coherence and remarkably low parameterization distortion, while eliminating both 3D spatial projection errors and artificial sequential-order bias present in autoregressive frameworks.
AI.conclusion: SeamFlow represents a significant advancement in 3D surface cutting by combining flow matching with topological awareness, successfully balancing semantic coherence with low parameterization distortion.

title: Continual Graph Memory for Adaptive Recommendation under Intent Drift
summary: This paper studies adaptive recommendation under intent drift, where feedback from each recommendation outcome can reveal whether the relational evidence used for ranking is useful, missing, or misleading. While Knowledge Graphs (KGs) provide essential semantic structure to handle these shifts, traditional KG-enhanced systems treat the graph as a static retrieval substrate, making it brittle to evolving intents, noisy metadata, and recurring failure patterns. This paper proposes CGM-Rec, a continual graph memory framework for adaptive recommendation. CGM-Rec treats the graph state as a writable memory and maintains two complementary components. Therein, a Semantic Graph Memory is updated conservatively through quality-gated typed operations for storing stable and high-confidence relational knowledge. Meanwhile, an Episodic Lesson Memory acts as a fast reactive memory that learns recent outcomes, failure cases, and corrective hints. During testing, model parameters remain frozen and adaptation occurs only through memory writes. We evaluate CGM-Rec under a frozen-parameter, one-pass reranking protocol, where encoders and prompts remain fixed during testing and adaptation occurs only through memory writes. Experiments across multiple recommendation settings show that CGM-Rec improves over evaluated neural and LLM-based baselines on most metrics. Particularly, under sampled-candidate reranking, CGM-Rec improves HR@1 by up to 29.58% over the strongest LLM baseline on Bundle, and outperforms K-RagRec on metadata-rich ML-100K with HR@5 of 0.5941 versus 0.4746.

AI.tldr: CGM-Rec is a continual graph memory framework for adaptive recommendation under intent drift. It treats the Knowledge Graph as a writable memory with two components: a conservatively updated Semantic Graph Memory for stable relational knowledge, and a fast reactive Episodic Lesson Memory for recent outcomes and failure cases. Adaptation occurs through memory writes only, with frozen model parameters during testing.
AI.motivation: Traditional KG-enhanced recommendation systems treat the graph as a static retrieval substrate, making them brittle to evolving intents, noisy metadata, and recurring failure patterns. This paper addresses the challenge of intent drift where feedback reveals whether relational evidence is useful, missing, or misleading.
AI.method: CGM-Rec maintains two complementary memory components: (1) Semantic Graph Memory updated conservatively through quality-gated typed operations for storing stable, high-confidence relational knowledge; (2) Episodic Lesson Memory acting as fast reactive memory for recent outcomes, failure cases, and corrective hints. During testing, model parameters remain frozen and adaptation occurs only through memory writes under a frozen-parameter, one-pass reranking protocol.
AI.result: CGM-Rec improves over neural and LLM-based baselines on most metrics. Under sampled-candidate reranking, it improves HR@1 by up to 29.58% over the strongest LLM baseline on Bundle, and outperforms K-RagRec on metadata-rich ML-100K with HR@5 of 0.5941 versus 0.4746.
AI.conclusion: The proposed continual graph memory framework effectively handles intent drift in recommendation systems by separating stable relational knowledge from fast-reactive episodic learning, achieving significant performance improvements without requiring parameter updates during inference.

title: Simulation-free Unbalanced Dynamic Optimal Transport with General Growth Penalty
summary: Inferring cellular dynamics from unpaired single-cell snapshots requires modeling both state transitions and population growth or death. Unbalanced dynamic optimal transport (UDOT) addresses this by penalizing growth along transport paths, making the choice of growth penalty a key way to encode biological priors on proliferation and apoptosis. However, existing UDOT solvers either rely on computationally expensive NeuralODE simulations or depend on analytical solutions of conditional paths, restricting their efficiency solely to quadratic penalties, i.e. Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao (WFR) geodesics. To enable an efficient UDOT solver for general growth penalties, we first show that concave growth penalties lead to degenerate solutions where growth and transport are separated. We then introduce \textbf{S}imulation-free \textbf{U}nbalanced \textbf{D}ynamic \textbf{O}ptimal transport (SUDO), a simulation-free framework for UDOT with general non-quadratic convex growth penalties. SUDO learns the conditional paths and transport costs, solves the induced semi-coupling problem, and subsequently leverages unbalanced flow matching to achieve a simulation-free solution. On WFR benchmarks, SUDO matches the accuracy of efficient, analytical solution-driven algorithms while outperforming simulation-based methods in computational speed. Beyond WFR, SUDO supports asymmetric penalties that encode proliferation-dominant priors and produce more plausible trajectories and growth estimates on synthetic and single-cell datasets.

AI.tldr: SUDO is a simulation-free framework for Unbalanced Dynamic Optimal Transport (UDOT) that handles general non-quadratic convex growth penalties, enabling efficient modeling of cellular dynamics including proliferation and apoptosis from unpaired single-cell data.
AI.motivation: Current UDOT solvers are limited: they either require computationally expensive NeuralODE simulations or are restricted to quadratic penalties (Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao geodesics) due to analytical solution requirements. The choice of growth penalty is crucial for encoding biological priors on proliferation and apoptosis, but existing methods cannot efficiently handle general growth penalties.
AI.method:
1) Show that concave growth penalties lead to degenerate solutions where growth and transport separate
2) Develop SUDO - a simulation-free framework that:
   - Learns conditional paths and transport costs
   - Solves the induced semi-coupling problem
   - Leverages unbalanced flow matching for simulation-free solution
3) Supports asymmetric penalties for encoding proliferation-dominant biological priors
AI.result: On WFR benchmarks: SUDO matches the accuracy of efficient analytical solution-driven algorithms while significantly outperforming simulation-based methods in computational speed. Beyond WFR: produces more plausible trajectories and growth estimates on synthetic and single-cell datasets when using asymmetric penalties that encode proliferation-dominant priors.
AI.conclusion: SUDO enables efficient UDOT computation with general non-quadratic convex growth penalties, expanding the toolkit for single-cell dynamics inference. The method successfully balances computational efficiency with accuracy and allows biological priors to be encoded through asymmetric growth penalties, leading to more biologically plausible results.

title: Ritgard: T(r)opical Islands of Socio-Technical Artifacts on GitHub
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, tool demo paper accepted at VISSOFT 2026
summary:
A software project is more than just code. Non-code artifacts often document the human processes and decisions behind source code. The rationale behind a library change, an architectural decision, a problem encountered by a user are all examples of information typically present in socio-technical artifacts (STAs), created and persisted in channels separate from the repository itself (yet sometimes very close---e.g., GitHub Issues with GitHub repositories). These STAs are a trove of information about the project's architecture and its evolution, containing details and insights that code alone cannot provide. Unfortunately, this information is not easily extracted and explored as STAs are frequently fragmented over different communication channels, and are written in natural language.
  We present Ritgard, a tool that mines GitHub repositories for their STAs, namely Issues, Pull Requests, and Discussions, and visualizes them as 3D islands covered with trees. Each tree represents a single artifact and each island is a topic extracted from the artifacts through a combination of text embedding and text summarization. The terrain of the islands rises out of the ocean as the topic becomes active and sinks back in when it becomes stale, thus depicting the evolution of features and concerns throughout the project's lifetime. We describe the tool's usage and implementation, showing the numerous technical challenges behind Ritgard's visualization.

AI.tldr: Ritgard is a tool that mines GitHub repositories for socio-technical artifacts (Issues, Pull Requests, and Discussions) and visualizes them as 3D islands covered with trees, where each tree represents an artifact and each island represents a topic extracted through text embedding and summarization.
AI.motivation: Socio-technical artifacts (STAs) contain valuable information about project architecture and evolution that code alone cannot provide, but this information is hard to extract and explore because STAs are fragmented across different communication channels and written in natural language.
AI.method: The tool mines GitHub repositories for STAs (Issues, Pull Requests, and Discussions), then uses text embedding and text summarization to extract topics from these artifacts. The extracted topics are visualized as 3D islands where each tree represents a single artifact and each island represents a topic. The terrain rises and sinks based on topic activity over time.
AI.result: A 3D visualization tool that depicts the evolution of features and concerns throughout a project's lifetime, with terrain rising out of the ocean when topics become active and sinking back when they become stale.
AI.conclusion: Ritgard provides an innovative approach to exploring fragmented socio-technical artifacts through 3D visualization, enabling developers to better understand project architecture and evolution through a visual representation of topic activity over time.

title: LUMIN: Lightweight Universal Manufacturing Inspection Network for Anomaly Detection
summary: Industrial anomaly detection faces two engineering bottlenecks: memory bank construction latency and inference efficiency. Traditional sampling algorithms (Farthest Point Sampling, K-Means, etc.) rely on numerous backbone forward passes and iterative distance computations, with construction times ranging from minutes to hours; heavy computation components such as multi-scale feature extraction struggle to meet the millisecond-level real-time requirements of production lines. This paper focuses on sampling efficiency and inference optimization for industrial deployment with two core contributions: (1) PSP (Plugin Sampler Pipeline)---a four-stage adaptive memory bank sampling pipeline based on 18-dimensional pixel metadata and five complementary visual plugins. PSP completes all sampling with zero backbone forward passes; coarse filtering is sub-second numerical sorting, and metadata extraction is a one-time offline cost. PSP supports progressive deployment and incremental updates. (2) Two engineering optimization strategies---parallel memory bank similarity computation (reducing inference memory and latency by over 95\%) and stratified pixel sampling for large-scale evaluation (reducing computation time by 20$\times$ while keeping metrics stable). As a vehicle for validation, we introduce LUMIN (Lightweight Universal Manufacturing Inspection Network) with extreme segmentation-head compression, systematically exploring the accuracy-efficiency frontier against strong baselines. Experiments on five benchmarks demonstrate that PSP matches state-of-the-art sampling accuracy at near-random construction cost (341$\times$ faster than FPS), while inference optimizations reduce evaluation time by 20$\times$ with negligible accuracy loss.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses industrial anomaly detection bottlenecks (memory bank construction latency and inference efficiency) by proposing PSP (Plugin Sampler Pipeline) - a four-stage adaptive sampling method using 18-dimensional pixel metadata and five visual plugins that requires zero backbone forward passes. Combined with two engineering optimization strategies (parallel similarity computation and stratified pixel sampling), the method achieves 341× faster construction than FPS and 20× reduction in evaluation time with negligible accuracy loss.
AI.motivation: Industrial anomaly detection faces two critical engineering bottlenecks: (1) memory bank construction latency - traditional sampling algorithms like Farthest Point Sampling and K-Means require numerous backbone forward passes and iterative distance computations, with construction times ranging from minutes to hours; (2) inference efficiency - heavy computation components like multi-scale feature extraction cannot meet millisecond-level real-time requirements of production lines.
AI.method: The paper proposes two core contributions: (1) PSP (Plugin Sampler Pipeline) - a four-stage adaptive memory bank sampling pipeline based on 18-dimensional pixel metadata and five complementary visual plugins. It completes all sampling with zero backbone forward passes, where coarse filtering uses sub-second numerical sorting and metadata extraction is a one-time offline cost. PSP supports progressive deployment and incremental updates. (2) Two engineering optimization strategies: parallel memory bank similarity computation and stratified pixel sampling for large-scale evaluation. Validation is performed using LUMIN (Lightweight Universal Manufacturing Inspection Network) with extreme segmentation-head compression.
AI.result: Experiments on five benchmarks demonstrate that PSP matches state-of-the-art sampling accuracy at near-random construction cost (341× faster than FPS), while inference optimizations reduce evaluation time by 20× with negligible accuracy loss. The parallel memory bank similarity computation reduces inference memory and latency by over 95%.
AI.conclusion: The proposed PSP sampling pipeline and engineering optimization strategies successfully address industrial anomaly detection deployment challenges. PSP achieves comparable sampling accuracy to state-of-the-art methods at a fraction of the construction cost, while the inference optimizations enable practical real-time evaluation without significant accuracy degradation, making the system suitable for millisecond-level real-time production line requirements.

title: Harness-agnostic detection and immunization of reward hacking in self-evolving language models
summary: Self-evolving language models improve by proposing candidate updates and keeping whatever raises a visible score. When that score is an imperfect proxy for the capability one actually wants, sustained selection widens the gap between the two. This is reward hacking. We introduce HackProbe, a monitor that attaches to an arbitrary self-evolving loop through two black-box hooks, with no access to weights or activations.
