It keeps a secret, distribution-fixed comparison core, whose frozen distribution makes its capability proxy comparable across generations, alongside a rotated fresh layer that hardens the bank against co-adaptation. Four tests built on that proxy cover the level gap, a scale-aligned divergence with online change-point detection, capability stagnation, and a conditional confidently-wrong rate; a Sidak correction turns them into a calibrated family-wise p-value. Diagnosis alone recovers nothing, so a risk-aware immunization layer reselects an honest candidate from the proposal pool using the core together with a purely structural gaming footprint, disclosing at most log2 Pi bits per generation to the host. We prove a detectability bound that converts a target error rate into an explicit probe-size budget, and we delimit what probe rotation does and does not buy. On a controlled prompt-level host with four injected hacking channels and ground-truth labels, HackProbe reaches 0.763 AUROC against 0.663 for the strongest baseline and cuts the false-positive rate from 0.706 to 0.434. Its bandwidth-limited reselection is the only immunization level that returns more true capability under hacking, 5.2 points on average, than it forfeits on clean runs, 4.7; per-channel effects are mostly not individually significant.

AI.tldr: HackProbe is a monitor system that detects reward hacking in self-evolving language models by using a distribution-fixed comparison core with a rotated fresh layer to prevent co-adaptation. It employs four statistical tests and a risk-aware immunization layer to both detect hacking and reselect honest candidates, achieving 0.763 AUROC and reducing false-positive rate from 0.706 to 0.434.
AI.motivation: Self-evolving language models can experience "reward hacking" where they optimize for an imperfect proxy score rather than the actual desired capability, causing a widening gap between the proxy and true capability over generations.
AI.method: HackProbe attaches to self-evolving loops through two black-box hooks with no access to weights/activations. It uses: (1) a distribution-fixed comparison core with frozen distribution for comparable capability proxy across generations, (2) a rotated fresh layer to harden against co-adaptation, (3) four tests covering level gap, scale-aligned divergence with online change-point detection, capability stagnation, and conditional confidently-wrong rate, (4) Sidak correction for calibrated family-wise p-value, (5) risk-aware immunization layer reselecting honest candidates using core plus structural gaming footprint, (6) bandwidth-limited disclosure of at most log2 Pi bits per generation.
AI.result: HackProbe achieves 0.763 AUROC vs 0.663 for strongest baseline, reduces false-positive rate from 0.706 to 0.434. Its bandwidth-limited reselection is the only immunization level that returns more true capability under hacking (5.2 points average) than it forfeits on clean runs (4.7 points).
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a provable detectability bound converting target error rate into explicit probe-size budget, demonstrates effective detection and mitigation of reward hacking, and shows that the rotated probe design prevents co-adaptation while maintaining capability monitoring.

title: Locating and Steering Refusal Beyond Attention
comment: 33 pages, 6 figures, 26 tables; 10-page main text plus technical appendix
summary: Where inside a language model does refusal live, and does that place change when the architecture does? In a transformer, refusal is governed by a single direction in the residual stream, a finding that safety and interpretability tooling now depend on. State-space models (SSMs) route information through a recurrent update instead of attention, sharing no token-mixing mechanism with a transformer. Does the same safety representation survive this shift, or must it be rediscovered per architecture? It survives. A single rigid rotation, which can only reorient a space and not reshape it, aligns one model's representation space with another's, so the two genuinely share the representation. A harm probe trained on a transformer then flags an SSM's harmful inputs, and removing the aligned direction makes a model answer attacks it would otherwise refuse, while a random direction of the same size does far less. What is architecture-specific is not where the direction is steered but where it must be read. Each layer computes a fresh output that is then added into the residual stream, and harm is cleanly readable at this output, the write site, before the addition. A control that holds the intervention's strength fixed shows that what matters is where the direction is estimated, not where it is applied. Applied through a detector-triggered gate, this direction lowers jailbreak success in all four architecture families we test (SSM, transformer, recurrent, hybrid), and on the SSM it holds against an attacker that tunes its prompt against the defense. The gate only matches a trivial rule that returns a fixed refusal whenever the same detector fires, so what transfers across architectures is the direction itself, not defense strength. Safety tooling built on refusal therefore ports to a new architecture by re-estimating the direction at that architecture's write site, not by rebuilding it.

AI.tldr: Refusal (safety) representations in language models exist as a single direction in the residual stream. This representation can be transferred across different architectures (transformers, SSMs, recurrent, hybrid) via a rigid rotation, without retraining. The key architecture-specific factor is not where the direction is applied, but where it is estimated—the "write site" (layer output before addition to residual stream). A harm probe trained on one architecture can flag harmful inputs in another after alignment, and removing this direction enables jailbreak. A detector-triggered gate using this direction reduces jailbreak success across all four architecture families tested.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether safety representations discovered in transformers can transfer to state-space models (SSMs), which lack attention mechanisms. The question is whether refusal lives in the same place across architectures, or must be rediscovered for each.
AI.method: Trained harm probes on transformers, then applied the same direction to SSMs after alignment via rigid rotation. Tested intervention effects by removing the aligned direction vs. random directions. Compared effectiveness across four architecture families (SSM, transformer, recurrent, hybrid). Tested against an attacker that tunes prompts against the defense.
AI.result: A single rigid rotation aligns representation spaces between different architectures, enabling a harm probe trained on transformers to flag harmful inputs in SSMs. Removing the aligned direction enables models to answer attacks they would otherwise refuse, while random directions have minimal effect. The write site (layer output before residual addition) is where harm is cleanly readable. A detector-triggered gate using this direction lowers jailbreak success across all architectures, even against an adaptive attacker.
AI.conclusion: Safety tooling built on refusal representations can port to new architectures by re-estimating the direction at that architecture's write site, not by rebuilding from scratch. The direction itself transfers across architectures, but the location where it must be read is architecture-specific.

title: Trace2Tower: Transition-Aware EigenTrace Induction of Multi-Level Skills for LLM Agents
summary: Large language model agents increasingly rely on execution traces to master complex interactive tasks. However, current paradigms are bottlenecked by shallow trajectory retrieval and flat skill summarization, fundamentally ignoring the temporal dependencies and outcome-conditioned topology of agent behavior. We introduce Trace2Tower, a transition-aware EigenTrace framework that distills raw trajectories into a robust skill hierarchy. Trace2Tower abstracts step-level interactions into canonical events, constructing a unified graph governed by semantic compatibility, transition dynamics, and outcome evidence. Through a novel contrastive spectral decomposition, it isolates stable, success-aligned behavioral modes while rigorously suppressing failure-prone shortcuts. These modes organically populate a dynamic skill tower of action templates, procedural routines, and overarching task strategies, continuously refined via verifier-guided feedback. On ALFWorld, Trace2Tower achieves 87.31% success requiring only 10.35 steps and 0.26 invalid actions; on WebShop, it reaches 50.67% exact success. Across both benchmarks, Trace2Tower significantly outperforms existing baselines in task mastery and context-efficient experience reuse.

AI.tldr: Trace2Tower introduces a transition-aware EigenTrace framework that transforms raw execution traces into a hierarchical skill structure for LLM agents. It uses contrastive spectral decomposition to extract success-aligned behavioral patterns while suppressing failure-prone shortcuts, creating a dynamic skill tower of action templates, routines, and strategies refined through verifier feedback.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agent paradigms are limited by shallow trajectory retrieval and flat skill summarization that ignore temporal dependencies and outcome-conditioned topology of agent behavior, creating a fundamental bottleneck in mastering complex interactive tasks.
AI.method: Trace2Tower abstracts step-level interactions into canonical events, constructs a unified graph governed by semantic compatibility, transition dynamics, and outcome evidence, then applies novel contrastive spectral decomposition to isolate stable success-aligned behavioral modes while suppressing failure-prone shortcuts. These modes populate a dynamic skill tower continuously refined via verifier-guided feedback.
AI.result: On ALFWorld: 87.31% success rate with only 10.35 steps and 0.26 invalid actions. On WebShop: 50.67% exact success. Significantly outperforms existing baselines in task mastery and context-efficient experience reuse across both benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Trace2Tower successfully addresses the trajectory retrieval and skill summarization bottlenecks through its transition-aware spectral approach, enabling effective hierarchical skill extraction and verifier-guided refinement that substantially improves LLM agent performance on complex interactive tasks.

title: CoMLP: Cooperatively-Gated MLPs for Fine-Grained Cross-Modal Information Fusion in Medical Image Segmentation
summary: Multi-modal medical images and clinical reports provide complementary anatomical, functional, and semantic information for medical image segmentation. Effectively exploiting these heterogeneous sources requires fine-grained cross-modal information fusion that preserves subtle spatial details while capturing semantic dependencies across modalities. Existing fusion approaches frequently rely on cross-attention, whose computational burden increases rapidly with spatial resolution, making dense cross-modal interaction difficult on high-resolution feature maps, particularly for volumetric medical images. In this work, we propose CoMLP, a cooperatively-gated MLP module for fine-grained cross-modal information fusion in medical image segmentation. CoMLP models cross-modal dependencies through cooperative cross-gating, built upon complementary regional and dilated MLP interactions, to capture local and global cross-modal dependencies. We further develop a multi-source fusion architecture in which CoMLP performs both inter-image fusion across imaging modalities and vision-language fusion between visual features and textual reports, enabling heterogeneous information to be integrated without relying on dense cross-attention. Extensive experiments on five medical segmentation benchmarks, covering 2D/3D images, clinical reports, multiple imaging modalities, and diverse anatomical regions, demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art multi-modal and language-guided segmentation methods. Ablation studies further show that fine-grained interaction at high spatial resolutions and complementary local-global fusion are critical to the performance gains. These results demonstrate the potential of MLP-based interaction as an effective alternative for fine-grained cross-modal information fusion in medical image segmentation.

AI.tldr: CoMLP proposes a cooperatively-gated MLP module for fine-grained cross-modal information fusion in medical image segmentation, using cooperative cross-gating with complementary regional and dilated MLP interactions to capture local and global cross-modal dependencies without dense cross-attention.
AI.motivation: Existing cross-attention based fusion approaches have high computational burden that increases rapidly with spatial resolution, making dense cross-modal interaction difficult on high-resolution feature maps, particularly for volumetric medical images.
AI.method: CoMLP uses cooperative cross-gating built upon complementary regional and dilated MLP interactions to capture both local and global cross-modal dependencies. The multi-source fusion architecture enables inter-image fusion across imaging modalities and vision-language fusion between visual features and textual reports without relying on dense cross-attention.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on five medical segmentation benchmarks (covering 2D/3D images, clinical reports, multiple imaging modalities, and diverse anatomical regions) demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art multi-modal and language-guided segmentation methods.
AI.conclusion: MLP-based interaction is an effective alternative for fine-grained cross-modal information fusion in medical image segmentation, with ablation studies confirming that fine-grained interaction at high spatial resolutions and complementary local-global fusion are critical to performance gains.

title: ERPBench: Evaluating LLM Agents for Enterprise Decision-Making Across Competitive Market Ecologies
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly proposed for enterprise workflows, yet existing evaluations rarely test whether business-decision conclusions transfer across competitive market ecologies. We introduce ERPBench, an execution-instrumented benchmark for enterprise decision agents in a six-round Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) simulation with coupled pricing, production, procurement, inventory, finance, and shared-market competition. ERPBench evaluates the same 100 fixed problems in two matched competitive market ecologies: Solo, where each evaluated LLM agent competes against fixed rule-based opponents, and Arena, where six evaluated LLM agents compete in a shared market. Across six model families, this yields 1,200 model-level trajectories spanning 7,200 decision rounds. Under the observed service configuration, the leading model differs between ecologies: DeepSeek leads in Solo (252.29M mean valuation; mean rank 1.67), whereas Gemini leads in Arena (263.95M; 1.76). The two ecologies identify the same task-level winner on only 21 of 100 problems, and Gemini's bottom-rank rate falls from 22 % to 0 % in Arena. ERPBench supports paired evaluation of whether enterprise-agent rankings transfer across competitive market ecologies, supplemented by aggregate execution-intervention analysis. Code and benchmark resources are available in our https://github.com/GAIR-NLP/erp-bench.

title: Training Large Language Models for Small-Molecule Design with Synthetic Task Scaling
summary: Designing viable drug candidates requires searching a combinatorially large and rugged chemical space for molecules that satisfy multiple, often competing, objectives. Large language models (LLMs) provide a useful generative prior for this problem because of their representational capacity, reasoning ability, and flexibility when incorporating information from the external environment. While reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) can be used to improve the capabilities of LLMs, many chemically relevant scoring functions require hours or even days per evaluation, making them prohibitively expensive to use directly during online training. Here, we investigate whether LLMs can learn molecular design strategies from cheaper synthetic tasks that generalize to expensive molecular lead optimization settings. We find that curriculum-based training recipes that gradually incorporate more challenging synthetic design tasks enable strong performance that surpasses that of much larger frontier models on structure-based lead optimization. Our results suggest that scaling post-training using synthetic tasks is an effective strategy for adapting LLMs to high-cost experimental scenarios that are too expensive to directly train on.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates using LLMs with reinforcement learning for molecular drug design, where expensive scoring functions make direct training impractical. The authors propose curriculum-based training on cheaper synthetic tasks that can generalize to expensive real-world lead optimization scenarios.
AI.motivation: Drug candidate design requires searching combinatorially large chemical spaces for molecules satisfying multiple competing objectives. While LLMs show promise, RLVR training requires many scoring function evaluations that can take hours to days per molecule, making direct training prohibitively expensive for realistic molecular lead optimization tasks.
AI.method: The authors investigate curriculum-based training recipes that gradually incorporate more challenging synthetic design tasks. They explore whether learning from cheaper synthetic tasks can generalize to expensive molecular lead optimization settings, using a curriculum that progresses from simpler to more complex synthetic problems.
AI.result: Curriculum-based training recipes that gradually incorporate more challenging synthetic design tasks enable strong performance that surpasses much larger frontier models on structure-based lead optimization.
AI.conclusion: Scaling post-training using synthetic tasks is an effective strategy for adapting LLMs to high-cost experimental scenarios that are too expensive to directly train on. This approach allows LLMs to learn molecular design strategies without requiring expensive real-world evaluations during training.

title: CLON: Cue-Calibrated Linguistic Object Onboarding for Zero-Shot 6D Pose Front-Ends
summary: Zero-shot 6D pose estimation pipelines increasingly rely on strong downstream pose solvers, but their performance is often limited by the front-end: object proposals must preserve partially visible true positives while rejecting semantically plausible distractors. We introduce Cue-Calibrated Linguistic Object Onboarding (CLON), a front-end requiring no task-specific training for new objects. Given rendered templates of the onboarded object set, CLON constructs a linguistic semantic memory for top-down proposal generation and object-set cue weights for calibrated proposal scoring. The linguistic memory guides SAM 3 toward high-recall proposals for onboarded objects, while cue weights are computed once from the onboarded object set before scene inference and kept fixed during online scoring. On seven BOP-Classic-Core datasets, CLON improves detection AP by 8.1 percentage points (pp), segmentation AP by 6.2 pp, and downstream 6D pose AR by up to 4.1 pp over CNOS and SAM-6D front-ends.

AI.tldr: CLON is a front-end for zero-shot 6D pose estimation that requires no task-specific training for new objects. It uses linguistic semantic memory to guide SAM 3 for high-recall proposals and calibrated cue weights for proposal scoring. It achieves significant improvements in detection AP (+8.1pp), segmentation AP (+6.2pp), and 6D pose AR (+4.1pp) over prior methods on seven BOP-Classic-Core datasets.
AI.motivation: Zero-shot 6D pose estimation pipelines rely on strong downstream pose solvers, but their performance is limited by the front-end: object proposals must preserve partially visible true positives while rejecting semantically plausible distractors. Existing front-ends lack effective ways to handle new objects without task-specific training.
AI.method: CLON uses rendered templates of the onboarded object set to construct a linguistic semantic memory for top-down proposal generation and object-set cue weights for calibrated proposal scoring. The linguistic memory guides SAM 3 toward high-recall proposals for onboarded objects, while cue weights are computed once from the onboarded object set before scene inference and kept fixed during online scoring.
AI.result: On seven BOP-Classic-Core datasets, CLON improves detection AP by 8.1 percentage points, segmentation AP by 6.2 percentage points, and downstream 6D pose AR by up to 4.1 percentage points over CNOS and SAM-6D front-ends.
AI.conclusion: CLON provides an effective front-end for zero-shot 6D pose estimation that requires no task-specific training for new objects, achieving significant improvements in detection, segmentation, and pose estimation performance over existing methods.

title: Train What You Deploy:Token-Faithful Post-Training of a Production Coding
summary: Existing post-training pipelines for coding and terminal agents suffer severe token and control fidelity errors: simplified training environments mismatch production deployments, and offline token reconstruction from agent logs distorts original prompts and conflates policy calls with background model operations. We present a fidelity-aware training coupling framework that retains trainer-side sampling over original prompts, eliminates spurious model calls via a negotiated training protocol, and restricts loss computation to verifiable token spans with closed-failure guarantees. We further propose Certified Divergence Proximal Policy Optimization (C-DPPO), which establishes tight two-sided TV certification bounds, adaptive-K rules, budget-aware sequence guarantees, and error-robust policy masking atop standard DPPO. Evaluated on matched Baize5B and Baize10B models with identical training and test protocols on TMax-100, C-DPPO yields a consistent +3.0-point performance gain over standard DPPO across model scales. Certificate audits validate the reliability and full operational coverage of our certified training pipeline.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses token and control fidelity errors in post-training pipelines for coding and terminal agents by proposing a fidelity-aware training coupling framework and Certified Divergence Proximal Policy Optimization (C-DPPO). The approach retains trainer-side sampling, eliminates spurious model calls, and provides TV certification bounds. Experiments on Baize models show +3.0-point improvement over standard DPPO.
AI.motivation: Existing post-training pipelines for coding and terminal agents suffer from severe token and control fidelity errors due to: (1) simplified training environments that mismatch production deployments, and (2) offline token reconstruction from agent logs that distorts original prompts and conflates policy calls with background model operations.
AI.method: The paper proposes two key innovations: (1) A fidelity-aware training coupling framework that retains trainer-side sampling over original prompts, eliminates spurious model calls via a negotiated training protocol, and restricts loss computation to verifiable token spans with closed-failure guarantees. (2) Certified DPPO (C-DPPO) which adds tight two-sided TV certification bounds, adaptive-K rules, budget-aware sequence guarantees, and error-robust policy masking atop standard DPPO.
AI.result: Evaluated on matched Baize5B and Baize10B models with identical training and test protocols on TMax-100, C-DPPO yields a consistent +3.0-point performance gain over standard DPPO across model scales. Certificate audits validate the reliability and full operational coverage of the certified training pipeline.
AI.conclusion: The proposed C-DPPO approach successfully addresses fidelity errors in post-training pipelines, achieving consistent performance improvements across model scales while providing certified reliability and full operational coverage through its TV certification bounds and error-robust mechanisms.

title: A Fairness Audit of the Duckworth-Lewis-Stern Method: Format-Specific and Gender-Differential Bias, with an Interpretable Calibration Layer for Cricket Target Revision
comment: Accepted for publication in the Journal of Quantitative Analysis in Sports (JQAS); forthcoming
summary: The Duckworth-Lewis-Stern (DLS) method has been the international standard for revising target scores in rain-interrupted limited-overs cricket since 1999. Despite over two decades of operational use, no large-scale empirical audit of its prediction bias has been published. We conduct such an audit on 8,150 international matches (3,095 ODIs, 5,055 T20Is) from Cricsheet, generating 233,550 synthetic interruption scenarios with temporal splits. We document two structured biases. First, DLS prediction error spans a 137-run range across (overs-remaining, wickets-lost) match-state buckets. Second, DLS exhibits a gender-differential bias on ODIs that has not previously been quantified: on the training split, mean over-prediction is +1.51 runs for men but +7.63 runs for women, a gap of +6.13 runs (F = 195.16, p < 10^-43). We benchmark DLS against five modern alternatives: Bi-LSTM, XGBoost, an enriched XGBoost variant, a deep context-aware model, and a stacking ensemble, and propose DLS-Cal, a lightweight interpretable calibration layer (27K parameters) outputting a state-conditioned correction added to DLS. DLS-Cal reduces absolute bias by 31% on ODI and 19% on T20I, and a gender-aware variant reduces women's ODI residual bias from +6.19 to +0.65 runs while leaving men's calibration unchanged. We release code, models, and data.

AI.tldr: This paper conducts the first large-scale empirical audit of the DLS (Duckworth-Lewis-Stern) method using 8,150 international cricket matches, discovering significant prediction biases including a previously unquantified gender differential (women's ODI over-prediction of +7.63 runs vs men's +1.51 runs). The authors propose DLS-Cal, a lightweight calibration layer that reduces bias by 31% in ODIs and 19% in T20Is.
AI.motivation: Despite over two decades of operational use of the DLS method as the international standard for revising target scores in rain-interrupted limited-overs cricket, no large-scale empirical audit of its prediction bias has been published. This gap in the literature needed to be addressed to understand and potentially improve the method's accuracy.
AI.method: The authors analyzed 8,150 international matches (3,095 ODIs, 5,055 T20Is) from Cricsheet, generating 233,550 synthetic interruption scenarios with temporal splits. They benchmarked DLS against five modern alternatives: Bi-LSTM, XGBoost, an enriched XGBoost variant, a deep context-aware model, and a stacking ensemble. They proposed DLS-Cal, a lightweight interpretable calibration layer (27K parameters) with state-conditioned corrections.
AI.result: Two structured biases were documented: (1) DLS prediction error spans a 137-run range across (overs-remaining, wickets-lost) match-state buckets; (2) A gender-differential bias exists in ODIs with mean over-prediction of +1.51 runs for men but +7.63 runs for women (gap of +6.13 runs, F = 195.16, p < 10^-43). DLS-Cal reduces absolute bias by 31% on ODI and 19% on T20I. A gender-aware variant reduces women's ODI residual bias from +6.19 to +0.65 runs while leaving men's calibration unchanged.
AI.conclusion: The DLS method contains significant, structured biases that can be effectively corrected through a lightweight calibration layer. The discovered gender differential bias is particularly important, as the gender-aware DLS-Cal variant nearly eliminates the women's ODI bias (+6.19 to +0.65 runs) while maintaining men's calibration. The authors release code, models, and data for reproducibility.

title: An Attention-Guided Global and Local Fusion Framework for Lesion-Focused Image Classification
summary: Lesion-focused image classification presents a core analytical challenge, as discriminative signals are often sparse, spatially dispersed, and easily obscured by background noise, while conventional convolutional neural networks (CNNs) process entire images uniformly and may dilute signal relevance. This study hypothesizes that adaptive fusion of global contextual information and lesion-focused local information can improve classification performance compared with using either representation independently. We propose a three-branch, attention-guided deep learning framework built on Densely Connected Convolutional Network-121 (DenseNet-121) to improve feature attribution, interpretability, and classification reliability. The architecture consists of a global branch that learns representations from full images, followed by Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) to generate attention maps that highlight prediction-relevant regions and produce masked inputs, and a local branch enhanced with a Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) to extract refined spatial and channel-wise features from these focused regions. An adaptive fusion branch integrates global and local representations by learning instance-specific weights, allowing dynamic prioritization between contextual and localized information. The framework is evaluated on a synthetic Spot Pattern Dataset (SSPD) and three benchmark datasets, including skin lesion, guava leaf, and grape leaf image datasets, where the fusion branch outperformed the individual global and local branches, reaching 97.75% accuracy on the skin lesion dataset and 99.64% on the guava leaf dataset. The results highlight the value of attention-guided architectures in healthcare analytics by improving model transparency, strengthening feature relevance, and supporting more reliable data-driven decision-making in medical image analysis.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a three-branch attention-guided deep learning framework (built on DenseNet-121) that adaptively fuses global contextual information and lesion-focused local information for improved medical image classification. The framework uses Grad-CAM for attention map generation and CBAM for refined feature extraction, achieving 97.75% accuracy on skin lesion dataset and 99.64% on guava leaf dataset.
AI.motivation: Lesion-focused image classification faces challenges: discriminative signals are sparse, spatially dispersed, and easily obscured by background noise. Conventional CNNs process entire images uniformly, diluting signal relevance. This study hypothesizes that adaptive fusion of global and local representations can improve classification performance.
AI.method: A three-branch framework built on DenseNet-121: (1) Global branch learns full-image representations and uses Grad-CAM to generate attention maps highlighting prediction-relevant regions; (2) Local branch enhanced with CBAM extracts refined spatial and channel-wise features from focused regions; (3) Adaptive fusion branch integrates both representations by learning instance-specific weights for dynamic prioritization.
AI.result: The fusion branch outperformed individual global and local branches, achieving 97.75% accuracy on the skin lesion dataset and 99.64% on the guava leaf dataset. Evaluated on SSPD (synthetic) and three benchmark datasets (skin lesion, guava leaf, grape leaf).
AI.conclusion: Attention-guided architectures improve model transparency, strengthen feature relevance, and support more reliable data-driven decision-making in medical image analysis. The adaptive fusion approach effectively handles sparse and dispersed discriminative signals in lesion-focused classification tasks.

title: Predicting Spatiotemporal Mobile Sensing-Based PM2.5 Concentrations Using Low-Rank Adapted Spatially Attentive Graph Neural Network
comment: 24 Pages, 14 Figures, World Conference of Transport Research2026 Transport Research
summary: Urban air quality can vary significantly along transit corridors, necessitating high-resolution monitoring. This work introduces a novel mobile-sensing dataset from Surat, Gujarat, India, comprising PM$*{2.5}$ concentrations, meteorological variables (temperature, humidity, wind speed, wind direction), and land-use features. To represent the spatiotemporal data as a graph, two node-definition strategies were used: (i) uniform segmentation (200--400~m intervals) and (ii) DBSCAN clustering to adaptively group dense observations. For each node, rolling mean and standard deviation of meteorological variables were computed. To model this high-dimensional data, we propose a SA-GNN for fine-grained, short-term PM$*{2.5}$ forecasting and hotspot identification. We compared SA-GNN with LSTM, RNN, GRU, and ANN models. These models performed well on low-resolution data but had difficulty capturing rapidly changing patterns in urban air quality. SA-GNN employs cluster-specific GRUs to capture localized temporal dependencies and a Graph Attention Network to learn spatial heterogeneity. This hybrid architecture effectively models rapid fluctuations and complex spatial interactions. On our dataset, SA-GNN achieved $R^2 = 0.95$, RMSE $= 6.8$, and MAE $= 4.2~\si{\micro\gram\per\meter\cubed}$, outperforming all baseline models. Combining spatial clustering with adaptive attention significantly improves forecasting, enabling real-time, fine-grained monitoring and supporting personalized exposure tracking and timely alerts for healthier cities.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel mobile sensing dataset from Surat, India for PM2.5 forecasting, featuring a Spatial Attention Graph Neural Network (SA-GNN) that combines cluster-specific GRUs for temporal dependencies and Graph Attention Network for spatial heterogeneity. SA-GNN achieved R²=0.95, outperforming LSTM, RNN, GRU, and ANN models.
AI.motivation: Urban air quality varies significantly along transit corridors, requiring high-resolution monitoring. Traditional models struggle with rapidly changing patterns in urban air quality, necessitating a more sophisticated approach to capture both spatial heterogeneity and temporal dynamics.
AI.method: The study created a mobile-sensing dataset with PM2.5, meteorological variables (temperature, humidity, wind speed, wind direction), and land-use features. Two node-definition strategies were employed: uniform segmentation (200-400m intervals) and DBSCAN clustering. Rolling mean and standard deviation of meteorological variables were computed for each node. The proposed SA-GNN model combines cluster-specific GRUs to capture localized temporal dependencies and a Graph Attention Network to learn spatial heterogeneity.
AI.result: SA-GNN achieved superior performance with R² = 0.95, RMSE = 6.8 μg/m³, and MAE = 4.2 μg/m³, outperforming all baseline models (LSTM, RNN, GRU, ANN). The baseline models performed well on low-resolution data but struggled to capture rapidly changing patterns in urban air quality.
AI.conclusion: Combining spatial clustering with adaptive attention significantly improves PM2.5 forecasting accuracy. The proposed SA-GNN enables real-time, fine-grained monitoring and supports personalized exposure tracking and timely alerts for healthier cities.

title: Resilience Beyond Stationary Client Unavailability: Unlocking Efficient and Unbiased Federated Learning
summary: Due to resource constraints or external and internal uncertainties, clients in real-world federated learning systems are often intermittently available edge devices. In highly dynamic environments, the parameter server lacks prior real-time knowledge of clients' availability, making it challenging to adapt traditional federated learning algorithms to be resilient to uncertainties in client availability. If not carefully addressed, complex client availability can introduce significant bias, potentially harming the performance of the trained model. Most prior work either fails to account for non-stationary client availability dynamics or demands significant memory and computational overhead. This paper aims to develop efficient federated learning algorithms that are provably resilient to heterogeneous and non-stationary stochastic client availability. We propose FedSWE, which admits novel algorithmic structures to (i) compensate for missed computations, (ii) stabilize and diffuse the global updates over rounds, and (iii) evenly mix the local updates through implicit gossiping, despite being agnostic to non-stationary dynamics. Compared with the standard FedAvg, FedSWE introduces light additional memory and computation overhead. We show that FedSWE converges to a stationary point of non-convex objectives while achieving the desired linear speedup property in certain special cases. We corroborate our analysis with numerical experiments over diversified client unavailability dynamics on real-world data sets.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the challenge of intermittent client availability in federated learning systems, where clients are often intermittently available edge devices. The authors propose FedSWE, a novel algorithm that compensates for missed computations, stabilizes global updates, and enables implicit gossiping to mix local updates, all while being agnostic to non-stationary client availability dynamics. The algorithm adds minimal overhead compared to FedAvg while providing theoretical convergence guarantees to stationary points of non-convex objectives and linear speedup properties in certain cases.
AI.motivation: In real-world federated learning systems, clients are often intermittently available edge devices due to resource constraints or uncertainties. The parameter server lacks prior real-time knowledge of client availability, making it challenging to adapt traditional federated learning algorithms. Complex client availability can introduce significant bias, potentially harming model performance. Prior work either fails to account for non-stationary client availability dynamics or requires significant memory and computational overhead.
AI.method: The authors propose FedSWE, which incorporates three novel algorithmic structures: (i) compensating for missed computations, (ii) stabilizing and diffusing global updates over rounds, and (iii) evenly mixing local updates through implicit gossiping. The algorithm is designed to be agnostic to non-stationary dynamics while introducing only light additional memory and computation overhead compared to the standard FedAvg.
AI.result: FedSWE converges to a stationary point of non-convex objectives while achieving the desired linear speedup property in certain special cases. The analysis is corroborated by numerical experiments over diversified client unavailability dynamics on real-world datasets.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents FedSWE as an efficient federated learning algorithm that is provably resilient to heterogeneous and non-stationary stochastic client availability. The algorithm successfully addresses the challenges of client availability uncertainty while maintaining computational efficiency and providing theoretical convergence guarantees.

title: Intrinsic Temporal Adaptation of CLIP for Partially Relevant Video Retrieval
summary: Partially Relevant Video Retrieval (PRVR) aims to retrieve untrimmed videos that contain moments relevant to a text query. Since the target moment occupies only a portion of the video, PRVR requires retrieval based on fine-grained understanding beyond coarse video-level matching. However, existing methods often rely on frozen CLIP frame features, which lack temporal understanding. Even with recent progress in parameter-efficient CLIP adaptation, video-level predictions can still be supported by imprecise frame-level evidence. In this paper, we propose an Intrinsic Temporal Adaptation (ITA) framework for PRVR. First, our Backbone-Internal Temporal Adaptation allows the last few visual transformer layers to attend over groups of neighboring frames. This provides temporally aware frame embeddings while keeping CLIP frozen and training only adaptation parameters. Second, we introduce Affinity-Weighted Gradient Propagation to address the weakly supervised nature of PRVR, softly aggregating top-$k$ frames based on text-frame affinities and propagating learning signals to multiple query-relevant frames. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on PRVR benchmarks, demonstrates robust cross-dataset transfer, and retrieves substantially more accurate frame-level evidence within ground-truth query-relevant moments. Our code is available at github.com/hynnsk/ITA.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an Intrinsic Temporal Adaptation (ITA) framework for Partially Relevant Video Retrieval (PRVR), which retrieves untrimmed videos containing moments relevant to text queries. The method addresses limitations of existing frozen CLIP-based approaches by introducing temporal awareness through grouped frame attention and handles weakly supervised learning via affinity-weighted gradient propagation.
AI.motivation: Existing PRVR methods rely on frozen CLIP frame features that lack temporal understanding. Even with parameter-efficient CLIP adaptation, video-level predictions can be supported by imprecise frame-level evidence, which is problematic since the target moment occupies only a portion of the video.
AI.method: The ITA framework has two main components: (1) Backbone-Internal Temporal Adaptation - allows the last few visual transformer layers to attend over groups of neighboring frames, providing temporally aware frame embeddings while keeping CLIP frozen and training only adaptation parameters; (2) Affinity-Weighted Gradient Propagation - addresses weakly supervised nature by softly aggregating top-k frames based on text-frame affinities and propagating learning signals to multiple query-relevant frames.
AI.result: The method achieves state-of-the-art performance on PRVR benchmarks, demonstrates robust cross-dataset transfer, and retrieves substantially more accurate frame-level evidence within ground-truth query-relevant moments.
AI.conclusion: The proposed ITA framework effectively addresses temporal understanding limitations in frozen CLIP-based PRVR methods through grouped frame attention and handles weakly supervised learning via affinity-weighted gradient propagation, leading to improved retrieval accuracy and better frame-level evidence localization.

title: SQL-Zero: Self-Evolving Text-to-SQL
summary: Training a competitive Text-to-SQL agent usually depends on human-annotated natural-language/SQL pairs, which are expensive, domain-specific, and a bottleneck for scaling to new databases. We show it is possible to train a competitive solver with zero annotated pairs. We introduce SQL-Zero, a proposer-solver self-play in which a challenger and a solver start from the same base LLM and the only ground truth is execution against the database itself. The challenger generates SQL pairs calibrated to the solver's current difficulty (targeting "hard but solvable"), and both roles are updated with GRPO in alternating turns, with a template-level repetition penalty on the challenger to prevent diversity collapse. Training on BIRD databases with no labels, self-play improves over the zero-shot base on BIRD dev by 6.6 points at 3B and 7.3 points at 7B. It also scores higher than a matched control trained under the same recipe on human BIRD gold over the same databases, although an exact paired test does not resolve that margin. Transfer depends on scale: at 3B every iteration outperforms the base on unseen Spider databases and under lexical perturbation (Spider-Syn), where it also degrades less than the matched BIRD-gold control, whereas at 7B only the first iteration preserves transfer.

AI.tldr: SQL-Zero trains a competitive Text-to-SQL solver using self-play with zero human-annotated examples. A challenger generates SQL pairs calibrated to solver difficulty ("hard but solvable"), and both roles are updated with GRPO in alternating turns. On BIRD databases without labels, it improves 6.6 points at 3B and 7.3 points at 7B over zero-shot baseline, outperforming a matched control trained on human BIRD gold. Transfer to unseen Spider databases works at 3B scale but degrades at 7B.
AI.motivation: Text-to-SQL training typically requires expensive human-annotated natural-language/SQL pairs, which are domain-specific and create a bottleneck for scaling to new databases. This paper addresses the need for training methods that don't depend on costly human annotations.
AI.method: SQL-Zero uses a proposer-solver self-play framework where a challenger and solver start from the same base LLM. The only ground truth is execution against the database itself. The challenger generates SQL pairs calibrated to the solver's current difficulty (targeting "hard but solvable"), and both roles are updated with GRPO (Gradient-Free Policy Optimization) in alternating turns. A template-level repetition penalty on the challenger prevents diversity collapse.
AI.result: Self-play training on BIRD databases with no labels improves over zero-shot base by 6.6 points at 3B scale and 7.3 points at 7B scale on BIRD dev. It also scores higher than a matched control trained on human BIRD gold over the same databases. At 3B scale, every iteration outperforms the base on unseen Spider databases and under lexical perturbation (Spider-Syn), with less degradation than the BIRD-gold control. At 7B scale, only the first iteration preserves transfer.
AI.conclusion: It is possible to train a competitive Text-to-SQL solver without any human-annotated pairs through self-play. Transfer performance depends on model scale: at 3B, self-play maintains transfer to unseen databases and under perturbations, while at 7B scale, transfer benefits are more limited. The approach demonstrates that database execution feedback alone can replace human annotations for training effective SQL solvers.

title: A Robust Watermark-based Fingerprint Framework for GNNs Ownership Verification
summary: The high training cost of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) has raised growing concerns regarding model ownership infringement, such as model stealing and unauthorized misuse. To verify model ownership and prevent significant economic losses, two groups of GNN Ownership Verification (OV) methods have been proposed: watermark-based methods and fingerprint-based methods. However, these methods typically face three limitations: (1) the performance degradation of protected models caused by out-of-distribution (OOD) watermark graphs with respect to the training set; (2) the unrealistic assumption that surrogate models have been trained on a watermark-containing training set; and (3) over-reliance on specific output levels for fingerprint extraction. In this paper, we propose a Robust watErMArk-based fingeRprint frameworK for GNNs, named REMARK. REMARK first generates carefully crafted in-distribution watermark graphs that maximize output differences between GNN models, thus mitigating OOD-induced performance degradation. REMARK then extracts robust fingerprints from these output differences to verify GNN ownership, thereby removing the assumptions that surrogate models must be trained on a watermark-containing dataset or expose specific output levels. Extensive experiments across widely used real-world datasets and GNN architectures demonstrate that REMARK achieves state-of-the-art OV accuracy and robustness while preserving the utility of protected models.

AI.tldr: REMARK is a novel framework for robust ownership verification of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) that combines watermark-based and fingerprint-based methods. It generates in-distribution watermark graphs to maximize output differences between GNN models and extracts robust fingerprints for ownership verification, addressing three key limitations of prior methods: OOD-induced performance degradation, unrealistic surrogate model assumptions, and over-reliance on specific output levels.
AI.motivation: The high training cost of GNNs has raised concerns about model ownership infringement (model stealing and unauthorized misuse). Existing GNN Ownership Verification (OV) methods (watermark-based and fingerprint-based) face three limitations: (1) performance degradation from out-of-distribution (OOD) watermark graphs; (2) unrealistic assumption that surrogate models are trained on watermark-containing datasets; and (3) over-reliance on specific output levels for fingerprint extraction.
AI.method: REMARK proposes a two-stage approach: (1) Generate carefully crafted in-distribution watermark graphs that maximize output differences between GNN models, thereby mitigating OOD-induced performance degradation; (2) Extract robust fingerprints from these output differences to verify GNN ownership, eliminating the need for surrogate models to be trained on watermark-containing datasets or expose specific output levels.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across widely used real-world datasets and GNN architectures demonstrate that REMARK achieves state-of-the-art OV accuracy and robustness while preserving the utility of protected models.
AI.conclusion: REMARK successfully addresses the three limitations of prior GNN ownership verification methods by using in-distribution watermark graphs and robust fingerprint extraction, achieving superior OV accuracy and robustness without compromising model utility.

title: Linguistic Trajectory Encoding for Efficient Long-Horizon Spatial Memory in Embodied Agents
summary: Embodied agents performing long-horizon tasks require a memory representation in which the state transitions of dynamic objects remain queryable in natural language across hours-to-days observation horizons. Existing systems either drop fine-grained motion (clip-level video-language embeddings), keep it only as raw coordinates (geometric SLAM), or organise it around immediate task context (agent working memories). None of them gives the agent a per-object timeline whose state transitions are themselves queryable in language. Our key contribution is \textbf{Linguistic Trajectory Encoding} (LTE), which compresses dynamic object motion histories via a hybrid representation combining natural language descriptions, sparse spatial anchors, and visual anchors. LTE adapts compression to motion complexity by anchoring periods without reliable observations to the last seen location, while representing motion with geometric waypoints and linguistic descriptions to preserve accuracy. To evaluate these capabilities across extended time horizons, we construct the \textbf{Spatial Memory Benchmark} (SMB) from EgoLife multi-day recordings, targeting capabilities absent in existing benchmarks: semantic trajectory retrieval and long-horizon object retrieval. On SMB, the LTE-based system achieves $45.3\%$ success in semantic trajectory retrieval and $48.7\%$ in long-horizon object retrieval, outperforming structured-memory and VLM baselines (best prior: $31.9\%$ and $34.4\%$). LTE achieves trajectory compression by factors of $8.7\times$ to $26.1\times$ with sub-second query latency on $24$\,h video. On Ego4D natural-language queries, the system reaches $28.75\%$ / $55.10\%$ R@1/R@5, $+15.80$ / $+31.30$ pts over EgoVLPv2.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Linguistic Trajectory Encoding (LTE), a hybrid memory representation for embodied agents that compresses dynamic object motion histories by combining natural language descriptions, sparse spatial anchors, and visual anchors. It enables queryable per-object timelines across long observation horizons (hours-to-days). The system achieves 45.3% semantic trajectory retrieval and 48.7% long-horizon object retrieval on the new Spatial Memory Benchmark, outperforming baselines by significant margins, with 8.7x-26.1x compression on 24h video.
AI.motivation: Embodied agents performing long-horizon tasks require memory representations where state transitions of dynamic objects remain queryable in natural language across extended time horizons. Existing approaches have critical limitations: video-language embeddings drop fine-grained motion (clip-level), geometric SLAM keeps only raw coordinates, and agent working memories organize around immediate task context. None provides per-object timelines with language-queryable state transitions.
AI.method: LTE compresses dynamic object motion histories via a hybrid representation combining natural language descriptions, sparse spatial anchors, and visual anchors. The method adapts compression to motion complexity by anchoring periods without reliable observations to the last seen location, while representing motion with geometric waypoints and linguistic descriptions to preserve accuracy. The Spatial Memory Benchmark (SMB) was constructed from EgoLife multi-day recordings to evaluate semantic trajectory retrieval and long-horizon object retrieval capabilities.
AI.result: On SMB, LTE achieves 45.3% success in semantic trajectory retrieval and 48.7% in long-horizon object retrieval, outperforming structured-memory and VLM baselines (best prior: 31.9% and 34.4%). LTE achieves trajectory compression by factors of 8.7x to 26.1x with sub-second query latency on 24-hour video. On Ego4D natural-language queries, the system reaches 28.75% / 55.10% R@1/R@5, achieving +15.80 / +31.30 point improvements over EgoVLPv2.
AI.conclusion: LTE successfully provides embodied agents with per-object timelines whose state transitions are queryable in natural language across extended time horizons. The hybrid representation combining linguistic, spatial, and visual anchors enables effective compression while preserving queryability, outperforming existing memory systems and video-language models on long-horizon retrieval tasks.

title: Model Retirement Creates Reproducibility Risk in Biomedical AI Publications
summary:
Background. Large language models (LLMs) are being adopted in biomedical research at a rapid and accelerating pace, yet commercial services that host many widely used models operate under deprecation schedules that can complicate scientific reproducibility.
  Methods. We searched PubMed for original research articles from 2022 through March 2026 that applied a specific LLM to a biomedical task. An extraction agent identified model names from 61,077 article abstracts with human reviewers validating a subset for extraction accuracy. Extracted model names were normalized to canonical model identifiers. Lifecycle data (release date, retirement date, status) were compiled for the 50 most frequently used models.
  Results. We identified 8,931 paper-model mentions spanning 5,242 unique publications after restricting the analysis to the 50 most frequently used models. Among these mentions, 77.7% cited a commercial closed-weight model. Overall, 42% involved a model that was already retired by the time of official publication or is scheduled to retire within two years of publication. The median interval from publication to model retirement was 538 days.
  Conclusion. Many biomedical publications using LLMs are on a trajectory toward computational non-reproducibility after publication. Model deprecation should be treated as a core reporting and preservation issue for biomedical research.

AI.tldr: This study examines the reproducibility crisis in biomedical research caused by LLM model deprecation. Analyzing 8,931 paper-model mentions across 5,242 publications, the authors find that 77.7% use commercial closed-weight models and 42% involve retired or soon-to-be-retired models, with a median of only 538 days between publication and model retirement.
AI.motivation: The rapid adoption of LLMs in biomedical research coincides with commercial model deprecation schedules that threaten scientific reproducibility. The authors aim to quantify this emerging problem by systematically tracking LLM usage and model lifecycle data in biomedical literature.
AI.method: The researchers searched PubMed for original research articles from 2022 through March 2026 that applied a specific LLM to biomedical tasks. An extraction agent identified model names from 61,077 article abstracts, with human reviewers validating a subset for accuracy. Extracted model names were normalized to canonical identifiers. Lifecycle data (release date, retirement date, status) were compiled for the 50 most frequently used models.
AI.result: Among 8,931 paper-model mentions spanning 5,242 unique publications: 77.7% cited a commercial closed-weight model; 42% involved a model that was already retired at publication or scheduled to retire within two years; the median interval from publication to model retirement was 538 days.
AI.conclusion: Many biomedical publications using LLMs face computational non-reproducibility after publication. Model deprecation should be treated as a core reporting and preservation issue for biomedical research, requiring new standards for model documentation and availability.

title: Persistent Teacher Anchoring for Tool-Using Agents
comment: 16 pages, 4 figures, 8 tables. Accepted at EMNLP 2026 (Main Conference)
summary: Distillation is common in LLM post-training, where on-policy knowledge distillation (OPKD) uses student-generated trajectories to prepare the student for downstream RL. At each state, the student matches a next-token distribution supplied by the teacher. As the rollout enters states the teacher would not visit, the teacher-student distribution gap can accumulate. In tool use, this gap becomes consequential because student-written calls execute before supervision and their observations shape later prefixes. Proposer-verifier generation addresses this drift by letting the teacher decide which student-proposed text is retained during generation. Existing formulations govern text but leave tool execution outside their scope. We propose Persistent Teacher Anchoring (PTA), a student-induced but teacher-committed rollout construction. PTA retains chunk-level verification and adds turn-level commitment, allowing a call to reach the environment only after the teacher has verified the entire turn. Treating verified chunks as atomic generation units, we introduce persistent lookahead, which fills idle rollout capacity by advancing future samples and carrying unfinished ones across student updates under the fixed verifier. Across Search-R1-style retrieval and DeepEyes-style perception RL, applying PTA before downstream RL improves macro best@4 by 2.5 and 2.8 points over OPKD under the same downstream RL budget, while lookahead improves throughput by 24%.

AI.tldr: PTA (Persistent Teacher Anchoring) addresses distribution drift in LLM knowledge distillation for tool use by requiring teacher verification of entire turns before environment execution, combined with persistent lookahead to improve throughput.
AI.motivation: In on-policy knowledge distillation (OPKD), the distribution gap between teacher and student accumulates as student-generated trajectories enter states the teacher wouldn't visit. This is particularly consequential in tool use scenarios where student-written calls execute before supervision and shape later prefixes.
AI.method: PTA introduces student-induced but teacher-committed rollout construction with: (1) chunk-level verification retained, (2) turn-level commitment added—calls reach environment only after teacher verifies entire turn, (3) treated verified chunks as atomic generation units, (4) persistent lookahead fills idle rollout capacity by advancing future samples and carrying unfinished ones across student updates.
AI.result: Applying PTA before downstream RL improves macro best@4 by 2.5 and 2.8 points over OPKD under the same downstream RL budget, while lookahead improves throughput by 24%.
AI.conclusion: PTA effectively mitigates distribution drift in tool-use distillation by maintaining teacher verification at turn level, and persistent lookahead significantly improves training efficiency without compromising quality.

title: Weather-Conditioned Depth Anything
summary: Monocular depth estimation foundation models, such as the Depth Anything series, have achieved remarkable performance across diverse domains. However, they still suffer from critical failures under adverse weather conditions, such as fog, rain, snow, or at night. To address this, we present Weather-Conditioned Depth Anything (DA-W), a framework that explicitly disentangles style from content for weather-robust depth estimation. Specifically, we introduce a Style Filter trained on a curated mix of real and synthetic degradation datasets to extract content-independent, degradation-aware weather embeddings. This style embedding is then injected into the Depth Anything backbone using a parameter-efficient, zero-initialized adapter. Such a lightweight modulation allows a single unified model to robustly adapt to diverse conditions, including fog, rain, snow, and low-light, while avoiding catastrophic forgetting of its core generalization abilities in normal conditions. We train the adapter using a pseudo-label distillation and alignment strategy. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed DA-W achieves state-of-the-art robust depth estimation, improving AbsRel by an average of 3.7% on our curated weather benchmarks, while matching or slightly outperforming performance on standard clean benchmarks. Our project page is available at https://zhaoming-tamu.github.io/WCDA/.

AI.tldr: DA-W is a weather-robust depth estimation framework that extends Depth Anything by disentangling style from content. It uses a Style Filter to extract weather embeddings and a zero-initialized adapter to modulate the backbone, achieving 3.7% average improvement in AbsRel on adverse weather benchmarks while maintaining clean benchmark performance.
AI.motivation: Monocular depth estimation foundation models like Depth Anything suffer critical failures under adverse weather conditions (fog, rain, snow, night), limiting their real-world applicability.
AI.method: 1) Style Filter trained on real and synthetic degradation datasets to extract content-independent, degradation-aware weather embeddings; 2) Zero-initialized parameter-efficient adapter to inject style embeddings into Depth Anything backbone; 3) Pseudo-label distillation and alignment strategy for training the adapter.
AI.result: State-of-the-art robust depth estimation with 3.7% average improvement in AbsRel on curated weather benchmarks, while matching or slightly outperforming performance on standard clean benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: DA-W successfully enables a single unified model to adapt to diverse weather conditions (fog, rain, snow, low-light) while avoiding catastrophic forgetting of its core generalization abilities in normal conditions.

title: FinalityBench: An Effect-Level Benchmark for Agent Decisions Under Delayed and Conflicting Financial Finality
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables. Code, corpus generator and all result files: https://github.com/abhisheksharma2411/finalitybench Archived at doi:10.5281/zenodo.22262591
summary: A merchant's payment processor, ledger, ERP and bank feed are updated by messages that get delayed, duplicated, dropped and reordered, so for minutes at a time the four hold contradictory beliefs about the same order. An agent resolving the exception must decide whether to ship goods, re-submit a capture, refund or wait, knowing some of those cannot be undone. We present FinalityBench, an executable benchmark for that decision. It keeps a hidden canonical event log and derives each system's view from a separately faulted delivery stream, so disagreement follows from specified fault semantics rather than being authored. Grading is on executed monetary effects: an episode is scored by the merchant's terminal economic position, relative to a privileged reference told when the pending capture resolves. The corpus of 321 tasks includes 45 twin pairs (90 tasks): tasks whose four system views are identical at the decision instant, whose authoritative probes both return unknown, and whose eventual correct dispositions differ. That snapshot indistinguishability is checked under every evaluation seed rather than assumed; equivalence over all interaction traces is not claimed. Over 14,445 graded episodes from nine programmatic policies, ranking by single-task accuracy and by paired loss disagree in 7 places: a ship-on-first-sign policy is second-best by accuracy at 65.7% and worst in the suite by paired loss, because it cannot tell the two members apart. A runtime gating irreversible actions on an authoritative finality probe reaches 85.4% and, unlike every polling policy, loses nothing to pass^5; its residual loss is almost entirely one archetype, which prices finality information directly. Language models reach the same exact rate as the hand-written gate on a stratified subset, lose about twice as much money, and discover the finality-gating strategy without being told it.

AI.tldr: FinalityBench is an executable benchmark for evaluating decision-making in payment processing systems where multiple components (processor, ledger, ERP, bank feed) hold contradictory beliefs due to message faults. The benchmark uses hidden canonical event logs and faulted delivery streams to test 321 tasks, including 45 twin pairs where systems are indistinguishable but require different actions.
AI.motivation: In payment systems, messages get delayed, duplicated, dropped, and reordered, causing different components to hold contradictory beliefs about transactions. An agent must make irreversible decisions (ship goods, re-submit capture, refund, or wait) without knowing the true state, and some actions cannot be undone. Existing benchmarks don't capture this specific problem of "indistinguishable but require different actions" scenarios.
AI.method: FinalityBench maintains a hidden canonical event log and derives each system's view from separately faulted delivery streams. Grading is based on executed monetary effects - scoring by the merchant's terminal economic position relative to a privileged reference. The corpus includes 45 twin pairs (90 tasks) where all four system views are identical at decision instant, both authoritative probes return unknown, but eventual correct dispositions differ. Testing involved 14,445 graded episodes from nine programmatic policies plus language models.
AI.result: Ranking by single-task accuracy and by paired loss disagree in 7 places. A ship-on-first-sign policy achieves 65.7% accuracy (second-best) but is worst by paired loss because it cannot distinguish twin pairs. A runtime gating irreversible actions on an authoritative finality probe achieves 85.4% accuracy and loses nothing to pass^5, with residual loss almost entirely from one archetype that prices finality information directly. Language models achieve the same accuracy as hand-written gate on stratified subset but lose about twice as much money, and discover the finality-gating strategy without being told it.
AI.conclusion: The distinction between accuracy and paired loss metrics reveals that twin pair tasks are critical for evaluating payment decision systems. Finality probing is the superior strategy, achieving 85.4% accuracy. Language models can discover optimal strategies autonomously but with higher monetary loss. The benchmark successfully captures the core challenge of making correct decisions under indistinguishable system states.

title: Dynamic Heterogeneous Graph Representation Learning: A Survey
summary: Graph representation learning (GRL) serves as a canonical paradigm for modeling complex networks. However, real-world AI systems inherently manifest as evolving heterogeneous entities with complex interactions, posing significant challenges to static or homogeneous modeling. To address these complexities, representation learning for Dynamic Heterogeneous Graphs (DHGs) has emerged as a vital approach for learning low-dimensional representations that simultaneously preserve structural semantics and temporal dynamics. This survey presents the first systematic review of DHG representation learning methods. We first introduce a unified formal definition that encompasses both discrete-time and continuous-time DHGs from the perspective of temporal granularity. Building upon this formulation, we propose a novel algorithm-centric taxonomy that categorizes existing literature, including early embedding-based approaches, graph neural network (GNN)-based models, and relatively recent Transformer-based DHG methods, while explicitly highlighting their intrinsic modeling biases with respect to dynamic granularity. Furthermore, we summarize representative applications of DHG representation learning, along with commonly used datasets and benchmarks. Finally, we discuss promising research directions that guide future advances in this rapidly evolving field.

AI.tldr: This survey presents the first systematic review of Dynamic Heterogeneous Graph (DHG) representation learning methods, covering early embedding-based approaches, GNN-based models, and Transformer-based methods, along with applications, datasets, and future research directions.
AI.motivation: Real-world AI systems are evolving heterogeneous entities with complex interactions, posing challenges to static or homogeneous modeling. There was a need for a systematic review of DHG representation learning methods.
AI.method: The authors propose a unified formal definition encompassing both discrete-time and continuous-time DHGs from temporal granularity perspective, and introduce a novel algorithm-centric taxonomy to categorize existing literature while highlighting modeling biases regarding dynamic granularity.
AI.result: The survey covers early embedding-based approaches, graph neural network (GNN)-based models, and Transformer-based DHG methods, along with representative applications, commonly used datasets, benchmarks, and promising research directions.
AI.conclusion: This survey provides the first systematic review of DHG representation learning, offering a unified formal definition, a novel taxonomy, and guidance for future advances in this rapidly evolving field.

title: PAPT++: Risk-Aware Adversarial Tuning and Generation for Single Domain Generalization
summary: Single domain generalization (SDG) aims to learn a model from one labeled source domain that generalizes to unseen target domains. A common strategy is to enrich the source distribution with augmented or generated samples, and recent text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models provide a strong generative prior for this purpose. However, diversity alone is insufficient for robust generalization, because useful generated samples should also capture variations that the current classifier finds difficult. Motivated by distributionally robust optimization (DRO), we define a semantic ambiguity set in the class-conditional generative space of a pretrained T2I model and search it for samples with high classification loss under the current classifier. To this end, we introduce PAPT++, a risk-aware adversarial generation-training framework for SDG. PAPT++ first learns diverse semantic reference images for each class through image-text alignment and intra-class diversity regularization. These references then serve as denoising targets during classifier-guided diffusion synthesis, reducing semantic drift while guiding generation toward challenging variations. The generated samples are combined with the source data to update the classifier, and the updated classifier guides the next synthesis round in return. In this way, PAPT++ progressively exposes the classifier to challenging yet semantically consistent variations. Extensive experiments on standard SDG benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of the proposed PAPT++ method and the effectiveness of its main components.

AI.tldr: PAPT++ is a risk-aware adversarial generation-training framework for single domain generalization (SDG) that uses text-to-image diffusion models to generate challenging yet semantically consistent samples. It iteratively synthesizes samples with high classification loss under the current classifier to progressively improve robustness to unseen target domains.
AI.motivation: Current SDG methods using text-to-image diffusion models rely on diversity alone, but this is insufficient for robust generalization. The key insight is that useful generated samples should capture variations that the current classifier finds difficult, not just diverse samples. This is motivated by distributionally robust optimization (DRO) principles.
AI.method: PAPT++ works in an iterative loop: (1) Learn diverse semantic reference images for each class via image-text alignment and intra-class diversity regularization; (2) Use these references as denoising targets during classifier-guided diffusion synthesis to reduce semantic drift while targeting challenging variations; (3) Combine generated samples with source data to update the classifier; (4) The updated classifier guides the next synthesis round. This creates a adversarial generation-training process that progressively exposes the classifier to difficult variations.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on standard SDG benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of PAPT++ over existing methods and validate the effectiveness of its main components.
AI.conclusion: PAPT++ effectively addresses the limitation of diversity-only approaches by incorporating risk-aware adversarial generation that targets classifier weakness. The framework successfully bridges the gap between source domain training and generalization to unseen target domains through iterative adversarial training with text-to-image diffusion models.

title: PLUME: Parameter-Efficient Personalization of Large Language Models via Low-Rank User Modulation in Shared Subspaces
summary: Personalizing large language models (LLMs) is essential for delivering AI assistance that aligns with individual users' styles, intents, and preferences. While per-user fine-tuning can substantially enhance personalization quality, it introduces significant parameter and storage overhead, limiting scalability to large user populations. We propose PLUME (Personalized Low-Rank Adaptation through User Modulation and Shared Subspace), a lightweight framework that achieves efficient and expressive per-user adaptation by leveraging a shared task-specific subspace. Specifically, PLUME first learns a global task subspace from aggregated user data. Personalization is then achieved by training only a lightweight small square matrix within this subspace, enabling each user to obtain a tailored model while keeping shared components fixed. Cross-layer shared parameters and rank-1 residual terms are further introduced to significantly reduce redundancy while maintaining expressiveness. Experiments on multiple personalized text generation benchmarks demonstrate that PLUME achieves comparable or superior performance to strong baselines, while reducing per-user parameters by over 95%. These results establish shared-subspace modulation with minimal residuals as a scalable and semantically grounded approach to LLM personalization.

AI.tldr: PLUME is a lightweight framework for personalizing large language models by learning a shared task-specific subspace and training only small per-user matrices within it, reducing per-user parameters by over 95% while maintaining performance.
AI.motivation: Per-user fine-tuning for LLM personalization introduces significant parameter and storage overhead, making it unscalable for large user populations. Current approaches lack a balance between personalization quality and efficiency.
AI.method: PLUME first learns a global task subspace from aggregated user data. Personalization is achieved by training only a lightweight small square matrix within this subspace, keeping shared components fixed. Cross-layer shared parameters and rank-1 residual terms are introduced to reduce redundancy while maintaining expressiveness.
AI.result: PLUME achieves comparable or superior performance to strong baselines on multiple personalized text generation benchmarks, while reducing per-user parameters by over 95%.
AI.conclusion: Shared-subspace modulation with minimal residuals provides a scalable and semantically grounded approach to LLM personalization, effectively balancing personalization quality and parameter efficiency.

title: Learning-Augmented Algorithms: Guarantees, Construction Mechanisms, and System-Level Implications
summary: Learning-augmented algorithms use fallible predictions while retaining formal performance guarantees. This survey synthesizes prediction interfaces, error measures, consistency--robustness trade-offs, and five representative construction mechanisms across online optimization, caching, learned data structures, graph problems, and mechanism design. An orthogonal theorem-level axis distinguishes achieved upper bounds from matched asymptotic dependence. Formal guarantees are separated from empirical systems evidence, with explicit treatment of prediction cost, feedback, and composition. The resulting synthesis states sufficient conditions for limited end-to-end reasoning and delineates open problems in cost-aware prediction, endogenous error, semantic predictors, and benchmarking.

AI.tldr: This is a survey paper synthesizing learning-augmented algorithms that use fallible predictions while maintaining formal performance guarantees. It covers prediction interfaces, error measures, consistency-robustness trade-offs, and five construction mechanisms across online optimization, caching, learned data structures, graph problems, and mechanism design.
AI.motivation: The motivation appears to be synthesizing the emerging field of learning-augmented algorithms, which combine machine learning predictions with traditional algorithmic guarantees. The paper aims to provide a systematic framework for understanding how to use predictions while maintaining worst-case performance guarantees.
AI.method: The survey method involves: (1) categorizing prediction interfaces and error measures, (2) analyzing consistency-robustness trade-offs, (3) examining five representative construction mechanisms across different domains, (4) distinguishing achieved upper bounds from matched asymptotic dependence at the theorem level, (5) separating formal guarantees from empirical evidence, and (6) explicitly treating prediction cost, feedback, and composition.
AI.result: The synthesis identifies sufficient conditions for limited end-to-end reasoning and delineates open problems in cost-aware prediction, endogenous error, semantic predictors, and benchmarking.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes by stating sufficient conditions for limited end-to-end reasoning and outlines four key open problems: (1) cost-aware prediction, (2) endogenous error, (3) semantic predictors, and (4) benchmarking in learning-augmented algorithms.

title: LetOccVote: Learning Weakly Supervised 3D Occupancy through Consensus
summary: Weakly supervised 3D occupancy prediction reduces the reliance on costly 3D annotations by learning from 2D pseudo-labels generated by vision foundation models. However, existing methods typically use these imperfect pseudo-labels directly as supervision, making occupancy learning vulnerable to erroneous geometric and semantic targets. We observe that agreement across repeated observations provides an inexpensive and reliable cue for assessing pseudo-label reliability.
