Based on this observation, we propose \textbf{LetOccVote}, a weakly supervised Gaussian-based occupancy framework that leverages cross-frame voting to improve both geometric and semantic supervision. For geometry, Depth Vote exploits cross-frame geometric agreement to refine supported pseudo depth and reject contradictory estimates before volumetric lifting and depth supervision. For semantics, Semantic Vote aggregates pseudo-semantic observations in a shared 3D space to identify reliable and contested evidence, strengthening reliable semantic supervision while filtering unreliable pseudo-label segments. The entire framework is trained solely with 2D pseudo-label supervision without requiring 3D occupancy annotations. On Occ3D-nuScenes, LetOccVote achieves 53.27 IoU and 20.39 mIoU, establishing state-of-the-art performance among methods with 2D pseudo-label supervision.

AI.tldr: LetOccVote is a weakly supervised 3D occupancy prediction framework that leverages cross-frame voting to improve both geometric and semantic supervision from imperfect 2D pseudo-labels. It uses agreement across repeated observations to assess pseudo-label reliability, achieving state-of-the-art performance (53.27 IoU, 20.39 mIoU) on Occ3D-nuScenes without requiring 3D annotations.
AI.motivation: Weakly supervised 3D occupancy prediction aims to reduce reliance on costly 3D annotations by using 2D pseudo-labels from vision foundation models. However, existing methods treat these pseudo-labels as ground truth, making learning vulnerable to erroneous geometric and semantic targets. The key insight is that agreement across repeated observations provides an inexpensive and reliable cue for assessing pseudo-label reliability.
AI.method: LetOccVote employs a Gaussian-based framework with two voting mechanisms: (1) Depth Vote for geometry - exploits cross-frame geometric agreement to refine supported pseudo depth and reject contradictory estimates before volumetric lifting and depth supervision; (2) Semantic Vote for semantics - aggregates pseudo-semantic observations in a shared 3D space to identify reliable and contested evidence, strengthening reliable semantic supervision while filtering unreliable pseudo-label segments. The entire framework is trained solely with 2D pseudo-label supervision without requiring 3D occupancy annotations.
AI.result: On Occ3D-nuScenes benchmark, LetOccVote achieves 53.27 IoU and 20.39 mIoU, establishing state-of-the-art performance among methods with 2D pseudo-label supervision.
AI.conclusion: The proposed cross-frame voting mechanism effectively addresses the noise problem in 2D pseudo-labels by leveraging temporal consistency. By distinguishing between reliable and unreliable pseudo-labels through agreement analysis, LetOccVote significantly outperforms existing weakly supervised methods, demonstrating the efficacy of using cross-frame agreement as a reliable cue for pseudo-label quality assessment.

title: Aplaud: Adaptive Personalized Low-Rank Decomposition for User-Specific LLM
summary: In this paper, we study the problem of personalized survey response prediction using fine-tuned large language models (LLMs). This task poses unique challenges: limited per-user training data, scalability of model storage, and the need to exploit shared structure across survey questions. To address these issues, we propose Aplaud (Adaptive Personalized Low-rank and User-specific Nested Decomposition), a lightweight and scalable framework for LLM personalization. Aplaud extends the LoRA paradigm by separating adaptation into a frozen, shared low-rank basis and a compact user-specific correction, augmented with a rank-one residual for finer personalization. To further reduce per-user parameter cost and mitigate overfitting, the correction matrix can be factorized into an even lower-rank form. Empirical results demonstrate that Aplaud achieves efficient, scalable personalization across users while outperforming state-of-the-art LoRA-based personalized LLM approaches in both generalization and inference efficiency.

AI.tldr: Aplaud is a lightweight framework for personalizing large language models to predict survey responses for individual users. It extends LoRA by separating adaptation into a frozen shared low-rank basis and a compact user-specific correction with a rank-one residual, where the correction can be further factorized to reduce parameters and mitigate overfitting.
AI.motivation: Personalized survey response prediction using LLMs faces three key challenges: limited per-user training data, scalability of model storage, and the need to exploit shared structure across survey questions.
AI.method: Aplaud (Adaptive Personalized Low-rank and User-specific Nested Decomposition) extends the LoRA paradigm by separating adaptation into: (1) a frozen, shared low-rank basis, (2) a compact user-specific correction matrix augmented with a rank-one residual for finer personalization, and (3) optional factorization of the correction matrix into an even lower-rank form to reduce per-user parameters and mitigate overfitting.
AI.result: Aplaud achieves efficient, scalable personalization across users while outperforming state-of-the-art LoRA-based personalized LLM approaches in both generalization and inference efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Aplaud framework successfully addresses the challenges of personalized LLM survey response prediction through its hierarchical low-rank decomposition approach, enabling effective personalization with reduced parameters and improved generalization.

title: How Faithful Is Attribution for Sales Forecasting? A Counterfactual Study
summary: Deep models for sales forecasting, such as WaveNet-style dilated convolutional networks, are accurate but opaque: when a single model predicts sales for one of many series, it offers no account of why. We add a post-hoc, architecture-agnostic counterfactual interpretability layer to a multi-series WaveNet forecaster trained on the full Corporacion Favorita grocery dataset (174,685 series over 1,688 days). The method decomposes each forecast into contributions that sum exactly to the predicted value, avoiding the allocation artifacts we observed with additive SHAP-style attribution. We evaluate faithfulness with a deletion/insertion protocol and find a statistically significant effect on both tests (deletion gap 0.22, p<0.001; insertion gap 0.27, p<0.01; robust across five background-sampling seeds), establishing that the attributions reflect genuine model behavior rather than plausible-looking artifacts. We then characterize, honestly, where attribution is and is not informative: reliance on the promotion signal is heterogeneous across series (median ratio approximately 1.0, with roughly 20% of series showing a strong effect), and the model captures the shape of the weekly sales cycle (day-of-week r=0.78) while systematically under-predicting its amplitude. Our contribution is not improved accuracy but an interpretability layer with a rigorous faithfulness evaluation and a candid account of its limits.

AI.tldr: This paper adds a post-hoc counterfactual interpretability layer to a WaveNet sales forecasting model trained on a large grocery dataset (174K+ series). The method decomposes forecasts into contributions that sum exactly to the prediction, avoiding allocation artifacts. The approach is evaluated using deletion/insertion protocols showing statistically significant faithfulness, and the authors honestly characterize where attribution is and isn't informative.
AI.motivation: Deep models like WaveNet are accurate for sales forecasting but opaque - they don't explain why a particular prediction was made. Existing interpretability methods like SHAP can introduce allocation artifacts. The authors sought to add a post-hoc, architecture-agnostic interpretability layer that provides faithful attributions.
AI.method: Post-hoc counterfactual interpretability layer applied to a multi-series WaveNet forecaster. Uses deletion/insertion protocol for evaluation with 5 background-sampling seeds. Characterizes attribution informativeness by examining promotion signal heterogeneity and day-of-week cycle capture.
AI.result: Deletion gap 0.22 (p<0.001), insertion gap 0.27 (p<0.01), both statistically significant across five seeds. Promotion signal reliance is heterogeneous (median ratio ~1.0, ~20% of series showing strong effect). Model captures weekly cycle shape (r=0.78) but systematically under-predicts amplitude.
AI.conclusion: The contribution is not improved accuracy but an interpretability layer with rigorous faithfulness evaluation and candid acknowledgment of its limitations. The method avoids allocation artifacts and provides statistically verified faithful attributions, while honestly reporting where attribution is and isn't informative.

title: Mitigating Performance Discrepancy in Cross-Domain 3D Class-Incremental Learning
summary: 3D perception plays a crucial role in real-world applications such as autonomous driving, robotics, and AR/VR. In practical scenarios, 3D perception models need to continually adapt to newly emerging 3D object categories, making class-incremental learning (CIL) particularly important. However, unlike 2D images, 3D point clouds are inherently heterogeneous: objects from the same class may not only come from the clean CAD domain, but also from RGB-D camera scans of varying quality, video reconstructions, or even corrupted observations. We discover that such heterogeneity introduces a new challenge beyond catastrophic forgetting: the degree of performance degradation can vary substantially across domains, a phenomenon we term performance discrepancy. To investigate this problem, we establish the Domain3D-CIL training and evaluation protocol, which contains point cloud categories from heterogeneous domains. We further adapt a wide range of mainstream CIL methods to the 3D modality. The results demonstrate that this performance discrepancy consistently appears across these baselines. To mitigate this issue, we introduce PolyMem, an exemplar-free approach that implicitly models rich high-order statistics of the feature distribution to enhance cross-domain robustness. Experiments demonstrate that our method effectively alleviates the performance discrepancy while improving the model's performance across domains. Code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses class-incremental learning (CIL) for 3D point clouds, identifying a new challenge called "performance discrepancy" where model degradation varies across heterogeneous domains (CAD, RGB-D scans, video reconstructions, corrupted data). The authors establish Domain3D-CIL benchmark, adapt existing CIL methods to 3D, and propose PolyMem - an exemplar-free method using high-order feature statistics to enhance cross-domain robustness.
AI.motivation: 3D perception is crucial for autonomous driving, robotics, and AR/VR. Real-world applications require continual adaptation to new 3D object categories (class-incremental learning). Unlike 2D images, 3D point clouds are heterogeneous - objects from the same class can come from different domains (CAD, RGB-D scans, video reconstructions, corrupted observations), causing varying performance degradation across domains - a phenomenon termed "performance discrepancy."
AI.method: 1) Established Domain3D-CIL training and evaluation protocol with heterogeneous point cloud domains; 2) Adapted mainstream CIL methods to 3D modality; 3) Proposed PolyMem - an exemplar-free approach that implicitly models rich high-order statistics of the feature distribution to enhance cross-domain robustness.
AI.result: The performance discrepancy consistently appears across all baseline CIL methods. The proposed PolyMem effectively alleviates the performance discrepancy while improving the model's performance across domains.
AI.conclusion: PolyMem successfully addresses the performance discrepancy issue in 3D class-incremental learning by using high-order statistics of feature distributions, providing robust cross-domain performance without requiring exemplars. Code will be publicly available.

title: DCFA: Dual-view Causal-inspired Attribution for Failure Reasoning in LLM-based Multi-agent Systems
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems have experienced rapid growth in recent years. Despite their promise, such systems remain fragile, frequently exhibiting reasoning and coordination errors that can lead to system-level failures. Failure attribution in such systems relies on tracing natural language interactions among agents to identify the decisive error, which refers to the earliest action whose correction can reverse system failure. There are two key challenges: 1) Shallow attribution: Existing methods often capture only minor deviations, such as incomplete retrievals or formatting errors, which verification mechanisms can correct, while missing the decisive cause of system failure. 2) Contextual degradation: As the length of the system traces increases, the model's reasoning ability rapidly deteriorates. To address these challenges, we propose DCFA, a training-free framework for failure attribution. DCFA integrates a global module that constructs structured causal-inspired dependency graphs from system traces to identify the initial decisive error, and a local module that applies local counterfactual-inspired reasoning to refine causal-inspired attribution. Experiments on the Who&When benchmark across six LLMs show that DCFA improves step-level accuracy by up to 8.27% over state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: DCFA is a training-free framework for failure attribution in LLM-based multi-agent systems that identifies the decisive error (the earliest action whose correction can reverse system failure) by integrating a global module constructing causal dependency graphs and a local module applying counterfactual-inspired reasoning.
AI.motivation: LLM-based multi-agent systems are fragile and frequently exhibit reasoning and coordination errors leading to system failures. Existing failure attribution methods suffer from shallow attribution (capturing only minor deviations while missing decisive causes) and contextual degradation (declining reasoning ability as trace length increases).
AI.method: DCFA integrates two modules: (1) A global module that constructs structured causal-inspired dependency graphs from system traces to identify the initial decisive error; (2) A local module that applies local counterfactual-inspired reasoning to refine causal attribution. The framework is training-free.
AI.result: DCFA improves step-level accuracy by up to 8.27% over state-of-the-art baselines on the Who&When benchmark across six LLMs.
AI.conclusion: The proposed DCFA framework effectively addresses both shallow attribution and contextual degradation challenges in failure attribution for LLM-based multi-agent systems through its dual-module approach combining global causal graph construction and local counterfactual reasoning.

title: Federated Attack Campaign Detection via Contrastive Encoding of Threat Indicators in Gradient Updates
comment: Accepted to ECML-PKDD 2026, 4th Workshop on Advancements in Federated Learning - Towards Trustworthy Federated Learning
summary: Detecting orchestrated cyberattack campaigns that span multiple organizations traditionally requires sharing sensitive telemetry and threat intelligence across institutional boundaries and country borders, a barrier that Federated Learning removes by training shared threat detectors directly on local data. We propose FedIoC, a modular framework in which clients fold locally available structured threat indicators into their gradient updates; we instantiate the client-side encoder with a supervised contrastive loss over IoC-matched flows. Within each training batch, flows that match any known indicator pattern form the positive set; the contrastive objective pulls their learned embeddings together and pushes non-IoC embeddings away, so that campaign-relevant structure is, by design, expressed in the gradient direction. Clients sharing indicators for the same attack campaign then produce aligned gradient components, which the server clusters by the cosine similarity of their updates to recover global campaign patterns without any direct IoC transmission. We evaluate FedIoC on two public threat-detection benchmarks distributed across FL clients that each observe only a fragment of every active campaign and hold disjoint indicator sets derived from their local telemetry. In this regime the FL server recovers cross-organizational campaign cohorts directly from gradient geometry. We contribute FedIoC as a modular framework for this setting, and use it to pinpoint the non-IID gradient structure as the main driver of recovery and to define the open problem of designing encoders that improve on it.

AI.tldr: FedIoC is a federated learning framework that enables multiple organizations to collaboratively detect orchestrated cyberattack campaigns without sharing sensitive threat intelligence. It uses a supervised contrastive loss over IoC (Indicators of Compromise)-matched network flows, where clients train on local data and share gradient updates instead of raw data. The server clusters gradient updates by cosine similarity to recover cross-organizational campaign patterns without direct IoC transmission.
AI.motivation: Detecting orchestrated cyberattack campaigns spanning multiple organizations traditionally requires sharing sensitive telemetry and threat intelligence across institutional boundaries and borders, which is a significant barrier. The paper aims to remove this barrier by using Federated Learning to train shared threat detectors directly on local data without exposing sensitive information.
AI.method: The proposed method (FedIoC) uses a modular framework where clients encode locally available structured threat indicators into gradient updates. The client-side encoder uses a supervised contrastive loss over IoC-matched flows within each training batch. Flows matching known indicator patterns form a positive set, and the contrastive objective pulls their embeddings together while pushing non-IoC embeddings away. Clients sharing indicators for the same attack campaign produce aligned gradient components, which the server clusters by cosine similarity to recover global campaign patterns.
AI.result: The evaluation was conducted on two public threat-detection benchmarks distributed across FL clients. Each client observes only a fragment of every active campaign and holds disjoint indicator sets derived from local telemetry. In this regime, the FL server successfully recovers cross-organizational campaign cohorts directly from gradient geometry.
AI.conclusion: The paper contributes FedIoC as a modular framework for this setting and identifies the non-IID (non-identically distributed) gradient structure as the main driver of recovery. They define the open problem of designing encoders that improve on this approach.

title: SimFuse3D: Source-Guided Target Simulation and Confidence-Guided Multi-Stage Localization Reweighting for Cross-Platform 3D Object Detection
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures. Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters
summary: Changes in sensor height and viewpoint alter object-level point distributions, making cross-platform LiDAR unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) difficult. Self-training uses labeled source scans and unlabeled target scans, yet a retained prediction may provide a useful target location while enclosing sparse foreground returns, background clutter, or points inconsistent with the predicted box. We refer to this mismatch as box-point inconsistency. We introduce SimFuse3D, which preserves the target placement and repairs the associated pseudo-object using measured geometry from labeled source scans. Object Memory retrieves a compatible labeled source instance. Target Simulation places its ground-truth box at the target location, aligns its points with the target viewing geometry, and filters the aligned crop to approximate the target observation. Confidence-Guided Multi-Stage Localization Reweighting (CMLR) maps each target pseudo-object confidence score to a bounded weight shared by RPN localization and R-CNN box regression. All components operate only during adaptation, leaving the detector architecture and inference graph unchanged. Across six cross-platform transfers, SimFuse3D exceeds Pi3DET-Net on every reported AP metric and ranks first among the compared adaptation methods on nearly all metrics. On nuScenes-to-KITTI, it ranks first among the compared adaptation methods with both evaluated detectors.

AI.tldr: SimFuse3D is a LiDAR unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) method that addresses cross-platform transfer challenges caused by sensor height and viewpoint differences. It repairs box-point inconsistencies in pseudo-objects using geometry from labeled source scans, and uses confidence-guided reweighting to improve adaptation performance.
AI.motivation: Cross-platform LiDAR UDA is difficult due to changes in sensor height and viewpoint altering object-level point distributions. Self-training methods suffer from "box-point inconsistency" where retained predictions may have sparse foreground returns, background clutter, or points inconsistent with the predicted box.
AI.method: SimFuse3D has three components: (1) Object Memory retrieves compatible labeled source instances; (2) Target Simulation places ground-truth boxes at target locations, aligns points with target viewing geometry, and filters crops to approximate target observation; (3) Confidence-Guided Multi-Stage Localization Reweighting (CMLR) maps pseudo-object confidence scores to bounded weights for RPN localization and R-CNN box regression. All components operate only during adaptation, leaving detector architecture unchanged.
AI.result: Across six cross-platform transfers, SimFuse3D exceeds Pi3DET-Net on every reported AP metric and ranks first among compared adaptation methods on nearly all metrics. On nuScenes-to-KITTI, it ranks first with both evaluated detectors.
AI.conclusion: SimFuse3D effectively addresses box-point inconsistency in LiDAR UDA through target simulation and confidence-guided reweighting, achieving state-of-the-art performance across diverse cross-platform transfers.

title: Shadow Queries for Private Retrieval in Vector Databases
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) increasingly rely on information retrieval (IR) systems, such as Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), to incorporate domain-specific knowledge without costly re-training. These systems often store pre-computed document embeddings in cloud-based vector databases. However, such embeddings are vulnerable to embedding inversion attacks (EIAs), which can reconstruct their underlying text. Existing defenses, such as adding noise or scaling embeddings, often provide limited privacy or significantly reduce retrieval utility.
  We propose SHAQ (shadow query generation), a semantic-decomposition and embedding-decoupling defense against EIAs. SHAQ is based on the insight that EIAs rely on the strong coupling between an embedding and its original text. Instead of storing document embeddings directly, SHAQ uses a generative language model to create diverse shadow queries that capture different semantic aspects of each document. These queries are then encoded and stored in place of the original document embeddings, thereby decomposing document semantics and decoupling stored embeddings from the source text.
  Experiments across diverse IR datasets show that SHAQ substantially improves privacy while preserving retrieval utility, achieving a recovery rate as low as 0.2104, defending up to 19.50% more tokens than baseline defenses, and reaching up to 0.7967 MAP@10 with up to 5.53% utility improvement. These results demonstrate that semantic decomposition and embedding decoupling provide an effective alternative to directly modifying embeddings for defending against EIAs.

AI.tldr: SHAQ is a defense mechanism against embedding inversion attacks (EIAs) in retrieval-augmented generation systems. It uses a generative language model to create diverse shadow queries capturing different semantic aspects of documents, which are then encoded and stored instead of original embeddings, thereby decoupling embeddings from source text while preserving retrieval utility.
AI.motivation: Large language models increasingly rely on information retrieval systems like RAG to incorporate domain-specific knowledge. These systems store pre-computed document embeddings in cloud-based vector databases, which are vulnerable to embedding inversion attacks (EIAs) that can reconstruct the original text. Existing defenses (adding noise or scaling embeddings) provide limited privacy or significantly reduce retrieval utility.
AI.method: SHAQ proposes a semantic-decomposition and embedding-decoupling defense. Instead of storing document embeddings directly, it uses a generative language model to create diverse shadow queries that capture different semantic aspects of each document. These queries are then encoded and stored in place of the original document embeddings, thereby decomposing document semantics and decoupling stored embeddings from the source text.
AI.result: Experiments across diverse IR datasets show that SHAQ substantially improves privacy while preserving retrieval utility: achieving a recovery rate as low as 0.2104, defending up to 19.50% more tokens than baseline defenses, and reaching up to 0.7967 MAP@10 with up to 5.53% utility improvement.
AI.conclusion: Semantic decomposition and embedding decoupling provide an effective alternative to directly modifying embeddings for defending against EIAs, offering better privacy-utility tradeoffs than existing baseline defenses.

title: Communication-Efficient Personalized Federated Learning via Layer-Wise Multi-Threshold Random Sketching
summary: Personalized federated learning (PFL) is a promising paradigm for collaborative learning over distributed devices, where edge nodes collaboratively train personalized models without sharing raw data. Although PFL addresses data heterogeneity by learning client-specific models, it still suffers from substantial uplink and downlink communication costs when exchanging high-dimensional parameters in bandwidth-constrained systems. Recent one-bit methods achieve extreme compression, but they usually rely on a single thresholding rule applied to the whole model. This design has two limitations. First, it overlooks layer-wise differences in parameter distributions and quantization sensitivities. Second, a single threshold provides only coarse binary information and cannot capture fine-grained variations in parameter distributions. To address these issues, we propose a communication-efficient PFL framework via layer-wise multi-threshold random sketching. In the proposed method, each layer is assigned its own set of quantization thresholds, so that the compressed representation can adapt to layer-specific statistics while using multiple intervals to provide a finer low-bit description of sketched parameters. The proposed method supports bidirectional communication using compact low-bit sketches and improves the communication-accuracy tradeoff compared with existing one-bit compression approaches.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a communication-efficient personalized federated learning (PFL) framework using layer-wise multi-threshold random sketching to address high communication costs in bandwidth-constrained systems. The method assigns each layer its own quantization thresholds to adapt to layer-specific statistics and provide finer low-bit descriptions of parameters.
AI.motivation: Existing one-bit compression methods for PFL rely on a single thresholding rule applied to the whole model, which has two key limitations: (1) it overlooks layer-wise differences in parameter distributions and quantization sensitivities, and (2) a single threshold provides only coarse binary information without capturing fine-grained variations in parameter distributions.
AI.method: The proposed framework uses layer-wise multi-threshold random sketching where each neural network layer is assigned its own set of quantization thresholds. This allows the compressed representation to adapt to layer-specific statistics while using multiple intervals to provide finer low-bit descriptions of sketched parameters. The method supports bidirectional communication using compact low-bit sketches.
AI.result: The proposed method improves the communication-accuracy tradeoff compared with existing one-bit compression approaches in personalized federated learning.
AI.conclusion: The layer-wise multi-threshold approach effectively addresses the limitations of single-threshold methods by capturing layer-specific parameter distributions and providing finer-grained quantization, leading to better performance in communication-constrained PFL scenarios.

title: Diffusion Language Models for Mobile Edge Agentic AI: Foundations, Applications, and Challenges
summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer a non-autoregressive alternative for mobile edge agentic artificial intelligence (AI) by refining tokens through iterative denoising rather than left-to-right decoding. Compared with autoregressive Transformer-based large language models (LLMs), DLMs can update multiple uncertain tokens in parallel and exploit bidirectional context throughout the generation process, enabling more flexible quality-latency trade-offs beyond fixed sequential decoding. These properties are particularly attractive for edge agents, where partial refinement, early exit, and constraint-guided correction can reduce response delay and communication overhead while improving robustness under noisy, incomplete, or dynamic contexts. This survey reviews DLM foundations and analyzes their suitability for edge settings under latency, memory, energy, bandwidth, privacy, and reliability constraints. We cover resource-efficient architectures, training and inference acceleration, compression, edge/cloud deployment, communication-aware serving, Internet of Things (IoT)/wireless applications, and evaluation of DLM-based agents. We further discuss open issues in long-context state management, split inference, trustworthy execution, multimodal grounding, and reproducible benchmarking. The goal is to connect DLM modeling properties, including bidirectionality, parallel refinement, controllability, and quality-latency elasticity, with system-level requirements of future mobile edge intelligence.

AI.tldr: This survey examines Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) as a non-autoregressive alternative for mobile edge agentic AI. DLMs refine tokens through iterative denoising rather than sequential decoding, enabling parallel token updates and bidirectional context exploitation. The paper analyzes DLM suitability for edge settings under latency, memory, energy, bandwidth, privacy, and reliability constraints, covering architectures, compression, deployment, and evaluation.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive Transformer-based LLMs face limitations for edge AI due to sequential decoding constraints. DLMs offer advantages including parallel token refinement, bidirectional context, and flexible quality-latency trade-offs. These properties are particularly attractive for edge agents requiring partial refinement, early exit, and constraint-guided correction to reduce response delay and communication overhead while improving robustness in noisy, incomplete, or dynamic contexts.
AI.method: This survey reviews DLM foundations and analyzes their suitability for edge settings by covering: resource-efficient architectures, training/inference acceleration, compression techniques, edge/cloud deployment strategies, communication-aware serving, IoT/wireless applications, and evaluation of DLM-based agents.
AI.result: The survey connects DLM modeling properties (bidirectionality, parallel refinement, controllability, quality-latency elasticity) with system-level requirements of future mobile edge intelligence, identifying key optimization areas for edge deployment.
AI.conclusion: DLMs present a promising paradigm for mobile edge AI by enabling flexible quality-latency trade-offs beyond fixed sequential decoding. Open challenges remain in long-context state management, split inference, trustworthy execution, multimodal grounding, and reproducible benchmarking.

title: PACE: Propagation-Aware Collaborative Correction for One-Shot Personalized Federated Graph Learning
summary: Client heterogeneity creates both an opportunity and a risk in personalized federated graph learning. Knowledge held by other subgraphs may complement a receiver's Local model, but an incompatible transfer can override reliable predictions. One-shot communication sharpens this tension because an unsuitable server return cannot be corrected later. We introduce PACE, which treats collaborative knowledge as a compact correction to a complete Local predictor rather than as its replacement. Each client uploads a rank-r update carrier and a diagonal sketch of propagated message moments. The server uses them to construct a propagation-aware, receiver-anchored correction, while the receiver retains its full Local model. Convex negative-log-likelihood calibration (CNLL) then selects one coefficient between Local and External logits using validation nodes; model parameters remain fixed and no feedback is sent. At Rank-6, personalized returns occupy 9.6-17.6% of dense tensor bytes across the six evaluated datasets. The correction receives nonzero weight and improves both Accuracy and weighted-F1 over Local on five datasets; on ogbn-arxiv, CNLL assigns zero predictive weight to the correction and preserves Local predictions exactly. Applying the same CNLL rule to matched baselines on three citation datasets does not account for these gains. The central result is therefore that a small transported correction can augment a complete Local model when receiver evidence supports it while leaving the Local prediction unchanged otherwise.

AI.tldr: PACE is a personalized federated graph learning method that treats collaborative knowledge as a compact correction to a complete local predictor rather than a replacement. It uses rank-r update carriers and diagonal sketches for one-shot communication, with convex negative-log-likelihood calibration (CNLL) to select between local and external predictions using validation nodes.
AI.motivation: Client heterogeneity in personalized federated graph learning creates tension between opportunity (knowledge complementarity) and risk (incompatible transfers overriding reliable predictions). One-shot communication intensifies this problem as unsuitable server returns cannot be corrected later.
AI.method: PACE introduces: (1) Rank-r update carriers and diagonal sketches of propagated message moments for compact communication; (2) Server constructs propagation-aware, receiver-anchored correction using these carriers; (3) Receiver retains full local model; (4) CNLL selects one coefficient between Local and External logits using validation nodes with fixed model parameters and no client feedback.
AI.result: At Rank-6, personalized returns occupy 9.6-17.6% of dense tensor bytes across six datasets. The correction improves Accuracy and weighted-F1 over Local on five datasets. On ogbn-arxiv, CNLL assigns zero predictive weight to correction and preserves Local predictions exactly. Matched baselines on three citation datasets do not achieve these gains.
AI.conclusion: A small transported correction can augment a complete local model when receiver evidence supports it, while leaving local predictions unchanged otherwise. The method successfully balances the opportunity-risk tension in heterogeneous federated graph learning.

title: InterSing: Explicit Interaction Dynamics for 3D Duet Singing Animation and Beyond
summary: We present InterSing, a framework for generating realistic 3D head animations for duet singing performances. Unlike solo singing, duet performance requires each singer to balance individual expressiveness with intermittent interaction at musically salient moments, such as phrase boundaries, synchronized rhythms, and call-and-response passages. Because these interactions are sparse and rhythm-dependent, existing audio-driven animation methods and conversational interaction models do not adequately capture their structure. Our key insight is that duet coordination can be represented as a time-varying signal that reflects how strongly performers engage with one another throughout a song. Based on this observation, we introduce interaction logits, an interpretable latent representation that models the degree of cross-performer engagement at each time step. We learn these logits using weak supervision and use them to condition an interaction-aware diffusion model jointly driven by audio features and interaction dynamics. This formulation enables unified multi-mode generation, spanning independent motion, coordinated behavior, and smooth transitions between them. Experiments show that InterSing generates realistic and expressive singing head animations with stronger coordination and musical alignment than existing methods, while preserving each performer's characteristic motion style. We further demonstrate that the same formulation generalizes to multi-singer performances and provides intuitive control over when and how performers engage.

AI.tldr: InterSing is a framework for generating realistic 3D head animations for duet singing performances by modeling performer coordination as a time-varying signal using interaction logits, which condition an interaction-aware diffusion model driven by audio features.
AI.motivation: Existing audio-driven animation methods and conversational interaction models inadequately capture duet coordination structure because interactions are sparse and rhythm-dependent. The key challenge is balancing individual expressiveness with intermittent interaction at musically salient moments (phrase boundaries, synchronized rhythms, call-and-response).
AI.method: 1) Represent duet coordination as a time-varying signal using interaction logits (interpretable latent representation modeling cross-performer engagement degree at each time step). 2) Learn interaction logits using weak supervision. 3) Condition an interaction-aware diffusion model jointly driven by audio features and interaction dynamics. This enables unified multi-mode generation spanning independent motion, coordinated behavior, and smooth transitions.
AI.result: InterSing generates realistic and expressive singing head animations with stronger coordination and musical alignment than existing methods, while preserving each performer's characteristic motion style. The formulation generalizes to multi-singer performances and provides intuitive control over engagement timing and manner.
AI.conclusion: The proposed interaction logits approach successfully models the sparse, rhythm-dependent nature of duet coordination, enabling a unified framework that handles both independent and coordinated behaviors with natural transitions. This represents a novel approach to modeling multi-performer temporal coordination in audio-driven animation.

title: DODR: Deterministic Operator-Driven Reasoning in Latent Space
summary: Autoregressive (AR) large language models formulate reasoning as token-level probabilistic sampling, which induces three fundamental defects in complex logical reasoning: error accumulation, probability substituting necessity, and the linear-chain information bottleneck. This paper proposes the Deterministic Operator-Driven Reasoning in Latent Space architecture (DODR), which reconstructs reasoning as reasoning-graph computation in a high-dimensional linear-algebraic space. Reasoning states are represented as snapshot vectors whose primitives are semantic units (phrases or sentences) rather than tokens, and each inference step is a deterministic matrix operation with no token sampling. Peirce's three inference types are formalized as three trainable matrix operators: a rank-deficient deduction operator (information collapse), a full-rank induction operator (information expansion), and an abduction operator defined as the Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse of deduction (information hypothesizing). We prove that the operator set is minimal and complete given Peirce's trichotomy, that no single "super-operator" can realize all three types (a rank obstruction), and that reasoning graphs are Turing-complete with contractive backflow converging by Banach's fixed-point theorem. Experiments on 503 sample records (420 deduplicated samples) across dedicated and end-to-end settings show: deduction loss converges to 1.40e-05; induction achieves 0.9996 generalization coverage with 20/20 hard vetoes on counterexamples; abduction solutions exceed the random baseline by 28x with judgment accuracies of 72.5% (58/80, Wilson 95% CI [61.9%, 81.1%]) and 81.7% (49/60, CI [70.1%, 89.4%]); frozen operators attain 100% (60/60) on unseen cross-domain deduction. The architecture provides a structural zero-hallucination guarantee and a three-layer continual-learning mechanism. All data and code are released.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes DODR (Deterministic Operator-Driven Reasoning in Latent Space), a novel architecture that replaces token-level probabilistic sampling in autoregressive LLMs with deterministic matrix operations on semantic-unit vectors. It formalizes Peirce's three inference types (deduction, induction, abduction) as trainable matrix operators and provides theoretical guarantees including Turing-completeness and zero-hallucination.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to address three fundamental defects in autoregressive LLMs: error accumulation, probability substituting necessity, and the linear-chain information bottleneck. Traditional AR models formulate reasoning as token-level probabilistic sampling, which is inherently probabilistic and prone to errors in complex logical reasoning tasks.
AI.method: DODR reconstructs reasoning as reasoning-graph computation in high-dimensional linear-algebraic space. Reasoning states are represented as snapshot vectors with semantic primitives (phrases/sentences) instead of tokens. Three matrix operators are defined: (1) rank-deficient deduction operator for information collapse, (2) full-rank induction operator for information expansion, and (3) abduction operator defined as Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse of deduction for information hypothesizing.
AI.result: Experiments on 503 samples (420 deduplicated) show: deduction loss converges to 1.40e-05; induction achieves 0.9996 generalization coverage with 20/20 vetoes on counterexamples; abduction exceeds random baseline by 28x with 72.5% (58/80) and 81.7% (49/60) judgment accuracies; frozen operators achieve 100% (60/60) on cross-domain deduction. The architecture provides structural zero-hallucination guarantee and three-layer continual learning.
AI.conclusion: The DODR architecture successfully addresses the three fundamental defects of AR models through deterministic matrix operations. The theoretical proofs establish minimality, completeness, and Turing-completeness of the operator set. Experimental results demonstrate strong performance across deduction, induction, and abduction tasks, with zero-hallucination guarantee and strong cross-domain generalization.

title: KVMem: Virtualizing Million-Token Agent Workspaces on a Consumer GPU
summary:
Modern LLM agents operate in persistent workspaces whose accumulated history can exceed both GPU KV capacity and the model's native context window. Existing systems typically compact older context into summaries or retrieve it later as text, either losing fine-grained execution evidence or repeatedly prefilling content that the model has already processed. We present KVMem, a KV-context virtualization system that preserves overflowed workspace history as paged KV state across GPU memory, host memory, and NVMe. KVMem uses lightweight, model-native attention-space indexes to select relevant historical blocks and materializes a query-dependent execution view bounded by the model's native context window. Extensive evaluations on long-context agent benchmarks spanning histories up to one million tokens, including LongMemEval, MemoryAgentBench, and AgentLongBench, show that KVMem generally achieves higher task utility and greater inference efficiency than compaction-based approaches, the de facto standard for handling context overflow. In the DeepSWE long-context test with Qwen3.8-27B, KVMem improves task success from 43.8% with compaction-only context management to 48.4%.
  In our local-deployment evaluation, KVMem runs Qwen3.6/3.8-27B NVFP4 with MTP on an off-the-shelf laptop equipped with a 24\,GB RTX 5090 Laptop GPU, virtualizing agent workspaces of up to 1M tokens-four times the model's native 256K-token context window. In a single-session setting, KVMem generates $\sim$50 tokens/s, providing interactive responsiveness for local agent execution. More broadly, by decoupling addressable workspace size from the LLM's native context window, KVMem provides a practical path toward long-running agents whose workspaces can grow beyond that window.

AI.tldr: KVMem is a KV-context virtualization system that preserves overflowed workspace history as paged KV state across GPU memory, host memory, and NVMe, enabling LLM agents to handle workspaces exceeding their native context window (e.g., 1M tokens with 256K context) using attention-space indexes for relevant block retrieval.
AI.motivation: Modern LLM agents in persistent workspaces accumulate history exceeding GPU KV capacity and the model's context window. Existing compaction-based approaches either lose fine-grained execution evidence or cause repeated prefilling of already-processed content, creating efficiency and utility issues.
AI.method: KVMem uses lightweight, model-native attention-space indexes to select relevant historical blocks and materializes a query-dependent execution view bounded by the model's native context window. It virtualizes KV state across GPU memory, host memory, and NVMe storage.
AI.result: On long-context agent benchmarks (LongMemEval, MemoryAgentBench, AgentLongBench) with histories up to 1M tokens, KVMem achieves higher task utility and inference efficiency than compaction-based approaches. In DeepSWE long-context test with Qwen3.8-27B, task success improved from 43.8% to 48.4%. On local deployment, Qwen3.6/3.8-27B NVFP4 with MTP on a 24GB RTX 5090 Laptop GPU achieves ~50 tokens/s for 1M token workspaces.
AI.conclusion: KVMem decouples addressable workspace size from the LLM's native context window, providing a practical path toward long-running agents with workspaces growing beyond the native context window while maintaining interactive responsiveness.

title: Methane Detection On Board Satellites from Unorthorectified Imagery
summary: As a potent greenhouse gas, methane is a major driver of climate change. Its effective mitigation relies on timely detection. Conventional detection methods rely on orthorectification to correct geometric distortions and matched filters to enhance plume signals, which are steps designed for ground processing and poorly suited to onboard execution. We introduce UnorthoDOS, a dataset and approach for training machine learning models directly on unorthorectified hyperspectral imagery, bypassing both orthorectification and matched-filter products. Our U-Net models trained on unorthorectified data approach the performance of models trained on orthorectified data (IoU 16.91% vs. 18.47% on all plumes), while both substantially outperform the mag1c matched-filter baseline (IoU 4.76%). We further demonstrate the feasibility of onboard deployment: FP16 compression halves model size with under 0.3% output deviation. The trained ML models and two ML-ready datasets -- orthorectified and unorthorectified hyperspectral imagery from the EMIT sensor -- are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/SpaceML/UnorthoDOS, with code at https://github.com/spaceml-org/plume-hunter.

AI.tldr: UnorthoDOS is a dataset and machine learning approach for detecting methane plumes directly from unorthorectified hyperspectral imagery, enabling onboard processing without traditional orthorectification or matched-filter steps. U-Net models trained on this data achieve comparable performance to orthorectified models (16.91% vs 18.47% IoU), both significantly outperforming the mag1c matched-filter baseline (4.76% IoU).
AI.motivation: Conventional methane detection methods rely on orthorectification to correct geometric distortions and matched filters to enhance plume signals. These steps are designed for ground processing and are poorly suited to onboard execution, creating a need for methods that can process unorthorectified data directly on satellites for timely methane detection.
AI.method: The approach trains U-Net models directly on unorthorectified hyperspectral imagery from the EMIT sensor, bypassing both orthorectification and matched-filter products. The study also explores FP16 compression for onboard deployment feasibility.
AI.result: U-Net models trained on unorthorectified data achieve IoU of 16.91%, approaching the performance of models trained on orthorectified data (18.47% IoU). Both substantially outperform the mag1c matched-filter baseline (IoU 4.76%). FP16 compression halves model size with less than 0.3% output deviation.
AI.conclusion: It is feasible to train ML models directly on unorthorectified hyperspectral imagery for methane detection, achieving performance close to orthorectified models while enabling onboard deployment. The trained models and ML-ready datasets (both orthorectified and unorthorectified) are publicly available.

title: ProtLingo: Efficient Protein Language Modeling via Conditional Memory and Expert Routing
summary: Proteins perform diverse cellular functions, and even single amino-acid substitutions can alter stability, activity, or molecular interactions. Protein language models (PLMs) provide a scalable approach for modeling such sequence--function relationships from unlabeled sequences, but increasing the size of dense Transformer backbones often brings substantial computational cost without consistently improving mutation-sensitive prediction. We introduce ProtLingo, an efficient PLM framework that augments a pretrained single-sequence backbone with conditional local memory and sparse expert routing. ProtLingo maps contextual residue representations into route-specific discrete codes, composes centered local windows into latent $N$-gram addresses, and retrieves reusable residual signals associated with recurring local sequence contexts. In parallel, selected feed-forward blocks are upcycled into sparse Mixture-of-Experts layers with shared and routed experts, enabling residue-dependent computation while activating only a subset of parameters. Experiments on protein fitness prediction, FLIP benchmarks, and supervised contact prediction show that ProtLingo achieves competitive performance with a 150M-scale backbone, including strong parameter efficiency on mutation-effect prediction and preserved long-range structural representations.

AI.tldr: ProtLingo is an efficient protein language model that augments pretrained single-sequence backbones with conditional local memory and sparse expert routing, achieving competitive performance with 150M-scale backbone while maintaining strong parameter efficiency on mutation-effect prediction and preserving long-range structural representations.
AI.motivation: Protein language models (PLMs) provide scalable approaches for modeling sequence-function relationships, but increasing the size of dense Transformer backbones brings substantial computational cost without consistently improving mutation-sensitive prediction. Even single amino-acid substitutions can significantly alter protein stability, activity, or molecular interactions.
AI.method: ProtLingo augments a pretrained single-sequence backbone with two key mechanisms: (1) conditional local memory - mapping contextual residue representations into route-specific discrete codes, composing centered local windows into latent N-gram addresses, and retrieving reusable residual signals associated with recurring local sequence contexts; (2) sparse expert routing - upcycling selected feed-forward blocks into sparse Mixture-of-Experts layers with shared and routed experts, enabling residue-dependent computation while activating only a subset of parameters.
AI.result: ProtLingo achieves competitive performance with a 150M-scale backbone, including strong parameter efficiency on mutation-effect prediction and preserved long-range structural representations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed ProtLingo framework demonstrates that efficient PLMs can achieve competitive performance through conditional local memory and sparse expert routing mechanisms, offering a promising direction for reducing computational costs while maintaining prediction quality for mutation effects and structural representations.

title: When Genomic Masking Priors Fail to Transfer: Strong Variant Prediction, Weak Functional Generation
summary: Bidirectional discrete diffusion model appears naturally suited to genomic modeling because it can reconstruct missing sequence from both flanks. We developed GenDA (Genomic Density-optimized Absorbing Diffusion) under the additional hypothesis that entropy-guided span placement would concentrate reconstruction pressure on compositionally complex regions, improving both downstream variant-effect prediction and functional sequence generation. Our results only partially support this premise. After supervised fine-tuning, the 202M-parameter GenDA model reaches a pooled ClinVar SNV AUROC of 0.774, exceeding a similarly scaled autoregressive model by 0.103. However, a matched random-span variant reaches 0.777, providing no evidence that entropy guidance causes the ClinVar improvement. More unexpectedly, GenDA fails a zero-shot functional inpainting stress test: across promoters, enhancers, exon boundaries, and intron boundaries, it does not consistently outperform a control that shuffles the native gap while exactly preserving 3-mer composition. Failure is already present for 50--500-bp gaps, although enhancer degradation worsens at longer gaps. Diagnostics identify several boundary conditions: entropy measures local sequence complexity rather than functional importance; 1-mer tokenization limits physical context; training spans are capped at 300 bp; and high absolute AlphaGenome fidelity can coexist with negative control-normalized restoration. These results show that strong fine-tuned variant prediction, a plausible corruption prior, and functional generation are distinct claims that require separate validation.

AI.tldr: GenDA, a 202M-parameter bidirectional discrete diffusion model for genomic modeling, achieves superior variant-effect prediction (ClinVar AUROC 0.774) but fails zero-shot functional inpainting stress tests. The improvement over autoregressive models (0.103 gain) appears unrelated to entropy guidance, as random-span controls perform similarly.
AI.motivation: The hypothesis was that entropy-guided span placement would concentrate reconstruction pressure on compositionally complex regions, thereby improving both downstream variant-effect prediction and functional sequence generation. The additional hypothesis was that entropy guidance would help identify functionally important regions.
AI.method: A 202M-parameter bidirectional discrete diffusion model (GenDA) was developed with entropy-guided span placement. It was compared against: (1) a similarly scaled autoregressive model, and (2) a matched random-span control. Evaluation included ClinVar SNV variant-effect prediction and zero-shot functional inpainting stress tests across promoters, enhancers, exon boundaries, and intron boundaries.
AI.result: GenDA achieved a pooled ClinVar SNV AUROC of 0.774, exceeding the autoregressive model by 0.103. However, a matched random-span variant achieved 0.777, providing no evidence that entropy guidance contributes to ClinVar improvement. GenDA failed the zero-shot functional inpainting stress test—it did not consistently outperform controls that shuffle native gaps while preserving 3-mer composition. Failure was observed for 50-500 bp gaps, with enhancer degradation worsening at longer gaps. Diagnostic analysis identified limitations: entropy measures local complexity rather than functional importance; 1-mer tokenization limits physical context; training spans are capped at 300 bp; and high AlphaGenome fidelity can coexist with negative control-normalized restoration.
AI.conclusion: Strong fine-tuned variant prediction, a plausible corruption prior, and functional generation are distinct claims requiring separate validation. The ClinVar improvement may not derive from entropy guidance as hypothesized. The model fails functional inpainting despite good variant prediction, suggesting these capabilities are not directly coupled. Several boundary conditions were identified that may explain the failure, including tokenization limitations, training span caps, and the mismatch between entropy-based and functional importance.

title: TourPhysics: Bringing Physics to World Models for Exploration and Manipulation from a Single Image
summary: Interactive visual world models must distinguish observation from physical intervention. Camera motion reveals new surfaces, whereas intervention changes object motion, contact, and deformation. Current video world models are largely driven by appearance priors and often lose physical or spatial consistency over long horizons. We present TourPhysics, an online framework initialized from a single image and a declarative physical configuration. TourPhysics extends PhysOmni, our ACM Multimedia 2026 work, from finite physics-grounded video synthesis to persistent exploration and manipulation. TourPhysics combines deterministic simulation with video generation while assigning separate roles to simulator state, geometric evidence, generator controls, and appearance memory. For each action, the simulator computes a finite physical and camera trajectory before the corresponding observation is generated. Accepted observations publish the terminal state and update the appearance memory and subsequent generator controls, while the committed state and simulator geometry remain fixed throughout synthesis and retry. We further separate the simulator geometry used for projection and visibility from the relative depth used to condition the generator. A reference-anchored memory retrieves accepted static appearance through geometric cross-view correspondence and incorporates it through a bounded residual that reverts to the native path when no valid correspondence exists. On simulator-defined camera tours and object manipulations, TourPhysics follows prescribed camera and object trajectories more closely than the evaluated baselines, preserves the input scene, and reduces appearance drift during long-horizon revisits.

AI.tldr: TourPhysics is an online video world model framework that extends PhysOmni to enable persistent exploration and manipulation from a single image. It combines deterministic physics simulation with video generation, distinguishing between camera motion (observation) and physical intervention (object manipulation) while maintaining spatial consistency over long horizons.
AI.motivation: Current video world models are driven by appearance priors and lose physical or spatial consistency over long horizons. They cannot distinguish observation (camera motion revealing new surfaces) from physical intervention (changing object motion, contact, deformation). The authors aim to create a framework that maintains physical consistency and preserves the input scene during extended exploration and manipulation.
AI.method: TourPhysics combines deterministic simulation with video generation with four separated components: (1) Simulator state - computes finite physical and camera trajectories before observation generation; (2) Geometric evidence - separate simulator geometry for projection/visibility from relative depth for generator conditioning; (3) Generator controls; (4) Appearance memory via reference-anchored retrieval using geometric cross-view correspondence. Accepted observations publish terminal state and update appearance memory. A bounded residual reverts to native path when no valid correspondence exists.
AI.result: TourPhysics follows prescribed camera and object trajectories more closely than evaluated baselines, preserves the input scene, and reduces appearance drift during long-horizon revisits.
AI.conclusion: The framework successfully enables persistent exploration and manipulation in video world models while maintaining physical consistency and reducing appearance drift. The separation of simulator geometry from depth conditioning, along with reference-anchored memory, enables effective long-horizon operation.

title: Whose record is this? Diagnosing and authorizing record use in personalized multimodal models
summary: Contextualized visual personalization can retrieve a true record yet apply it to the wrong visual subject. We formalize when a record may condition an answer as \emph{record authorization}: subject presence ($P$), record-edge validity ($E$), and answer support ($S$) must all hold. We call violations visual memory misbinding (VMM). We construct RecordAuth-Diag, a 3,690-case matched diagnostic suite that changes one image--record edge while holding the query, question, record text, and image multiset fixed. Card removal and nonce relabeling attribute these failures to supplied records. Raw-bank failures span Qwen-, Phi-, and Gemma-family interfaces: Gemma-3-4B-IT reaches 63.69\% local unauthorized use at 25.75\% clean recall. CoViP remains at 26.02\%, versus 22.49\% for its Qwen backbone at similar clean recall. Typed pre-generation authorization reduces Qwen card exposure on RecordAuth-Diag from 43.63\% to 3.06\%, while positive recall changes from 86.26\% to 60.90\%. Full $P\wedge E\wedge S$ validation uses 560 localized DAVIS cases: top-1 relevance and typed authorization have comparable release (28.93\% and 28.39\%) but 6.79\% and 0.89\% unsafe release, respectively. Of the 33 additional unsafe cases removed, 27 are support, 4 edge, 2 clean, and 0 boundary cases. Thus the observed increment is an $E\wedge S$ decision dominated by support, not an edge check alone. Appearance supplies $E$ evidence only conditional on $P$; authenticated subject tokens instantiate the missing presence witness as a sufficiency control. The claims concern the evaluated contracts, not natural prevalence, consent, or visual identity

AI.tldr: This paper addresses visual memory misbinding (VMM) in contextualized visual personalization systems, where retrieved records are incorrectly applied to wrong visual subjects. The authors formalize record authorization as three conditions (Subject Presence P, Record-Edge Validity E, Answer Support S) that must all hold, and construct a diagnostic suite (RecordAuth-Diag) to evaluate this problem across multiple model families.
AI.motivation: The core problem is that visual personalization systems can retrieve a true record but apply it to the wrong visual subject - a critical security and accuracy issue. The motivation is to formalize when a record can legitimately condition an answer (record authorization) and diagnose where failures occur.
AI.method: The authors constructed RecordAuth-Diag, a 3,690-case matched diagnostic suite that changes one image-record edge while holding query, question, record text, and image multiset fixed. They used card removal and nonce relabeling to attribute failures to supplied records. They evaluated multiple model families (Qwen, Phi, Gemma) and tested typed pre-generation authorization and full P∧E∧S validation using 560 DAVIS cases.
AI.result: Gemma-3-4B-IT shows 63.69% local unauthorized use at 25.75% clean recall. CoViP has 26.02% failure versus 22.49% for its Qwen backbone. Typed pre-generation authorization reduces Qwen card exposure from 43.63% to 3.06%, while positive recall drops from 86.26% to 60.90%. Full validation shows top-1 relevance (28.93% release, 6.79% unsafe) versus typed authorization (28.39% release, 0.89% unsafe). Of 33 additional unsafe cases removed, 27 are support, 4 edge, 2 clean, and 0 boundary cases.
AI.conclusion: The observed safety improvement is an E∧S decision dominated by support (not edge check alone). Appearance supplies E evidence only conditional on P; authenticated subject tokens instantiate the missing presence witness as a sufficiency control. The claims apply to evaluated contracts only, not natural prevalence, consent, or visual identity.

title: From Deep to Shallow: Unconstrained and Efficient Layer Merging Strategy
comment: 13 pages, 3 figures, accepted at the ITEM Workshop at ECML PKDD 2026
summary: Although Deep Neural Networks have become foundational in many areas of Machine Learning, high computational demands limit their application in resource-constrained environments. To address this issue, depth compression methods have been proposed to identify and linearize redundant activation functions, thereby allowing for the merging of layers without intermediate non-linearities. However, these methods face two key challenges: they cannot be directly applied to convolutions with padding due to the absence of an analytical solution for merging these layers, and they typically increase the kernel size of merged layers, thus limiting speed-up gains. To overcome these limitations, we propose an efficient strategy that enables merging of layers without an existing analytical solution, and also without increasing kernel size. We validate our approach across multiple architectures and datasets, and measure inference speed-up gains on real embedded platforms. We publicly released the code at https://github.com/ShulzhenkoPetr/deep-to-shallow.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses computational limitations of Deep Neural Networks in resource-constrained environments by proposing a depth compression method that enables merging of layers without intermediate non-linearities, overcoming two key limitations of prior approaches: inability to handle convolutions with padding and kernel size increase.
AI.motivation: Deep Neural Networks have become foundational in many ML applications but their high computational demands limit deployment in resource-constrained environments. Existing depth compression methods that merge layers by linearizing redundant activation functions face two critical challenges: they cannot handle convolutions with padding due to lack of analytical solutions, and they typically increase kernel size which limits speed-up gains.
AI.method: The paper proposes an efficient strategy that enables merging of layers without an existing analytical solution, and does so without increasing kernel size. The approach is validated across multiple architectures and datasets, with inference speed-up measured on real embedded platforms.
AI.result: The method achieves inference speed-up gains on real embedded platforms. Specific quantitative results are not provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach successfully enables layer merging for cases without analytical solutions while maintaining kernel size, providing a practical solution for deploying deep neural networks in resource-constrained environments. Code is publicly available.

title: One Diffusion Model, Two Roles: Guided Trajectory Planning and Safety-Critical Scenario Generation in Closed-Loop Simulation
comment: Accepted at ECCV 2026 workshop. Arka and Rajesh have equal contribution
summary: Diffusion probabilistic models can capture the multi-modal, interaction-rich distribution of joint future trajectories in driving scenes. We show that a single pretrained diffusion traffic model can serve two complementary roles in the autonomous driving development loop: as an ego motion planner, and as a controllable generator of safety-critical scenarios for stress-testing the planners. On the planning side, we introduce a Single-Stream Dual-Stream (SSDS) diffusion-transformer decoder that fuses scene context via joint attention rather than late cross-attention, improving closed-loop performance on nuPlan. We further propose Decoupled Annealing Posterior Sampling with Energy (DAPSE), a training-free guidance scheme that injects arbitrary energy functions at the clean-sample level, avoiding the first-order approximation errors while requiring no auxiliary networks. Beyond planning, we leverage the same diffusion model as a controllable scenario generator to create realistic long-tail driving interactions for closed-loop evaluation. Through inference-time guidance, selected agents are steered toward safety-critical behaviors, including aggressive cut-ins, lead-vehicle braking, and combined longitudinal-lateral interactions, while preserving realistic traffic behaviors. Evaluated in closed-loop nuPlan simulations with independent black-box planners, the generated scenarios expose failure modes that remain hidden under standard benchmarks. Although the SSDS-based planner achieves stronger nominal performance, it experiences larger degradation under these challenging scenarios, demonstrating that benchmark superiority does not necessarily translate to robustness. These results demonstrate that a single learned traffic prior can simultaneously improve motion planning and provide a realistic framework for systematic planner robustness evaluation.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a unified diffusion probabilistic model for autonomous driving that serves dual roles: as an ego motion planner and as a controllable scenario generator for stress-testing planners. The approach introduces SSDS diffusion-transformer decoder for planning and DAPSE for training-free energy-based guidance.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to address two key challenges in autonomous driving: 1) Improving motion planning by better capturing multi-modal, interaction-rich distributions of future trajectories, and 2) Creating realistic safety-critical scenarios for systematic robustness evaluation of planners, since standard benchmarks fail to expose failure modes.
AI.method: Two main technical contributions: (1) SSDS diffusion-transformer decoder using joint attention for fusing scene context, improving over late cross-attention approaches; (2) DAPSE (Decoupled Annealing Posterior Sampling with Energy), a training-free guidance scheme that injects arbitrary energy functions at the clean-sample level to steer generated scenarios toward safety-critical behaviors (aggressive cut-ins, lead-vehicle braking, combined longitudinal-lateral interactions).
AI.result: The SSDS planner achieves improved closed-loop performance on nuPlan benchmark. The diffusion-based scenario generator successfully creates realistic long-tail driving interactions through inference-time guidance. Generated scenarios expose failure modes in black-box planners that remain hidden under standard benchmarks. Notably, planners with stronger nominal performance exhibit larger degradation under challenging scenarios.
AI.conclusion: A single learned traffic prior (diffusion model) can simultaneously improve motion planning and provide a realistic framework for systematic planner robustness evaluation. Benchmark superiority does not necessarily translate to robustness, highlighting the importance of evaluating planners under safety-critical scenarios.

title: Hierarchical Possession-Aware Graph Pointer Network for Pass Receiver Selection
comment: This paper has been accepted by the 27th International Conference on Web Information Systems Engineering (WISE 2026)
summary: Pass receiver selection is a fundamental task in football analytics, aiming to predict the intended receiver under a given game state. This task is challenging with event-centered freeze-frame observations, a broadcast-like setting that provides only partial and variable player visibility without complete trajectories or stable player identities. The model must therefore reason over anonymous visible candidates, opponent pressure, and recent context under partial observation. To address this setting, we propose a Hierarchical Possession-aware Graph Pointer Network (HPGPN), which formulates pass receiver selection as variable-size candidate prediction over visible teammates. HPGPN jointly models current player interactions, local event context, and possession-level temporal dynamics. It represents the current pass situation with a graph, incorporates fixed event context, and uses dynamic possession history to capture how the attacking sequence evolves. Candidate representations are refined hierarchically by integrating spatial, contextual, and historical evidence, and a glimpse pointer head scores the receiver candidates. Experiments on public football event and freeze-frame data show that HPGPN improves pass receiver selection performance. Ablation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of graph-based interaction modeling, fixed event context, and dual-branch dynamic possession-history modeling.

AI.tldr: HPGPN is a novel neural network approach for predicting pass receivers in football using freeze-frame data. It uses graph-based modeling to represent player interactions, incorporates event context and possession history, and employs a hierarchical refinement with pointer mechanism to select from variable-size visible teammates. The method shows improved performance over baseline approaches on public football datasets.
AI.motivation: Pass receiver selection is a fundamental but challenging task in football analytics. The challenge arises from using event-centered freeze-frame observations, which provide only partial and variable player visibility without complete trajectories or stable player identities. The model must reason over anonymous visible candidates, opponent pressure, and recent context under partial observation.
AI.method: The paper proposes a Hierarchical Possession-aware Graph Pointer Network (HPGPN), which formulates pass receiver selection as variable-size candidate prediction over visible teammates. HPGPN jointly models: 1) Current player interactions using graph representation, 2) Fixed event context, and 3) Dynamic possession history to capture attacking sequence evolution. Candidate representations are refined hierarchically by integrating spatial, contextual, and historical evidence, with a glimpse pointer head scoring the receiver candidates.
AI.result: Experiments on public football event and freeze-frame data show that HPGPN improves pass receiver selection performance. Ablation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of graph-based interaction modeling, fixed event context, and dual-branch dynamic possession-history modeling.
AI.conclusion: HPGPN effectively addresses the pass receiver selection problem under partial observation settings by hierarchically integrating spatial, contextual, and historical evidence through graph-based interaction modeling and dynamic possession history.

title: Adaptation Interfaces for In-Context Tabular Foundation Models in Time-to-Event Prediction
summary: Tabular foundation models (TabFMs) achieve strong performance on structured data, particularly for standard classification and regression problems. Yet, extending them to censored time-to-event prediction is challenging because it requires properly handling censoring and event-time dynamics. Building on our prior work, we further link TabFMs with CoxPH and DeepHit and revise the context-resampled training procedure. We evaluate temporal zero-shot reformulation, classification-based fine-tuning, and survival-head adaptation using frozen TabFM backbones on 74 single-risk data sets, and we additionally study 4 competing-risk data sets. Zero-shot inference is effective on smaller single-risk data sets, whereas supervised adaptation becomes increasingly advantageous as data sets scale. Cox provides the most reliably strong interface, especially for Integrated Brier Score (IBS) on larger data sets. DeepHit is relatively stronger for the time-dependent Concordance Index than for IBS, while cause-specific MTLR ranks highest among the TabFM survival heads in the four-data-set competing-risk analysis. Classification fine-tuning becomes more competitive with zero-shot inference as data sets grow but remains weaker for probabilistic prediction. Overall, our results indicate that effective TabFM transfer depends on the data regime and on the statistical structure represented by the chosen adaptation interface. The implementation scripts used for this work are available at https://github.com/kaylode/survival-fm.

AI.tldr: This paper extends tabular foundation models (TabFMs) to censored time-to-event prediction tasks by integrating them with survival analysis methods (CoxPH, DeepHit, MTLR). The study evaluates three adaptation approaches on 74 single-risk and 4 competing-risk datasets, finding that zero-shot inference works well for smaller datasets while supervised adaptation benefits larger ones. CoxPH shows strongest performance for IBS, while DeepHit excels at time-dependent Concordance Index.
AI.motivation: Extend TabFMs (which excel at standard classification/regression) to censored time-to-event prediction, which is challenging due to the need to properly handle censoring and event-time dynamics. The field lacks comprehensive evaluation of how pretrained TabFMs transfer to survival analysis tasks.
AI.method: Evaluate three adaptation approaches: (1) temporal zero-shot reformulation, (2) classification-based fine-tuning, (3) survival-head adaptation using frozen TabFM backbones. Test on 74 single-risk and 4 competing-risk datasets. Link TabFMs with CoxPH and DeepHit, and revise context-resampled training procedure.
AI.result: Zero-shot inference effective on smaller single-risk datasets; supervised adaptation advantages increase with data scale. CoxPH provides most reliable strong interface, especially for Integrated Brier Score (IBS) on larger datasets. DeepHit stronger for time-dependent Concordance Index than IBS. Cause-specific MTLR ranks highest in competing-risk analysis. Classification fine-tuning becomes more competitive with scale but remains weaker for probabilistic prediction.
AI.conclusion: Effective TabFM transfer to survival prediction depends on data regime (dataset size) and the statistical structure of the chosen adaptation interface. No single approach dominates across all settings; the optimal method depends on dataset characteristics and evaluation metrics.

title: LensStyle: Learning the Optical Aesthetics for Controllable Stylized Lens Effect Rendering
summary: The visual aesthetics of photographs are deeply influenced by lens characteristics such as aperture shape, optical vignetting and optical diffraction, which together define a camera's unique optical style. Existing lens effect rendering methods primarily focus on accurately simulating the blur transition from small to large apertures but overlook the stylistic aspects of lens effects. As a result, they fail to produce diverse bokeh effects under large apertures or capture distinctive photographic phenomena such as starbursts that emerge under small apertures.
