Randomized telemetry can address this but is scarce due to potential disruption of normal operation.
AI.method: Confounding-Valid Counterfactual Conformal Inference (CV-CCI) uses the General Synthetic-Powered Inference (GESPI) principle to combine abundant but potentially confounded observational telemetry with limited randomized data. This approach leverages observational data for efficiency while using randomized data to retain finite-sample coverage guarantees.
AI.result: CV-CCI remains valid under hidden confounding while producing more efficient prediction sets than state-of-the-art confounding-valid baselines in experiments on two representative radio access network (RAN) control tasks.
AI.conclusion: CV-CCI successfully addresses the challenge of counterfactual inference under hidden confounding by effectively combining observational and randomized data, providing both statistical validity and practical efficiency for network operators.

title: Compositional Reward Models for Conditional Medical Image Generation
summary:
Acquiring high quality annotated medical image data is critical for training deep learning models; however, annotation is expensive, time consuming, and requires domain expertise. Conditional diffusion models, such as ControlNet, offer an alternative by generating images conditioned on semantic masks and text. However, existing approaches fail to capture fine grained properties (e.g., intensity and texture), as well as semantic consistency expected by domain experts, limiting their effectiveness for downstream tasks. Recent attempts to address these issues using reinforcement learning fine-tuning remain limited due to the reliance on a single scalar reward, which conflates diverse failure modes and provides weak corrective signals. We propose PRISM, a Compositional Reward Model (CRM) framework for conditional medical image generation. Instead of assigning a single reward, we decompose image quality into verifier grounded stages, each evaluating a distinct aspect of correctness from fine to coarse properties, including low level attributes (intensity and texture), structural alignment with conditioning inputs, and high level semantic fidelity. These stage wise rewards are composed through a Hierarchical Constrained Propagation (HCP) mechanism that enforces a fine to coarse notion of correctness, ensuring that lower level deficiencies are resolved before higher level rewards are accrued, preventing easier objectives from masking critical failures.
  We evaluate PRISM across three datasets spanning diverse medical imaging tasks: PanNuke (multi-class cell segmentation), CeDeM (villi/crypt detection and measurement), and ISIC (skin lesion classification). Training downstream models with data generated by PRISM yields improvements over closest baselines, including a 2.3% increase in mDice on PanNuke, a 8.5% reduction in Mean Relative Error (MRE) on CeDeM, and increases ISIC F1 by 5.9%.

AI.tldr: PRISM is a framework for conditional medical image generation that uses a compositional reward model with hierarchical constrained propagation to evaluate image quality across multiple stages (low-level attributes, structural alignment, and semantic fidelity), improving downstream task performance on PanNuke, CeDeM, and ISIC datasets.
AI.motivation: Acquiring high-quality annotated medical image data is expensive, time-consuming, and requires domain expertise. Existing conditional diffusion models like ControlNet fail to capture fine-grained properties (intensity, texture) and semantic consistency. Prior reinforcement learning fine-tuning approaches rely on a single scalar reward that conflates diverse failure modes and provides weak corrective signals.
AI.method: PRISM decomposes image quality into verifier-grounded stages evaluating: (1) low-level attributes (intensity and texture), (2) structural alignment with conditioning inputs, and (3) high-level semantic fidelity. These stage-wise rewards are composed through a Hierarchical Constrained Propagation (HCP) mechanism that enforces a fine-to-coarse notion of correctness, ensuring lower-level deficiencies are resolved before higher-level rewards are accrued.
AI.result: Training downstream models with PRISM-generated data yields: 2.3% increase in mDice on PanNuke (multi-class cell segmentation), 8.5% reduction in Mean Relative Error (MRE) on CeDeM (villi/crypt detection and measurement), and 5.9% increase in F1 on ISIC (skin lesion classification).
AI.conclusion: PRISM's compositional reward framework with hierarchical constrained propagation effectively improves conditional medical image generation quality, leading to significant downstream task performance improvements across diverse medical imaging datasets.

title: LLM-Assisted Behavioural and Scenario Augmentation for Agent-Based Energy Adoption Models
summary: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) create opportunities to enrich simulation-based energy policy analysis, particularly by supporting structured behavioural assumptions and exploratory techno-economic scenarios. However, directly replacing adoption models with LLM reasoning raises concerns regarding interpretability, reproducibility, and behavioural validity. This paper proposes a hybrid framework for LLM-assisted specification design, integrating bounded behavioural rubrics and structured scenario specifications into a calibrated agent-based model (ABM) of solar photovoltaic (PV) adoption by Irish dairy farms. The proposed approach preserves the original techno-economic adoption mechanism while augmenting it with bounded behavioural modulation and scenario-driven uncertainty analysis. Behavioural effects are represented through interpretable conservative, balanced, and optimistic rubrics, while future policy and market conditions are explored through fixed, rule-validated scenario specifications. Experimental results across multiple policy settings, Monte Carlo worlds, and random seeds demonstrate stable and economically plausible behaviour, with adoption outcomes remaining bounded and monotonic across behavioural regimes. The framework achieves up to approximately 13% behavioural adoption increase relative to the corresponding logistic case without producing unstable or unrealistic saturation dynamics. The results demonstrate that LLM-assisted specifications can be integrated into calibrated energy ABMs in a controlled, reproducible, and policy-relevant manner.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a hybrid framework that integrates large language models (LLMs) into calibrated agent-based models (ABMs) for energy policy analysis, specifically examining solar photovoltaic (PV) adoption by Irish dairy farms. The approach addresses concerns about interpretability, reproducibility, and behavioral validity by using bounded behavioral rubrics and structured scenario specifications rather than directly replacing adoption models with LLM reasoning.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to leverage recent advances in LLMs to enrich simulation-based energy policy analysis while addressing critical limitations: directly replacing adoption models with LLM reasoning raises significant concerns about interpretability, reproducibility, and behavioral validity. The authors seek to preserve the original techno-economic adoption mechanism while augmenting it with bounded behavioral modulation and scenario-driven uncertainty analysis.
AI.method: The proposed hybrid framework integrates bounded behavioral rubrics (conservative, balanced, and optimistic) and structured scenario specifications into a calibrated agent-based model of solar PV adoption by Irish dairy farms. The framework was tested across multiple policy settings, Monte Carlo worlds, and random seeds to validate stability and economic plausibility.
AI.result: Experimental results demonstrate stable and economically plausible behavior across all tested conditions. Adoption outcomes remain bounded and monotonic across behavioral regimes. The framework achieves up to approximately 13% behavioral adoption increase relative to the corresponding logistic case without producing unstable or unrealistic saturation dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The conclusion states that LLM-assisted specifications can be successfully integrated into calibrated energy ABMs in a controlled, reproducible, and policy-relevant manner. This approach preserves the benefits of LLM augmentation while maintaining the interpretability and reliability required for energy policy analysis.

title: Deep Microcompression: Structured Pruning and Bit-packed Quantization for Microcontrollers
comment: Presented at the Global South ML Workshop at the International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026), Seoul, South Korea
summary: This paper introduces Deep Microcompression (DMC), a hardware-aware pipeline for deep learning inference on bare-metal microcontrollers. DMC integrates structured pruning, quantization-aware training, and fixed-length bit-packing to achieve a 55.8$\times$ weight compression ratio on LeNet-5 (98.77\% accuracy), generating a dependency-free C library with deterministic latency. On the RP2040 (Cortex-M0+), DMC reduces binary size by 3$\times$ versus TensorFlow Lite while matching its accuracy. Critically, DMC enables the first documented deployment of a standard CNN on the ATmega328P, a device constrained to 2KB SRAM, previously considered infeasible for CNN inference.

AI.tldr: Deep Microcompression (DMC) is a hardware-aware compression pipeline that enables deep learning inference on ultra-constrained microcontrollers by combining structured pruning, quantization-aware training, and fixed-length bit-packing, achieving 55.8× weight compression on LeNet-5 while preserving 98.77% accuracy and enabling the first CNN deployment on the ATmega328P with only 2KB SRAM.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to enable deep learning inference on extremely resource-constrained microcontrollers (bare-metal MCUs with minimal SRAM), which were previously considered infeasible for CNN inference. Existing frameworks like TensorFlow Lite produce binaries that are too large for such devices, and there is a need for a hardware-aware approach that can achieve significant compression while maintaining accuracy.
AI.method: DMC integrates three key techniques: (1) structured pruning to remove weights while maintaining hardware-friendly structures, (2) quantization-aware training to train models with quantized weights, and (3) fixed-length bit-packing to compress weights into compact representations. The pipeline generates a dependency-free C library with deterministic latency, making it suitable for real-time embedded applications.
AI.result: DMC achieves a 55.8× weight compression ratio on LeNet-5 while maintaining 98.77% accuracy. On the RP2040 (Cortex-M0+), it reduces binary size by 3× compared to TensorFlow Lite while matching its accuracy. Most significantly, DMC enables the first documented deployment of a standard CNN on the ATmega328P, a device with only 2KB SRAM that was previously considered infeasible for CNN inference.
AI.conclusion: DMC represents a breakthrough in embedded deep learning by enabling CNN inference on extremely constrained microcontrollers through aggressive but accuracy-preserving compression. The approach demonstrates that with hardware-aware optimization, even devices with only 2KB SRAM can run standard CNNs, significantly expanding the applicability of deep learning in ultra-low-power embedded systems.

title: PuTR-CouT: Counting-by-Tracking in Camera-Trap Image Sequences
summary: Species identification in camera trap images has been widely studied, but key ecological modeling tasks such as species abundance or density estimation also require counting individual animals. However, the lack of counting labels in most datasets and low frame rates (typically ~1 frame per second) make sequence-level tracking and count estimation particularly challenging. In this work, we present PuTR-CouT, a counting-by-tracking framework built on a transformer-based learned association mechanism for sequence-level animal counting in camera trap images. To address the scarcity of annotated tracking data, we generate synthetic training data by exploiting structural priors, such as static backgrounds and short temporal bursts, to heuristically create pseudo-tracking labels in a weakly supervised manner. The resulting tracker associates detections across frames, using these tracks to estimate per-species counts. We also refine the MaxBoxCount heuristic used by the top solutions of the iWildCam 2021 challenge as a strong baseline, setting the highest score reported to date. When evaluated on the iWildCam 2021 benchmark, our framework PuTR-CouT delivers competitive counting results compared to the improved MaxBoxCount, with the added capability of multi-species predictions and track-level verification.

AI.tldr: PuTR-CouT is a counting-by-tracking framework using transformer-based learned association for individual animal counting in camera trap image sequences, addressing the challenge of limited counting labels and low frame rates through weakly supervised synthetic data generation.
AI.motivation: While species identification in camera trap images has been widely studied, ecological modeling tasks like species abundance or density estimation require counting individual animals. However, the lack of counting labels and low frame rates (~1 fps) make sequence-level tracking and count estimation challenging.
AI.method: The framework uses a transformer-based learned association mechanism to associate detections across frames. To address the scarcity of annotated tracking data, synthetic training data is generated using structural priors (static backgrounds and short temporal bursts) to create pseudo-tracking labels in a weakly supervised manner. The method also refines the MaxBoxCount heuristic from the iWildCam 2021 challenge.
AI.result: PuTR-CouT achieves competitive counting results compared to the improved MaxBoxCount on the iWildCam 2021 benchmark, setting the highest score reported to date for MaxBoxCount. The framework provides multi-species predictions and track-level verification capabilities.
AI.conclusion: The proposed PuTR-CouT framework delivers competitive counting performance while offering additional capabilities including multi-species predictions and track-level verification, making it suitable for ecological monitoring applications.

title: From Interaction Traces to Persistent Skills: Online Evolution for Computer-Use Agents
summary: Computer-use agents can execute increasingly complex tasks in graphical interfaces, but their interaction experience is typically transient: procedural knowledge acquired from one rollout is not systematically retained, refined, and reused in later tasks. Existing skill libraries provide external procedural knowledge, yet their incremental value over the same agent operating without skills, as well as their longitudinal dynamics under repeated interaction, remain insufficiently characterized. We present an online skill-evolution framework that converts interaction trajectories and evaluator feedback into a persistent, versioned library of reusable procedures. Each iteration executes against a frozen library snapshot, and evidence-guided skill updates become available in subsequent iterations without changing model parameters. We compare the full evolving-library system with a configuration-matched empty-library control across four OSWorld application domains under the same fixed action-generation and GUI-grounding stack, task sets, and iteration horizons. Following a five-iteration empty-library warm-up, Full attains a higher post-warm-up mean evaluator score in all four observed domain runs, with mean differences ranging from 5.7 to 18.6 percentage points and domain-dependent temporal stability. In GIMP, provenance-aware analysis reveals retrieval across task-of-origin boundaries and revision churn, where repeated accepted edits fail to recover the originating task. These findings characterize evolving skill libraries as auditable, shared procedural memory that can improve a fixed computer-use stack, while showing that their benefits are conditional and repeated revision does not guarantee recovery. Code is released at https://github.com/LongtaoHu/Skill-Evo4GUI.

AI.tldr: An online skill-evolution framework that converts interaction trajectories and evaluator feedback into a persistent, versioned skill library for computer-use agents. The system is compared against an empty-library control across four OSWorld domains over five iterations, showing improved evaluator scores (5.7-18.6 percentage points higher) but with conditional benefits and revision challenges.
AI.motivation: Computer-use agents lack systematic retention and reuse of procedural knowledge across tasks. Existing skill libraries' incremental value and longitudinal dynamics under repeated interaction remain insufficiently characterized.
AI.method: Online skill-evolution framework that converts interaction trajectories and evaluator feedback into a persistent, versioned library of reusable procedures. Each iteration executes against a frozen library snapshot, with evidence-guided skill updates becoming available in subsequent iterations without changing model parameters.
AI.result: Full evolving-library system outperforms empty-library control in all four domains: 5.7-18.6 percentage points higher post-warm-up mean evaluator score, with domain-dependent temporal stability. In GIMP, provenance-aware analysis reveals retrieval across task-of-origin boundaries and revision churn, where repeated accepted edits fail to recover the originating task.
AI.conclusion: Evolving skill libraries function as auditable, shared procedural memory that can improve a fixed computer-use stack, but benefits are conditional and repeated revision does not guarantee recovery.

title: NEAT-POCKET: Pocket-Conditioned Autoregressive 3D Molecular Generation with a Neighborhood-Guided Set Transformer
summary: AI-driven de novo molecular design offers a promising route to accelerate early-stage drug discovery by generating novel ligands directly within target protein binding pockets. We present NEAT-POCKET, a pocket-conditioned extension of the autoregressive NEAT model for 3D molecular generation. NEAT-POCKET generates molecules atom by atom in protein pocket environments while preserving atom permutation invariance and explicitly modeling hydrogen atoms. Benchmarks on the CrossDocked and SPINDR datasets show that NEAT-POCKET achieves competitive structure-based generation performance while sampling substantially faster than existing baselines. Beyond full-molecule generation, NEAT-POCKET naturally enables pocket-conditioned fragment completion, a task directly relevant to lead optimization and scaffold elaboration. These results position NEAT-POCKET as a fast, flexible, and practical framework for structure-based drug design.

AI.tldr: NEAT-POCKET is a pocket-conditioned 3D molecular generation model that generates molecules atom-by-atom within protein binding pockets, achieving competitive performance while being substantially faster than existing methods.
AI.motivation: Accelerate early-stage drug discovery by generating novel ligands directly within target protein binding pockets using AI-driven de novo molecular design.
AI.method: Pocket-conditioned extension of the autoregressive NEAT model for 3D molecular generation. Generates molecules atom-by-atom in protein pocket environments while preserving atom permutation invariance and explicitly modeling hydrogen atoms.
AI.result: Achieves competitive structure-based generation performance on CrossDocked and SPINDR datasets. Samples substantially faster than existing baselines. Enables pocket-conditioned fragment completion for lead optimization and scaffold elaboration.
AI.conclusion: NEAT-POCKET represents a fast, flexible, and practical framework for structure-based drug design, with particular utility in lead optimization through fragment completion.

title: Efficient Multi-Timescale Event Representations for Feed-Forward Object Detection
comment: Accepted to the Workshop on Neuromorphic Vision (NEVi) at ECCV 2026, 16 pages
summary: Autonomous systems require robust low-latency perception under rapidly changing scene dynamics and challenging illumination. In event cameras object detection commonly relies on recurrent architectures to accumulate sparse temporal information over time. This work investigates how temporal information can be encoded directly within the event representation. We propose a confidence-normalized continuous multi-timescale representation based on logarithmic B-spline temporal encoding together with a geometry-aware local confidence mechanism that exploits the spatial structure of event generation. Using a fixed feed-forward EventCenterNet detector, we show that the proposed representations consistently outperform the compact CSTR representation on PEDRo and Gen1 datasets. We further introduce a recursive exponential-polynomial approximation that enables efficient event-by-event updates while largely preserving detection performance. These results demonstrate that carefully designed event representations can capture a substantial portion of the temporal information learned through recurrent temporal modeling, providing a promising foundation for efficient feed-forward, event-driven, and future neuromorphic object detection.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel event camera representation that encodes temporal information directly within the event representation, eliminating the need for recurrent architectures. The method uses logarithmic B-spline temporal encoding with a geometry-aware confidence mechanism, achieving better performance than compact CSTR representation while enabling efficient event-by-event updates.
AI.motivation: Autonomous systems require robust low-latency perception under rapidly changing scene dynamics and challenging illumination. Current event camera object detection relies on recurrent architectures to accumulate sparse temporal information over time, which is computationally expensive. This work investigates encoding temporal information directly within the event representation for more efficient feed-forward processing.
AI.method: The proposed method includes: (1) Confidence-normalized continuous multi-timescale representation using logarithmic B-spline temporal encoding; (2) Geometry-aware local confidence mechanism exploiting spatial structure of event generation; (3) Fixed feed-forward EventCenterNet detector; (4) Recursive exponential-polynomial approximation for efficient event-by-event updates.
AI.result: The proposed representations consistently outperform the compact CSTR representation on PEDRo and Gen1 datasets. The recursive exponential-polynomial approximation enables efficient event-by-event updates while largely preserving detection performance.
AI.conclusion: Carefully designed event representations can capture a substantial portion of the temporal information learned through recurrent temporal modeling. This provides a promising foundation for efficient feed-forward, event-driven, and future neuromorphic object detection systems.

title: CHAMP: Cross-domain Hybrid Architecture for Matchmaking and Prediction in Online Multi-Player Games
summary:
Multiplayer Online Battle Arena (MOBA) games rely on matchmaking to maintain competitive balance. Our prior work, CUPID, framed matchmaking as an assignment re-optimization problem and showed that a single-mode win-rate predictor can meaningfully rebalance teams. However, deploying such a system across diverse player populations exposes three practical bottlenecks: most queueing players lack sufficient in-mode match history (cold start), skill distributions shift drastically across rank tiers (distribution inconsistency), and extreme skill segments are severely data-starved.
  We present CHAMP, a cross-domain matchmaking framework that resolves these deployment bottlenecks. To address data sparsity and cold starts, CHAMP replaces the target-mode-only player profile with a hybrid domain feature collection: a timestamp-ordered cross-mode short-term sequence whose slices are annotated with target-domain features, plus per-mode breakdowns of long-term, real-time and team statistics. We further propose the Domain-Aware Win-rate Network (DAWN): a Domain-aware Knowledge Extractor (DAKE) compiles target-mode attributes into learnable representations that feed Domain-Aware Temporal/Spatial/Permutation OmniNet Encoders (DATOE/DASOE/DAPOE), so that mode-conditioned representations and per-mode debiasing are learned jointly inside a single shared network. Online, one trained DAWN serves every supported mode, with per-mode position-satisfaction thresholds as the only mode-specific knob.
  Offline, DAWN achieves 67.73% win-rate prediction accuracy, outperforming all evaluated attention and sequence baselines. Online A/B tests across the entire League ladder of a large-scale MOBA game, from novice players up to the top-expert players served by Elite Mode, demonstrate consistent drops in imbalanced matches. For lower-tier players, CHAMP reduces the 5-minute kill crushing rate by up to 20.73%.

AI.tldr: CHAMP is a cross-domain matchmaking framework for MOBA games that addresses cold start, distribution inconsistency, and data starvation bottlenecks through hybrid domain feature collection and a unified neural network (DAWN) for win-rate prediction across multiple game modes.
AI.motivation: Deploying matchmaking systems like CUPID across diverse player populations faces three practical bottlenecks: (1) cold start - most players lack sufficient in-mode match history, (2) distribution inconsistency - skill distributions vary drastically across rank tiers, and (3) data starvation - extreme skill segments have severely limited data. These issues limit the effectiveness of single-mode win-rate predictors in real-world deployment.
AI.method: CHAMP uses a hybrid domain feature collection combining: (1) timestamp-ordered cross-mode short-term sequences with target-domain feature annotations, and (2) per-mode breakdowns of long-term, real-time, and team statistics. The DAWN architecture includes a Domain-aware Knowledge Extractor (DAKE) that compiles target-mode attributes into learnable representations, feeding three Domain-Aware Encoders (DATOE for temporal, DASOE for spatial, DAPOE for permutation patterns). A single trained DAWN serves all supported modes, with only per-mode position-satisfaction thresholds as mode-specific configuration.
AI.result: Offline evaluation shows DAWN achieves 67.73% win-rate prediction accuracy, outperforming all evaluated attention and sequence baselines. Online A/B tests across the entire League ladder (from novice to Elite Mode experts) demonstrate consistent reductions in imbalanced matches. For lower-tier players, CHAMP reduces the 5-minute kill crushing rate by up to 20.73%.
AI.conclusion: CHAMP successfully resolves deployment bottlenecks in cross-domain matchmaking through its hybrid feature approach and unified DAWN architecture. The system achieves strong offline performance and delivers measurable improvements in online match quality across all skill tiers, particularly benefiting lower-tier players by reducing early-game stomps.

title: A Comparative Study of Counterfactual Explainers for Graph Neural Networks Enabling Multiple Types of Graph Edit
summary: Counterfactual explanations for graph-structured data seek to determine minimal and realistic modifications required in an input graph to alter a model's prediction to a predefined output. Although counterfactual explainers that support modifying the graph by both adding and removing edges have recently emerged, there is still a lack of general and efficient methods, especially when considering the quality of the generated explanations. Moreover, the problem remains far from solved, as existing methods exhibit different strengths and weaknesses, often trading off between explanation size, coverage and quality. For this reason, it is important to identify where each method performs well and where it falls short, so as to guide future research in the field. Thus, our study compares six state-of-the-art (SOTA) models on a diverse set of real-world and synthetic datasets, covering both binary and multi-class graph and node classification tasks, and evaluates their performance using diverse quantitative and qualitative metrics.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a comprehensive benchmark study comparing six state-of-the-art counterfactual explanation methods for graph-structured data across diverse datasets and classification tasks, evaluating them using multiple quantitative and qualitative metrics.
AI.motivation: While counterfactual explainers for graphs that support both adding and removing edges have emerged, there is a lack of general and efficient methods with good explanation quality. Existing methods exhibit different strengths and weaknesses, often trading off between explanation size, coverage, and quality, necessitating a systematic comparison to guide future research.
AI.method: The study compares six SOTA models on diverse real-world and synthetic datasets, covering binary and multi-class graph and node classification tasks, evaluated using diverse quantitative and qualitative metrics.
AI.result: The abstract does not provide specific quantitative results, but establishes a comprehensive comparative framework identifying where each method performs well and where it falls short.
AI.conclusion: This benchmark study provides guidance for future research in graph counterfactual explanations by identifying the strengths and limitations of existing SOTA methods across different tasks and evaluation criteria.

title: Adaptive Multi-Granularity Temporal Modeling for Weakly Supervised Video Anomaly Detection
summary: As the scale of video surveillance data outpaces manual annotation capacities, weakly supervised video anomaly detection (WSVAD) has emerged as a critical research frontier. Most existing approaches formulate WSVAD within a Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) framework that relies on rigid, hand-crafted temporal priors to supervise anomaly scoring. However, such formulations exhibit limited adaptability to the wide variation in anomaly durations and temporal dynamics observed in real-world videos, often leading to unstable or unreliable snippet-level predictions. To address this limitation, we propose an adaptive temporal modeling framework for WSVAD that explicitly accounts for variations in video dynamics across multiple temporal granularities. First, we introduce a Temporal Refinement Module (TRM) that leverages dynamic positional encoding and a learnable class token to model long-range temporal dependencies while distilling a stable global video-level representation. Second, to capture anomalous events with varying frequency and duration, we develop an adaptive Event Segmentation Module (ESM) that identifies event boundaries through temporal discontinuity analysis and aggregates snippet features into discriminative event-level representations. Finally, for snippet-level and event-level predictions, we propose an adaptive similarity-based fusion strategy that dynamically integrates anomaly scores into video-level predictions, replacing fixed top-k aggregation heuristics with global semantic relevance. Extensive experiments on two benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an adaptive temporal modeling framework for weakly supervised video anomaly detection (WSVAD) that addresses limitations of traditional Multiple Instance Learning approaches. The framework includes a Temporal Refinement Module for long-range dependencies, an Event Segmentation Module for identifying anomaly boundaries, and an adaptive similarity-based fusion strategy for score integration.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address limitations in existing WSVAD methods that rely on rigid, hand-crafted temporal priors within a Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) framework. These approaches fail to adapt to varying anomaly durations and temporal dynamics in real-world videos, leading to unstable or unreliable snippet-level predictions. The core problem is the lack of adaptability to the wide variation in anomaly durations and temporal dynamics.
AI.method: The proposed framework consists of three key components: (1) Temporal Refinement Module (TRM) - uses dynamic positional encoding and learnable class token to model long-range temporal dependencies while distilling stable global video-level representations; (2) Adaptive Event Segmentation Module (ESM) - identifies event boundaries through temporal discontinuity analysis and aggregates snippet features into discriminative event-level representations to capture anomalous events with varying frequency and duration; (3) Adaptive similarity-based fusion strategy - dynamically integrates anomaly scores into video-level predictions, replacing fixed top-k aggregation heuristics with global semantic relevance for both snippet-level and event-level predictions.
AI.result: The proposed framework consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods on two benchmarks, demonstrating the effectiveness of the adaptive temporal modeling approach for WSVAD.
AI.conclusion: The adaptive temporal modeling framework successfully addresses the limitations of traditional MIL-based WSVAD approaches by explicitly accounting for variations in video dynamics across multiple temporal granularities. The combination of TRM, ESM, and adaptive fusion strategy provides a more robust and adaptable solution for video anomaly detection in real-world scenarios.

title: AutoLR: Automating the Path from Research to Launch Review in Industrial Recommender Systems
summary: Improving an industrial recommender is an iterative research-and-engineering process rather than a direct path from idea to deployment. In \textbf{DASHEN, NetEase's gaming-community app}, algorithm engineers typically identify promising directions from research papers, technical reports, and prior production experiments; reproduce or adapt the underlying methods; implement them in the production codebase; and evaluate the resulting models through training and offline experiments. Promising candidates are then advanced to online A/B tests, and those demonstrating robust gains are submitted to Launch Review---the internal gate for full-traffic rollout. Large language models (LLMs) can assist with individual stages of this workflow, but the overall process remains human-dependent without a harness that can reliably coordinate them across long-running, often multi-day experimental cycles. We present \textbf{AutoLR}, initially built as \textbf{Auto Launch Review} and later extended upstream into an autonomous research-to-launch harness. AutoLR combines three system mechanisms: a \textbf{multi-expert council} that debates and adversarially reviews proposals; a \textbf{deterministic evidence-weighted exploration--exploitation selector} that allocates a limited trial budget across candidate directions and uses Council reranking; and a layered knowledge system that combines external research, production-system knowledge, and DASHEN-specific domain knowledge---such as game communities, player characteristics, and content-interaction patterns---with posterior evidence from configurations, patches, logs, failures, and offline outcomes. LLM agents perform semantic reasoning and code generation, while deterministic controllers retain authority over execution, metric extraction, guardrails, and persistent state transitions.

AI.tldr: AutoLR is an autonomous research-to-launch harness developed for NetEase's gaming community app DASHEN to improve industrial recommender systems. It combines a multi-expert council for adversarial proposal review, a deterministic evidence-weighted exploration-exploitation selector for budget allocation, and a layered knowledge system integrating external research, production knowledge, and domain-specific game community data. LLM agents handle semantic reasoning and code generation while deterministic controllers manage execution, metrics, guardrails, and state transitions.
AI.motivation: Industrial recommender system improvement is an iterative, multi-day process requiring human coordination across research, implementation, offline evaluation, online A/B testing, and launch review stages. Existing LLMs can assist individual stages but lack a harness to reliably coordinate the entire experimental cycle autonomously.
AI.method: AutoLR integrates three system mechanisms: (1) A multi-expert council that debates and adversarially reviews candidate proposals; (2) A deterministic evidence-weighted exploration-exploitation selector that allocates limited trial budgets across candidates using Council reranking; (3) A layered knowledge system combining external research, production-system knowledge, DASHEN-specific domain knowledge (game communities, player characteristics, content-interaction patterns), with posterior evidence from configurations, patches, logs, failures, and offline outcomes. LLM agents perform semantic reasoning and code generation while deterministic controllers retain authority over execution, metric extraction, guardrails, and persistent state transitions.
AI.result: AutoLR extends beyond its initial Auto Launch Review function (reviewing candidates for full-traffic rollout) to become an autonomous research-to-launch harness that can coordinate the entire experimental cycle from research to deployment.
AI.conclusion: The system demonstrates a viable approach to automating the iterative research-and-engineering process in industrial recommender systems by combining LLM-based reasoning with deterministic control mechanisms, enabling autonomous coordination across long-running multi-day experimental cycles.

title: Single-Query Black-Box Calibration Auditing via Logit Bias
summary: Evaluating the calibration of Large Language Models (LLMs) is critical for their safe deployment as zero-shot classifiers. Yet, commercial API providers increasingly hide the continuous output probabilities required by standard calibration metrics. To bypass this opacity, we demonstrate that any LLM API exposing a logit\_bias parameter can be mathematically manipulated to evaluate exact probability thresholds using strictly one query per sample. Leveraging this mechanism, we introduce a novel and provably consistent estimator of the True Calibration Error for binary tasks. Our approach therefore provides an efficient framework for auditing black-box foundation models.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a method to evaluate LLM calibration when API providers hide output probabilities, using the logit_bias parameter to estimate exact probability thresholds with only one query per sample, enabling auditing of black-box foundation models.
AI.motivation: Commercial LLM API providers increasingly hide continuous output probabilities, which are required by standard calibration metrics. This opacity prevents users from assessing how well-calibrated these models are—a critical issue for safe deployment as zero-shot classifiers. There is a need for methods to audit black-box foundation models without requiring access to internal probability outputs.
AI.method: The authors demonstrate that any LLM API exposing a logit_bias parameter can be mathematically manipulated to evaluate exact probability thresholds using strictly one query per sample. This mechanism is used to develop a provably consistent estimator of the True Calibration Error for binary tasks.
AI.result: The proposed approach provides an efficient framework for auditing black-box foundation models by enabling exact probability threshold evaluation through a single query per sample, with provable consistency guarantees for the calibration error estimator.
AI.conclusion: This work enables practitioners to assess LLM calibration even when APIs hide probability outputs, facilitating safer deployment of LLMs as zero-shot classifiers. The method represents a practical solution for transparency and accountability in black-box AI systems.

title: MultiAttenGastro: Multi-Dimensional Attention Augmentation for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy Classification
summary: Automated gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy classification requires models that generalize across diverse modalities and class distributions, often far from natural-image pretraining. We propose MultiAttenGastro, a plug-and-play attention framework with parallel 1-D channel, 2-D spatial, and 3-D contextual heads, and present the first systematic cross-dataset evaluation across eight CNN and transformer backbones on five public GI datasets (80 backbone--dataset runs). We find that attention effectiveness is not universal but tracks the representational gap between ImageNet features and the target distribution: MultiAttenGastro improves 6 of 8 backbones on Kvasir-Capsule (14-class WCE, large gap; best macro F1 98.33\%), is uniformly negative on the small-gap Kvasir-v2 benchmark (0/8), and shows mixed outcomes on datasets with intermediate gap. Five-seed ablation on the strongest case (Kvasir-Capsule, ConvNeXt-Tiny) shows this improvement is directionally consistent, but not statistically decisive (paired $t$: $p=0.47$; Wilcoxon: $p=0.63$), and that individual attention heads are not uniformly beneficial in isolation only their combination yields a positive mean effect. Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) analysis links this pattern to representational redundancy: low inter-head CKA under large domain gaps coincides with the framework's only consistent gains, while high redundancy under small gaps coincides with its losses. We report these results, including the non-significant margins, as evidence for when and why multi-dimensional attention helps GI endoscopy classification, rather than as a claim that MultiAttenGastro is a strictly superior architectural choice.

AI.tldr: MultiAttenGastro is a plug-and-play attention framework with parallel 1-D channel, 2-D spatial, and 3-D contextual heads for GI endoscopy classification. The first systematic cross-dataset evaluation across 8 CNN/transformer backbones on 5 GI datasets (80 runs) reveals that attention effectiveness depends on the representational gap between ImageNet pretraining and target distribution - beneficial for large gaps (Kvasir-Capsule: 6/8 backbones improved, best macro F1 98.33%), neutral/negative for small gaps (Kvasir-v2: 0/8), and mixed for intermediate gaps. Statistical significance is not achieved, but CKA analysis links gains to low inter-head redundancy under large domain gaps.
AI.motivation: Automated GI endoscopy classification requires models that generalize across diverse modalities and class distributions, often far from natural-image pretraining. The authors seek to understand when and why multi-dimensional attention mechanisms help in this domain, rather than simply proposing another SOTA method.
AI.method: Proposed MultiAttenGastro with parallel 1-D channel, 2-D spatial, and 3-D contextual attention heads. Conducted systematic cross-dataset evaluation across 8 backbones (CNN and transformer) on 5 public GI datasets (80 backbone-dataset runs). Used Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) to analyze representational redundancy between attention heads. Performed five-seed ablation and statistical tests (paired t-test, Wilcoxon).
AI.result: Attention effectiveness tracks the representational gap: (1) Kvasir-Capsule (large gap): 6/8 backbones improved, best macro F1 98.33%; (2) Kvasir-v2 (small gap): 0/8 backbones improved; (3) Intermediate gap datasets: mixed outcomes. Statistical analysis shows directionally consistent but non-significant improvement (paired t: p=0.47; Wilcoxon: p=0.63). Individual heads not uniformly beneficial - only combination yields positive mean effect. CKA reveals low inter-head redundancy under large gaps coincides with gains, high redundancy under small gaps coincides with losses.
AI.conclusion: Multi-dimensional attention helps GI endoscopy classification only when there is a large representational gap between ImageNet features and target distribution, and when attention heads provide complementary (non-redundant) representations. The framework is not a universally superior architectural choice - its effectiveness is context-dependent. Results are reported with appropriate statistical uncertainty.

title: MARLA: A Conceptual Scaffold for Regulatory Learning under the EU AI Act
summary: The EU AI Act positions regulation as part of the infrastructure for safe, trustworthy and market-ready innovation. Realising this ambition requires regulatory learning: the evidence generated during implementation must be translated into governance and legal knowledge that supports consistent interpretation, effective oversight, and adaptation as technologies evolve. Yet the actors who produce this evidence and those who rely on it operate in different professional worlds. This paper proposes MARLA (Map, Assess, Report, Learn, Adapt), a conceptual scaffold organising regulatory learning as a five-stage cycle centred on the implementation of legal requirements into socio-technical practices, situated at the Local, National and European levels of the AI Act's governance architecture. Deliberately non-prescriptive, MARLA gives technical and legal stakeholders a shared vocabulary in which each of the first three stages generates its own documentable form of regulatory learning. We illustrate the scaffold with two piloted case studies and a prospective National-to-European illustration.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes MARLA (Map, Assess, Report, Learn, Adapt), a five-stage conceptual framework for regulatory learning in the context of the EU AI Act. The framework organizes regulatory learning across Local, National, and European governance levels, designed to translate implementation evidence into governance knowledge for consistent interpretation, effective oversight, and technology adaptation.
AI.motivation: The EU AI Act aims to position regulation as infrastructure for safe, trustworthy, and market-ready innovation. However, there exists a disconnect between actors who produce evidence during implementation and those who rely on it for governance—operating in different professional worlds. This gap necessitates a systematic approach to regulatory learning.
AI.method: The paper proposes a deliberately non-prescriptive conceptual scaffold (MARLA) that organizes regulatory learning into five stages: Map, Assess, Report, Learn, and Adapt. Each of the first three stages generates its own documentable form of regulatory learning. The framework is illustrated through two piloted case studies and a prospective National-to-European illustration.
AI.result: The MARLA framework provides a shared vocabulary for technical and legal stakeholders to bridge their different professional worlds. It enables regulatory learning to be organized around the implementation of legal requirements into socio-technical practices across Local, National, and European governance levels.
AI.conclusion: MARLA offers a practical tool for organizing regulatory learning that can support consistent interpretation, effective oversight, and adaptation as AI technologies evolve under the EU AI Act. The framework's non-prescriptive nature allows flexibility while maintaining a structured approach to translating implementation evidence into governance knowledge.

title: Coarse-Graining Hidden Representations: Unsupervised Neuron Selection via Mapping Entropy
summary: Overparameterized neural networks carry far more hidden units than a task nominally requires, raising the question of which neurons are essential and whether that distinction is legible in the representation itself, without labels or gradients. We cast neuron selection as the problem of coarse-graining the hidden layer by retaining a subset of its neurons, and score each putative selection by the mapping entropy (ME). This quantity measures the loss of discriminatory power inherent in discarding part of the network neurons, and the selection that minimises the ME is taken as particularly informative. This criterion is fully unsupervised, in that it depends only on hidden-activation statistics. In teacher-student networks, ME optimisation recovers the minimal teacher-consistent representation and retains extra units in proportion to the hidden layer's residual variability; in a non-linear Gaussian process task, it selects coherent functional-class mappings whose preferred class shifts across training. On this task and on translation-augmented MNIST, ME-selected subnetworks outperform random subsets of equal size, most clearly under strong compression - linking configurational distinguishability to predictive performance.

AI.tldr: A method for selecting essential neurons in overparameterized neural networks using mapping entropy (ME), which measures the loss of discriminatory power when discarding neurons. The approach is fully unsupervised, relying only on hidden-activation statistics.
AI.motivation: Overparameterized neural networks contain more hidden units than necessary, raising the question of which neurons are truly essential and whether this can be determined without labels or gradients.
AI.method: The method casts neuron selection as a coarse-graining problem where a subset of neurons is retained. Each selection is scored by mapping entropy (ME), which measures the loss of discriminatory power when discarding neurons. The selection that minimizes ME is chosen as optimal.
AI.result: In teacher-student networks, ME optimization recovers the minimal teacher-consistent representation and retains extra units proportional to residual variability. In non-linear Gaussian process tasks, it selects coherent functional-class mappings. On MNIST and translation-augmented MNIST, ME-selected subnetworks outperform random subsets of equal size, especially under strong compression.
AI.conclusion: Mapping entropy provides an effective unsupervised criterion for neuron selection that links configurational distinguishability to predictive performance, with particular strength under high compression scenarios.

title: Training-Free Logical and Structural Anomaly Detection via Calibrated Fusion
summary: Industrial anomaly detection must handle two distinct defect families: structural anomalies, which manifest as local texture corruptions, and logical anomalies, which violate global rules on object count, composition, or arrangement. Existing detectors typically favor one family at the expense of the other. In particular, training-free methods effectively exploit frozen representations but lack an explicit notion of object count, while methods that reason about counts usually rely on category-specific component modeling. We show that counting ability can be introduced into training-free anomaly detection without additional training or part-level supervision. Our key idea is a normal-set calibration that aligns heterogeneous anomaly cues using statistics from normal images, enabling their direct fusion within a unified training-free framework. Built upon this calibration, our detector combines complementary frozen cues to address both logical and structural anomalies. On MVTec-LOCO, our method achieves image-level AUROCs of 89.0 and 95.9 on logical and structural anomalies, respectively, yielding a 92.5 average---the best among training-free detectors in our comparison. It remains competitive with methods requiring network training or part annotations, while its structural variant matches PatchCore on MVTec-AD (99.1 image-AUROC), suggesting that the proposed calibration generalizes beyond logical anomaly detection.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a training-free anomaly detection method that addresses both structural and logical anomalies in industrial inspection by introducing counting ability through normal-set calibration, which aligns heterogeneous anomaly cues from frozen representations using statistics from normal images.
AI.motivation: Existing industrial anomaly detectors favor either structural or logical anomalies but not both. Training-free methods effectively use frozen representations but lack object count reasoning, while count-based methods require category-specific component modeling. There's a need for a unified training-free approach that can detect both defect families without additional training or part-level supervision.
AI.method: The proposed method introduces a normal-set calibration technique that aligns heterogeneous anomaly cues using statistics from normal images, enabling their direct fusion within a unified training-free framework. This calibration enables the combination of complementary frozen cues to address both logical and structural anomalies without any network training or part annotations.
AI.result: On MVTec-LOCO, the method achieves image-level AUROCs of 89.0 (logical) and 95.9 (structural), with an average of 92.5—best among training-free detectors. It remains competitive with methods requiring network training or part annotations. On MVTec-AD, the structural variant achieves 99.1 image-AUROC, matching PatchCore performance.
AI.conclusion: The normal-set calibration successfully introduces counting ability into training-free anomaly detection without additional training or part-level supervision. The method achieves state-of-the-art performance among training-free detectors for both logical and structural anomalies, while remaining competitive with methods requiring training or annotations, demonstrating good generalization beyond logical anomaly detection.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Sequential Solar PV Policy Design under Uncertainty: An Agent-Based Approach
summary: Designing effective and fiscally sustainable policies for solar photovoltaic (PV) adoption requires balancing adoption gains against public expenditure under uncertainty and heterogeneous decision-making. This study formulates PV policy design as a sequential decision problem and integrates reinforcement learning (RL) with a stochastic agent-based model (ABM) that simulates yearly solar PV adoption under uncertainty. A policymaker agent selects annual incentives, including capital grants, subsidised loan rates, and feed-in tariffs, over a 16-year horizon. Adoption--cost trade-offs are explored by varying policy preferences within a scalarised reward framework. Policies are learned using PPO, SAC, and TD3 and evaluated under stochastic simulation. The results show that this approach produces a clear trade-off structure: the highest-adoption policy (TD3, $w_{\text{cost}}=0.5$) achieves approximately 4,145 adopters at a cost of EUR 41.73 million, while the lowest-cost policy (PPO, $w_{\text{cost}}=2.0$) reduces expenditure to EUR 7.27 million with 2,682 adopters. The balanced policy (PPO, $w_{\text{cost}}=1.6$) achieves 3,495 adopters at a cost of EUR 22.47 million. Across algorithms, consistent trade-off patterns are observed, indicating robustness of the adoption--cost relationship. Compared with static baseline policies, the RL framework explores a broader range of policy configurations. These findings demonstrate the potential of RL as a flexible tool for adaptive policy design under uncertainty.

AI.tldr: This study uses reinforcement learning (PPO, SAC, TD3) combined with a stochastic agent-based model to design optimal solar PV adoption policies over a 16-year horizon, balancing adoption gains against public expenditure under uncertainty.
AI.motivation: Designing effective and fiscally sustainable policies for solar PV adoption requires balancing adoption gains against public expenditure under uncertainty and heterogeneous decision-making. Traditional policy design methods struggle to handle this complexity.
AI.method: The study formulates PV policy design as a sequential decision problem and integrates reinforcement learning (RL) with a stochastic agent-based model (ABM) that simulates yearly solar PV adoption under uncertainty. A policymaker agent selects annual incentives (capital grants, subsidised loan rates, and feed-in tariffs) over a 16-year horizon. Policy preferences are varied within a scalarised reward framework. Three RL algorithms (PPO, SAC, and TD3) are used and evaluated under stochastic simulation.
AI.result: The results show a clear trade-off structure: highest-adoption policy (TD3, w_cost=0.5) achieves ~4,145 adopters at EUR 41.73M cost; lowest-cost policy (PPO, w_cost=2.0) costs EUR 7.27M with 2,682 adopters; balanced policy (PPO, w_cost=1.6) achieves 3,495 adopters at EUR 22.47M. Consistent trade-off patterns are observed across algorithms, indicating robustness. The RL framework explores a broader range of policy configurations compared with static baseline policies.
AI.conclusion: RL combined with ABM is a flexible tool for adaptive policy design under uncertainty, producing robust and consistent trade-offs between adoption and cost across different algorithms.

title: MomentQuant: an even more minimalist interval method with linear time complexity for time series classification
summary: Time series data is very common in many real-world applications and in numerous domains, with increasing interest for automated information extraction using machine learning. One of these subfields is time series classification, which consists in assigning a label to each new, unseen time series. Many algorithms have been developed over the past decades, with the trade-off between predictive performance and computational cost being consistently discussed. Quant, an interval-based algorithm extracting quantiles from recursive, fixed, dyadic intervals, was shown to achieve high accuracy, while being very fast. We propose two changes to make this algorithm even faster. The first one is a better optimized implementation of the exact same algorithm. The second one is to derive approximate quantiles, using the Cornish-Fisher expansion, instead of exact quantiles. This change removes the necessity to sort the time series, leading to a smaller computational complexity. We call this novel algorithm MomentQuant. We provide evidence that our implementation of Quant is faster than the original one, and that MomentQuant is even faster than our implementation of Quant, at the cost of a tiny decrease in predictive performance. These improvements are especially relevant for real-life applications, where inference is performed much more often than training.

title: VoxelFix: Post-Hoc Semantic Correction of Completed 3D Voxel Maps
summary: Semantic 3D maps are increasingly constructed automatically for aerial robotics by integrating learned semantic predictions into 3D representations. While this avoids costly manual 3D annotation, errors in the perception and mapping pipeline can persist in the resulting map, reducing its reliability for downstream autonomous tasks. Existing 3D semantic map refinement methods either rely on the original observations, treat occupancy as part of the prediction problem, or apply non-learned local regularization to completed maps. Instead, we study post-hoc semantic correction, asking whether semantic accuracy can be recovered directly from the completed map while keeping its geometry and occupancy fixed. We introduce \method, a graph-based model that corrects voxel labels based on local geometry and neighboring semantic information. To obtain training pairs, we corrupt contiguous regions of annotated OccuFly maps according to class confusions observed in upstream maps. We evaluate \method on completed OccuFly maps generated from predictions of four independently trained 2D segmentation models. \method consistently improves mIoU by 4.23--5.00 percentage points, with gains broadly distributed across the evaluated semantic classes and particularly strong improvements for tree, roof, and wall. Results on an independently reconstructed out-of-distribution aerial scene further suggest that the learned correction can transfer beyond the environments seen during training.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses error correction in automatically constructed semantic 3D maps for aerial robotics. The proposed method, a graph-based model, corrects voxel labels in completed maps while keeping geometry and occupancy fixed, achieving consistent mIoU improvements of 4.23-5.00 percentage points across different segmentation models.
AI.motivation: While semantic 3D maps can be constructed automatically for aerial robotics by integrating learned semantic predictions, errors in the perception and mapping pipeline persist in the resulting maps, reducing reliability for downstream autonomous tasks. Existing methods either rely on original observations, treat occupancy as part of the prediction problem, or apply non-learned local regularization. The authors investigate whether semantic accuracy can be recovered directly from the completed map while keeping geometry and occupancy fixed.
AI.method: The authors introduce a graph-based model that corrects voxel labels based on local geometry and neighboring semantic information. To obtain training pairs, they corrupt contiguous regions of annotated OccuFly maps according to class confusions observed in upstream maps. The method is evaluated on completed OccuFly maps generated from predictions of four independently trained 2D segmentation models.
AI.result: The method consistently improves mIoU by 4.23-5.00 percentage points, with gains broadly distributed across evaluated semantic classes and particularly strong improvements for tree, roof, and wall classes. Results on an independently reconstructed out-of-distribution aerial scene further suggest that the learned correction can transfer beyond environments seen during training.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that semantic accuracy can be recovered directly from completed 3D maps through a graph-based post-hoc correction approach, without requiring access to original observations or modifying the map's geometry and occupancy. The method shows consistent improvements across different segmentation models and generalizes to out-of-distribution aerial scenes.

title: From Language Models to World-Acting Systems: Progress and Limits of Agentic AI across Digital, Social, Virtual, and Physical Environments
comment: Review article. 29 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Literature cutoff: 31 August 2026
summary: Large language models become consequential agents when surrounding systems let outputs change external state. Models now call tools, operate interfaces, delegate work, retain state, inhabit generated worlds, and control robots or laboratory equipment. Such advances are often narrated as one march toward autonomy, conflating model competence, system integration, persistence, and safe authority. This critical review synthesizes primary research and official technical specifications available by 31 August 2026. We organize the evidence along delegated authority, temporal persistence, and environmental coupling, while separating model, harness, and environment. Within the evidence examined, action-interface expansion is documented more convincingly than robust completion, recovery, authorization, or independent verification. Model Context Protocol and Agent2Agent improve interoperability but do not establish trustworthy delegation; multi-agent organization adds specialization alongside cost and correlated failure. Persistent simulations and world models support training and planning but do not themselves demonstrate agency; robotics and self-driving laboratories establish bounded feasibility rather than unattended open-world reliability. We propose justified delegation as an analytical and normative heuristic, not an observed law or certified score: expand action scope only where evidence supports provenance, bounded authority, failure detection, safe recovery, and calibrated human control. This framing yields a research agenda for coupled model-harness evaluation, capability-based permissions, durable state, cross-agent accountability, and staged physical validation.

AI.tldr: This critical review examines the state of large language models as agents in external systems, finding that while action-interface capabilities have expanded, claims of autonomy are overstated. The paper proposes "justified delegation" as a normative framework for evaluating LLM agent systems.
AI.motivation: The field increasingly conflates model competence with system autonomy, persistence, and safe authority. This review aims to clarify what is actually demonstrated vs. what is merely narrated as progress toward autonomy.
AI.method: Critical review synthesizing primary research and official technical specifications available by August 2026, organized along delegated authority, temporal persistence, and environmental coupling dimensions, while separating model, harness, and environment.
AI.result: Action-interface expansion is documented more convincingly than robust completion, recovery, authorization, or independent verification. MCP and A2A improve interoperability but do not establish trustworthy delegation. Multi-agent organization adds specialization alongside cost and correlated failure. Persistent simulations support training/planning but do not demonstrate agency. Robotics and self-driving labs show bounded feasibility, not unattended open-world reliability.
AI.conclusion: The paper proposes "justified delegation" as an analytical and normative heuristic: expand action scope only where evidence supports provenance, bounded authority, failure detection, safe recovery, and calibrated human control. This yields a research agenda for coupled model-harness evaluation, capability-based permissions, durable state, cross-agent accountability, and staged physical validation.

title: From 80x to 385x: A Best-Matching-Unit Search at the L2 Roof, Measured Against a Symmetrically Tuned Baseline
comment: 15 pages, 8 tables, 3 figures. Companion to arXiv:2608.24067. Both implementations were tuned symmetrically; cuSPARSE became 2-3x faster in the process. Code, data and frozen results: doi:10.5281/zenodo.22245712 (tag v2.0)
summary: Comparisons between GPU implementations are usually asymmetric: one side is tuned by its author, the other is run as found. I report a programme that tuned both a novel SOM algorithm (SparseBin) and the baseline algorithm it was being compared to (cuSPARSE). The best-matching-unit search that dominates self-organizing map training was tuned through four levers - tile size, tile-membership clustering, neuron-axis chunking and vectorised loads - reaching 5.6-10.1x per epoch over the previously published configuration at map sizes from 32x32 to 512x512, and lifting the margin over the CUDA implementation behind our earlier MEDLINE atlases from ~80x to ~385x. cuSPARSE, the implementation SparseBin is compared against, received every lever with an analogue on its side, and became 2-3x faster in the process. The tuned kernel pressed the L2 bandwidth roof at 77% of peak with every other unit at 40-65%, bounding any further lever at ~1.3x - a terminal result rather than a waypoint, and every untested lever was either capped by that bound by construction or measured null.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses asymmetric GPU implementation comparisons by tuning both a novel SOM algorithm (SparseBin) and its baseline (cuSPARSE). Four optimization levers were applied to the best-matching-unit search: tile size, tile-membership clustering, neuron-axis chunking, and vectorised loads. SparseBin achieved 5.6-10.1x speedup over previous configuration, while cuSPARSE became 2-3x faster. The tuned kernel reached 77% of L2 bandwidth peak, with further optimization bounded at ~1.3x.
AI.motivation: GPU implementation comparisons are typically asymmetric - one algorithm is optimized while the baseline runs as-is. The author aimed to create a fair comparison by tuning both SparseBin (novel SOM algorithm) and cuSPARSE (baseline) to demonstrate true performance differences.
AI.method: Four optimization levers were applied to the best-matching-unit search (which dominates SOM training): (1) tile size, (2) tile-membership clustering, (3) neuron-axis chunking, and (4) vectorised loads. Analogous optimizations were applied to cuSPARSE. Performance was measured across map sizes from 32x32 to 512x512.
AI.result: SparseBin achieved 5.6-10.1x speedup per epoch over previously published configuration, lifting the margin over CUDA implementation from ~80x to ~385x. cuSPARSE became 2-3x faster. The tuned kernel achieved 77% of L2 bandwidth peak (other units at 40-65%), bounding further optimization at ~1.3x.
AI.conclusion: The result is considered "terminal" rather than a waypoint - meaning further significant optimization is unlikely. Any untested levers were either capped by the bandwidth bound by construction or measured to have no effect. This demonstrates a fair comparison methodology where both implementations are optimized to their theoretical limits.

title: WeAgent-MMGenEdit: A Full-Stack Recipe for Multimodal Agentic Image Generation and Editing
summary: Image generation and editing models have advanced rapidly, yet remain unreliable when prompts require external world knowledge. Bounded and long-tail parametric knowledge prevents direct or reason-then-generate approaches from recovering the required facts and visual appearances. Existing agentic generation and editing methods mitigate this limitation with retrieval tools, yet remain constrained by insufficient visual verification, overloaded policy models, and weak integration of retrieved textual and visual evidence. To address these limitations, we present WeAgent-MMGenEdit, a full-stack recipe including a multimodal harness, a scalable data construction pipeline, a comprehensive benchmark, and post-training methods for the agent policy and image backend. We first introduce WeAgent-Harness, a multimodal runtime with persistent evidence management and dedicated verification and integration tools that organize retrieved multimodal evidence into a dense carrier. Upon this, we develop a scalable pipeline for prompt synthesis and agentic trajectory collection, yielding 23K supervised trajectories and 14.7K RL tasks with three-layer verifiable checklists. We further introduce WeBench-MMGenEdit, a bilingual benchmark covering both knowledge-intensive image generation and multi-image editing. Finally, a two-sided post-training recipe based on SFT and RL improves the agent policy and image backend. Together, WeAgent-MMGenEdit enables a 30B-total/3B-active policy to outperform similarly sized policy models and approach the performance of a 1T-parameter agent.

AI.tldr: WeAgent-MMGenEdit is a full-stack solution for knowledge-intensive image generation and editing, addressing limitations of existing agentic methods through a multimodal harness, scalable data pipeline, comprehensive benchmark, and post-training methods. It enables a 30B-parameter model to approach the performance of a 1T-parameter agent.
AI.motivation: Image generation and editing models fail when prompts require external world knowledge due to bounded parametric knowledge. Existing agentic methods suffer from insufficient visual verification, overloaded policy models, and weak integration of retrieved textual and visual evidence.
AI.method: The solution includes: (1) WeAgent-Harness, a multimodal runtime with persistent evidence management and dedicated verification/integration tools; (2) A scalable pipeline for prompt synthesis and agentic trajectory collection (23K supervised trajectories, 14.7K RL tasks with three-layer verifiable checklists); (3) WeBench-MMGenEdit, a bilingual benchmark for knowledge-intensive image generation and multi-image editing; (4) Two-sided post-training recipe based on SFT and RL for both agent policy and image backend.
AI.result: WeAgent-MMGenEdit enables a 30B-total/3B-active policy to outperform similarly sized policy models and approach the performance of a 1T-parameter agent.
AI.conclusion: The full-stack approach successfully integrates multimodal retrieval with visual verification, addressing the key limitations of prior agentic generation and editing methods. The combination of dedicated harness, large-scale training data, comprehensive benchmark, and two-sided post-training achieves significant performance improvements with efficient model sizes.

title: Compact-Memory LLM Agents via Online Max-Member Clustering and Atom-Aware Packing
summary:
Many long-horizon LLM deployments face tight prompt budgets: latency, cost, and context limits make full-context prompting impractical as interaction length grows. The key question is then not raw recall alone, but which memory design gives the best quality--token trade-off in the compact-memory regime. We present \textbf{RSM-full}, an online clustered-memory pipeline designed for a strong quality--token Pareto point.
  RSM-full combines two design choices: a cosine-gated \emph{max-member merge} write rule and an atom-aware grouped context packer. On AMA-Bench, our primary compact-memory benchmark, it reaches $83%$ of Full-Context quality at $32%$ of the token cost at a $4$k budget; under four-seed averaging it beats the closest streaming-clustered baseline (Online K-Means) by $+3.5$--$6.0$,pp ($p{<}.001$) across the whole ${\sim}2.6$k--${\sim}5$k regime. Three-seed ablations show most of this gain comes from the merge rule ($+5.7$,pp over Online K-Means and matched-$τ$ DP-means) and the grouped packer ($+5.0$,pp over flat concatenation).
  The pattern reproduces on RealMem, an independent long-horizon persona-memory benchmark: RSM-full improves on Budget-RAG ($+0.69$,pp, $p{=}.006$), is on par with BM25-RAG (paired $Δ{=}{+}0.27$,pp, $p{=}.47$; we do \emph{not} claim BM25 equivalence in the equivalence-test sense), and significantly outperforms Streaming-Proto ($+2.97$,pp) and the closest reproduced 2025 agentic-memory baseline A-MEM ($+1.65$,pp, $p{<}.001$). Across benchmarks the message is consistent: under tight budgets, compact-memory performance is driven mainly by how streaming memories are merged and how retrieved content is assembled.
  Overall, RSM-full is most useful when answeroughly $2k$--$5k$ prompt tokens, where itdefines a strong compact-memory Pareto point; higher-token baselines remain stronger outside this regime.

AI.tldr: RSM-full is an online clustered-memory pipeline for LLMs that achieves 83% of full-context quality at only 32% token cost in compact-memory regimes (2k-5k tokens). It combines a cosine-gated max-member merge write rule with an atom-aware grouped context packer, outperforming baselines like Online K-Means, Budget-RAG, and A-MEM on AMA-Bench and RealMem benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon LLM deployments face tight prompt budgets due to latency, cost, and context limits. The key challenge is designing memory systems that maximize quality-token trade-offs in the compact-memory regime, rather than just maximizing raw recall.
AI.method: RSM-full integrates two novel design choices: (1) a cosine-gated max-member merge write rule for streaming memory consolidation, and (2) an atom-aware grouped context packer for assembling retrieved content. The approach is evaluated on AMA-Bench (primary compact-memory benchmark) and RealMem (independent long-horizon persona-memory benchmark).
AI.result: On AMA-Bench at 4k token budget: achieves 83% of Full-Context quality at 32% token cost; beats Online K-Means by +3.5-6.0pp (p<.001). Ablations show merge rule contributes +5.7pp and packer contributes +5.0pp. On RealMem: +0.69pp over Budget-RAG (p=.006), on par with BM25-RAG (+0.27pp, p=.47), +2.97pp over Streaming-Proto, +1.65pp over A-MEM (p<.001).
AI.conclusion: RSM-full defines a strong compact-memory Pareto point in the ~2k-5k token regime. Performance is primarily driven by how streaming memories are merged and how retrieved content is assembled. Higher-token baselines remain stronger outside this regime.

title: Beyond Stationarity in Time Series: Discovering Causal Structures and Latent Regimes via Markov Blankets
comment: Accepted at the 11th AALTD Workshop at ECML PKDD 2026, Naples, Italy
summary: This paper introduces Regime-aware Constraint-Based and Noise-Based causal discovery with Markov Blankets (RCBNB-MB), a novel causal discovery algorithm for time series that relaxes the common assumption of a single, time-consistent causal structure. Time series are typically observed at discrete time points and often exhibit regime changes that challenge the assumption of a static causal structure, a limitation in many real-world dynamic systems. To address this challenge, RCBNB-MB identifies latent causal regimes, defined as subsets of time points within which a stable causal structure holds. The algorithm follows an iterative strategy that segments the time series into regimes and discovers the causal graph within each regime. By leveraging the Markov blanket rather than direct parents, RCBNB-MB gains robustness to errors in causal discovery and preserves predictive information. We provide theoretical guarantees for RCBNB-MB's ability to recover both regime transitions and causal graphs under reasonable assumptions. Furthermore, we validate its effectiveness through extensive experiments on simulated datasets with known ground truth and real-world IT monitoring data, where taking into account regime shifts is critical. Empirical results show that RCBNB-MB systematically outperforms baseline approaches in accurately detecting regime changes and their associated causal graphs, positioning it as a robust and versatile framework for non-stationary time series analysis.

AI.tldr: RCBNB-MB is a novel causal discovery algorithm for time series that handles regime changes (non-stationarity) by identifying latent causal regimes and discovering causal graphs within each regime. It uses Markov blankets instead of direct parents for robustness and provides theoretical guarantees for recovering regime transitions and causal graphs.
AI.motivation: Existing causal discovery algorithms assume a single, time-consistent causal structure, which is violated in real-world dynamic systems that exhibit regime changes. This assumption limitation needed to be addressed for practical applications.
AI.method: The algorithm uses an iterative strategy that: 1) Segments time series into regimes (subsets of time points with stable causal structure), 2) Discovers causal graphs within each regime, 3) Leverages Markov blankets rather than direct parents for robustness to errors in causal discovery.
AI.result: Empirical results show RCBNB-MB systematically outperforms baseline approaches in accurately detecting regime changes and their associated causal graphs, validated on both simulated datasets with known ground truth and real-world IT monitoring data.
AI.conclusion: RCBNB-MB provides a robust and versatile framework for non-stationary time series causal discovery, with theoretical guarantees and strong empirical performance.

title: SMILE: Self-Explainable Multimodal Information Bottleneck for Medical Diagnosis
summary: Explainability is increasingly seen as a crucial requirement in AI-based medical diagnosis, particularly in safety-critical clinical decision-making. Most existing explainability methods in healthcare operate in a post-hoc manner and are predominantly designed for unimodal data, which limits their applicability in increasingly prevalent multimodal diagnostic settings.
