In sequential transfer optimization, pointwise B-spline trajectory evaluation is reformulated using a blending-matrix representation for trajectory and collision computations. Both reformulations maintain close numerical agreement with their reference evaluations and substantially reduce runtime, yielding $256.72\times$ and $93.91\times$ end-to-end speedups, respectively. These results demonstrate problem-side reformulation as a practical route toward scalable ETO. Both application implementations and experimental scripts are released as open source to support reproducibility and reuse.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses runtime scaling in Evolutionary Transfer Optimization (ETO) by reformulating serial computations into parallel forms. Two case studies are presented: matrix-recursive kinematic-arm evaluation (256.72× speedup) and pointwise B-spline trajectory evaluation (93.91× speedup), both maintaining numerical accuracy with reference methods.
AI.motivation: As ETO scales to larger task collections, problem evaluation becomes a computational bottleneck. The authors identify this as a major source of runtime growth and seek practical solutions for scalable ETO.
AI.method: The authors organize evaluation scaling into two levels: (1) scaling the number of evaluated tasks, and (2) scaling the workload within each task. They reformulate serial computations using matrix representations: accumulation-matrix for cumulative link directions in kinematic-arm evaluation, and blending-matrix for trajectory and collision computations in B-spline trajectory evaluation.
AI.result: Both reformulations achieve substantial speedups while maintaining close numerical agreement with reference evaluations: 256.72× end-to-end speedup for multi-task optimization (kinematic-arm) and 93.91× speedup for sequential transfer optimization (trajectory evaluation).
AI.conclusion: Problem-side reformulation is demonstrated as a practical route toward scalable ETO. The implementations and experimental scripts are released as open source to support reproducibility and reuse.

title: How Does mHC Use Its Residual Streams? Selective Routing and Near-Identity Mixing
summary: Hyper-Connections and their manifold-constrained variant mHC widen a residual pathway from one stream to n, yet how trained models use this capacity remains unclear: how broadly blocks read and write, how strongly the residual pathway mixes streams, and whether the streams carry distinct representations. We examine these properties in the four-stream residual pathway of DeepSeek-V4-Flash using effective stream counts, cross-stream residual weights, and inter-stream cosine similarity. Read/write routing is concentrated but varies across depth: a typical attention or FFN site effectively uses about two streams, while the dominant stream changes across layers and the representations remain directionally distinct. Residual mixing is modest and occurs primarily in early layers; in layers 22-42, the pathway mostly carries each stream forward separately. Targeted interventions establish the functional significance of these patterns. Replacing the late mixers by identity increases C4 perplexity by only 1.9% and preserves the six-task average score, whereas replacing the early mixers increases perplexity by 41%. Fixing each early mixer to its C4 diagnostic mean increases perplexity by only 0.2% and reduces the average score by 0.25 percentage points, showing that its site-specific structure matters more than its token-wise variation on the evaluated metrics. Likewise, retaining the three largest routing weights per token at every site increases perplexity by at most 2.7% and changes the average score by at most 0.4 points. Thus, the studied model realizes only part of the flexibility afforded by four-stream mHC: individual blocks rarely require all four streams, and late residual mixing provides little measured benefit.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how DeepSeek-V4-Flash uses the four-stream residual pathway in mHC architecture. Despite having capacity for four streams, the model primarily uses about two streams per block, with residual mixing concentrated in early layers and providing minimal functional benefit.
AI.motivation: Hyper-Connections and mHC widen residual pathways from one stream to n, but it remains unclear how trained models actually utilize this capacity—whether blocks read/write broadly, how strongly streams are mixed, and whether streams carry distinct representations.
AI.method: Analyzed DeepSeek-V4-Flash's four-stream residual pathway using three metrics: effective stream counts (measuring how many streams blocks effectively use), cross-stream residual weights (measuring mixing strength), and inter-stream cosine similarity (measuring representation distinctness). Conducted targeted interventions: replacing late/early mixers with identity, fixing early mixers to C4 diagnostic mean, and retaining only three largest routing weights per token.
AI.result: Read/write routing is concentrated: typical attention or FFN sites effectively use ~2 streams. The dominant stream changes across layers, and representations remain directionally distinct. Residual mixing is modest and occurs primarily in early layers (layers 1-21); in layers 22-42, the pathway mostly carries each stream forward separately. Intervention results: (1) Late mixers → identity: +1.9% perplexity, zero score change. (2) Early mixers → identity: +41% perplexity. (3) Fixing early mixers to mean: +0.2% perplexity, -0.25 score. (4) Keeping 3 largest routing weights: +2.7% perplexity max, ±0.4 score change.
AI.conclusion: DeepSeek-V4-Flash realizes only part of the four-stream mHC flexibility: individual blocks rarely require all four streams, and late residual mixing provides little measured benefit. The model relies heavily on early-layer mixing but not late-layer mixing, and token-wise routing variation has minimal impact on downstream performance.

title: Adaptive Gated Deepfake Detection for Low-Resolution and Resource-Constrained Environments
summary: Deepfake detection models often rely on high-quality inputs, fixed inference paths, and computationally expensive architectures, limiting their use in low-resolution and resource-constrained settings. This paper proposes AdaGate-DF, an adaptive gated deepfake detection framework that uses image-quality cues to route samples through a dual multi-exit system so high-quality images can exit earlier and save compute. We evaluated AdaGate-DF against MaD-CoRN, DefakeHop++, and ShuffleNetV2 on two benchmark datasets (Celeb-DF and FaceForensics++) under multiple configurations to test image resolution dependence and training and inference efficiency. On Celeb-DF, AdaGate-DF achieves an AUC of 0.9370, outperforming MaD-CoRN and DefakeHop++ while maintaining a low inference latency. Resolution-based testing shows consistent improvement as input resolution increases, reaching an AUC of 0.9708 at 384 by 384. The FaceForensics++ results highlight that AdaGate-DF remains effective under class imbalance, following competitive results with evaluated models. Overall, AdaGate-DF demonstrated a practical balance between detection performance, uncertainty-aware prediction, and computational efficiency for variable-quality deepfake detection.

AI.tldr: AdaGate-DF is an adaptive gated deepfake detection framework that uses image-quality cues to route samples through a dual multi-exit system, enabling high-quality images to exit early and save computational resources. It achieves AUC of 0.9370 on Celeb-DF and 0.9708 at 384x384 resolution, outperforming MaD-CoRN and DefakeHop++ while maintaining low inference latency.
AI.motivation: Current deepfake detection models rely on high-quality inputs, fixed inference paths, and computationally expensive architectures, making them unsuitable for low-resolution and resource-constrained settings. There is a need for an efficient, adaptive approach that can handle variable-quality inputs.
AI.method: The proposed AdaGate-DF framework uses image-quality cues to route samples through a dual multi-exit system. High-quality images can exit earlier in the pipeline to save compute, while lower-quality images continue through additional processing. The model was evaluated against MaD-CoRN, DefakeHop++, and ShuffleNetV2 on Celeb-DF and FaceForensics++ datasets under multiple configurations testing resolution dependence and training/inference efficiency.
AI.result: On Celeb-DF, AdaGate-DF achieves an AUC of 0.9370, outperforming MaD-CoRN and DefakeHop++ while maintaining low inference latency. Resolution-based testing shows consistent improvement as input resolution increases, reaching an AUC of 0.9708 at 384x384 resolution. On FaceForensics++, the method remains effective under class imbalance, showing competitive results with evaluated models.
AI.conclusion: AdaGate-DF demonstrates a practical balance between detection performance, uncertainty-aware prediction, and computational efficiency for variable-quality deepfake detection. The adaptive gating mechanism effectively reduces computational burden while maintaining high detection accuracy across different input qualities.

title: MePo++: Unifying Representation Refinement and Reconciliation for General Continual Learning
summary: General continual learning (GCL) aims to learn from evolving data streams without task identities, explicit boundaries, or repeated access to previous data, making it a realistic yet challenging setting for continual intelligence. Although pretrained models (PTMs) provide rich prior knowledge for addressing the limited supervision and non-stationary nature of GCL, existing PTM-based methods often directly adapt pretrained representations and overlook two critical gaps: the misalignment between upstream pretraining and downstream continual adaptation, and the unreliability of conventional output alignment under blurry streams. Here we propose MePo++, a unified post-training framework that bridges pretrained knowledge and downstream GCL through representation refinement and reconciliation. MePo++ introduces two complementary components: MetaPrep, which improves representation plasticity for continual adaptation through unsupervised meta-refinement over pseudo continual sequences; and StreamAlign, which reinforces representation stability by reconciling evolving online features with a stable pretrained geometry. By improving representation learnability before adaptation and preserving alignment during continual learning, MePo++ enables PTMs to remain both plastic for new concepts and stable over evolving streams. Experiments across diverse PTMs, datasets, and continual learning baselines demonstrate the consistent effectiveness and generality of MePo++ for PTM-based GCL. Our code is available at https://github.com/SunGL001/MePo_Plus.

AI.tldr: MePo++ is a unified post-training framework for pretrained model-based general continual learning (GCL). It addresses two key gaps: misalignment between pretraining and downstream adaptation, and unreliable output alignment under blurry data streams. The framework consists of MetaPrep (for representation plasticity) and StreamAlign (for representation stability).
AI.motivation: Existing PTM-based continual learning methods directly adapt pretrained representations without addressing: (1) the misalignment between upstream pretraining and downstream continual adaptation, and (2) the unreliability of conventional output alignment under blurry streams. GCL is challenging because it learns from evolving data streams without task identities, explicit boundaries, or repeated access to previous data.
AI.method: MePo++ introduces two complementary components: (1) MetaPrep - improves representation plasticity for continual adaptation through unsupervised meta-refinement over pseudo continual sequences; (2) StreamAlign - reinforces representation stability by reconciling evolving online features with a stable pretrained geometry. The approach improves representation learnability before adaptation and preserves alignment during continual learning.
AI.result: Experiments across diverse PTMs, datasets, and continual learning baselines demonstrate consistent effectiveness and generality of MePo++ for PTM-based GCL.
AI.conclusion: MePo++ enables pretrained models to remain both plastic for new concepts and stable over evolving streams, providing a unified post-training framework that bridges pretrained knowledge and downstream GCL through representation refinement and reconciliation.

title: Optimal Rates for Agentic Networked Information Aggregation
comment: Initial version submitted to SODA 2027 on July 9, 2026
summary:
Building on the pioneering paper of Kearns, Roth, and Ryu (SODA'26), we study information aggregation in a networked learning model. The model captures a central pattern in agentic AI: each agent sees only part of the data and passes on only its own conclusion. Their model considers a linear regression problem with the mean squared error (MSE) loss. Agents sit in a DAG and each sees only a subset of the features and its parents' predictions, fits a linear predictor, and passes only its prediction forward. The benchmark is the full-feature learner that sees all raw features. A path of depth $D$ is $M$-covered if every block of $M$ consecutive agents collectively sees all raw features. Kearns, Roth, and Ryu proved that the excess mean squared error of the last agent on such a path is $O(M/\sqrt D)$, and gave a cyclic instance with excess error $Ω(M/D)$ for $D<M^2$.
  We close this gap: the correct rate is constant up to depth $M^2$, and $Θ(M^2/D)$ beyond it. We first give a sharper analysis of the cyclic instance and improve its lower bound to $Ω(\sqrt{M/D})$ for $D<M^2$. We then construct, for every depth $D\ge M^2$, an $M$-covered path of depth $D$ with excess error $Ω(M^2/D)$. The same instance gives the constant lower bound for all $D < M^2$. We also show that for any fixed distribution the excess error contracts geometrically along the path, ruling out any single instance that witnesses any polynomial lower bound at every depth.
  Finally, we prove the same optimal rate for logistic classification in the logit-passing model of Bateni et al., which considers the binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss. The same improved upper bound of $O(M^2/D)$ holds, and we transfer all the regression lower bounds by showing that on those examples the logistic path follows the least-squares path up to rescaling.

AI.tldr: This paper studies information aggregation in a networked learning model where agents see only partial features and pass predictions forward in a DAG. It resolves an open problem from Kearns, Roth, and Ryu regarding the excess mean squared error of the last agent in a path. The key finding is that the correct rate is constant for depth D < M², and Θ(M²/D) for D ≥ M², improving the previous O(M/√D) bound. The results also extend to logistic classification with binary cross-entropy loss.
AI.motivation: The model captures a central pattern in agentic AI where each agent sees only part of the data and passes only its conclusion forward. Understanding the error rates in such networked learning is crucial for designing efficient multi-agent AI systems. The previous work by Kearns, Roth, and Ryu had a gap between their upper bound O(M/√D) and lower bound Ω(M/D) for D < M², which this paper resolves.
AI.method: The analysis involves: (1) Sharper analysis of the cyclic instance to improve the lower bound to Ω(√(M/D)) for D < M²; (2) Construction of M-covered paths of depth D with excess error Ω(M²/D) for every D ≥ M²; (3) Showing geometric contraction of excess error along paths for fixed distributions; (4) Transferring regression lower bounds to logistic classification by demonstrating that logistic paths follow least-squares paths up to rescaling on the constructed examples.
AI.result: The paper establishes the optimal rate: excess error is constant (Θ(1)) for depths D < M², and Θ(M²/D) for D ≥ M². Key contributions include: (1) Improved lower bound of Ω(√(M/D)) for D < M²; (2) Construction of paths achieving Ω(M²/D) error for D ≥ M²; (3) Proof that no single instance can witness polynomial lower bounds at all depths; (4) Extension of the optimal O(M²/D) rate to logistic classification in the logit-passing model.
AI.conclusion: The gap in the literature is closed—the correct information aggregation rate in networked learning is now fully characterized. The results show that for shallow networks (D < M²), constant error is unavoidable, while for deeper networks (D ≥ M²), the error decreases as M²/D. This fundamental understanding applies to both linear regression with MSE loss and logistic classification with BCE loss, providing guidance for designing agentic AI systems with appropriate depth relative to the number of features each agent can access.

title: Scalable Detection of Fossil Palynomorphs in Multifocal Digital Microscopy Images
summary: Palynomorphs (microscopic, organic-walled fossils such as pollen, spores, and dinoflagellates) are important high-resolution records of past climates and are critical to the study of ancient ecosystems. Existing methods rely on manual analysis of high-resolution, multifocal digital microscopy images, which is slow and time-consuming and requires researchers to compromise on the scale of their investigations. To the best of our knowledge, our work proposes the first ever scalable end-to-end pipeline for automated palynomorph detection in whole slide images that addresses this bottleneck through: (1) efficient methods for decomposing and compressing digitized multifocal microscope slide images into tractable 2-dimensional tiles for analysis; (2) benchmarking modern object detection models, including RF-DETR, for the detection of palynomorphs, achieving an AP@50 of 0.879; (3) an efficient algorithm for the synthesis of detection outputs across large-scale, high-resolution images; and (4) an I/O optimization resulting in faster inference time. Our methods drastically reduce the time required for palynomorph detection in a single slide from often days of manual inspection to under one hour of automated analysis, enabling palynological research at a substantially greater scale.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first scalable end-to-end pipeline for automated palynomorph detection in whole slide microscopy images, reducing analysis time from days to under one hour.
AI.motivation: Manual analysis of palynomorphs (pollen, spores, dinoflagellates) in high-resolution multifocal digital microscopy images is slow, time-consuming, and limits the scale of palynological research.
AI.method: The pipeline includes: (1) efficient decomposition and compression of digitized multifocal microscope slides into 2D tiles; (2) benchmarking modern object detection models including RF-DETR; (3) an algorithm for synthesizing detection outputs across large-scale images; and (4) I/O optimization for faster inference.
AI.result: Achieved AP@50 of 0.879 using RF-DETR model, reducing detection time from days of manual inspection to under one hour of automated analysis per slide.
AI.conclusion: The proposed pipeline enables palynological research at a substantially greater scale by providing an efficient, automated solution for palynomorph detection in whole slide images.

title: TruthInsightBench: An Evidence-Grounded Benchmark for Automated Evaluation of Open-Ended Scientific Discovery Agents
summary: Autonomous coding agents are increasingly proposed as AI-scientist systems that conduct analyses and write research reports, but executing a prescribed analysis is not the same as making a discovery. Existing benchmarks are configured for reproduction: tasks, data, and rubrics are built around a hidden target study, and recovery of its result is rewarded. We present TruthInsightBench, a benchmark configured for discovery. Its 40 blind tasks, drawn from 40 peer-reviewed studies across 10 scientific domains, expose only a neutral scientific objective and frozen data; source conclusions, expected values, and analysis paths are withheld, leaving the agent to determine what claim the data support. A fixed LLM-based judge scores the evidentiary maturity of an agent's own claims along six dimensions, operationalized as 29 artifact-grounded items, with automated, deterministic aggregation and no per-instance human grading, so evaluation can be repeated automatically as agents evolve. On one frozen base model, four coding agents form a narrow plateau (58.4-60.3 of 100) with no statistically reliable pairwise separation: they execute and document analyses competently, with comparatively strong evidence auditability and novelty, but largely lack the discriminating acts that establish a trustworthy claim (controls, robustness, falsifiability, and cross-dataset generalization). The bottleneck is scientific judgment rather than coding, and genuine discovery remains out of reach. TruthInsightBench makes this gap a measurable target; data and scoring code are at https://github.com/TruthInsight-stack/TruthInsightBench.

AI.tldr: TruthInsightBench is a new benchmark for evaluating AI coding agents' ability to make scientific discoveries, rather than just reproduce existing results. It uses 40 blind tasks from peer-reviewed studies where agents must determine what claims the data support without any target answers. Testing four coding agents revealed a narrow performance plateau (58.4-60.3/100), with agents showing competence in execution and documentation but lacking the scientific judgment needed for genuine discovery.
AI.motivation: The authors argue that existing benchmarks for AI coding agents are configured for "reproduction" - they reward recovering a hidden target study's results. However, executing a prescribed analysis is fundamentally different from making a discovery. The authors present TruthInsightBench to address this gap and make the discovery capability of AI agents measurable.
AI.method: The benchmark uses 40 blind tasks drawn from 40 peer-reviewed studies across 10 scientific domains. Only a neutral scientific objective and frozen data are provided; source conclusions, expected values, and analysis paths are withheld. An LLM-based judge scores the evidentiary maturity of an agent's claims along six dimensions, operationalized as 29 artifact-grounded items, with automated deterministic aggregation.
AI.result: Four coding agents tested on one frozen base model achieved a narrow plateau of 58.4-60.3 out of 100, with no statistically reliable pairwise separation. Agents showed competence in executing and documenting analyses, with comparatively strong evidence auditability and novelty. However, they largely lacked the discriminating acts that establish trustworthy claims: controls, robustness, falsifiability, and cross-dataset generalization.
AI.conclusion: The bottleneck is scientific judgment rather than coding capability. Genuine discovery remains out of reach for current AI coding agents. TruthInsightBench makes this gap a measurable target, enabling systematic evaluation as agents evolve.

title: Embedded Graph Flows for Categorical Graph Generation
summary: Generating categorical graphs requires choosing node and edge types that form a coherent structure without depending on node order. Many graph generators encode categories as fixed one-hot vectors, which can impose an artificial geometry in which categories are equidistant. We propose Embedded Graph Flows (EGF), a generative model that learns continuous embeddings for node and unordered-edge categories and transports Gaussian noise towards these learnt endpoints using a permutation-equivariant graph transformer. A terminal readout maps the embeddings back to discrete graph categories. Across molecular benchmarks, EGF achieved competitive performance. On QM9, EGF gives the best result on all four reported metrics among the three methods, including a Fréchet ChemNet Distance (FCD) of 0.150, compared with 0.717 for the categorical-diffusion baseline DiGress and 0.812 for the bridge-based baseline GruM. When applied to larger molecules in ZINC250k, EGF retains the lowest maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) using the neighbourhood subgraph pairwise distance kernel (NSPDK), indicating close agreement with the local substructures of the reference molecules. Our code is available at https://github.com/Trusted-System-Lab/EGF.

AI.tldr: EGF is a generative model for categorical graphs that learns continuous embeddings for node/edge categories and uses a graph transformer to transport Gaussian noise to these embeddings, applied to molecular generation with state-of-the-art results on QM9 and ZINC250k benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing graph generators use fixed one-hot vectors for categories, which imposes artificial geometry where categories are equidistant. This limits the model's ability to learn meaningful relationships between different node and edge types.
AI.method: EGF uses three key components: (1) continuous embeddings for node and unordered-edge categories learned during training, (2) a permutation-equivariant graph transformer that transports Gaussian noise towards learned embeddings, and (3) a terminal readout that maps embeddings back to discrete graph categories.
AI.result: On QM9, EGF achieves the best results on all four reported metrics among three methods, with FCD of 0.150 compared to 0.717 for DiGress and 0.812 for GruM. On ZINC250k, EGF retains the lowest MMD using NSPDK, indicating close agreement with local substructures of reference molecules.
AI.conclusion: EGF successfully addresses the limitation of one-hot encoding by learning continuous embeddings for categorical graph elements, achieving superior performance on molecular benchmarks compared to categorical-diffusion (DiGress) and bridge-based (GruM) baselines.

title: Lightweight Vision Transformer Compression for On-Device Plant Disease Detection in Resource-Constrained Agricultural Field Conditions
summary: Chilli (Capsicum annuum) is one of India's most economically significant crops, yet its productivity is persistently threatened by diseases that are difficult to identify without expert intervention. While Vision Transformers (ViTs) have achieved high classification accuracy, their large computational footprint makes deployment on resource constrained devices challenging. Existing compression approaches typically address pruning, quantization, and knowledge distillation in isolation, leaving the potential benefits and interactions of their combined application insufficiently explored. We propose a unified Vision Transformer compression framework that combines Hessian-Balanced Adaptive Block Pruning (H-BAC), guided by second-order sensitivity estimation, with quantization and attention-based knowledge distillation. To systematically identify the most effective configuration within each compression family, each technique is first evaluated independently through controlled ablation studies, after which the best-performing components are integrated into a sequential deployment pipeline tailored to real-world agricultural constraints. On a chilli 3-class village-split dataset with a genuine cross-village, cross-device out-of-distribution test split, the resulting compressed models match or exceed the 95.13% FP32 baseline's accuracy, alongside 74-98% model size reduction, and the fully integrated compression pipeline achieves a 54.5x size reduction (327.42 MB to 6.01 MB) at 95.13 +/- 2.32% accuracy across four tested configurations. A direct comparison further reveals that, on this dataset, a directly-trained student of the same final size, without pruning or distillation, reaches comparable accuracy of 94.87%, at the same 6.01 MB INT8 size, indicating where H-BAC and knowledge distillation are, and are not yet shown to be, worth their computational cost.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a unified Vision Transformer compression framework for chilli disease classification, combining Hessian-Balanced Adaptive Block Pruning (H-BAC), quantization, and attention-based knowledge distillation. The framework achieves 54.5x model size reduction (327.42 MB to 6.01 MB) while maintaining 95.13% accuracy, though direct training achieves comparable accuracy at the same model size.
AI.motivation: Chilli is economically significant in India but disease identification requires expert intervention. Vision Transformers achieve high accuracy but are computationally expensive for resource-constrained devices. Existing compression approaches (pruning, quantization, knowledge distillation) are typically explored in isolation, leaving their combined potential unexplored.
AI.method: The framework combines: (1) H-Balanced Adaptive Block Pruning (H-BAC) guided by second-order Hessian sensitivity estimation, (2) quantization, and (3) attention-based knowledge distillation. Each technique is first evaluated independently through controlled ablation studies, then the best components are integrated into a sequential deployment pipeline. Dataset: 3-class chilli village-split with cross-village, cross-device out-of-distribution test split.
AI.result: The compressed models match or exceed the 95.13% FP32 baseline accuracy with 74-98% model size reduction. The fully integrated pipeline achieves 54.5x size reduction (327.42 MB to 6.01 MB) at 95.13 ± 2.32% accuracy across four tested configurations. Direct training of a student model of the same final size achieves 94.87% accuracy at 6.01 MB INT8.
AI.conclusion: The compression framework effectively reduces ViT model size by 54.5x while maintaining baseline accuracy. However, direct training achieves comparable accuracy, questioning the computational cost-benefit of H-BAC and knowledge distillation in this specific application. The ablation studies provide systematic guidance for real-world agricultural deployment constraints.

title: Measuring AI Accountability Through Argumentation Analysis: Can Model Reasoning Withstand Scrutiny?
comment: 27 pages (19 main text + appendix and references), 5 figures, 6 tables. Accepted for publication in the Paris Journal of AI and Digital Ethics (2026); presented at PCAIDE 2026
summary: AI oversight methods rely on ground truth for validation, but what constitutes appropriate AI behavior is contested. This leaves evaluation of moral reasoning in LLMs and debate-based oversight implicitly avoiding realistic ambiguity. We investigate an alternative standard designed to function despite such ambiguity: structural quality of the defence a model can mount for its verdicts in response to critical questions, measured through a four-phase dialectical protocol grounded in Walton's theory of argumentation schemes and Govier's criteria for argument cogency. The protocol is adaptive to different frames of reasoning, extends beyond multiple-choice framing, and treats both the reasoning that precedes a verdict and its post-hoc justification. Across nine frontier models and 200 high-ambiguity MoralChoice items -- $6,778$ judge-scored cells, validated against $89.6\%$ inter-judge agreement on the binary failure judgment -- models defend their reasoning well above the rubric minimum on every dimension. Failure mass concentrates on grounds and sufficiency, and correlates with epistemic hedging rather than argument length. Reasoning is better defended than post-hoc justification, on every model and every Govier dimension. The scheme a model presents in its justification differs from the one it reasoned with on a substantial share of dilemmas ($\geq 20\%$ per model), despite value-based practical reasoning dominating both tracks. The protocol catches strictly indefensible defences (self-contradiction, false premises), and it surfaces difficulties in characterizing the role of retraction in AI alignment, suggesting a need for more situated evaluations.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel AI oversight method that evaluates moral reasoning in LLMs not by comparing verdicts to ground truth, but by assessing the structural quality of a model's defense of its judgments through a four-phase dialectical protocol. Testing across 9 frontier models on 200 high-ambiguity moral dilemmas reveals models perform well above minimum thresholds, with failures concentrating on argument grounds and sufficiency rather than reasoning depth.
AI.motivation: Current AI oversight methods rely on ground truth for validation, but what constitutes "appropriate AI behavior" is fundamentally contested in moral contexts. This creates a gap where evaluation of moral reasoning in LLMs and debate-based oversight implicitly avoid realistic ambiguity. The authors seek an alternative evaluation standard that can function despite such ambiguity.
AI.method: Four-phase dialectical protocol grounded in Walton's theory of argumentation schemes and Govier's criteria for argument cogency. The protocol is adaptive to different reasoning frames, extends beyond multiple-choice, and evaluates both reasoning preceding verdicts and post-hoc justification. Applied to 9 frontier models across 200 high-ambiguity MoralChoice items (6,778 judge-scored cells), validated against 89.6% inter-judge agreement on binary failure judgment.
AI.result: Models defend reasoning well above rubric minimum on every dimension. Failure mass concentrates on grounds and sufficiency, correlating with epistemic hedging rather than argument length. Reasoning is better defended than post-hoc justification across every model and Govier dimension. Scheme presented in justification differs from reasoning scheme in ≥20% of dilemmas per model, despite value-based practical reasoning dominating both tracks. The protocol catches strictly indefensible defenses (self-contradiction, false premises).
AI.conclusion: The protocol successfully evaluates moral reasoning quality independent of contested ground truth. It surfaces difficulties in characterizing the role of retraction in AI alignment and suggests a need for more situated evaluations. The findings indicate that models can mount structurally sound defenses of moral judgments, but struggle with post-hoc justification and certain argument components (grounds, sufficiency).

title: Variational Continuation for Double Pendulum Periodic Orbits
summary: We present a Hessian-based approach to numerically continue periodic orbits in dynamical systems. A loop (periodic orbit candidate) is parametrized as a Fourier series; a loss function is defined based on the deviation of the loop from the physical differential equations. Unlike previous work relying on hand-derived Jacobians, our method automates the process by leveraging automatic differentiation, a common machine learning technique. The continuation direction can be determined by the flat directions of the loss landscapes (directions with zero eigenvalues), making the search of periodic orbits efficient and guided. Our method is integrator-free, precisely initializes oscillations around unstable fixed points, and efficiently detects orbit family intersections and subharmonic bifurcations. As a demonstration, we present full continuations of periodic double pendulum oscillations from fixed points, showing bifurcations along orbit families and categorizing branches of periodic orbits. In particular, we find periodic orbits where both pendulum masses are never simultaneously at rest, which to our knowledge has been missing in the literature.

AI.tldr: A Hessian-based method using automatic differentiation for numerically continuing periodic orbits in dynamical systems, demonstrated on the double pendulum to discover previously unreported periodic orbits.
AI.motivation: Previous approaches to continuing periodic orbits relied on hand-derived Jacobians, which is labor-intensive and error-prone. The authors aimed to automate this process using automatic differentiation (a machine learning technique) and leverage the loss landscape geometry (flat directions/zero eigenvalues) to guide the continuation search efficiently.
AI.method: The method parametrizes periodic orbit candidates (loops) as Fourier series and defines a loss function measuring deviation from the physical differential equations. It uses automatic differentiation to compute gradients and Hessians, eliminating the need for hand-derived Jacobians. The continuation direction is determined by identifying flat directions in the loss landscape (directions with zero eigenvalues).
AI.result: The method successfully performed full continuations of periodic double pendulum oscillations from fixed points, identifying bifurcations along orbit families and categorizing branches of periodic orbits. Notably, the method discovered previously undocumented periodic orbits where both pendulum masses are never simultaneously at rest.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Hessian-based approach using automatic differentiation provides an efficient, integrator-free method for periodic orbit continuation. It successfully identifies orbit family intersections, subharmonic bifurcations, and discovers novel periodic orbits in the double pendulum system, demonstrating the power of machine learning techniques for classical dynamical systems analysis.

title: MEOX: Compact Multimodal Mixture-of-Experts for Earth Observation
comment: Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Geoscience and Remote Sensing
summary: Recent advances in Earth Observation representation learning accommodate heterogeneous sensors and missing observations, often through larger architectures. We present MEOX (Multimodal Earth Observation with eXperts), a multimodal masked autoencoder with a 2.939 million-parameter encoder and 3.115 million parameters in total. Sensor-specific adapters, explicit validity signals, and a shared sparse-expert block preserve modality-dependent processing before a learned patch-wise fusion. Four metadata tokens then accompany a single spatial sequence through fourteen further encoder blocks. Shared expert projections with private low-rank residuals constrain parameter growth, while rotary attention supports downstream spatial grids different from pretraining. The model is pretrained on 1.228 million MMEarth64 samples using modality-balanced masked reconstruction and structured sensor dropout. Frozen transfer is evaluated on six GEO-Bench tasks at both 64 and 224 pixels. The model reaches 64.42% mean intersection-over-union on cashew segmentation at 64 pixels and 90.56% average accuracy on EuroSAT at 224 pixels, exceeding the corresponding reported CSMoE results. BigEarthNet finetuning reaches 72.95% micro-average precision. Routing diagnostics distinguish expert participation, spatial dependence, modality association, and functional contribution. A held-out WorldCover probe measures a 0.64-percentage-point benefit from metadata, while retrieval separates same-sensor semantics from cross-sensor alignment. These results demonstrate sensor-flexible representation learning and strong task transfer using a compact parameter budget.

AI.tldr: MEOX is a compact multimodal masked autoencoder (3.1M parameters) for Earth Observation that uses sensor-specific adapters, shared sparse-expert blocks, and rotary attention to enable flexible sensor processing and strong transfer learning across GEO-Bench tasks.
AI.motivation: Earth Observation representation learning needs to handle heterogeneous sensors and missing observations, typically requiring large architectures. This work aims to achieve strong performance with a compact parameter budget through efficient design choices.
AI.method: MEOX uses sensor-specific adapters with explicit validity signals and a shared sparse-expert block for modality-dependent processing before learned patch-wise fusion. Four metadata tokens accompany spatial sequences through 14 encoder blocks. Parameter growth is constrained via shared expert projections with private low-rank residuals. The model employs rotary attention supporting downstream grids different from pretraining. Pretraining uses 1.228M MMEarth64 samples with modality-balanced masked reconstruction and structured sensor dropout.
AI.result: 64.42% mean IoU on cashew segmentation at 64px; 90.56% average accuracy on EuroSAT at 224px (exceeding CSMoE); BigEarthNet finetuning reaches 72.95% micro-average precision. Metadata provides 0.64-percentage-point benefit on WorldCover. Routing diagnostics reveal expert participation, spatial dependence, modality association, and functional contribution patterns.
AI.conclusion: MEOX demonstrates sensor-flexible representation learning with strong task transfer using a compact 3.1M parameter model, outperforming reported CSMoE results on key benchmarks while maintaining parameter efficiency through shared expert projections and low-rank residual designs.

title: Constructing and Evaluating Clinical Reasoning Trajectories for Medical Agent
summary: Evaluation of medical artificial intelligence agents remains predominantly answer-centric, assessing only the correctness of final outputs while overlooking the quality of intermediate reasoning. In clinical settings, however, a correct answer reached through fabricated evidence or incoherent logic is as dangerous as an incorrect one. We propose MedTraj, a framework that treats reasoning trajectories as critical objects for construction, evaluation, and optimization. The pipeline generates structured multi-step reasoning chains from medical reasoning sources. Each trajectory is then parsed into clinical observations, evidence, numbered reasoning steps, and a final conclusion, and scored across five quality dimensions: coherence, evidence support, hallucination, completeness, and traceability. Controlled error injection introduces targeted faults into otherwise correct trajectories to establish causal links between specific reasoning failures and measurable quality degradation. Building on this, step-level filtering based on marginal contribution identifies which individual reasoning steps drive or undermine trajectory quality. Finally, quality-weighted context learning feeds trajectory evaluations back into the model at inference time, allowing it to learn from both strong and weak reasoning demonstrations. Experiments across CareQA, PubMedQA, and CECMed demonstrate that trajectory context consistently improves reasoning coherence, with gains of +0.029 to +0.041 over a zero-shot baseline. On CECMed, quality-weighted context nearly doubles the correctness over the zero-shot baseline while cutting the hallucination ratio by 87%. Marginal-contribution analysis further shows that a small minority of reasoning steps carry most of the quality signal, and that extending chains beyond four steps yields diminishing returns.

AI.tldr: MedTraj is a framework for evaluating medical AI reasoning by treating reasoning trajectories as critical objects. It generates multi-step reasoning chains, parses them into clinical observations/evidence/reasoning steps/conclusions, and scores them across five quality dimensions (coherence, evidence support, hallucination, completeness, traceability). The framework uses controlled error injection to establish causal links between reasoning failures and quality degradation, step-level filtering based on marginal contribution, and quality-weighted context learning at inference time. Experiments on CareQA, PubMedQA, and CECMed show trajectory context improves reasoning coherence (+0.029 to +0.041), nearly doubles correctness on CECMed while reducing hallucination by 87%, and reveals that a small minority of reasoning steps carry most quality signal.
AI.motivation: Current medical AI evaluation is answer-centric, assessing only final output correctness while ignoring intermediate reasoning quality. In clinical settings, correct answers reached through fabricated evidence or incoherent logic are equally dangerous. There's a need to evaluate the reasoning process itself, not just the final answer.
AI.method: 1) Generate structured multi-step reasoning chains from medical reasoning sources; 2) Parse trajectories into clinical observations, evidence, numbered reasoning steps, and final conclusions; 3) Score across five quality dimensions: coherence, evidence support, hallucination, completeness, traceability; 4) Controlled error injection introduces targeted faults to establish causal links between reasoning failures and quality degradation; 5) Step-level filtering based on marginal contribution identifies quality-driving steps; 6) Quality-weighted context learning feeds trajectory evaluations back at inference time.
AI.result: Trajectory context consistently improves reasoning coherence (+0.029 to +0.041 over zero-shot baseline). On CECMed, quality-weighted context nearly doubles correctness while cutting hallucination ratio by 87%. Marginal-contribution analysis shows a small minority of reasoning steps carry most quality signal, and extending chains beyond four steps yields diminishing returns.
AI.conclusion: MedTraj provides a comprehensive framework for evaluating medical AI reasoning quality beyond final answers. The trajectory-based approach, quality-weighted context learning, and step-level analysis significantly improve reasoning coherence and reduce hallucinations. The finding that few reasoning steps drive most quality signal offers practical guidance for efficient reasoning chain construction.

title: Distill Globally, Adapt Locally: Reasoning Distillation and Product-Type Test-Time Training for Scalable Trade-Up Recommendation
comment: Accepted at the Third Workshop on Agentic and Generative AI for E-Commerce (GenAIECommerce 2026), co-located with ACM RecSys 2026
summary: Trade-up recommendation identifies higher-quality alternatives that preserve a customer's purchase intent while offering upgraded benefits. Large language models (LLMs) can reason about such distinctions, but applying them directly to hundreds of millions of product pairs is operationally impractical. We introduce a two-level framework that distills LLM reasoning into an efficient non-generative student and adapts its decision boundary to product-type-specific trade-up criteria. At Level 1, a retrieval-augmented few-shot LLM teacher generates structured relation labels and natural-language rationales. These rationales supervise a compact embedding-pair classifier through alignment and contrastive objectives; at inference, the student uses only two precomputed 768-dimensional product embeddings, with no LLM calls or text generation. On a fixed human-annotated benchmark of 8,352 pairs, a 15.5M-parameter four-class reasoning-distilled student achieves AUC 0.924 (95% CI [0.918, 0.929]), compared with 0.912 for the four-class label-only student. At Level 2, product-type test-time training (PT-TTT) uses few-shot demonstrations to optimize lightweight category-specific adapters over the frozen student. PT-TTT improves AUC from 0.924 to 0.941 and average precision from 0.920 to 0.940. On a 100K-pair proxy catalog, the distilled student on a single eight-GPU machine is approximately 5,000x faster and 10,000x lower in estimated cost than direct LLM inference.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a two-level framework for trade-up recommendation that distills LLM reasoning into an efficient student model. The approach uses an LLM teacher to generate structured labels and rationales, which supervise a compact 15.5M-parameter classifier. A second level uses product-type-specific adapters (PT-TTT) to further improve performance. The system achieves AUC 0.941 and is 5,000x faster than direct LLM inference.
AI.motivation: Direct application of LLMs to hundreds of millions of product pairs for trade-up recommendation is operationally impractical due to computational cost and latency. There is a need to capture LLM reasoning capabilities in an efficient non-generative student model that can scale to production workloads.
AI.method: The framework operates at two levels: (1) Level 1 uses a retrieval-augmented few-shot LLM teacher to generate structured relation labels and natural-language rationales, which supervise a compact embedding-pair classifier through alignment and contrastive objectives; the student uses only two precomputed 768-dimensional product embeddings at inference. (2) Level 2 applies product-type test-time training (PT-TTT), which uses few-shot demonstrations to optimize lightweight category-specific adapters over the frozen student.
AI.result: On a human-annotated benchmark of 8,352 pairs, the 15.5M-parameter reasoning-distilled student achieves AUC 0.924 (95% CI [0.918, 0.929]), compared with 0.912 for the label-only student. PT-TTT improves AUC from 0.924 to 0.941 and average precision from 0.920 to 0.940. On a 100K-pair proxy catalog, the distilled student is approximately 5,000x faster and 10,000x lower in estimated cost than direct LLM inference.
AI.conclusion: The two-level framework successfully distills LLM reasoning into an efficient student model that achieves high accuracy (AUC 0.941) while being computationally practical. The reasoning distillation with rationales outperforms label-only distillation, and PT-TTT provides additional gains by adapting to product-type-specific criteria. The approach enables scalable trade-up recommendation at production scale with significant cost and speed advantages.

title: Reflection-aware Generative Novel View Synthesis
summary: We propose Ref-GeNVS, a training-free, reflection-aware method for generative novel view synthesis (NVS) in mirror scenes. Existing multi-view diffusion models often fail to recognize the mirror in the scene and cannot exploit reflected content for scene generation. To fix this issue without additional training, our key idea is to treat a mirror image as two complementary views. From input images, we estimate the mirror plane and reflect camera poses to form virtual views. Based on this virtual view setup, we propose a two-stage generation method consisting of Mirror-gated attention and Reflection injection, which enables reflection-consistent NVS by explicitly leveraging reflection relationships in a multi-view diffusion model. Ref-GeNVS inherits the strong generalizability of the multi-view diffusion backbone, while it does not require finetuning. On synthetic and real scenes including mirrors, Ref-GeNVS outperforms recent generative NVS methods by generating reflection-consistent and contextually coherent novel views, revealing scene structure visible only through mirrors. Project page: https://kim-geonu.github.io/Ref-GeNVS/

AI.tldr: Ref-GeNVS is a training-free method for generative novel view synthesis in mirror scenes that treats mirror images as complementary views. It estimates mirror planes, reflects camera poses to form virtual views, and uses a two-stage generation approach (Mirror-gated attention and Reflection injection) to enable reflection-consistent NVS without fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-view diffusion models fail to recognize mirrors in the scene and cannot exploit reflected content for scene generation. There is a need to explicitly leverage reflection relationships to generate accurate novel views in mirror scenes.
AI.method: 1) Estimate mirror plane from input images; 2) Reflect camera poses to form virtual views; 3) Two-stage generation consisting of Mirror-gated attention and Reflection injection; 4) Explicitly leverage reflection relationships in a multi-view diffusion model while inheriting its generalizability without fine-tuning.
AI.result: On synthetic and real scenes including mirrors, Ref-GeNVS outperforms recent generative NVS methods by generating reflection-consistent and contextually coherent novel views, revealing scene structure visible only through mirrors.
AI.conclusion: Ref-GeNVS successfully generates reflection-consistent novel views in mirror scenes without requiring additional training or fine-tuning, outperforming existing state-of-the-art generative NVS methods.

title: LLM-Guided Program Evolution for Circle Packing: Breaking 10 Packomania Records for $28
summary: We present Discovery Loop, a lightweight system that uses a large language model (LLM) to iteratively evolve optimization algorithms. Starting from a simple seed solver, the LLM proposes algorithmic improvements guided by a scoreboard of results and a history of prior ideas. Each candidate is evaluated against an independent verifier; improvements are kept and failures discarded. Applied to the Packomania circle-packing benchmark (csqv: maximize the sum of radii of N variable-radius circles in the unit square), the system improved the best known solutions for 10 values of N in the range 101-114, with gains of 2.4%-5.4% over prior records, all within 15 iterations and at a total LLM cost of $27.72. These results have been independently accepted by Packomania. We describe the method, analyze cost-efficiency dynamics including an adaptive plateau-detection mechanism, and discuss implications for democratizing automated scientific discovery.

AI.tldr: Discovery Loop uses an LLM to iteratively evolve optimization algorithms for circle-packing problems. Starting from a seed solver, the LLM proposes algorithmic improvements guided by a scoreboard and history. Each candidate is evaluated against an independent verifier, with improvements kept and failures discarded. The system improved best known solutions for 10 values of N (101-114) with gains of 2.4%-5.4%, at a total cost of $27.72 within 15 iterations.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of automating scientific discovery, specifically in optimization algorithm design. The motivation is to democratize automated scientific discovery by using LLMs to iteratively evolve algorithms without requiring extensive human expertise or computational resources.
AI.method: The method involves: (1) Starting from a simple seed solver, (2) Using an LLM to propose algorithmic improvements guided by a scoreboard of results and history of prior ideas, (3) Evaluating each candidate against an independent verifier, (4) Keeping improvements and discarding failures, (5) Implementing an adaptive plateau-detection mechanism to identify when further iterations are unlikely to yield improvements.
AI.result: The system improved the best known solutions for 10 values of N in the range 101-114 on the Packomania circle-packing benchmark (csqv problem - maximize sum of radii of N variable-radius circles in unit square). The improvements ranged from 2.4%-5.4% over prior records, achieved within 15 iterations at a total LLM cost of $27.72. These results were independently accepted by Packomania.
AI.conclusion: The system demonstrates a cost-effective approach to automated scientific discovery using LLMs. The low cost ($27.72) and rapid convergence (15 iterations) suggest potential for democratizing optimization algorithm design. The adaptive plateau-detection mechanism helps optimize resource allocation. The successful independent verification of results validates the approach.

title: RegionFed: Federated Learning for Personalized Query Understanding in Heterogeneous Retail Environments
summary: Retail search systems serve diverse geographic regions with distinct query patterns, vocabularies, and product preferences, creating significant data heterogeneity that challenges both privacy-preserving training and model personalization. Federated learning offers a natural solution for privacy, but standard FL methods produce global models that sacrifice regional performance, while existing personalized FL approaches operate at the parameter level and catastrophically collapse on modern transformers (below 10\% accuracy on T5) due to tied embeddings and LayerNorm interactions. We introduce RegionFed, an \textit{architecture-robust} federated learning framework that sidesteps this failure by operating entirely at the gradient level. RegionFed uses the $\ell_2$ conflict between regional and global gradients as a unified signal that (i) diagnoses heterogeneity, (ii) routes each region to the cheapest sufficient personalization strategy, and (iii) adaptively controls personalization strength. Because it treats models as differentiable black boxes, RegionFed deploys on T5-Small, T5-3B, RoBERTa, and CNN with zero code changes, providing large gains on transformers (where parameter-level methods collapse) and consistent improvements on CNNs. Across three public datasets (Amazon ESCI, Amazon Reviews, LEAF-FEMNIST) and four architectures, RegionFed-Meta achieves 92.27\%, closing the gap to the privacy-violating centralized upper bound (Centralized + Regional Weighting: 92.04\%, $Δ$=0.23pp, within 1$σ$) while providing $(ε{\approx}0.60)$-differential privacy and $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{T})$ convergence.

AI.tldr: RegionFed is an architecture-robust federated learning framework that operates at the gradient level to address data heterogeneity in retail search systems across diverse geographic regions. It uses ℓ2 gradient conflict as a unified signal for diagnosing heterogeneity, routing personalization strategies, and controlling personalization strength. The method deploys on multiple architectures (T5, RoBERTa, CNN) with zero code changes and achieves 92.27% accuracy, closing the gap to centralized training within 0.23pp while providing differential privacy.
AI.motivation: Retail search systems serve diverse geographic regions with distinct query patterns, vocabularies, and product preferences, creating significant data heterogeneity. This challenges both privacy-preserving training and model personalization. Standard federated learning produces global models that sacrifice regional performance, while existing personalized FL approaches catastrophically collapse on modern transformers (below 10% accuracy on T5) due to tied embeddings and LayerNorm interactions.
AI.method: RegionFed operates entirely at the gradient level, treating models as differentiable black boxes. It uses the ℓ2 conflict between regional and global gradients as a unified signal that (i) diagnoses heterogeneity, (ii) routes each region to the cheapest sufficient personalization strategy, and (iii) adaptively controls personalization strength.
AI.result: RegionFed achieves 92.27% accuracy on Amazon ESCI, closing the gap to the privacy-violating centralized upper bound (Centralized + Regional Weighting: 92.04%, Δ=0.23pp, within 1σ). It provides (ε≈0.60)-differential privacy and O(1/√T) convergence. Large gains on transformers (where parameter-level methods collapse) and consistent improvements on CNNs across three public datasets (Amazon ESCI, Amazon Reviews, LEAF-FEMNIST) and four architectures (T5-Small, T5-3B, RoBERTa, CNN).
AI.conclusion: RegionFed successfully addresses the challenge of data heterogeneity in federated learning for retail search systems across diverse geographic regions. By operating at the gradient level rather than the parameter level, it avoids the catastrophic collapse observed in existing personalized FL approaches on modern transformers. The framework is architecture-robust, deploying on multiple architectures with zero code changes while providing differential privacy guarantees and theoretical convergence rates.

title: Think-Verify-Revise: Neuro-Symbolic Visual Reasoning with Vision-Language Models and Dynamic Logic Tensor Networks
comment: Accepted at the MARS2 Workshop @ ECCV 2026
summary: Visual reasoning tasks require a system to jointly perceive visual content and apply formal relational constraints---a combination that neither pure neural nor purely symbolic approaches handle well in isolation. This paper proposes a Neuro-Symbolic (NeSy) framework that closes this gap by tightly coupling a Vision-Language Model (VLM) for automatic First-Order Logic (FOL) rule induction with a Dynamic Logic Tensor Network (D-LTN) for differentiable rule verification, in a closed iterative feedback loop. The VLM receives a small set of labelled visual examples and proposes candidate FOL rules conforming to a strict grammar (Think); the D-LTN is automatically assembled from these rules at runtime and evaluates them grounding on CNN-produced visual embeddings (Verify); and verification failures are fed back to guide the VLM's next hypothesis (Revise). Evaluated on the ViSudo-PC benchmark across four visual domains (MNIST, EMNIST, KMNIST, FMNIST), the system induces valid Sudoku constraint rules using only three training examples as visual context. The proposed method achieves AUC scores matching or outperforming previous methods (NeuPSL, LTN), showing the potential for automatic rule discovery through VLM. Code is available at https://github.com/homayoun-afshari/nesy.

AI.tldr: A Neuro-Symbolic framework that combines a Vision-Language Model (VLM) for First-Order Logic (FOL) rule induction with a Dynamic Logic Tensor Network (D-LTN) for differentiable rule verification in a closed-loop feedback system. The system achieves automatic rule discovery from visual examples.
AI.motivation: Visual reasoning tasks require jointly perceiving visual content and applying formal relational constraints, which neither pure neural nor purely symbolic approaches handle well in isolation. This paper aims to close this gap by combining the strengths of both approaches.
AI.method: The framework uses three components in an iterative loop: (1) VLM receives labeled visual examples and proposes candidate FOL rules conforming to a strict grammar (Think); (2) D-LTN is automatically assembled from these rules at runtime and evaluates them using CNN-produced visual embeddings (Verify); (3) Verification failures are fed back to guide the VLM's next hypothesis (Revise).
AI.result: Evaluated on ViSudo-PC benchmark across MNIST, EMNIST, KMNIST, and FMNIST domains, the system induces valid Sudoku constraint rules using only three training examples. AUC scores match or outperform previous methods (NeuPSL, LTN).
AI.conclusion: The proposed NeSy framework demonstrates the potential for automatic rule discovery through VLM, achieving competitive performance with minimal training examples by tightly coupling neural perception with symbolic reasoning.

title: ProCA: Progressive Contrastive Alignment for Robust EEG Visual Decoding
summary: Electroencephalogram (EEG) visual decoding aims to recover visual semantics from non-invasive neural time-series signals, for which robust alignment between noisy neural responses and stable semantic representations is key to achieving high-performance decoding. Despite recent advances in contrastive learning, robust EEG decoding remains challenging because existing methods rely on fixed visual or textual anchors whose semantic relations may become misaligned with EEG representations that vary across trials, subjects, and learning stages. Our empirical evidence shows that this instability appears across both standard EEG decoding protocols and more challenging robustness settings, including strict cross-subject transfer and realistic personalized continual adaptation. We provide a formal analysis showing that fixed semantic supervision can bias optimization when EEG-specific relations evolve, and that structure-agnostic perturbations may distort semantically important EEG components. To address these issues, we propose Progressive Contrastive Alignment (ProCA), a unified and model-agnostic framework for adaptive neural-semantic alignment. ProCA progressively refines class-level contrastive supervision from frozen vision-language priors to EEG-aware semantic relations, and introduces structure-consistent interpolation to constrain feature mixing according to channel-wise and temporal importance. Across subject-dependent, subject-independent, strict cross-subject transfer, and continual adaptation settings, ProCA achieves average relative Top-1/Top-5 gains of 7.4%/3.9%, 10.0%/4.6%, 28.1%/17.8%, and 16.8%/11.6%, respectively.

AI.tldr: ProCA is a progressive contrastive alignment framework for EEG visual decoding that addresses the misalignment problem between fixed semantic anchors and variable EEG representations. It achieves 7.4%/10.0%/28.1%/16.8% relative Top-1 gains across subject-dependent, subject-independent, cross-subject transfer, and continual adaptation settings respectively.
AI.motivation: EEG visual decoding aims to recover visual semantics from non-invasive neural time-series signals. The key challenge is achieving robust alignment between noisy neural responses and stable semantic representations. Existing contrastive learning methods rely on fixed visual or textual anchors whose semantic relations may become misaligned with EEG representations that vary across trials, subjects, and learning stages. This instability appears across standard EEG decoding protocols and challenging robustness settings including strict cross-subject transfer and personalized continual adaptation.
AI.method: ProCA (Progressive Contrastive Alignment) is proposed as a unified and model-agnostic framework for adaptive neural-semantic alignment. It has two main components: (1) Progressively refines class-level contrastive supervision from frozen vision-language priors to EEG-aware semantic relations, and (2) Introduces structure-consistent interpolation to constrain feature mixing according to channel-wise and temporal importance.
AI.result: ProCA achieves average relative Top-1/Top-5 gains of 7.4%/3.9% (subject-dependent), 10.0%/4.6% (subject-independent), 28.1%/17.8% (strict cross-subject transfer), and 16.8%/11.6% (continual adaptation) respectively.
AI.conclusion: The formal analysis shows that fixed semantic supervision can bias optimization when EEG-specific relations evolve, and structure-agnostic perturbations may distort semantically important EEG components. ProCA provides a solution by adaptively aligning neural and semantic representations, demonstrating significant improvements across diverse EEG decoding scenarios.

title: Interface-Induced Trajectory Censoring
comment: 39 pages, 14 pages main text. Code, data, and pre-registrations: https://github.com/nebula-1999/Interface-Induced-Trajectory-Censoring
summary:
Agent evaluations report a tool-call rate read off the serving stack. That number can be zero while the model is emitting well-formed calls: the interface censors the trajectory before anything downstream sees it.
  On BFCL v4's own data, executor and scorer, holding weights, cases, decoding and seeds fixed and changing only the serving adapter, the same model scores 0.00 or 0.96 / 0.19. A 2x2 over chat template and parser locates the effect exactly: both main effects are exactly zero and all of it sits in the interaction -- no component is defective, and repairing one side of the contract buys precisely nothing. On tau-bench's 115 interactive retail tasks the same swap moves server-parsed calls from 0 to 636 and tasks reaching any tool execution from 0 to 103. Our probe reproduces the funnel across a 21x scale range of Qwen2.5-Coder: the server parses 0/100 at every size while well-formed emitted calls rise to 80/100 at 32B (~72 after calibration against an adjudicated gold standard). Under a matched envelope, across a comparable scale span, the silent fraction stays at 0-2, a prediction committed to the repository before the run. Llama-3.1-8B's 23% rate of calling the task function itself as a tool falls to 0 under one strict:true flag.
  The mismatch reaches inside the training loop, and its consequence is scale-dependent: in verl's AgentLoop at 7B, 45 of 115 generations carry a complete call; 0 are accepted, 0 execute, 0 return an observation. At 1.5B the same zero is over-determined, so we report the two scales separately. At evaluation time, repairing the adapter restores the mechanism but not a significant outcome gain: parsing 0->84, rescues 0->9, pass rate 53->62 (n.s.). We release a 98-line preflight check that catches every silent failure here. The observed tool-call rate is not a property of the model alone; it is a property of the model-interface stack that measures it.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals a critical evaluation artifact: AI models can emit well-formed tool calls that get silently censored by the serving interface, causing reported tool-call rates to be zero even when the model is functioning correctly. The authors demonstrate this "silent failure" phenomenon across multiple benchmarks (BFCL v4, tau-bench), model families (Qwen2.5-Coder, Llama-3.1), and scale ranges, showing that the interaction between chat template and parser determines success—not individual components.
AI.motivation: The authors observed that agent evaluations report tool-call rates directly from the serving stack, which can be zero even when models emit well-formed calls. This discrepancy appears to stem from interface-level censorship rather than model failures, motivating a systematic investigation of this "silent failure" phenomenon.
AI.method: The authors conducted controlled experiments by holding weights, test cases, decoding, and seeds fixed while swapping only the serving adapter. They performed a 2x2 factorial design over chat template and parser to localize the effect. They also probed the phenomenon across a 21x scale range of Qwen2.5-Coder, compared results against a matched envelope prediction, and tested Llama-3.1-8B with the strict:true flag. They additionally released a 98-line preflight check to detect silent failures.
AI.result: On BFCL v4, the same model scores 0.00 or 0.96/0.19 depending on the serving adapter. The 2x2 experiment reveals all effect sits in the interaction (no main effects). On tau-bench's 115 retail tasks, the swap moves server-parsed calls from 0 to 636 and tasks reaching any tool execution from 0 to 103. Qwen2.5-Coder shows server parsing 0/100 at all sizes while well-formed calls rise to 80/100 at 32B. Under a matched envelope, the silent fraction stays at 0-2%. Llama-3.1-8B's 23% self-call rate drops to 0 with strict:true. In training loop (verl's AgentLoop), at 7B, 45/115 generations carry complete calls but 0 execute; at 1.5B the zero is over-determined. At evaluation time, repairing the adapter yields parsing 0→84, rescues 0→9, pass rate 53→62 (not significant).
AI.conclusion: The observed tool-call rate is not a property of the model alone—it is a property of the model-interface stack that measures it. The silent failure problem stems from chat template × parser interactions, is scale-dependent, and requires interface-level fixes rather than model improvements. The authors provide a diagnostic tool (98-line preflight check) to catch these silent failures.

title: CrossDepth: Geometry-Constrained Attention for Generalizable Multi-View Surround Depth Estimation
summary: Reliable 3D understanding of the surrounding environment is a core requirement for autonomous driving. Multi-view surround camera rigs provide broad scene coverage, but the spatially adjacent images typically overlap only minimally. Consequently, the depth of most pixels must be inferred from monocular appearance cues. These cues can appear differently across images and may therefore be interpreted differently by the depth estimation model. We target two main sources of cross-image inconsistency: differences in camera intrinsics and the limited receptive field of each image. We address the former by conditioning the features on per-pixel camera-aware ray embeddings, enabling the network to account for camera-dependent variations in monocular cues. We address the latter by extending each pixel's context beyond its own image through cross-image attention constrained to geometrically plausible regions, derived from the calibrated rig setup. The model is trained in a fully self-supervised manner based on photometric consistency. Evaluations on DDAD and nuScenes show improved overall depth accuracy and cross-image depth consistency over state-of-the-art self-supervised methods under in-domain and cross-domain evaluation. Code is available at https://abualhanud.github.io/CrossDepthPage/.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses cross-image depth inconsistency in self-supervised multi-view surround camera depth estimation for autonomous driving by using camera-aware ray embeddings and cross-image attention mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Multi-view surround camera rigs provide broad scene coverage but have minimal overlap between adjacent images, requiring depth inference from monocular cues that can appear differently across images due to camera intrinsics and limited receptive fields.
AI.method: Two main approaches: (1) Per-pixel camera-aware ray embeddings to account for camera-dependent variations in monocular cues, and (2) Cross-image attention constrained to geometrically plausible regions derived from the calibrated rig setup. The model is trained in a fully self-supervised manner based on photometric consistency.
AI.result: Evaluations on DDAD and nuScenes datasets show improved overall depth accuracy and cross-image depth consistency over state-of-the-art self-supervised methods under in-domain and cross-domain evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method successfully addresses cross-image depth inconsistency in multi-view surround camera depth estimation by leveraging camera-aware ray embeddings and constrained cross-image attention, achieving state-of-the-art performance on benchmark datasets.

title: Compact Bellman-Grounded Cognitive Maps for Cost-Aware Navigation
summary: Biological agents navigate familiar environments not by re-solving routes for each new goal, but by reusing a learned map built once and read off as goals change. Existing artificial cognitive-map models mimic this reuse, yet their guidance is not explicitly grounded in additive heterogeneous route costs. Furthermore, they often struggle with memory efficiency: representative state-indexed and high-rank spectral constructions incur substantial storage growth as the environment scales. We present BCM, which grounds a reusable cognitive map in local edge costs through a self-supervised Bellman-grounded objective and a compact coordinate encoding, supporting changing goal queries without per-goal retraining. On weighted grids of up to $N=1600$ nodes, BCM maintains full success and only a 5\% mean Gap relative to exact Dijkstra search, compared with about $45\%$ for a connectivity-based spectral baseline. Notably, as the graph size increases from $N=400$ to $N=3600$, its memory footprint grows sublinearly while maintaining competitive performance, making our method scalable to complex environments. Together, these results show that additive route costs can be written into a compact, reusable cognitive-map representation, bridging the gap between biological flexibility and optimal path planning.

AI.tldr: BCM is a cognitive map model that grounds reusable navigation maps in additive edge costs using a Bellman-grounded objective, achieving near-optimal pathfinding (5% Gap vs Dijkstra) with sublinear memory scaling, outperforming spectral baselines by 40% in accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing artificial cognitive-map models fail to explicitly handle additive heterogeneous route costs and suffer from memory inefficiency (representative state-indexed and high-rank spectral constructions grow substantially with environment size). The goal is to create a method that matches biological flexibility while maintaining optimal path planning performance.
AI.method: BCM uses a self-supervised Bellman-grounded objective and a compact coordinate encoding to build a cognitive map grounded in local edge costs. This supports changing goal queries without per-goal retraining, in contrast to prior methods that require retraining for each new goal.
AI.result: On weighted grids of up to N=1600 nodes, BCM maintains full success rate with only 5% mean Gap relative to exact Dijkstra search, compared to ~45% for connectivity-based spectral baseline. Memory footprint grows sublinearly from N=400 to N=3600 while maintaining competitive performance.
AI.conclusion: BCM bridges biological flexibility and optimal path planning by encoding additive route costs into a compact, reusable cognitive map. The method achieves near-optimal performance (5% mean Gap vs Dijkstra) while maintaining sublinear memory growth as environment scales, making it scalable to complex environments.

title: From Interpretability Methods to Interpretable Models
summary: More than a decade in, explainable AI (XAI) for computer vision has assembled a mature toolbox: attribution, feature visualization, concept-based, and circuit-based methods. Yet almost all of the field's effort has gone into building and comparing these methods, and little into the question they were meant to answer---how interpretable are our models, and are we making progress as they evolve? We argue for shifting the field's focus from methods to models, along two complementary lines. One is already within reach: existing tools let us characterize and compare what different models represent and compute. The other is harder, and largely neglected: whether a model can actually be understood by the humans who rely on it---the independent evaluators on whom trust and certification depend, not the experts confirming what they already expect. It can only be measured, not inferred. We review why the toolbox is mature enough to support both, survey the thin body of work comparing models, draw a parallel to systems neuroscience, and close with a model-centric XAI agenda.

AI.tldr: This paper argues for shifting the focus of Explainable AI (XAI) for computer vision from developing and comparing methods to evaluating and improving model interpretability. The authors contend that while XAI has developed a mature toolbox (attribution, feature visualization, concept-based, and circuit-based methods), the field has neglected the fundamental question of whether models are actually understandable by humans. They propose two complementary research directions: characterizing model representations/computations (already achievable) and measuring human understandability (harder but crucial). The paper reviews the maturity of existing tools, surveys comparative work, draws parallels to systems neuroscience, and proposes a model-centric XAI agenda.
AI.motivation: The motivation behind this paper is to address a critical gap in the XAI field: despite significant effort in developing explanation methods, there has been little focus on evaluating whether these methods actually make models interpretable to humans or whether the field is making progress as models evolve. The authors argue that the field has been method-centric rather than model-centric, and that trust and certification in AI systems depend on independent evaluators (not just experts) being able to understand models.
AI.method: The paper takes a review and argumentative approach. It surveys the existing XAI toolbox (attribution, feature visualization, concept-based, and circuit-based methods), reviews the limited body of work comparing models, draws an analogy to systems neuroscience methodology, and proposes a new model-centric agenda for XAI research.
AI.result: The paper does not present experimental results but rather provides a conceptual framework and agenda. It establishes that: (1) the XAI toolbox is mature enough to support both characterizing models and measuring human understandability, (2) there is currently only thin body of work comparing models, and (3) a parallel can be drawn to systems neuroscience in terms of focusing on model behavior rather than just developing tools.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that the XAI field should shift from a methods-centric approach to a model-centric approach.
