They propose a research agenda focused on: (1) using existing tools to characterize and compare what different models represent and compute, and (2) measuring whether models can actually be understood by human evaluators (not just experts). This shift is essential for building trust, enabling certification, and determining whether the field is making genuine progress in model interpretability.

title: Unifying ICL, SFT, KL-Regularized RL Through a Bayesian Lens
summary: Large language models are now trained and evaluated under a diverse set of paradigms: supervised fine-tuning (SFT), few-shot in-context learning (ICL), KL-regularized RLHF/RLVR, on-policy distillation (OPD), and test-time reasoning with search and chain-of-thought. These methods are often discussed as fundamentally different, and recent empirical results--such as the mixed impact of few-shot prompting on RL-tuned reasoning models--can appear puzzling. This note develops a Bayesian perspective that puts these procedures on the same footing. At the core is a two-step template: (i) construct a (generalized) Bayes or Gibbs posterior q* over outputs or actions given a context, using a prior/reference model and a utility signal (log-likelihood, reward, or advantage); and (ii) approximate q* by a forward-KL projection onto a parametric family, either in-weights (SFT/RL) or in-context (ICL). Part I formalizes few-shot ICL and SFT as amortized and-weights projections onto the Bayes posterior predictive. Parts II-IV show that KL-regularized RLHF/RLVR, reward-weighted SFT, reward-weighted ICL (RW-ICL), and advantage-weighted SFT (AWSFT) are all instances of forward-KL projection onto posteriors induced by rewards or advantages. We disentangle where these equivalences hold (objectives and first-order updates) and where they do not (source and granularity of the learning signal). Part V sketches implications for modern reasoning pipelines: RLHF/RLVR recipes as "posterior design + projection", why cold-start or supervised warm-up is practically unavoidable for importance-weighted KL projections, and DeepSeek-R1 and o1-style reasoning models as combining test-time Bayesian search with training-time KL amortization.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a unified Bayesian framework that shows SFT, ICL, KL-regularized RLHF/RLVR, and other LLM training paradigms are all instances of forward-KL projection onto posterior distributions.
AI.motivation: The empirical diversity of LLM training methods (SFT, ICL, RLHF, OPD, test-time reasoning) appears puzzling, and this work aims to provide a unifying theoretical perspective to understand their relationships and differences.
AI.method: The authors propose a two-step Bayesian template: (i) construct a generalized Bayes/Gibbs posterior using a prior/reference model and utility signal (log-likelihood, reward, or advantage); (ii) approximate this posterior via forward-KL projection onto a parametric family, either in-weights (SFT/RL) or in-context (ICL).
AI.result: The paper demonstrates that: (1) Few-shot ICL and SFT are amortized and in-weights projections onto the Bayes posterior predictive; (2) KL-regularized RLHF/RLVR, reward-weighted SFT, reward-weighted ICL (RW-ICL), and advantage-weighted SFT (AWSFT) are all instances of forward-KL projection onto reward/advantage-induced posteriors; (3) The framework clarifies where equivalences hold (objectives and first-order updates) and where they differ (source and granularity of learning signals).
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a "posterior design + projection" interpretation of RLHF/RLVR, explains why cold-start/supervised warm-up is necessary for importance-weighted KL projections, and characterizes modern reasoning models (e.g., DeepSeek-R1, o1-style) as combining test-time Bayesian search with training-time KL amortization.

title: A Generalizable Feature Extractor for Alzheimer's-Related Brain MRI Tasks
comment: 26 pages (excluding the references section), 7 figures (excluding sub-figures)
summary: When there is not enough labeled data to properly train deep learning models, transfer learning can help. We still do not fully understand how effective it is in neuroimaging, especially for Alzheimer's disease research. It is also not clear if these transferred models can work on new datasets without being retrained for each specific task. We evaluate whether a compact, supervised pretrained model can serve as a reusable foundation model for downstream neuroimaging tasks. We freeze the 7.18 million weights of a 3D CNN previously trained for brain-age prediction, and adapt it to each task using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), requiring only ~1% additional trainable parameters. We evaluate generalizability in six experiments. Adapting the model to classify cognitively normal versus Dementia on ADNI gave an AUC of 0.964 on held-out folds (Experiment #1). Applying that adapted model unchanged to OASIS-3, with no retraining, gave an AUC of 0.871 (Experiment #2). Reusing its output logit together with age and a cognitive score distinguished stable from progressing MCI with an AUC of 0.828 (Experiment #3). Adapting the same backbone to predict amyloid positivity from structural MRI gave an AUC of 0.804 (Experiment #4). Finally, the same approach estimated ICV-normalized hippocampal and white matter hypointensity volumes directly from the T1w image, with R^2 of 0.80 and 0.91 respectively, tasks normally addressed with much larger U-Net networks (Experiments #5 and #6). A compact model supervised on brain age can therefore serve as a reusable backbone, adapting to each task with ~1% additional parameters and transferring to an unseen cohort without any training. Our findings suggest that a carefully trained brain age model can serve as an effective foundation model for Alzheimer's related tasks, even under strict data constraints.

title: SciDocBench: A Workflow-Centered Benchmark and Data Pipeline for Scientific Document Understanding
comment: 52 pages, 21 figures, and 20 tables. Project page: https://github.com/InternLM/SciDocBench
summary: Scientific papers require models to reason jointly over text, equations, figures, tables, code, and datasets while preserving the provenance of supporting evidence. Existing benchmarks typically evaluate these capabilities in isolation, leaving unclear whether multimodal models can support realistic scientific-reading workflows. We introduce SciDocBench, a workflow-centered benchmark for scientific document understanding. It contains 124 expert-authored and difficulty-screened questions organized into seven research-assistant capability groups and 19 subtasks across five scientific domains. Each question is instantiated under four matched conditions combining English or Chinese questions with all-images-first or interleaved document representations, yielding 496 evaluation instances for controlled analysis. The strongest evaluated system achieves only 62.6/100, with pronounced weaknesses in document perception, evidence grounding, verification, and cross-document reasoning. To translate these diagnostics into scalable training signals, we introduce SciDocIR, a typed evidence-graph representation that preserves scientific document objects, layout and cross-reference relations, and provenance. Building on SciDocIR, we construct SciDocDataset, comprising approximately 15K supervised fine-tuning samples and 8K reinforcement-learning samples across 14 verifiable subtasks. Together, SciDocBench, SciDocIR, and SciDocDataset form an evaluation-to-training framework for diagnosing and improving scientific-document assistants. The project page is available at https://github.com/InternLM/SciDocBench.

AI.tldr: SciDocBench is a workflow-centered benchmark for scientific document understanding that evaluates multimodal models' ability to reason over scientific papers. It contains 124 questions across 7 capability groups and 19 subtasks, tested under 4 conditions (English/Chinese × different document representations). The best system achieves only 62.6/100, revealing significant weaknesses in document perception, evidence grounding, verification, and cross-document reasoning. The paper also introduces SciDocIR (evidence-graph representation) and SciDocDataset (~23K training samples) to enable scalable training.
AI.motivation: Scientific papers require models to jointly reason over multiple modalities (text, equations, figures, tables, code, datasets) while preserving evidence provenance. However, existing benchmarks evaluate these capabilities in isolation, leaving unclear whether multimodal models can support realistic scientific-reading workflows. There is a need for a comprehensive benchmark that assesses integrated scientific document understanding.
AI.method: The authors created SciDocBench with 124 expert-authored, difficulty-screened questions organized into 7 research-assistant capability groups and 19 subtasks across 5 scientific domains. Each question is instantiated under 4 matched conditions: English or Chinese questions combined with all-images-first or interleaved document representations, yielding 496 evaluation instances. They also introduced SciDocIR, a typed evidence-graph representation that preserves document objects, layout, cross-reference relations, and provenance. Based on SciDocIR, they constructed SciDocDataset with ~15K supervised fine-tuning samples and 8K reinforcement learning samples across 14 verifiable subtasks.
AI.result: The strongest evaluated system achieves only 62.6/100 on SciDocBench, with pronounced weaknesses in four areas: (1) document perception, (2) evidence grounding, (3) verification, and (4) cross-document reasoning. This indicates significant room for improvement in scientific document understanding capabilities.
AI.conclusion: SciDocBench, SciDocIR, and SciDocDataset form an evaluation-to-training framework for diagnosing and improving scientific-document assistants. The benchmark reveals substantial gaps in current models' ability to handle realistic scientific reading workflows, while the proposed training dataset provides a scalable path toward improvement. The project is available at https://github.com/InternLM/SciDocBench.

title: A Hybrid Predictive Ensemble of Machine Learning and Deep Neural Networks for Early Cardiovascular Disease Risk Assessment
summary: This study introduces an intelligent framework that integrates machine learning and deep neural network ensemble techniques for early detection and prognosis of cardiovascular diseases. The system utilizes real-time physiological data collected from Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) devices, including ECG sensors, heart rate monitors, and blood pressure trackers. To ensure the accuracy and reliability of input data, preprocessing steps such as noise reduction, normalization, and missing value imputation are employed. The most significant health indicators are identified through effective feature selection methods and then processed using optimized classifiers such as Support Vector Machines (SVM), Random Forests, and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), which are combined in an ensemble architecture to improve diagnostic precision. The framework demonstrates remarkable performance in predicting cardiovascular disease risk, achieving higher accuracy, reduced false positives, and enhanced consistency compared to conventional methods. It is designed on a cloud-based infrastructure that ensures scalability and real-time processing for continuous patient monitoring. Experimental evaluation on real-world cardiovascular datasets confirms the framework's efficiency in early-stage risk assessment and clinical decision support. The results highlight the potential of combining traditional machine learning and deep learning paradigms to achieve proactive healthcare management and improve patient outcomes.

AI.tldr: An intelligent framework combining machine learning and deep neural network ensemble techniques for early detection and prognosis of cardiovascular diseases using real-time IoMT data (ECG, heart rate, blood pressure). The system uses preprocessing, feature selection, and ensemble classifiers (SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost) deployed on cloud infrastructure.
AI.motivation: Early detection and prognosis of cardiovascular diseases (CVD) to enable proactive healthcare management and improve patient outcomes through continuous patient monitoring.
AI.method: Real-time physiological data collection from IoMT devices (ECG sensors, heart rate monitors, blood pressure trackers); preprocessing steps including noise reduction, normalization, and missing value imputation; feature selection for identifying significant health indicators; ensemble architecture combining SVM, Random Forests, and XGBoost classifiers; cloud-based infrastructure for scalability and real-time processing.
AI.result: The framework achieves higher accuracy, reduced false positives, and enhanced consistency compared to conventional methods. Experimental evaluation on real-world datasets confirms efficiency in early-stage risk assessment and clinical decision support.
AI.conclusion: Combining traditional machine learning and deep learning paradigms can achieve proactive healthcare management and improve patient outcomes. The ensemble approach with cloud-based deployment provides a scalable solution for continuous cardiovascular disease monitoring.

title: WorldSculpt: Generating Compositional Worlds from Grounded Videos
summary: We study the problem of generating a compositional 3D representation of a cluttered scene containing hundreds of objects. The goal is to represent the scene as a collection of individual object meshes placed in a shared world frame, as required by downstream applications such as gaming, AR/VR, simulation, and robotics. This task is challenging in densely cluttered scenes, where objects heavily occlude one another and each view reveals only a fraction of their geometry. Geometry-based approaches typically reconstruct the scene as a single representation and leave incomplete geometry in occluded regions, while existing compositional methods with generative priors are largely limited to relatively simple scenes. We show that complex scenes with hundreds of objects can instead be generated compositionally by adapting a strong single-object 3D generative prior to multi-view observations. We instantiate this paradigm with Pixal3D, extending it with a multi-view conditioning pathway that grounds object generation in multiple posed observations. Although the model is finetuned entirely on single objects in canonical space, it generalizes to large scenes with severe occlusion without any scene-level training, demonstrating the feasibility and scalability of this paradigm. We further introduce UE-MeshyScene, a photorealistic benchmark of densely cluttered scenes with hundreds of objects, per-object annotations, and ground-truth meshes. Across single-object, controlled multi-object, and UE-MeshyScene evaluations, our method consistently outperforms prior approaches, with larger gains as scene complexity and occlusion increase. Finally, we demonstrate broader applicability by converting generated 3DGS worlds, such as Marble and HY-World 2.0, into compositional mesh scenes.

AI.tldr: A method for generating compositional 3D representations of densely cluttered scenes with hundreds of objects by adapting a single-object 3D generative prior (Pixal3D) to multi-view observations, without requiring scene-level training.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches struggle with densely cluttered scenes where objects heavily occlude each other. Geometry-based approaches reconstruct incomplete geometry in occluded regions, while compositional methods with generative priors are limited to simple scenes. The key insight is that a strong single-object 3D generative prior can be adapted to multi-view observations for complex scenes.
AI.method: Extended Pixal3D with a multi-view conditioning pathway that grounds object generation in multiple posed observations. The model is finetuned entirely on single objects in canonical space but generalizes to large scenes with severe occlusion without any scene-level training.
AI.result: The method consistently outperforms prior approaches across single-object, controlled multi-object, and UE-MeshyScene evaluations, with larger gains as scene complexity and occlusion increase.
AI.conclusion: The approach generalizes from single-object training to complex cluttered scenes without scene-level training, outperforming prior methods especially in highly occluded scenarios. It also enables conversion of 3DGS worlds (Marble, HY-World 2.0) into compositional mesh scenes.

title: The Mirror Agent Model: a Bayesian Architecture for Interpretable Agent Behavior
comment: Accepted at the International Workshop on Explainable, Transparent Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Systems, 2022
summary: In this paper we illustrate a novel architecture generating interpretable behavior and explanations. We refer to this architecture as the Mirror Agent Model because it defines the observer model, that is the target of explicit and implicit communications, as a mirror of the agent's. With the goal of providing a general understanding of this work, we firstly show prior relevant results addressing the informative communication of agents intentions and the production of legible behavior. In the second part of the paper we furnish the architecture with novel capabilities for explanations through off-the-shelf saliency methods, followed by preliminary qualitative results.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Mirror Agent Model, a novel architecture that generates interpretable behavior and explanations by defining an observer model as a mirror of the agent's model. The architecture incorporates explanation capabilities through off-the-shelf saliency methods.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to provide a general understanding of how agents can communicate their intentions explicitly and implicitly, and produce legible behavior that is interpretable to human observers.
AI.method: The architecture uses a mirror mechanism where the observer model mirrors the agent's model. Explanation capabilities are added through off-the-shelf saliency methods, and preliminary qualitative results are provided.
AI.result: The paper presents prior relevant results on informative communication of agents' intentions and legible behavior, along with preliminary qualitative results of the proposed architecture.
AI.conclusion: The Mirror Agent Model offers a novel approach to generating interpretable behavior and explanations by leveraging the mirror concept and saliency methods, though the abstract suggests this is preliminary work with qualitative results.

title: What Matters in On-Policy Distillation? A Perspective on Data Efficiency and Data Selection
summary: On-Policy Distillation (OPD) has emerged as a widely adopted post-training paradigm for enhancing large language models in reasoning domains. However, the data-centric mechanisms in OPD remain relatively underexplored. This paper presents a empirical study of data efficiency and data selection in OPD. We begin by investigating an extreme setting: training OPD on only one example, namely 1-shot OPD. Surprisingly, we find that 1-shot OPD is consistently effective across all sampled training examples and harder examples often yield superior performance gain. We next investigate what actually drives the student model's improvement in the training data. Our analysis reveals that the improvement is not driven by high token entropy, but the longer CoT paths which hard problems naturally generate. Training on longer CoT can help maintain closer alignment with the teacher over a long reasoning horizon, and learn critical thinking patterns usually missing in short CoTs, such as reflection (e.g., ``Alternatively''). Based on these insights, we propose a simple data selection method that selects only hard examples for training, where even ``unsolvable'' examples that completely exceed the teacher's capability can be successfully used. Our experiments conducted on four models ranging from 1.5B to 7B show that training the student model on only 8 selected hard examples matches the performance of the 17K dataset baseline.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates data efficiency and data selection in On-Policy Distillation (OPD) for enhancing large language models in reasoning tasks. The key findings show that 1-shot OPD is surprisingly effective, harder examples yield better performance, and the improvement comes from longer CoT paths rather than high token entropy. Based on these insights, a simple data selection method using only hard examples (even "unsolvable" ones) can match the performance of a 17K dataset with just 8 selected examples.
AI.motivation: The data-centric mechanisms in On-Policy Distillation (OPD) remain relatively underexplored, despite OPD being a widely adopted post-training paradigm for enhancing LLMs in reasoning domains. The authors seek to understand what drives student model improvement and how to achieve better data efficiency.
AI.method: The authors conducted an empirical study with three main investigations: (1) Testing 1-shot OPD by training on only one example, (2) Analyzing what drives improvement (token entropy vs. CoT length), (3) Proposing a data selection method that selects only hard examples (including "unsolvable" ones that exceed teacher capability). Experiments were conducted on four models ranging from 1.5B to 7B parameters.
AI.result: Key findings include: (1) 1-shot OPD is consistently effective across all sampled training examples, (2) Harder examples yield superior performance gain, (3) Improvement is driven by longer CoT paths (not high token entropy), (4) Longer CoT helps maintain alignment with teacher over long reasoning horizons and learn critical thinking patterns like reflection (e.g., "Alternatively"), (5) Training on just 8 selected hard examples matches the performance of the 17K dataset baseline.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that data efficiency in OPD can be dramatically improved by selecting hard examples with longer CoT paths. Even "unsolvable" examples that exceed the teacher's capability can be successfully used for training. This challenges the conventional assumption that training data should be solvable and reveals that the quality of reasoning (CoT length) matters more than quantity or entropy in OPD.

title: CABAL: Multi-Agent Simulacra for Tracing the Effects of Collusive Bidding in Peer Review
summary: Recent reports during the AAAI-27 review cycle highlight the risk of reviewers coordinating bids for reciprocal assignment advantage. Prior work treats bidding, reviewer assignment, and review manipulation as separate stages, leaving the lifecycle effects of collusive bidding unclear. Real-world analysis is further constrained by typically unobservable collusive intent and the lack of counterfactuals for the same conference. Motivated by this gap, we introduce \alg, an end-to-end multi-agent simulacra framework for studying reviewer assignment integrity by holding the conference environment fixed and configuring LLM-driven reviewer agents with honest or collusive policies. We further develop an affinity-guided collusive bidding strategy that uses mutual reviewer-paper affinities to construct collusion rings and select target papers, producing expertise-consistent rather than arbitrarily targeted attacks. Controlled experiments show that collusive bidding more than doubles target-paper capture and that assigned colluders score target papers about two points higher than honest co-reviewers, while conference-wide effects remain comparatively modest. Evaluated bid-phase detectors provide only limited evidence of collusion: in a fixed-triplet detector stress test, native positive-bid graphs are confounded by benign affinity, while a Very-High-only diagnostic view enables precise but low-coverage local recovery.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a multi-agent simulation framework to study collusive bidding in academic conference reviewer assignment, demonstrating that collusive strategies significantly improve target paper capture while evading detection by existing methods.
AI.motivation: Prior work treats bidding, reviewer assignment, and manipulation as separate stages, leaving the lifecycle effects of collusive bidding unclear. Real-world analysis is constrained by unobservable collusive intent and lack of counterfactuals for the same conference.
AI.method: End-to-end multi-agent simulacra framework holding conference environment fixed, with LLM-driven reviewer agents configured with honest or collusive policies. Developed affinity-guided collusive bidding strategy using mutual reviewer-paper affinities to construct collusion rings and select target papers.
AI.result: Collusive bidding more than doubles target-paper capture. Assigned colluders score target papers about two points higher than honest co-reviewers. Conference-wide effects remain comparatively modest. Bid-phase detectors provide limited evidence: fixed-triplet detector stress test shows native positive-bid graphs confounded by benign affinity, while Very-High-only diagnostic view enables precise but low-coverage local recovery.
AI.conclusion: Existing bid-phase detectors struggle to identify collusion rings due to confounding by benign affinity patterns. More sophisticated detection methods are needed, though current approaches show limited precision and coverage.

title: ACE: Adaptive Calibration-Free Expert Skipping for MoE-based LLMs
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures provide an efficient paradigm for scaling large language models (LLMs), yet fixed top-k routing activates the same number of expert slots for every token, causing substantial redundant computation. Existing expert-skipping methods often rely on router confidence, calibration data, or additional training, and therefore cannot reliably estimate the actual contribution of routed experts. To this end, we propose ACE, a training-free, calibration-free, and checkpoint-preserving framework for token-adaptive expert skipping in MoE-based LLMs. ACE contains two complementary components: 1) Global Spectral Proxy (GSP), which estimates global transformation capacity from the coupled gate, up, and down projections together with RMSNorm scaling; and 2) Router-Conditioned Refinement (RCR), which constructs expert-specific direction prototypes from centered router weights and evaluates expert responses along routing-preferred directions. During inference, ACE combines both estimates with runtime router gates and skips an expert slot only when both views identify it as low-contribution, while always retaining the top-1 expert. All expert statistics are computed offline, leaving only table lookups and lightweight scalar operations online. Extensive experiments across three MoE-based LLMs and eight benchmarks demonstrate that ACE consistently outperforms existing static and dynamic baselines, with increasingly pronounced advantages under aggressive expert skipping. For instance, at a 50% skipping ratio on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, ACE reduces WikiText-2 perplexity by 7.96% and improves average downstream accuracy by 4.15 percentage points over the strongest competing method.

AI.tldr: ACE is a training-free, calibration-free framework for token-adaptive expert skipping in MoE-based LLMs. It uses two components (GSP and RCR) to estimate expert contributions and skip low-value experts during inference, achieving significant improvements in perplexity and accuracy at aggressive skipping ratios.
AI.motivation: Fixed top-k routing in MoE architectures activates the same number of expert slots for every token, causing redundant computation. Existing expert-skipping methods rely on router confidence, calibration data, or additional training, and cannot reliably estimate actual expert contributions.
AI.method: ACE comprises two complementary components: (1) Global Spectral Proxy (GSP) estimates global transformation capacity from coupled gate, up, and down projections with RMSNorm scaling; (2) Router-Conditioned Refinement (RCR) constructs expert-specific direction prototypes from centered router weights and evaluates expert responses along routing-preferred directions. During inference, both estimates are combined with runtime router gates; an expert slot is skipped only when both views identify it as low-contribution, while always retaining the top-1 expert. All expert statistics are computed offline, leaving only table lookups and lightweight scalar operations online.
AI.result: At 50% skipping ratio on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, ACE reduces WikiText-2 perplexity by 7.96% and improves average downstream accuracy by 4.15 percentage points over the strongest competing method. Experiments across three MoE-based LLMs and eight benchmarks demonstrate consistent outperformance over static and dynamic baselines, with increasingly pronounced advantages under aggressive expert skipping.
AI.conclusion: ACE provides an effective training-free solution for token-adaptive expert skipping in MoE-based LLMs, achieving superior performance-efficiency tradeoffs by combining global transformation capacity estimation with router-conditioned expert response evaluation.

title: Substrate-Aware AI Agents: Execution Context as a First-Class Input
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures. Reproducibility artifacts and source-linked evaluation code: https://github.com/manu2/Context-Aware-Agent-Experiment
summary: Autonomous AI agents increasingly select actions in environments whose memory, execution-time, runtime, compute, and operational constraints determine what counts as a suitable plan. We call the absence of this execution context from an agent's planning state substrate blindness. We test this general proposition through numerical code generation, where selected implementation choices and operational consequences are directly observable. Three frontier model configurations--Anthropic Claude Opus 5, OpenAI GPT-5.6-Sol, and Google Gemini 3.7 Flash--generate code for a high-dimensional pairwise Euclidean-distance task either from the task alone or with a 128 MB RAM and 10.0 s wall-time contract. Contract disclosure reduced measured peak process memory in 13 of 14 executable index-aligned task-only versus contract-disclosed comparisons and reduced mean wall time in all three cohorts, making execution up to 3.1x faster. Across the audited corpus, disclosure produced structural code changes including bounded blocking, float32 retention, upper-triangle traversal, and in-place or memory-mapped buffers. At a tighter 96 MB contract, independently sampled contract-disclosed cohorts achieved correct-and-within-budget outcomes of 4/5 for Claude Opus 5, 5/5 for GPT-5.6-Sol, and 3/5 for Gemini 3.7 Flash, compared with task-only outcomes of 0/5, 1/5, and 0/5; cohort mean MaxRSS and wall time were 49-74% and 35-64% lower than their task-only references. These results establish a controlled proof of concept for substrate-aware agent planning: a minimal execution contract induces proactive structural adaptation in generated programs, shifting computation away from unconstrained allocations and substantially improving observed resource-time profiles before execution.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the concept of "substrate blindness" in AI agents—where agents lack awareness of execution constraints like memory, time, and compute limits. The study tests whether providing explicit execution contracts (e.g., 128 MB RAM, 10s time limit) to three frontier AI models (Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6-Sol, Gemini 3.7 Flash) improves their code generation for a high-dimensional pairwise Euclidean-distance task. Results show that contract disclosure significantly reduces memory usage (13/14 cases) and execution time (up to 3.1x faster), with structural code adaptations like bounded blocking, float32 retention, and upper-triangle traversal. At tighter constraints (96 MB), contract-disclosed cohorts achieved 4-5/5 success rates vs 0-1/5 for control groups.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address a fundamental limitation in autonomous AI agents: they plan and generate actions without accounting for the execution context (memory, time, compute constraints). This "substrate blindness" can lead to plans that are theoretically correct but practically infeasible when deployed in real environments with resource constraints.
AI.method: The researchers conducted controlled experiments using three frontier AI models (Anthropic Claude Opus 5, OpenAI GPT-5.6-Sol, and Google Gemini 3.7 Flash). They generated code for a high-dimensional pairwise Euclidean-distance task under two conditions: (1) task-only (no constraints specified) and (2) contract-disclosed (with explicit 128 MB RAM and 10.0s wall-time constraints). They measured peak process memory (MaxRSS) and wall time, and audited structural code changes. A tighter 96 MB contract was also tested with independently sampled cohorts.
AI.result: Contract disclosure reduced measured peak process memory in 13 of 14 executable comparisons and reduced mean wall time in all three cohorts (up to 3.1x faster). Structural code changes included bounded blocking, float32 retention, upper-triangle traversal, and in-place or memory-mapped buffers. At 96 MB contract, success rates were 4/5 (Claude), 5/5 (GPT), 3/5 (Gemini) vs 0/5, 1/5, 0/5 for task-only. Mean MaxRSS and wall time were 49-74% and 35-64% lower respectively.
AI.conclusion: The study establishes a controlled proof of concept for substrate-aware agent planning. Even minimal execution contracts (RAM + time limits) induce proactive structural adaptation in generated programs, shifting computation away from unconstrained allocations and substantially improving observed resource-time profiles before execution. This suggests AI agents can respond to execution constraints when provided, opening pathways for resource-aware autonomous planning.

title: Uncensored Open-weight Models: Redistribution as the Persistence Layer
summary: A rapidly expanding ecosystem of actors is removing built-in safety guardrails from open-weight AI models. We profile this ecosystem by identifying key producers, downstream reproductions, and emerging applications. Between January 2024 and March 2026, we identified 3,471 original uncensored models on HuggingFace, each repackaged an average of 2.4 times; three actors account for 52% of all 8,164 compressed redistributions. Once quantized and mirrored across separate accounts, formats, and registries such as Ollama, these models persist regardless of upstream removal and become easier to deploy downstream. Of the 1,643 identified GitHub applications integrating uncensored large language models (ULLMs), 25% were classified as explicitly malicious.

AI.tldr: This paper documents the growing ecosystem of actors removing safety guardrails from open-weight AI models, identifying 3,471 original uncensored models on HuggingFace that have been repackaged 8,164 times, with 25% of downstream GitHub applications being explicitly malicious.
AI.motivation: The research addresses the rapidly expanding practice of removing built-in safety guardrails from open-weight AI models, which poses significant security and misuse risks. The authors seek to systematically profile this ecosystem by identifying key producers, distribution patterns, and malicious applications.
AI.method: The authors conducted a longitudinal measurement study from January 2024 to March 2026, identifying uncensored models on HuggingFace, tracking their redistributions across formats and registries (e.g., Ollama), and analyzing GitHub applications integrating these models.
AI.result: Between January 2024 and March 2026, 3,471 original uncensored models were identified on HuggingFace, each repackaged an average of 2.4 times (total 8,164 compressed redistributions). Three actors account for 52% of all redistributions. Models persist regardless of upstream removal through quantization and mirroring across separate accounts and registries. Of 1,643 identified GitHub applications integrating uncensored LLMs, 25% were classified as explicitly malicious.
AI.conclusion: The uncensored AI model ecosystem represents a significant and growing threat, with high concentration among few producers, persistence mechanisms that bypass removal efforts, and substantial malicious downstream usage. The findings highlight the need for improved countermeasures and coordinated governance.

title: Do LLMs Exhibit Coherent Knowledge Structures in Mathematical Reasoning? A Perspective from Knowledge Space Theory
summary: Human knowledge is inherently structured and interdependent: mastery of a concept requires prior mastery of its prerequisites, a principle formalized by Knowledge Space Theory (KST). While LLMs achieve strong performance on complex reasoning tasks, it remains unclear whether they exhibit coherent, human-like knowledge structure. We introduce a KST-grounded framework for evaluating LLM knowledge structure in mathematical reasoning, using it as a normative framework to analyze whether LLM behavior adheres to principled knowledge dependencies. Evaluating eight open- and closed-source LLMs against real human learners, we find that (1) LLMs do not adhere to human knowledge structure -- they frequently violate knowledge dependencies and fail to leverage related knowledge provided in context to improve performance on dependent questions; (2) LLMs do not share a consistent knowledge structure among themselves, as reflected by low overlap in their knowledge distributions. Furthermore, these structural deficiencies remain largely invisible to accuracy-based and LLM-as-judge evaluations. Together, our results provide behavioral evidence that current LLMs knowledge does not follow a human-like structure.

AI.tldr: This paper applies Knowledge Space Theory (KST) to evaluate whether large language models (LLMs) exhibit human-like knowledge structure in mathematical reasoning. The study tests eight LLMs against real human learners and finds that LLMs: (1) violate knowledge dependencies and fail to leverage related context, (2) lack consistent knowledge structure among themselves, and (3) these issues are invisible to traditional accuracy-based or LLM-as-judge evaluations.
AI.motivation: Current LLMs show strong performance on complex reasoning tasks, but it's unclear whether their knowledge is structured in a human-like, principled way with proper prerequisite relationships between concepts.
AI.method: Introduced a KST-grounded framework to evaluate LLM knowledge structure in mathematical reasoning. Evaluated eight open- and closed-source LLMs against real human learners, comparing their behavior against normative knowledge dependencies.
AI.result: LLMs do not adhere to human knowledge structure—they frequently violate knowledge dependencies and fail to leverage related knowledge in context. LLMs also lack consistent knowledge structure among themselves (low overlap in knowledge distributions). These structural deficiencies remain invisible to accuracy-based and LLM-as-judge evaluations.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs' knowledge does not follow a human-like structure, suggesting a fundamental difference between how LLMs and humans organize knowledge.

title: A Unified Physics-Aware Quantum Machine Learning Framework across Power GaN HEMTs and Logic Nanowire FETs: Predicting Unseen Process Splits and Held-Out Geometry Combinations with Lower Error and Tighter Split-to-Split Variability
summary: We present a unified reinforcement-learning (RL) framework that discovers compact parametrized quantum circuits (PQCs) for data-scarce device modeling. A graph neural network (GNN) policy optimized by proximal policy optimization (PPO) searches circuit architectures using leave-one-group-out cross-validation (LOGOCV) error on held-out process or geometry groups as the reward. The framework achieves the lowest mean absolute error (MAE) on all 11 targets versus six classical baselines, with 59% lower error (Ioff) and 81% tighter fold variability (VTH) for HEMTs and 84% lower error (VTH, SS, Ioff) and 82% tighter fold variability (Ioff) for NWFETs. These results demonstrate the potential of RL-selected, classically simulated PQCs as compact surrogates with low OOD error and improved physical consistency, despite imposing no explicit physical constraints, penalty terms, or device-specific equations, on the two evaluated device datasets.

AI.tldr: A unified reinforcement learning framework using a graph neural network (GNN) policy optimized by PPO discovers compact parametrized quantum circuits (PQCs) for data-scarce device modeling, achieving superior performance over classical baselines on HEMT and NWFET devices.
AI.motivation: Device modeling with limited data requires compact surrogate models with low out-of-distribution (OOD) error and improved physical consistency.
AI.method: Graph neural network (GNN) policy optimized by proximal policy optimization (PPO) searches circuit architectures using leave-one-group-out cross-validation (LOGOCV) error on held-out process or geometry groups as the reward.
AI.result: Achieves lowest mean absolute error (MAE) on all 11 targets versus six classical baselines: 59% lower error (Ioff) and 81% tighter fold variability (VTH) for HEMTs; 84% lower error (VTH, SS, Ioff) and 82% tighter fold variability (Ioff) for NWFETs.
AI.conclusion: RL-selected PQCs serve as compact surrogates with low OOD error and improved physical consistency, despite imposing no explicit physical constraints, penalty terms, or device-specific equations.

title: Commonsense Reasoning in Computer Vision: Foundations, Recent Advancements, and Future Directions
summary: Commonsense reasoning in computer vision encompasses integrating visual data and contextual knowledge, crucial for enhancing AI's understanding of everyday scenarios. This understanding not only improves machine learning models but also enhances their ability to interact meaningfully with humans and the environment. Unlike CNN-based conventional vision models, which are designed to identify objects within a specific image, incorporating commonsense knowledge enables models to interpret scenes in a more holistic manner, thereby improving their spatial ability to reason about relationships among objects and actions. This integration not only enhances object recognition but also facilitates a deeper understanding of the contextual factors, ultimately leading to more precise predictions and interactions in real-world applications. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of recent developments that integrate commonsense knowledge into computer vision tasks. We systematically review approaches based on knowledge graphs, scene graphs, neuro-symbolic models, and commonsense-augmented transformers. We also outline current limitations related to dataset bias, knowledge incompleteness, and integration challenges. Finally, we highlight prospective research trajectories in cross-modal reasoning, scalable commonsense knowledge injection, and neuro-symbolic hybrid architectures to develop truly intelligent visual systems.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive survey paper reviewing recent developments in integrating commonsense knowledge into computer vision tasks, covering knowledge graphs, scene graphs, neuro-symbolic models, and transformers, while identifying current limitations and future research directions.
AI.motivation: Current CNN-based vision models only identify objects within specific images but lack contextual understanding. Integrating commonsense knowledge enables more holistic scene interpretation, improving spatial reasoning about object relationships and actions, leading to more precise predictions in real-world applications.
AI.method: Systematic review of approaches based on four categories: (1) knowledge graphs, (2) scene graphs, (3) neuro-symbolic models, and (4) commonsense-augmented transformers.
AI.result: Identified three major limitations: dataset bias, knowledge incompleteness, and integration challenges. Outlined three prospective research trajectories: cross-modal reasoning, scalable commonsense knowledge injection, and neuro-symbolic hybrid architectures.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a comprehensive survey of commonsense reasoning in computer vision, systematically reviewing current approaches while highlighting the path toward developing truly intelligent visual systems through improved reasoning capabilities.

title: AI for Computational Design Science: A Responsible Human-AI Framework and Case Study on Short-Form Video Safety Surveillance
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming not only what information systems researchers design, but also how design research is conducted. Yet existing literature offers limited guidance for computational design science (CDS) when AI actively participates in problem formulation, resource construction, design search, evaluation, and knowledge abstraction. We develop AI for Computational Design Science (AI4CDS), a five-phase methodological framework in which AI expands problem and design search while researchers retain responsibility for domain grounding, admissibility, verification, and scientific judgment. Collaboration is governed by graduated trust, reversibility, auditability, and differentiated reproducibility. We instantiate AI4CDS through ChildRiskGuard, an interpretable artifact for detecting short-form videos inappropriate for children, while documenting AI interactions, rejected alternatives, corrections, and audit trails. The case translates audience-dependent safety and explanation faithfulness into three technical challenges and develops an artifact that separates generic from child-specific risk, represents distinct developmental-risk mechanisms, and makes concept-level explanations part of the predictive computation. ChildRiskGuard achieves an F1 score of 0.769, substantially outperforming direct application of a general-purpose content-safety model while remaining competitive with strong benchmarks. The primary contribution is AI4CDS as a responsible framework for AI-enabled CDS; ChildRiskGuard provides process and artifact evidence of how AI-expanded, researcher-governed design can generate and evaluate novel computational design knowledge.

AI.tldr: This paper develops AI4CDS, a five-phase methodological framework for computational design science where AI actively participates in design processes while researchers maintain governance through graduated trust, reversibility, auditability, and differentiated reproducibility. The framework is instantiated through ChildRiskGuard, an interpretable artifact for detecting child-inappropriate short-form videos, achieving an F1 score of 0.769.
AI.motivation: Existing literature offers limited guidance for computational design science (CDS) when AI actively participates in problem formulation, resource construction, design search, evaluation, and knowledge abstraction. There is a need for a responsible framework that balances AI's expanded capabilities with researcher oversight.
AI.method: The paper develops AI4CDS, a five-phase methodological framework where AI expands problem and design search while researchers retain responsibility for domain grounding, admissibility, verification, and scientific judgment. Collaboration is governed by graduated trust, reversibility, auditability, and differentiated reproducibility. The framework is instantiated through ChildRiskGuard, which translates audience-dependent safety and explanation faithfulness into three technical challenges.
AI.result: ChildRiskGuard achieves an F1 score of 0.769, substantially outperforming direct application of a general-purpose content-safety model while remaining competitive with strong benchmarks. The artifact separates generic from child-specific risk, represents distinct developmental-risk mechanisms, and makes concept-level explanations part of the predictive computation.
AI.conclusion: AI4CDS serves as a responsible framework for AI-enabled CDS. ChildRiskGuard provides process and artifact evidence of how AI-expanded, researcher-governed design can generate and evaluate novel computational design knowledge, demonstrating the feasibility of maintaining scientific judgment while leveraging AI capabilities.

title: Don't Drop Dropout: Optimizing Layer Sparsity for Efficient LLM Training and Inference
comment: This is a slightly extended version of the paper published at ICML 2026
summary: Layer dropout (a.k.a. stochastic depth) has been shown to enable faster training, higher accuracy, and robustness to zero-shot layer pruning in both language and vision transformers. However, as models and datasets have scaled, dropout - particularly layer dropout - has largely disappeared from large language models (LLMs) pre-training recipes. While some prior work has reported that dropout can degrade accuracy, no comprehensive study has quantified, let alone mitigated, this effect. In this study, we show that layer dropout should be used in state-of-the-art LLM training, establishing best practices and scaling analysis for both training and post-training benefits. Concretely, with optimal layer distribution, time schedule, and optimizer hyperparameters, we observe that at the same training FLOPs layer dropout leads to lower loss. For a given number of training steps, LLMs can achieve lower or similar validation loss while saving upto 25% of training FLOPs. Moreover, layer dropout enables significant post-training optimizations, such as early exit, intermediate-layer skipping, and self-speculative decoding, yielding up to 1.5x inference speedup with negligible accuracy loss. Across more than 2400 training experiments, spanning models from 271M to 8.2B parameters and datasets up to 160B tokens, we demonstrate that these findings extend reliably to large-scale training regimes. All pre-training experiments were run on Cerebras CS-3 systems.

AI.tldr: Layer dropout (stochastic depth), once common in vision/language transformers, has largely disappeared from LLM pre-training. This study demonstrates that with optimal configuration, layer dropout enables lower validation loss at equivalent FLOPs or up to 25% FLOPs savings, while also enabling post-training optimizations like early exit and self-speculative decoding that yield 1.5x inference speedup.
AI.motivation: While layer dropout was effective for smaller transformers, no comprehensive study has quantified its effects or mitigation strategies at LLM scale. This work addresses this gap by establishing best practices for layer dropout in modern LLM training.
AI.method: Across 2400+ experiments on models from 271M to 8.2B parameters trained on up to 160B tokens, the authors systematically investigated optimal layer distribution, time schedules, and optimizer hyperparameters for layer dropout on Cerebras CS-3 systems.
AI.result: With optimal configuration, layer dropout leads to lower loss at the same training FLOPs. For a given number of training steps, LLMs achieve similar or lower validation loss while saving up to 25% of training FLOPs. Additionally, layer dropout enables post-training optimizations (early exit, intermediate-layer skipping, self-speculative decoding) yielding up to 1.5x inference speedup with negligible accuracy loss.
AI.conclusion: Layer dropout should be reintroduced into state-of-the-art LLM training pipelines. It provides both training efficiency (lower loss per FLOP) and inference benefits (1.5x speedup via speculative decoding and related techniques), with findings reliably extending to large-scale training regimes.

title: Testing Interchangeability in LLM Agent Teams
summary: Production multi-agent systems replace agents constantly, on the assumption that an agent filling a role is interchangeable with any other agent that can do the job. We test that assumption. Eight teams per setting are formed independently from one base model on the same tasks, each agent keeping a private notebook across ten formation episodes; we then trade role-matched agents between teams and measure what changes on held-out tasks. Against a placebo that reproduces the disruption of a roster change without changing who occupies the seat, a swap costs little in task score but raises the communication a team spends per unit of progress by 16 to 63 percent, and in Hanabi a swapped agent is more expensive than an inexperienced one, consistent with interference from conventions learned with its former partner. In Collab-Overcooked, when the agent that sets the agenda is replaced, most of the extra communication comes from the agent that stayed. Three ablations, over base models, decoding temperature and formation length, move the swap penalty alongside one other quantity: how far independently formed teams drift apart. Greedy decoding lowers both; doubling a team's history raises both. In these settings, agents are more fungible in task outcome than in coordination efficiency, with larger swap effects after longer formation histories.

AI.tldr: This paper tests whether agents filling roles in multi-agent systems are truly interchangeable by swapping role-matched agents between independently formed teams and measuring the impact on task performance and communication efficiency. The key finding is that while task scores remain largely unaffected, communication costs increase significantly (16-63%), with agents learning coordination conventions with their original partners that interfere with performance in new teams.
AI.motivation: Production multi-agent systems assume agents are interchangeable when replacing team members. This assumption is tested to understand the real costs of roster changes in deployed multi-agent systems.
AI.method: Eight teams per setting formed from one base model on identical tasks, with each agent maintaining a private notebook across ten formation episodes. Role-matched agents are traded between teams and changes measured on held-out tasks. A placebo condition controls for disruption without personnel changes. Three ablations test base models, decoding temperature, and formation length.
AI.result: Swaps cost little in task score but raise communication per unit of progress by 16-63%. In Hanabi, swapped agents are more expensive than inexperienced ones, consistent with interference from conventions learned with former partners. In Collab-Overcooked, when the agenda-setting agent is replaced, extra communication comes from the staying agent. Greedy decoding lowers both the swap penalty and team drift; doubling team history raises both.
AI.conclusion: Agents are more fungible in task outcome than in coordination efficiency. Larger swap effects occur after longer formation histories, suggesting that teams develop unique coordination conventions that are not easily transferable.

title: GUT: Quantifying and Optimizing the Reasoning Uncertainty of LLMs via Graph Complexity
summary: Recent years have witnessed great advances in the reasoning ability of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, the reasoning processes of LLMs often exhibit uncertainty, where LLMs often produce a proliferation of divergent branches at each reasoning step even when fed the same prompting inputs, and certain branches exhibit evidently incredible, even nonsensical, reasoning chains and results. In this paper, we propose the Graph-complexity-based UncerTainty (GUT) method for investigating the reasoning uncertainty of LLMs. The key idea of GUT is to characterize the potential branches of each reasoning chain with a directed acyclic graph, thereby ensuring that all potential branches are comprehensively covered within the graph space. Building upon this recognition, we further build two modules of GUT, that is, a Quantification (GUT-Q) module and an Optimization (GUT-O) module, for quantifying and reducing the reasoning uncertainty of LLMs, respectively. GUT-Q measures LLM reasoning uncertainty by approximating the reasoning space complexity with graph complexity. GUT-O implements uncertainty optimization by treating negative uncertainty as the reward function in reinforcement learning. Experimental results conducted on four LLMs and five datasets validate the effectiveness of GUT.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes GUT (Graph-complexity-based UncerTainty), a method to investigate and reduce reasoning uncertainty in Large Language Models. GUT uses directed acyclic graphs to characterize potential reasoning branches, with two modules: GUT-Q for quantifying uncertainty via graph complexity, and GUT-O for optimizing uncertainty using reinforcement learning with negative uncertainty as reward.
AI.motivation: Recent advances in LLM reasoning ability have revealed a critical issue: reasoning processes exhibit uncertainty, where LLMs produce multiple divergent reasoning branches even with identical prompting inputs, and some branches contain nonsensical or incredible reasoning chains and results. This uncertainty undermines the reliability and consistency of LLM reasoning.
AI.method: The proposed GUT method characterizes potential branches of each reasoning chain using a directed acyclic graph (DAG) to comprehensively cover all potential branches within the graph space. The method consists of two modules: (1) GUT-Q (Quantification) - measures LLM reasoning uncertainty by approximating reasoning space complexity with graph complexity; (2) GUT-O (Optimization) - implements uncertainty reduction by treating negative uncertainty as the reward function in reinforcement learning.
AI.result: Experimental results conducted on four LLMs and five datasets validate the effectiveness of GUT.
AI.conclusion: The GUT method provides a novel framework for investigating, quantifying, and reducing reasoning uncertainty in LLMs through graph-based complexity analysis and reinforcement learning optimization. The approach demonstrates effectiveness across multiple models and datasets.

title: Beyond Aggregate Scores: Behavioral Correctness Assumptions for Assessing Reference-Based Automatic Evaluation Methods
summary: Automated reference-based evaluation methods play a critical role in assessing natural language generation systems. Existing meta-evaluation primarily measures agreement with human judgments or benchmark labels, providing limited insight into evaluator behavior under controlled conditions. We introduce behavioral correctness assumptions, a complementary framework for evaluating reference-based automatic evaluation methods. We define a taxonomy of correctness-preserving and correctness-altering assumptions and operationalize them through controlled response transformations that specify expected scoring behaviors. We evaluate diverse lexical, character-level, semantic, LLM-based, and hybrid evaluators and analyze their assumption-level behavior, stability, sensitivity, repeat-run variability, configuration sensitivity, and reproducibility. Our experiments reveal distinct behavioral trade-offs across evaluation paradigms: no evaluator satisfies all proposed correctness assumptions, and evaluators with similar aggregate performance can exhibit substantially different behavioral profiles. These findings demonstrate that behavioral correctness assumptions provide diagnostic information obscured by conventional aggregate meta-evaluation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "behavioral correctness assumptions" as a novel framework for evaluating reference-based automatic evaluation methods in natural language generation. It proposes a taxonomy of correctness-preserving and correctness-altering assumptions and tests various evaluators (lexical, character-level, semantic, LLM-based, hybrid) to analyze their behavioral properties including stability, sensitivity, and reproducibility.
AI.motivation: Current meta-evaluation methods primarily measure agreement with human judgments but provide limited insight into evaluator behavior under controlled conditions. The authors argue that aggregate performance metrics obscure important behavioral differences between evaluators.
AI.method: The authors operationalize behavioral correctness assumptions through controlled response transformations that specify expected scoring behaviors. They evaluate diverse types of evaluators including lexical, character-level, semantic, LLM-based, and hybrid approaches, analyzing assumption-level behavior, stability, sensitivity, repeat-run variability, configuration sensitivity, and reproducibility.
AI.result: The experiments reveal distinct behavioral trade-offs across evaluation paradigms: no evaluator satisfies all proposed correctness assumptions, and evaluators with similar aggregate performance can exhibit substantially different behavioral profiles.
AI.conclusion: Behavioral correctness assumptions provide diagnostic information that is obscured by conventional aggregate meta-evaluation, offering a complementary framework for assessing reference-based automatic evaluation methods.

title: RISE: Recursive Improvement via Self-Extrapolating Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense, per-token supervision for language model post-training, but its effectiveness is bottlenecked by teacher quality: external teachers suffer from distribution mismatch, while self-distillation with privileged conditioning is limited by in-context learning capacity. We propose \textbf{RISE} (\textbf{R}ecursive \textbf{I}mprovement via \textbf{S}elf-\textbf{E}xtrapolating Policy Distillation), which constructs a synthetic teacher directly from the model's own RLVR training trajectory. By extrapolating the displacement between the current checkpoint and a trailing anchor---in parameter space or output logit space---RISE converts a sparse outcome-induced parameter update into a dense token-level target, without any external model or privileged conditioning. RISE combines RLVR and OPD in a complementary loop: outcome rewards ground the extrapolation toward correct reasoning, while the extrapolated teacher refines token-level decisions. Moreover, since the teacher is refreshed every iteration as the student improves, distillation becomes a recursive improvement mechanism rather than a one-shot compression step. Experiments spanning mathematical reasoning, multi-domain STEM, code generation, and multi-turn agentic tasks show that RISE outperforms RLVR-only training and on-policy self-distillation across all settings.

AI.tldr: RISE proposes a novel method that combines RLVR with on-policy distillation by constructing a synthetic teacher from the model's own training trajectory, converting sparse outcome-based parameter updates into dense token-level supervision without external models or privileged conditioning.
AI.motivation: On-policy distillation provides dense per-token supervision but is bottlenecked by teacher quality - external teachers suffer distribution mismatch while self-distillation with privileged conditioning is limited by in-context learning capacity. The authors seek a way to create high-quality token-level targets without these limitations.
AI.method: RISE constructs a synthetic teacher by extrapolating the displacement between the current checkpoint and a trailing anchor (in parameter space or output logit space). This converts sparse outcome-induced parameter updates into dense token-level targets. RLVR and OPD are combined in a complementary loop where outcome rewards ground the extrapolation toward correct reasoning while the extrapolated teacher refines token-level decisions. The teacher is refreshed every iteration as the student improves, enabling recursive improvement.
AI.result: Experiments across mathematical reasoning, multi-domain STEM, code generation, and multi-turn agentic tasks show that RISE outperforms RLVR-only training and on-policy self-distillation across all settings.
AI.conclusion: RISE demonstrates that self-distillation can serve as a recursive improvement mechanism rather than a one-shot compression step, effectively addressing the teacher quality bottleneck in on-policy distillation by leveraging the model's own training trajectory.

title: Large Language Models for HVAC Operations in Building Energy Systems: A Critical Review of Methods, Applications, and Deployment Readiness
comment: 38 pages, 9 figures, 16 tables. Submitted to Energy and Buildings
summary: Building automation systems generate rich sensor data yet remain insight-poor because heterogeneous point naming, missing metadata, and fragmented documentation obstruct their operational use. This systematic review analyses and codes 66 peer-reviewed studies on large language models (LLMs) for HVAC operations published between 2023 and March 2026. Each study is classified across five application families and three LLM method families and assessed for evidence realism, deployment readiness, and the responsibility boundary between the LLM and physical HVAC decisions. The corpus is concentrated in building energy modelling (BEM, 32 of 66 papers), while load forecasting remains too sparse for subfield-level conclusions. Only four studies reach pilot-level evidence, and none reports sustained operational deployment. No study was classified as ready-now for industry adoption; three were near-term and 63 research-only. Nevertheless, several bounded, human-in-the-loop uses merit near-term trials, including point-name normalisation, document-grounded operator support, BEM workflow assistance, and advisory interfaces around physics-based controllers. Conventional machine learning (ML), model predictive control (MPC), reinforcement learning (RL) and ontology-based tools remain more adopted for high-frequency control, short-horizon numerical forecasting, and well-posed ontology mapping, while autonomous agentic operation and unvalidated occupant proxies remain research-stage. Current evidence therefore supports LLMs primarily as semantic and workflow layers rather than autonomous HVAC controllers. Future work should prioritise field-validated benchmarks, orchestration evaluation under operational constraints, and LLM-MPC/RL architectures with bounded latency and verifiable safety properties.

AI.tldr: This systematic review analyzes 66 peer-reviewed studies (2023-March 2026) on LLMs for HVAC operations. The field remains immature—only 4 studies reach pilot-level evidence, none report sustained deployment, and no study is ready for industry adoption. LLMs show promise as semantic/workflow layers (point-name normalization, document-grounded operator support, BEM workflow assistance) rather than autonomous controllers. Conventional ML, MPC, and RL remain superior for high-frequency control and numerical forecasting.
AI.motivation: Building automation systems generate rich sensor data but remain insight-poor due to heterogeneous point naming, missing metadata, and fragmented documentation. LLMs are emerging as potential solutions, but their actual readiness for HVAC operations remains unclear. This systematic review addresses the gap by comprehensively mapping the current evidence base.
AI.method: The authors conducted a systematic review of 66 peer-reviewed studies on LLMs for HVAC operations. Each study was classified across five application families and three LLM method families, and assessed for evidence realism, deployment readiness, and responsibility boundary between LLM and physical HVAC decisions.
AI.result: The corpus is concentrated in building energy modelling (BEM, 32/66 papers). Load forecasting remains too sparse for subfield conclusions. Only 4 studies reach pilot-level evidence; none reports sustained operational deployment. No study is ready-now for industry adoption (3 near-term, 63 research-only). Bounded, human-in-the-loop uses merit near-term trials: point-name normalization, document-grounded operator support, BEM workflow assistance, and advisory interfaces around physics-based controllers. Conventional ML, MPC, RL, and ontology-based tools remain more adopted for high-frequency control, short-horizon forecasting, and ontology mapping. Autonomous agentic operation and unvalidated occupant proxies remain research-stage.
AI.conclusion: Current evidence supports LLMs primarily as semantic and workflow layers rather than autonomous HVAC controllers. Future work should prioritize: (1) field-validated benchmarks, (2) orchestration evaluation under operational constraints, and (3) LLM-MPC/RL architectures with bounded latency and verifiable safety properties.

title: LLM-Driven Algorithm Design for Quantum Circuit Synthesis based on Binary Decision Diagrams
summary: Quantum circuits are central to implementing quantum algorithms on quantum devices, where quantum gates must be reversible. Many quantum algorithms rely on Boolean functions, which must therefore be implemented reversibly within quantum circuits. Reversible circuit synthesis provides a way to translate such Boolean functions into reversible circuits. Binary decision diagrams (BDDs) offer a scalable approach to this task, but the resulting BDDs and circuits depend heavily on variable ordering. Existing ordering heuristics commonly minimize BDD size because it is closely tied to the circuit size. However, BDD size is an imperfect proxy for the quantum cost of the synthesized circuit (QCC). We propose \texttt{QuantumEvo}, an evolutionary framework that uses an LLM as a heuristic generator for QCC-aware BDD variable ordering. Instead of predicting orderings directly, \texttt{QuantumEvo} searches over ordering heuristics initialized from multiple heuristic families. Candidate heuristics directly manipulate variable orderings using standard BDD operations and are selected by downstream QCC. The discovered heuristic, HGA-QE, modifies the sifting step inside a genetic algorithm so that the procedure is better aligned with QCC. Across the benchmark set, HGA-QE achieves a 70.9\% tie-or-win rate against the per-function best baseline and is strictly best on 13.5\% of the functions. The results demonstrate broadly competitive QCC performance, with HGA-QE showing a clearer relative advantage in strict wins on the two benchmark suites drawn from sources different from the data used for heuristic discovery.

AI.tldr: QuantumEvo is an evolutionary framework that uses an LLM as a heuristic generator to discover BDD variable ordering heuristics optimized for quantum circuit cost (QCC). It discovers HGA-QE, which modifies the sifting step in a genetic algorithm to better align with QCC, achieving 70.9% tie-or-win rate against baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing BDD variable ordering heuristics minimize BDD size as a proxy for circuit size, but BDD size is an imperfect proxy for quantum cost of the synthesized circuit (QCC). There is a need for heuristics directly optimized for QCC rather than BDD size.
AI.method: An evolutionary framework using an LLM as a heuristic generator for QCC-aware BDD variable ordering. The framework searches over ordering heuristics initialized from multiple heuristic families, where candidate heuristics manipulate variable orderings using standard BDD operations and are selected by downstream QCC. This discovers HGA-QE, which modifies the sifting step inside a genetic algorithm.
AI.result: HGA-QE achieves a 70.9% tie-or-win rate against the per-function best baseline across the benchmark set, and is strictly best on 13.5% of the functions. It shows a clearer relative advantage on benchmark suites drawn from sources different from the data used for heuristic discovery.
AI.conclusion: The evolutionary framework successfully discovers QCC-aware heuristics that outperform traditional BDD-size-minimizing heuristics. HGA-QE demonstrates broadly competitive QCC performance, with particularly strong results on out-of-distribution benchmarks.

title: Technical Manual for a Toolkit for Measuring Contextual Individuation in Transformer Language Models
comment: 29 pages, 2 figures (one with 2 subfigures), 1 table. Toolkit, source code, and corpora archived separately on Zenodo (see Section 9)
summary: A transformer language model assigns a single, context-independent vector to a word type at its embedding layer, yet is widely believed to individuate that word's occurrences by context in its later layers. Testing this belief cleanly requires a construct that holds the word form fixed while its context and intended sense vary in a controlled, labeled way. This manual documents an open toolkit built around such a construct, which we call a bridge form: a single written word that recurs, unchanged, across two or more subject domains with a different sense in each. We describe, and justify, every stage of the pipeline: the declarative specification of bridge forms and their source domains, corpus acquisition from Wikipedia, occurrence localization, layer-wise representation extraction, a domain-pairwise silhouette measurement of separation in the model's representation space, and a paired visualization protocol. Each design choice is presented together with the methodological failure mode it is meant to avoid (sense contamination from overly broad category labels, the multi-group bias of the silhouette coefficient, subword-tokenization misalignment, and axis-comparability artifacts in dimensionality-reduced plots, among others). This manuscript is a methodological and implementation reference: it does not report or interpret empirical outcomes of running the toolkit on any particular model or bridge-form set. The toolkit, its full source, and the corpora used to exercise it are archived separately (Section 9) under a persistent identifier, and are intended to be cited as an instrument by studies that use it to produce and interpret empirical results.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an open-source toolkit for testing whether transformer language models contextualize word meanings across different domains. The core construct is "bridge forms" - words with the same written form but different meanings across subject domains. The paper is purely methodological, describing the pipeline without reporting empirical results.
AI.motivation: To test the widely held belief that transformer language models contextualize word meanings in later layers (despite using context-independent embeddings at the input layer). The challenge was creating a controlled, labeled construct to isolate word form from context and meaning variation.
AI.method: The toolkit implements a multi-stage pipeline: (1) declarative specification of bridge forms and their domains, (2) Wikipedia corpus acquisition, (3) occurrence localization, (4) layer-wise representation extraction from transformer models, (5) domain-pairwise silhouette measurement for representation space separation, and (6) paired visualization protocol. Each stage is designed to avoid specific methodological failure modes.
AI.result: This is a methodological reference paper - no empirical outcomes are reported. The toolkit, source code, and corpora are archived separately with persistent identifiers for future use.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a complete methodological and implementation reference for studying how transformer models represent polysemous words across different domains. It explicitly addresses design choices and their failure modes, serving as a foundation for future empirical studies using the toolkit.

title: Does Your Agent's Memory Survive a Model Upgrade? A Controlled Study of Memory Portability
summary:
Model upgrades are routine; memory migrations are not. An agent can keep the same memory store and still forget: a new model may interpret old notes differently, mixed embedding versions may break retrieval, and repair may fail without the original evidence. We compare memory as the same history is preserved verbatim for long-context reading (LC-RAW), divided into chunks for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), compressed by a model into natural-language notes (NOTES), or normalized into a fixed-schema knowledge graph (KG-fixed). The study uses 48 synthetic histories with randomized answer codes, exact scoring, and two open-weight models with sub 10 billion parameters.
  Our measurements show that fixed-schema structures transfer reliably, with KG-fixed accuracy changing by only $+0.0004 \pm 0.0020$ following a writer swap. Conversely, compressed NOTES exhibit high model coupling, with accuracy shifting asymmetrically by $+9.91$ or $-13.28$ percentage points depending on the specific migration direction. In RAG systems, partial embedding migrations using a 50/50 mixed index capture only a 4.96-point accuracy improvement, forfeiting the majority of the 11.90-point gain achieved through full re-embedding. Diagnostic decomposition attributes 80% ($0.467 \pm 0.014$) of the NOTES accuracy deficit to information lost during initial construction, whereas retrieval failures drive 81% ($0.364 \pm 0.012$) of the RAG deficit. Finally, store-only repair of NOTES fails to reach a 90% performance recovery target in all 48 test cases, whereas retaining the raw source history enables successful recovery in 34 of 48 cases for one tested direction. These findings highlight the necessity of direction-specific migration testing, strict embedding space isolation, and the retention of source histories for memory repair.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates memory migration challenges when AI models are upgraded while keeping the same memory store. The study compares four memory representations (long-context raw, RAG chunks, compressed notes, and fixed-schema knowledge graphs) across 48 synthetic histories using two sub-10B parameter models. Results show that fixed-schema knowledge graphs transfer most reliably, while compressed notes exhibit severe model coupling. The findings emphasize the need for direction-specific migration testing, embedding space isolation, and retention of source histories for memory repair.
AI.motivation: Model upgrades are routine but memory migrations are not. When an agent upgrades to a new model while keeping the same memory store, various issues can arise: new models may interpret old notes differently, mixed embedding versions may break retrieval, and repair may fail without original evidence. This study addresses the lack of systematic understanding of how different memory representations behave under model changes.
AI.method: The study compares four memory representations: (1) LC-RAW: long-context reading with verbatim history preservation; (2) RAG: chunked for retrieval-augmented generation; (3) NOTES: compressed by model into natural-language notes; (4) KG-fixed: normalized into fixed-schema knowledge graph. Experiments used 48 synthetic histories with randomized answer codes, exact scoring, and two open-weight models with sub-10 billion parameters. The study measured accuracy changes after writer swaps, analyzed partial vs. full re-embedding in RAG, and performed diagnostic decomposition to attribute accuracy deficits to specific failure modes.
AI.result: Fixed-schema structures (KG-fixed) transfer reliably with minimal accuracy change (+0.0004 ± 0.0020) after model swap. Compressed notes (NOTES) show high model coupling with asymmetric accuracy shifts of +9.91 or -13.28 percentage points depending on migration direction. In RAG systems, 50/50 mixed index captures only 4.96-point improvement versus 11.90-point gain from full re-embedding. Diagnostic decomposition shows 80% (0.467 ± 0.014) of NOTES deficit stems from information loss during initial construction, while 81% (0.364 ± 0.012) of RAG deficit comes from retrieval failures.
