Store-only repair of NOTES fails to reach 90% performance recovery in all 48 cases, whereas retaining raw source enables recovery in 34/48 cases.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight three critical requirements: (1) direction-specific migration testing is necessary due to asymmetric model coupling; (2) strict embedding space isolation is required to prevent degradation; (3) retention of source histories is essential for memory repair. Fixed-schema knowledge graphs provide the most robust transfer, while compressed notes and RAG systems suffer from significant model-specific information loss and retrieval failures. Raw source history preservation enables successful recovery in the majority of cases.

title: Who Should Grade My Work? Student Perspectives on Transparent AI-Assisted Writing Assessment in Higher Education
summary: The integration of GenAI tools into higher education assessment raises important questions about how students understand, interpret, and respond to AI-mediated evaluation. As instructors increasingly explore AI tools for providing feedback, prior research has examined whether GenAI-generated feedback improves writing performance and how students perceive its usefulness; comparatively little is known, however, about how students interpret such evaluation when they are explicitly informed that an AI system, rather than a human instructor, produced the feedback and the score. This study reports findings from a qualitative pedagogical inquiry conducted in an undergraduate technical communication course for computing students at a Saudi public university. Thirteen male undergraduate computing students completed an in-class handwritten writing task; the scanned submissions were evaluated by ChatGPT using a rubric-based prompt aligned with the task objectives. Students were then explicitly informed that ChatGPT had generated the score and feedback and were invited to reflect on the evaluation in writing. Inductive thematic analysis of these reflections identified four themes: perceived usefulness of feedback; awareness of AI's contextual and pedagogical limitations; conditional trust, distinguishing feedback utility from evaluative authority; and reflection on the institutional and pedagogical role of the human instructor. Participants accepted GenAI feedback as useful for surface-level revision but consistently positioned the human instructor as the appropriate authority over grading decisions. The study identifies this as a distinction between feedback utility and evaluative authority, two judgments that students treat as analytically separate rather than as opposite ends of a single approval scale...

AI.tldr: This study investigates how undergraduate computing students in Saudi Arabia interpret and respond to AI-generated assessment feedback when explicitly told ChatGPT produced the score and feedback. Using qualitative thematic analysis of student reflections, the research identifies a key distinction students make between feedback utility (helpful for revision) and evaluative authority (who should decide grades).
AI.motivation: While prior research has examined whether GenAI-generated feedback improves writing performance and student perception of its usefulness, there is limited understanding of how students interpret AI-mediated evaluation when explicitly informed that an AI system (rather than a human instructor) produced the feedback and score. This gap is significant as higher education increasingly adopts AI tools for assessment.
AI.method: Qualitative pedagogical inquiry conducted in an undergraduate technical communication course at a Saudi public university. Thirteen male undergraduate computing students completed an in-class handwritten writing task. Submissions were evaluated by ChatGPT using a rubric-based prompt aligned with task objectives. Students were explicitly informed that ChatGPT generated the score and feedback, then invited to reflect on the evaluation in writing. Inductive thematic analysis was used to analyze student reflections.
AI.result: Four themes emerged: (1) perceived usefulness of feedback; (2) awareness of AI's contextual and pedagogical limitations; (3) conditional trust, distinguishing feedback utility from evaluative authority; and (4) reflection on the institutional and pedagogical role of the human instructor. Participants accepted GenAI feedback as useful for surface-level revision but consistently positioned the human instructor as the appropriate authority over grading decisions.
AI.conclusion: The study identifies a distinction between "feedback utility" and "evaluative authority"—two judgments that students treat as analytically separate rather than as opposite ends of a single approval scale. Students find AI feedback useful for revision but believe human instructors should retain evaluative authority over grades.

title: CUA-Universe: A Scalable and Dynamic Environment for Hybrid GUI+CLI Agents
summary: Computer-use agents have advanced on benchmarks like OSWorld and AndroidWorld, but still act mostly through the GUI, often producing inefficient trajectories. Real-world computer work is hybrid, combining visual-state inspection with precise, high-throughput command-line operations, so capable agents must coordinate both modalities over shared application state. Yet scalable hybrid environments remain scarce because supporting both GUI and CLI over real applications typically requires substantial manual engineering for each application. Existing agents also struggle to use the two interfaces complementarily: CLI-native agents lack visual perception for tasks involving interface state or layout, while GUI-native agents are inefficient for operations better executed through commands. We introduce CUA-Universe, a scalable environment-to-data pipeline that turns real desktop software into hybrid GUI+CLI environments. App-Forge adapts applications into reproducible VMs and command-line surfaces it discovers, wraps, or generates, scaling to 16 applications; Task-Weave synthesizes diverse hybrid tasks of controllable difficulty from reusable operations over seed files; and Path-Steer steers rollouts along efficient hybrid paths and harvests verified trajectories for post-training. Training on this data shifts behavior from inefficient GUI interaction and brittle CLI scripting toward effective GUI+CLI orchestration. Our 9B model improves both success and efficiency on CUA-Verse (Score +39.3 pts; -37% steps, -60% tokens), OSWorld (SR +16.8 pts; -57% steps, -44% tokens), and OSWorld-MCP (Score +7.84 pts; -27% steps, -30% tokens). CUA-Universe provides a scalable path toward more capable and efficient computer-use agents.

AI.tldr: CUA-Universe is a scalable pipeline that transforms real desktop software into hybrid GUI+CLI environments for training computer-use agents. It consists of App-Forge (adapts apps to VMs with CLI surfaces), Task-Weave (synthesizes hybrid tasks), and Path-Steer (harvests efficient trajectories). Training on this data enables a 9B model to achieve significant improvements in both success rate and efficiency across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current computer-use agents rely mainly on GUI, producing inefficient trajectories. Real-world work requires both visual-state inspection (GUI) and precise command-line operations (CLI), but scalable hybrid environments are scarce. Existing agents also struggle to use both interfaces complementarily - CLI-native agents lack visual perception, while GUI-native agents are inefficient for command-based operations.
AI.method: The paper proposes CUA-Universe with three components: (1) App-Forge - adapts real desktop software into reproducible VMs with discovered/wrapped/generated CLI surfaces, scaling to 16 applications; (2) Task-Weave - synthesizes diverse hybrid tasks of controllable difficulty from reusable operations over seed files; (3) Path-Steer - steers rollouts along efficient hybrid paths and harvests verified trajectories for post-training.
AI.result: A 9B model trained on harvested data shows significant improvements: On CUA-Verse (Score +39.3 pts, -37% steps, -60% tokens), OSWorld (SR +16.8 pts, -57% steps, -44% tokens), and OSWorld-MCP (Score +7.84 pts, -27% steps, -30% tokens). The training shifts behavior from inefficient GUI interaction and brittle CLI scripting toward effective GUI+CLI orchestration.
AI.conclusion: CUA-Universe provides a scalable path toward more capable and efficient computer-use agents by enabling hybrid GUI+CLI training data generation. The approach demonstrates that coordinating both modalities over shared application state leads to better performance and efficiency compared to GUI-only or CLI-only agents.

title: Molecular Déjà Vu: Digit-Level Retrieval of Published Values in Frontier Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated on molecular property benchmarks, but accuracy cannot distinguish a model that predicts a property from one that retrieves a published number. We audit 22 frontier models on 12 regression benchmarks for verbatim retrieval and find that it is widespread but relatively benchmark-specific: on five datasets more than $50\%$ of the LLMs show verbatim retrieval, while on the remaining datasets it appears only in isolated cells. We run our experiments at two reasoning levels and find that reasoning changes retrieval. The same experiments, on the same molecules and with the same prompt, are flagged $89\%$ more often at the higher reasoning level than at the lowest one. Finally, we test a way to interrupt retrieval in our most contaminated cases, and find that the strongest models in some cases still recognise a combination of transformed SMILES strings and original labels. Furthermore, suppressing retrieval moves the prediction errors of the different models closer together in relative terms, while their differing use of verbatim retrieval spreads them apart. This indicates that the general predictive capability of an LLM is not determined solely by the amount of memorised values. This work provides an overview of the amount and depth of verbatim retrieval in molecular regression benchmarks using LLMs.

AI.tldr: This paper audits 22 frontier LLMs on 12 molecular property regression benchmarks to distinguish genuine property prediction from verbatim retrieval of memorized published values. The study finds that verbatim retrieval is widespread but varies significantly across benchmarks, and that reasoning levels significantly impact retrieval behavior.
AI.motivation: The core problem is that accuracy metrics on molecular property benchmarks cannot distinguish between LLMs that genuinely predict properties versus those that retrieve memorized published numbers. This raises concerns about the validity of benchmark evaluations for assessing LLM capabilities in molecular science.
AI.method: The authors audited 22 frontier models on 12 regression benchmarks, testing for verbatim retrieval at two reasoning levels. They also tested interventions to interrupt retrieval in contaminated cases and analyzed how suppressing retrieval affects prediction error distributions.
AI.result: Verbatim retrieval is widespread but benchmark-specific: over 50% of LLMs show verbatim retrieval on five datasets, while on others it appears only in isolated cells. Reasoning level significantly impacts retrieval, with 89% more flags at higher reasoning levels. Strongest models can still recognize transformed SMILES with original labels. Suppressing retrieval moves prediction errors closer together in relative terms.
AI.conclusion: The general predictive capability of an LLM is not determined solely by the amount of memorized values. This work provides the first comprehensive overview of verbatim retrieval depth in molecular regression benchmarks using LLMs.

title: Necessary or Sufficient? Evaluating LLM Explanations With Behavioural Evidence
summary: LLM decision components that can operate within agent workflows often produce action-relevant recommendations or judgements together with explanations. Operators may use the named factors to monitor a system, diagnose errors, or decide when to escalate an output. Such use assumes that the explanations agree with the component's observable decision behaviour. We test two interpretations of the named factors: necessity, meaning that changing a factor would change the output, and sufficiency, meaning that retaining it while removing other changeable information would preserve the output. We evaluate these interpretations in two synthetic use cases: recommending advisors to clients and judging prompts for harmfulness or risk. Models return an output and the top three factors that most influenced it. Controlled black-box interventions estimate a necessity score for each factor by measuring how often changing it changes the output, and a sufficiency score by measuring how often retaining it preserves the output. Across eight models from the Claude, GPT, and Gemini families, the mean Spearman correlations between the cited ranking and the necessity and sufficiency scores are 0.349 and 0.354 for advisor recommendation, and 0.431 and 0.580 for prompt monitoring. Furthermore, an uncited factor scores above the lowest-scoring cited factor in 57.6% of advisor responses under necessity and 58.1% under sufficiency; the corresponding prompt-monitoring rates are 25.8% and 8.9%. The cited top three contain useful information but do not reliably identify the three factors with the strongest measured influence under necessity or sufficiency. The framework provides a black-box reliability check for explanations used in agent oversight while remaining scoped to individual LLM decisions.

AI.tldr: This paper tests whether LLM-provided explanations (named factors) actually reflect the model's decision behavior in agent workflows. Using black-box interventions across 8 models (Claude, GPT, Gemini), the study evaluates two interpretations of explanations: necessity (would changing the factor change the output?) and sufficiency (would retaining the factor preserve the output?). Results show moderate correlations (0.35-0.58) between cited rankings and measured influence, with uncited factors often scoring higher than cited ones, suggesting explanations contain useful but unreliable information for oversight.
AI.motivation: LLM decision components in agent workflows produce outputs with explanations, but operators need to know if these explanations actually reflect the model's decision behavior for monitoring, error diagnosis, and escalation decisions. This motivates testing whether cited factors truly influence outputs as claimed.
AI.method: Controlled black-box interventions across two synthetic use cases (advisor recommendation and prompt harmfulness/risk judgment) with 8 models. For each decision, necessity scores measure how often changing a factor changes the output, while sufficiency scores measure how often retaining a factor preserves the output. These are compared against the model's self-reported factor rankings.
AI.result: Mean Spearman correlations between cited rankings and measured scores were 0.349 (necessity) and 0.354 (sufficiency) for advisor recommendation, and 0.431 (necessity) and 0.580 (sufficiency) for prompt monitoring. An uncited factor exceeded the lowest-scoring cited factor in 57.6% (necessity) and 58.1% (sufficiency) of advisor responses, and 25.8% (necessity) and 8.9% (sufficiency) for prompt monitoring.
AI.conclusion: The cited top three factors contain useful information but do not reliably identify the three factors with the strongest measured influence under necessity or sufficiency interpretations. The framework provides a black-box reliability check for explanations used in agent oversight while remaining scoped to individual LLM decisions.

title: Multi-Step Tool-Calling over Korean Open Public APIs: A Benchmark and a Data-Synthesis Recipe
comment: 30 pages, 7 figures, 26 tables. Accepted to EMNLP 2026 Industry Track
summary: Data-sovereignty regulations increasingly require public institutions to deploy open-source, on-premise LLM agents that chain multiple tool-calls across live government APIs. However, open-source models consistently underperform in this multi-step setting, and no existing benchmark measures the gap. We introduce the Korean Open Public API Benchmark (KOPA-Bench), comprising 145 real-world tasks. To close this gap, we present EDGE, an Execution-grounded Dynamic Graph for tool-calling data synthEsis driven by live execution. EDGE builds a graph of how each tool's output can feed another's input, keeps only the links that succeed when actually called against the live APIs, and traverses these verified links to synthesize executable multi-step trajectories. Fine-tuned via GRPO on the resulting dataset, our 9B model nearly matches the untuned 27B model from the same family, improving substantially not only on KOPA-Bench but also on the BFCL benchmark.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the challenge of deploying open-source LLM agents for multi-step tool-calling in government APIs under data-sovereignty regulations. The authors introduce KOPA-Bench (145 Korean real-world tasks) and EDGE (a method that synthesizes executable multi-step trajectories by building and traversing a verified graph of tool dependencies using live API execution).
AI.motivation: Data-sovereignty regulations increasingly require public institutions to deploy open-source, on-premise LLM agents that can chain multiple tool-calls across live government APIs. However, open-source models consistently underperform in this multi-step setting, and no existing benchmark measures this gap.
AI.method: EDGE builds a graph of how each tool's output can feed another's input, keeps only the links that succeed when actually called against the live APIs, and traverses these verified links to synthesize executable multi-step trajectories. The model is then fine-tuned using GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) on the resulting dataset.
AI.result: The 9B model fine-tuned via GRPO on EDGE-generated data nearly matches the untuned 27B model from the same family, showing substantial improvement not only on KOPA-Bench but also on the BFCL benchmark.
AI.conclusion: EDGE effectively bridges the performance gap between small and large open-source models in multi-step tool-calling tasks, enabling feasible deployment of efficient open-source LLMs for government API applications under data-sovereignty constraints.

title: A Deep Generative Model for Synthesizing Labeled Wireless Signals
summary: Wireless signals with position-related labels are pivotal for both performance evaluation and model training in the realm of wireless sensing. However, acquiring real-world datasets is often challenged by significant measurement and labeling costs. Traditional methods for synthesizing labeled wireless signals typically rely on environmental models, leading to extensive hyper-parameter tuning and inadequate realism for comprehensive model training purposes. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel deep learning (DL)-based method, namely Inter-Instance Generative Adversarial Networks (IIns-GAN), to generate realistic labeled wireless signals. The generated signals are particularly adaptive to different environment scenarios and well-suited for various model training tasks, including distance estimation and environment identification. We have conducted extensive experiments on public Ultra-Wideband (UWB) datasets to evaluate the realism and utility of the generated signals. The results demonstrate that the signals generated by IIns-GAN mirror the physical characteristics of real-world measurements, and significantly contribute to the improvement of model training in diverse wireless sensing tasks.

AI.tldr: IIns-GAN is a deep learning-based method that generates realistic labeled wireless signals for wireless sensing tasks, addressing the high cost of acquiring real-world datasets.
AI.motivation: Acquiring real-world wireless signal datasets with position labels is expensive due to measurement and labeling costs. Traditional synthesis methods rely on environmental models, requiring extensive hyper-parameter tuning and lacking realism for comprehensive model training.
AI.method: A novel deep learning method called Inter-Instance Generative Adversarial Networks (IIns-GAN) is proposed to generate realistic labeled wireless signals that are adaptive to different environment scenarios.
AI.result: Experiments on public UWB datasets demonstrate that signals generated by IIns-GAN mirror the physical characteristics of real-world measurements and significantly improve model training for tasks including distance estimation and environment identification.
AI.conclusion: IIns-GAN effectively addresses the dataset acquisition challenge in wireless sensing by generating realistic synthetic signals that can be used for training various wireless sensing models, showing promise for practical applications.
